en: The Śrī-Nyāyamuktāvalī composed by the venerable Yati Rāghavendra.
Having bowed to the Consort of Lakṣmī and also to the teachers of Pūrṇabodha,
we compose this *Nyāyamuktāvalī* as an ornament for the necks of the learned.

Requested by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and others for the sake of knowledge, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa descended as Vyāsa; manifesting the lost Vedas, he composed this scripture consisting of the *Brahmasūtras* for the determination of their meaning and for the welfare of living beings.

This first aphorism (*sūtra*) is intended to establish that this scripture—which consists of a systematic arrangement of reasoning—should indeed be commenced by proving its possession of a subject matter and other necessary elements, and to establish the necessity of the inquiry known as *jijñāsā* (the desire to know), which is synonymous with reflection and investigation through reasoning, as being a prerequisite for it.
Oṃ. Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. Oṃ. 1.

Thus [it is said]. Because this first pentad of topics (*pañcādhikaraṇī*) serves as the pedestal for the chapters and sections (*pāda*), the others are for the most part included within the chapters and sections of the treatise (*śāstra*) itself; this will be clarified in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) in each respective section (*naya*). Furthermore, the connection of immediate succession (*anantara-saṅgati*) is of many kinds. As it has been stated:

"The connections are of the form of objection (*ākṣepikī*), extension (*ātideśikī*), introduction (*upoddhāta*), exception (*apavāda*), and incidental application (*prasaṅga*), and so forth; and that [connection] is characterized by immediate succession. Thus [ends the section].
Because this very [treatise] is the beginning, there is no prior connection here.

The subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*viśaya*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*uttara*), and the purpose (*prayojana*)— the ancients know these five to constitute a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Thus it has been said; the five-membered syllogism is elucidated according to the text, and the connection between the preceding and following parts [is established] by the grace of the Guru’s feet. In such passages as “Desire to know that—Brahman,” the object of inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is what is heard in the scripture. The doubt is whether this inquiry is something to be undertaken or not. The seed of that doubt is made clear in the commentary for each section. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not to be undertaken, because of the absence of a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth. This is because the non-Self (*anātman*) is unreal, and the Supreme Self (*parātman*) is already established through signs such as desire and the like.

Furthermore, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a supreme self other than one's own self, such a self does not exist. Moreover, whether the Vedāntas are of human origin or not, they lack authority due to the absence of the quality of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). Even if their authority were intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), they would fail to reveal Brahman as an established entity (*siddha-rūpa*) because they are intent upon [injunctions of] action (*kārya-paratva*). Even if they did reveal an established fact, according to the Advaitins, they are perceived as being solely concerned with the partless nature of one's own self. And since one's own self is established through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃdhī*), it cannot be an object of knowledge because there is no doubt regarding its existence.

Because qualities such as atomicity, which are distinct from the body and so forth, are also non-self and therefore unreal; and because even when knowledge of that [atomicity] exists, liberation or any other fruit is not perceived, it is impossible for that [knowledge] to have such a fruit. In the absence of both subject matter (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*), there is all the more an absence of the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) and the relationship [between them]. Or, let us grant that another Brahman is the subject matter; even so, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not fruitful. For the knowledge of Brahman is certainly not its fruit.

Knowledge is attained through that [action], as established by such passages as "He extends knowledge through action"; furthermore, because action itself is not an end in itself (*apumartha*). Nor is the grace of Brahman the fruit through that [action], since that too is established by action alone in such passages as "That action which pleases Hari..."; and because grace itself is not an end in itself. Nor is liberation the fruit through that [action], since that too is established by action alone in such passages as "We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal."

Furthermore, liberation, which consists in the cessation of false bondage, does not depend upon the grace [of the Lord]. Or, even if the fruit in the form of liberation were to occur through the medium of the grace of knowledge, she (Śakti) would still not be the qualified person for it. For if mere seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) were the qualified persons, then women, Śūdras, and others would also attain qualification; this would contradict such scriptural passages as, "The three Vedas are not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and base Brahmins. Moreover, there is no other qualified person whose qualification is excluded from that [category]. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): [it is as follows...]

Although [the Self] is not an object for those who hold the views of non-self, other-selves, or self-identity, it is nonetheless a fit subject of inquiry because it is established as a reality distinct from the individual soul (jīva)—namely the entity called Viṣṇu—by means of the word *brahman* used etymologically (*yaugika*) in the Veda, which denotes through its constituent parts a thing that is unconditioned by space, time, or qualities, as indicated by such scriptural passages as, "And why is it called *brahman*? For great (*bṛhantaḥ*) indeed are the qualities within it. Furthermore, since there is disagreement regarding this entity—due to its being characterized as having qualities, being devoid of qualities, or having few qualities—it is possible for it to be a subject of inquiry by virtue of its state of doubt.

The first position is not tenable, because there exists a relationship between [the Lord] and those qualified seekers who desire that [liberation], since liberation—known as the fruit—is produced by the grace arising from that knowledge. Nor is the second position tenable; for, according to the Smṛti cited in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) stating "hearing and reflection," inquiry in the form of hearing and so forth is the primary means for attaining knowledge, and ritual action is merely its subsidiary. Furthermore, although ritual action is not an end in itself, it possesses human purpose (puruṣārtha) by being a cause of liberation through the mediation of divine grace.

Furthermore, according to the Smṛti, one is considered "lowest" by virtue of action; moreover, since liberation has as its cause only the grace (*prasāda*) born of knowledge, while bondage is established through the means of perception and so forth, liberation necessarily depends upon grace. Furthermore, the statement that immortality is attained through action—such as "The soma-drinker indeed becomes immortal, as far as Indra [reaches]"—is merely figurative. Nor is the third alternative tenable.

Even though one who merely desires liberation (mumukṣu) lacks the qualification [for this inquiry], since a specific qualified person—one who possesses devotion to the Supreme Viṣṇu, as well as study, tranquility, self-control, and so forth—is possible according to such Smṛti texts as "one who is devoted to the Supreme Viṣṇu," the inquiry must indeed be undertaken. In this regard, although the doubt regarding whether liberation is produced by karma and its resolution are not explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya and the Ṭīkā, there is no contradiction because the word "only" (eva) in the Anuvyākhyāna—stating that "one is liberated only through His grace from the knowledge born of the inquiry"—indicates this very point.
Here, the results of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions are respectively the non-commencement and the commencement of the Śāstra. || 1 ||
|| Oṃ. [Brahman is that] from which there is the origin, etc., of this [world]. Oṃ. || 2 ||

The introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) arises because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised by way of a challenge to the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) characterized by the fullness of attributes belonging to an entity other than the individual soul, which has liberation as its fruit for a qualified person as previously described.

Alternatively, the connection with the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*) is that the definition of Brahman—the object of inquiry mentioned previously—is now being stated. In the *Taittirīya*, it is heard: "That from which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they depart—that, seek to know; that is Brahman. "When they depart" means at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). "Into which they enter of their own accord" means in liberation (*mukti*). Regarding this, there arises the doubt: Is the Brahman spoken of as "that is Brahman" the individual soul (*jīva*) or Viṣṇu?

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since it is stated that [the word *brahman*] applies to "the Great One (*bṛhat*), the genus (*jāti*), the individual soul (*jīva*), the lotus-seated one (*kamalāsana*), and the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*"), the word *brahman* is conventional (*rūḍha*) when applied to the individual soul (*jīva*), because its etymological meaning (*yaugika-artha*) is inapplicable there. Furthermore, since the word lacks conventionality when applied to Viṣṇu, and because the absence of a fullness of attributes would follow [if it were not conventional], its etymological application is untenable; for convention is stronger than etymology. Moreover, the causality mentioned in the preceding sentence, "from which [all this arises]," is possible even for the individual soul through the mediation of the unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*). For these very reasons, since the [causal] genus and so forth are impossible here, [the passage] "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen" and so on is an injunction for reflection (*manana*).

Furthermore, because the word "Self" (ātman), which is well-known in other passages to refer to the individual soul (jīva), is used here as well, this Brahman must be the jīva itself; and since that [jīva] is established by the notion of "I," there is no need for an inquiry [into it]. The final position (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

Since the causality of the origin and so forth of the world, as stated in the preceding passage beginning with "From which," is established as residing in Viṣṇu alone by the verse "He who [supports] the threefold earth and the heaven," and since the literal sense of words such as "born" would be lost if the passage were intended to mean that the individual soul (jīva) is the cause through an unseen force (adṛṣṭa); since there is no restrictive factor for the pronoun "these" (*imāni*); since the state of being reached by those already liberated, mentioned in the phrase "they enter into it," is in every way impossible [for the soul]; and since the agency of the soul will be refuted in the second [sūtra], "On account of the designation of another"—therefore, this [passage] serves as a sublater of the soul's status as the cause of the origin and so forth.

Because conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) must be set aside—in the passage "The Self, indeed, my dear," the word *ātman* heard there denotes Viṣṇu according to the principle to be stated later, namely "because of the word 'own'"; and because that very [word] has the status of being a conventional term for the wise (*vidvad-rūḍhi*) in the sense of "That indeed is Brahman, the supreme among the seers" (*tadeva brahma paramaṃ kavīnām*), and because such usage is stronger than the conventional usage of the ignorant; and because, by both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), Viṣṇu alone, who is full of all attributes, is Brahman—therefore, since He is the object of doubt, the desire to know Him (*taj-jijñāsā*) must certainly be undertaken.

Regarding the alternative view: there arises a doubt as to whether the word *brahman* refers to the well-known individual soul (*jīva*) or to some other meaning. In favor of the latter, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of having to postulate its denotative power for that meaning and its intended significance (*tātparya*) therein. In favor of the former, however, there is simplicity (*lāghava*), because the individual soul is not something to be newly postulated; since it is stated that "the genus *bṛhat* [is the root] and the individual soul [is the referent]," the primary signification (*śakti*) is already established, and its intended significance is also proven without contradiction. Thus, the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it refers only to the individual soul. [The Siddhāntin replies: "That which is unmixed with suffering, which is not overwhelmed, and which is uninterrupted..."

Based on the Śruti passage, "And the happiness brought about by desire has its locus in the state of heaven," it is argued that the established meaning of the term *svarga* (heaven)—such as sandalwood paste and the like—must be set aside in favor of an unestablished meaning; this constitutes the Siddhānta. Alternatively, since there is complexity (*gaurava*) in accepting an extraordinary subject (*viśeṣya*), whereas there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in accepting a well-known subject, it follows that, in accordance with that [simplicity], the basis for the application of the term is simply the fulfillment of qualities possible in the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, there is no intention to refer to the fulfillment of qualities as intended by the Siddhāntin; consequently, the term refers only to the individual soul. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the following refutation is given].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: first, by the subverting argument that [the term "Brahman"] refers only to a non-worldly subject (*alaukika-viśeṣya*) precisely because it functions as the cause [of the world], and consequently, due to the absence of any restrictive factor, the fulfillment of all attributes (*sarvaguṇapūrti*) alone is the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*); therefore, it refers exclusively to another meaning (Viṣṇu). This is one point. Another point is this: what was previously stated—that Viṣṇu is the liberator because he grants grace (*prasāda*) produced by the knowledge arising from the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), and therefore the desire to know should be undertaken—is incorrect. For if that were the case, since [the same knowledge] could also act as a binder, it would follow that the desire to know Him should not be undertaken either.

Nor is this [bondage] non-existent; for since it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to be either unbound or bound by itself, if one must speak of its being bound by another, then that other—whether conscious or unconscious—is itself dependent on the Lord. Consequently, the Lord would himself be the binder, and thus He could not be the object of inquiry.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the Lord is dependent on others, He cannot be the liberator from bondage brought about by one's own lack of dependence; therefore, the desire to know Him (*tajjijñāsā*) should not be undertaken. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that while the Lord who is displeased acts as a binder, He who is pleased acts as a liberator; thus, the desire to know Him must be undertaken in order to generate the knowledge that is the cause of His grace. Among these, the first [view] is intended by the *Ṭīkā*, while the latter is intended by the *Sudhā*. Furthermore, even within that, the latter should be meditated upon in the section concerning meditation (*upāsanāpāda*).

In the first [interpretation], the intention was not that the word *brahman* refers to Viṣṇu even in the sentence "from which" (*yato vā*), as it does in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the second, however, the distinction is that it refers to Viṣṇu everywhere. Regarding the last [interpretation], it should be understood that although the sūtra "liberation from this" (*mukteś cāsya*) ought to have been composed, the statement of the cause of creation and so forth in the form "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*) is intended to suggest the possibility of [Brahman] being the liberator. Here, the result to be clarified is the necessity of performing the inquiry (*jijñāsā*). || 2 ||
Om. [Brahman is] the source of the scriptures; Om. (Sūtra 3)

The connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the objection that the previously stated definition overextends (*ativyāpti*) to Rudra and others, it is now refuted. The doubt concerns whether the status of being the cause of the world—stated in such scriptural passages as "From which indeed... (*yato vā*)—belongs to Viṣṇu or to someone else. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it belongs to someone else, because the causehood of the world can be easily established for Rudra and others as well through inference. To explain: ... [as follows].

Even though the mere existence of an agent is established by the inference—"The earth and so forth have an agent because they are effects, like a pot"—this inference culminates either in the agent named Viṣṇu, as stated in the Śruti which denies its own authority in the words "one who does not know the Veda," or it culminates in an agent in the form of Śiva and others as taught in the Pāśupata and other Āgamas. Thus, the status of Śiva and others as the cause of the world's origin and so forth is established by the inference: "Śiva is the creator of the world's birth and so forth because he is omniscient; otherwise [it would be] like a potter. Nor is omniscience unestablished.

One prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) relies solely on inference, based either on an inference supported by scripture—such as the Pāśupata and other Āgamas which establish that [the world] is produced by Him—or on an inference from the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth, which establishes a creator possessed of eternal knowledge, will, and effort, or eternal effort. Since the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntin) does not accept that such a being is Viṣṇu, this [inference] culminates in identifying Him as Rudra and others, who are designated by such terms due to their role as the destroyer and so forth. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the scriptures cited by the opponent regarding Viṣṇu’s causality in this context.

[The opponent replies: "Because those [scriptures] merely intend to establish Viṣṇu as the cause, since they are contradicted by the aforementioned inference. But another [opponent] says: Since Rudra and others are perceived to be the causes of the world through the Pāśupata and other Āgamas—which are free from suspected defects because they were composed by the omniscient Śiva and others—Rudra and the rest are the creators of the world. Nor is there a contradiction with the Veda, which establishes Viṣṇu as the cause of the world due to its self-evident authority (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*); for there is no contradiction between the creatorship of both [Rudra and Viṣṇu], as their status as creators pertains to different times and so forth.

The proponent of the Āgamas argues that since the Vedas and Āgamas state that Viṣṇu and others created all this, such statements are logically consistent as referring either to the creation of everything produced at their respective times or to their general capacity; for just as the Vedic prohibition of Śiva’s causality and the Āgamic prohibition of Viṣṇu’s causality can be understood as intended to praise the non-sunrise sacrifice and the like by censuring the sunrise sacrifice and the like, so too the prohibitions regarding Viṣṇu and others can possibly be intended to enjoin the causality of [their respective deities]. Thus says the follower of the Āgamas.

And thus, if the characteristic [of God] is being the creator of the birth and so forth of the entire world, it is impossible; if it is being the creator of only some [parts], it is over-extensive; therefore, the prima facie conclusion is that such a definition is not tenable.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: The first prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not tenable. This is because, just as in the case of taste, smell, and so forth, the aforementioned inferences—which lack a basis in the Veda—are negated in their authority regarding the cause of the universe by such scriptural passages as, "One who does not know the Veda does not perceive this Great One," and "The Person known through the Upaniṣads. Furthermore, since such arguments could be applied even to the possession of horns by rabbits and the like, they would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*) and thus fail to establish the intended object. Therefore, the first prima facie position is not correct.

Likewise, since the invalidity of false scriptures has been stated by the Smṛti—beginning with "The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the Bhārata, and the Pañcarātra"—which is accepted as authoritative and embraced by the Śruti, it follows that [the opponent's position] is not supported even by Āgama; thus, Viṣṇu alone is the cause of the world. Therefore, the result in the final conclusion (siddhānta) is that the definition is not over-extensive (ativyāpta). That this [topic] does not have its meaning already established by the section on Smṛti will be explained in that very place. It should be understood here that the two preceding prima facie views (pūrvapakṣa) are based, respectively, on the Bhāṣya and the Anuvyākhyāna. || 3 ||
Oṃ. But that [Brahman is the cause of the world] because of the harmony [of all scriptural texts]; Oṃ. (4)

There is no over-extension [of the definition] because causality is to be understood solely through scripture; this constitutes the immediate connection [to the present topic] either by way of implying the result of the preceding section, or by way of investigating the specific point—established in the previous section—as to whether Viṣṇu or someone else is the one whose causality is known through scripture. Here, the doubt is whether the status of having scripture as its source belongs to Viṣṇu alone or to others as well. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that even Rudra and others possess causality that is to be understood solely through scripture.

From the Śaiva and other Āgamas—which are commentaries on the Veda and are not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—the intent of the Veda is ascertained regarding Rudra and others also being the cause. This is because it has been stated that "from a commentary, one attains a specific understanding [of the original], just as from a commentary on a poem, one understands the specific [meaning] of the poem. Nor should it be said that such [commentaries] lack authority; for when a commentary on a subject matter that is itself authoritative is authoritative, there is no need for further evidence in the event of a contradiction with other means of valid cognition. And in this case, the contradiction with other means of valid cognition has been established by the scriptural passage beginning with "Not by logic" (naiṣā tarkeṇa).

Nor does it follow from this that, because Viṣṇu is also a cause according to the *Pañcarātra* and other texts, there must be a determination of the Veda’s purport [in favor of him]. For even so, since his status as the cause is established through the aforementioned reasoning regarding differences of place and so forth, the claim that "Viṣṇu alone is the agent" remains unproven; this is because the opening statements (*upakrama*) and other criteria cannot determine the Veda’s purport due to the impossibility of deciding their relative strength. This is one argument stated in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*. Another argument is as follows: From scriptures such as the Vedas, the causality of Rudra and others indeed appears. And therein, the purport of those scriptures is established precisely because they are not sublated.

Nor can it be argued that a scriptural passage establishing Viṣṇu’s causality or one prohibiting Rudra’s and others’ [causality] acts as a sublater [of the other], because the reverse could equally be the case. Since both would then possess equal force, both could be agents; and since the passages can be explained by attributing Viṣṇu’s causality to one time-period and the absence of such causality in Rudra and others to another, this is the position supported by the *bhāṣya* based on the superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) produced by the Vedas. Alternatively, it should not be said that the Śaiva and other Āgamas lack the capacity to determine the intended meaning of the Vedas simply because their own authority has been denied.

"Since even in the Veda there is the perception of Rudra and others as the cause," thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based solely on scripture, accompanied by superficial perception, is one; here, according to the first alternative, there are two prima facie arguments—the former being favored by Sudhā and the latter by Īkā. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Since the Vedas are perceived as being mutually contradictory at first glance, their status as a single coherent whole can only be established by determining their intended meaning (*tātparya*). However, because the Śaiva and other Āgamas lack authority according to the aforementioned reasoning, they cannot serve as determiners of that intended meaning—even if they do not contradict other means of knowledge—when the subject matter is inconsistent with the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and so forth. Furthermore, since such an interpretation would be impossible for a work that does not accord with the introductory passages, and because a superficial perception rooted in ignorance is non-conclusive, the intended meaning of the Veda must be determined through the introductory passages and other such indicators, and [the Āgamas] cannot establish the Vedic intent by means of that [interpretation].

Since the purport of the Veda must be determined by means of the necessary *upakrama* (introductory statements) and other criteria—according to the method stated in the foundational texts (*mūlagrantha*)—and since the determination of strength and weakness is easily accomplished thereby, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is primarily the cause of the universe and the subject matter of the purport of all authentic scriptures. Thus, both the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on scripture (*āgama*) and those based on perception (*pratīti*) are untenable. Consequently, the final [prima facie] argument is also untenable; therefore, the definition [of the system] is not over-extended (*ativyāpta*). This is the result. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ. Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture. Oṃ. || 5 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is secondary, no, because of the word 'Self' (ātman). Oṃ. Because liberation is taught for one who is established in That. Oṃ. And because there is no statement of its being something to be abandoned. Oṃ. Because of merging into It. Oṃ. Because of merging into It. Oṃ. Because of the uniformity of the goal. Oṃ. And because it is so stated in scripture. The introductory connection (*saṅgati*) is one of objection (*ākṣepikī*), since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises by way of an objection to what was previously stated: namely, that Brahman is the subject matter intended by all the scriptures in their primary sense.

The doubt arises as to whether it is logically tenable that Brahman is primarily the source of all scriptures or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not tenable; for according to such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back," Brahman is said to be inexpressible. Nor should it be argued that because the scripture states, "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city," Brahman is an object of vision—and since that which is known through the Upanishads cannot be perceived by means other than words, its perception by words would be impossible without its being expressible—this argument is not valid. [The answer follows: It is indeed logical. For the scripture itself declares, "It is to be seen through the mind alone" (*manasaivānudraṣṭavyam*), and thus perception by means of words is not precluded. Furthermore, the statement "from which words turn back" refers to the cessation of words regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not to the fact that Brahman is entirely beyond verbal expression. Therefore, Brahman is primarily the source of all scriptures. This is established.

Since the scriptural mention of "seeing" refers to the secondary self (gauṇātman) and that [self] is indeed expressible by words, it is possible for even the pure Self—which is inexpressible—to be "seen" by means of a word through indication (lakṣaṇā). This is because the scripture, stating "He taught by means of non-speaking itself," implies that he instructed by means of indication, without the function of direct verbal expression.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of the theory of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), when the question "What is the indicated object (*lakṣya*) of this word? is raised, one would have to employ another word that is itself indicative; and since for that purpose the cognition of the relationship with the primary meaning (*vācya*) is required, the employment of yet another indicative word would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For even in the theory of direct denotation (*vācyatva*), a denotative word conveys its meaning only when its relationship [with that meaning] has been grasped, and the grasping of that relationship is dependent upon the grasping of the relata.

Because Brahman is the subject matter of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*), its realization occurs only through another scripture; thus, since the same infinite regress would apply, the claim that [the realization] occurs "by the primary function" (*mukhyavṛttyā*) is incorrect. Furthermore, as for the claim that Brahman is the source of all scriptures (*sarvaśāstrayonitva*), that too is not tenable. According to the Śruti, "The Vedas are indeed infinite"; because the Vedas are infinite, their very nature is difficult to grasp for persons endowed with limited lifespan, knowledge, and so forth. Consequently, it is difficult to know that "all scriptures have Brahman as their ultimate purport. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): [text continues]

In passages such as, "One should see the Self in the Self alone," and "He by whom the Self has been perceived and awakened—that is his world; indeed, that is the world itself"—the object of vision is the pure Self, because of the teaching on liberation through the word "Self" and its synonyms. And of that [pure Self]...

If [Brahman] were to be perceived through a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the aforementioned infinite regress would follow. Furthermore, since Brahman is eternally established by its own self-luminosity, it is improper to apply a definition, as this would result in the futility of the scripture (*śāstra*). On the other hand, regarding the position that [the scripture] is expressive (*vācaka*), since derivative words (*yaugika-pada*) are equivalent to sentences, they do not require the separate apprehension of grammatical relations (*saṅgati*); thus, there is no infinite regress. This is consistent with such scriptural passages as "whence speech turns back," which establish that Brahman is not the object of speech in its entirety.

Even though the Vedas are infinite, because of the scriptural hearing of a commonality of purpose in the statement, "All the Vedas are reasoning" (*yuktayaḥ*), and because one understands—by means of the analogy of observing a branch whose meaning has been determined by the omniscient author of the Sūtras—that other branches must also have that same meaning simply by virtue of being branches, it follows that Viṣṇu’s status as the source of all scriptures is primary; this is the explicit result.
Even though it serves to establish two distinct points, one should understand that the section (adhikaraṇa) is a single unit because it aims to prove the meaning of the term "one" (eka). || 5 ||

The remainder of this chapter is fruitful for the purpose of establishing—even by means of removing objections and so forth—the "harmonious convergence" (*samanvaya*) mentioned in the Śruti passage, "That state which all the Vedas proclaim. Here, within the remainder of the chapter, the harmonious convergence promised in the Sūtra on Convergence (*Samanvaya-sūtra*) is demonstrated through the reason of "denotability" (*vācyatva*) stated in the section on the term "Iksati" (*Īkṣati-naya*).

This is because, among the four types of Vedic words—those well-known in that [Brahman], those well-known elsewhere, those known both here and elsewhere, and those known neither here nor elsewhere—the harmonious convergence of those well-known in Brahman need not be stated.

Furthermore, since the other categories are each twofold according to the distinction between name (nāman) and gender (liṅga), following the maxim of "breaking a great wrestler," there is first the reconciliation in the first quarter of the names that are well-known elsewhere [in secular literature] but here denote the substratum (dharmin) directly; in the second quarter, the reconciliation of genders that indicate the substratum through its attributes (dharma); and in the third quarter, the reconciliation of both types—those well-known in both [Vedic and secular contexts]—which are twofold.

The distinction between the sections (pādas) and their sequence is as follows: although the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) of words well-known elsewhere is accomplished only with great effort, it is stated last because it is not accessible to all qualified seekers and is difficult to understand at first. The non-confusion of terms "well-known elsewhere" and so forth, as well as the distinction between names and gender based on conventional (*rūḍhi*) and etymological (*yaugika*) usage, should be understood from the *Candrikā*. **Oṃ. [Brahman is] the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because of repetition.** 6.1.12. Oṃ.

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [Brahman] because of words denoting modification, we say no, because of abundance. Oṃ. And because its cause is designated. Oṃ. And it is celebrated in the very words of the mantra. Oṃ. It is not the other, because that is untenable. Oṃ. And because of the designation of difference. Oṃ. And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference. Oṃ. And scripture teaches its union with this [Self] in this [state]."

Alternatively, because the great quality of being full-bliss—the object of the meditation that bestows all desired bliss—is the primary meaning [of the word "Self"], it is logical that the previously mentioned exclusion of the "secondary Self" follows from the word "Self. Or else, there is a contextual connection (*saṅgati*) based on an objection: since the previously stated objection arises through the challenge that the term "Self" might apply figuratively to what is not Brahman—such as the "Self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and so forth, as heard in the passage, "This very Self consisting of bliss"—the present discussion proceeds as a response to that objection. Thus, it is found in the *Taittirīya*.

The subject matter consists of the terms *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*—which denote the substrata (guṇin) as heard in the passage beginning with "This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣo'nnarasamayaḥ*)—as well as the words denoting the common attributes (*guṇasāmānya*) such as bliss (*ānanda*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding their meaning, there arises a doubt: is it some other being different from Viṣṇu, such as Caturmukha (Brahmā), or is it Viṣṇu? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is someone other than Viṣṇu. For instance:

Because the suffix *mayaṭ* in *annamaya* and the others denotes a modification (*vikāra*), whereas Brahman is described as "changeless," "imperishable," and "pure," and is therefore devoid of modification and does not identify with such modifications.

Even if the suffix *mayaṭ* were to mean "abundance," it would be untenable here because abundance is defined by the scarcity of heterogeneous elements, and since even a trace of suffering or the like is impossible in Brahman, such a meaning is precluded. Furthermore, the sense of "identity" (*tādātmya*) for *mayaṭ* is refuted by its redundancy; for after introducing the body—which is a modification of food and is denoted by the word "person" (*puruṣa*)—in the passage "From food, the person [arises]," the text states: "That very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*); this indeed is his head, this is his right wing, this is his left wing, this is his trunk, and this is his tail, the support."

Furthermore, because the head, arms, and other limbs are designated as being perceptible, the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *annamaya* must necessarily signify "modification" (*vikāra*). Since a dual meaning is untenable, it is logical that the suffix everywhere signifies modification alone. Moreover, in passages such as "Another inner self is the *prāṇamaya*," these [sheaths] are described as being distinct from one another; and by the statement "This very [self] is the body, this is the Self," they are described through the relationship of body and embodied. Yet, these five sheaths are manifold, whereas Brahman—according to such texts as "Brahman is indeed one without a second"—is singular and non-dual.

It is stated that "the self consisting of consciousness is bodiless" (*aśarīraḥ prajñātmā*), and it is also bodiless. Furthermore, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is said: "Joy (*priya*) is its head, delight (*moda*) is its right wing, rapture (*pramoda*) is its left wing, bliss (*ānanda*) is its trunk, and Brahman is its tail, the foundation. Thus, Brahman is described as a limb—specifically the foot—of the one consisting of bliss. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is not Brahman, because it is contradictory for two things to both be Brahman, and because it is impossible for a part and the whole to be identical.

Therefore, it is either the sheaths (*kośa*) themselves that are denoted by these terms because they possess the nature of all modifications (*vikāra*), or the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) because of its identification with those modifications, or the individual soul (*jīva*), or some other entity according to the direction stated in the Commentary; in no way is Viṣṇu [meant]. But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: all five, beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), are indeed Brahman.

Because the word "Brahman" is heard in each of the five [sheaths]—in the passages, "Those who meditate on food as Brahman," "Those who meditate on breath as Brahman," "He who knows bliss as Brahman," "If he knows consciousness as Brahman," and "If he knows that 'Brahman exists'"—and because there is a repetition of that term for the sheaths consisting of consciousness and bliss; and because the word "Self" is repeated in all five [sheaths] in such forms as, "There is another inner Self consisting of breath," and "This self consisting of food."

Likewise, in the *annamaya* (consisting of food), there are marks such as being the sustenance of all and the destroyer of all, as well as being the eldest and the goal to be attained by the worshiper, based on the passage beginning with "it is eaten and it eats beings. In the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), there are also marks such as being the object of the activity of all the gods and others, as stated in "the gods breathe after the breath," and being the object of knowledge which is the cause of liberation in the form of all life. In the *manomaya* (consisting of mind), there are marks such as being beyond the reach of speech and mind, and being the object of realization which is the cause of liberation in the form of fearlessness, based on the passage beginning with "from whence words return."

In the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness), there are signs such as being worshipped by all the gods, being the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*), being the cause of liberation, and being attainable by the worshipper—as stated in passages beginning with, "All the gods worship Brahman, the eldest consciousness. In the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), there are signs such as being the creator preceded by volition (*saṅkalpa*), being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all, and being the object of the knowledge that is the cause of liberation—as stated in passages beginning with, "He desired," and so forth. Likewise, [there is the sign]: "For who indeed would inhale, and who would exhale, if this bliss were not in the ether?"

It may be that the state of being composed of bliss—characterized by the fullness of bliss denoted by the word "Ānanda"—is the reason for its being the object of the universe's desire; for it is stated as the fruit to be attained that the knower of Brahman, described as "he who knows thus," approaches this very self consisting of food (annamaya).

Because it is heard that [Brahman] is to be attained by the knower of Brahman, and because there is an abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga*) in all five [sections], and because the phrase "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" refers to the Brahman described as having the characteristics stated in the Vedic verse "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," which is explained by these very words, and because it constitutes a context (*prakaraṇa*) concerning Brahman; and because of the title of the *Bhṛgu-vallī* starting with "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa," and so forth; and because they praised Hari with those very verses beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us."

Furthermore, because it occurs within a section of the Upaniṣads—which are determined to have Brahman as their subject matter through the traditional recollection (smṛti) stating "He is Janārdana"—and because words such as "Brahman" and "Self" are established as residing exclusively in Viṣṇu by means of the scriptural passages cited in the Commentary; and because the fact that the *Bhṛguvallī* constitutes a corroborative testimony (*samākhyāna*) has been demonstrated in the foundational texts; nor is there an incompatibility with the suffix *-mayaḥ*, since that suffix is justified here as signifying abundance (*prācurya*), being defined by the relative paucity of happiness found in things of the same class. And it has been said:

Just as there is a minimum of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with heterogeneous things, so too there is a minimum of co-occurrence with a locus distinct from its own genus; this is the defining characteristic (*nirūpaka*). Furthermore, the statement regarding "otherness" (*anyatva*) and "interiority" (*antaratva*) is justified by the force of such Smṛti passages as: "Because the sheaths (*kośa*), which constitute the substrata, are different," "because the Brahman is the body [of all]," "because Brahman possesses manifold forms," and "though non-different, it is designated by the word 'different'. If it is asked, "How then is the reference to the body in the passage *sa vā eṣa* [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1] to be understood?"—the answer is: no, it is not.

In the passage beginning with "From the Self, space" and ending with "From food, the person," the manifestation—which is a form of birth—of Hari, who possesses the nature of being the regulator of space and the rest, is stated; for by the word "person" (puruṣa), Hari is also referred to as the subject under discussion, as he will state later: "And [He is the cause] in space and the rest, by way of being the cause."

This is because the word "rasa" and the pronoun "saḥ"—which refers back to the distant subject "Ātman"—serve as qualifiers precisely to exclude the *annamaya* body under discussion; otherwise, the description would have been complete with the mere statement, "This is the *annamaya*. Furthermore, the direct reference "this is its head" is justifiable, like the expression "with knees bent" (*añjānu*) used for knees covered by a garment. Moreover, since the nature of Brahman as fullness has been established elsewhere for both the *ānandamaya* and its limbs, there is no contradiction in their being limbs.

Therefore, because there is no sublation and because there is proof, all five sheaths are indeed of the nature of Brahman, beginning with Aniruddha. As for the purpose [of this discussion]: since Brahman is the constituent part (*avayava*) of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), an inquiry into the parts is impossible without the whole; thus, this serves as the resolution to the objection regarding the inquiry [into Brahman]. 6.
Oṃ. [The inner self is Brahman] because of the teaching of its attributes. Oṃ. 7.
|| Oṃ, [the Self] is different because of the designation of difference; oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the objection raised previously: since the quality of "being invisible" (adṛśyatva), which is heard as an attribute of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) in the passage "invisible, bodiless," is also heard as belonging to the "one within" (antastha), and since that [one within] is not Viṣṇu, it follows that the former is also not Viṣṇu. In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], the one within is heard as being endowed with qualities such as invisibility: "Having entered within, he is the agent; him who moves within the moon by means of the mind, though existing together [with them], the gods do not perceive."

Since even the gods do not know "who else this might be," because invisibility is established through the principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so), there arises a doubt as to whether that one situated within is Viṣṇu or another such as Indra. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is Indra and others, on account of the scriptural mention of Indra in passages such as, "Indra is the king; Brahmā, Indra, Agni... and so forth; on account of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Sūrya in the verse, "Seven yoke the chariot with its single wheel..."; on account of the characteristic mark of Varuṇa in the phrase, "The leader of the waters..."; and on account of the scriptural mention of Tvaṣṭṛ in the passage, "Tvaṣṭṛ, transforming his forms... [1.2.24–27].

Although there are many marks (liṅgas) of Viṣṇu such as invisibility and so forth, because the intrinsic strength of the Śruti is more powerful—as it is said, "Between those two, the nature [of the Śruti] is stronger"—and because the marks are also stronger due to being non-contingent (niravakāśa), let Indra and others be one with Viṣṇu in accordance with both the subsequent Śruti and the marks. Regarding the passage, "Moving within the ocean by means of the mind, whose egg-shell they call the vital heat (*śuṣma*)," [the Lord is the subject] because the marks of Brahman—such as residing within the ocean, being the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and being the *vīrya* (potency)—have no other possible application according to the scriptural citations mentioned in the Commentary; and furthermore, because in this very context, the distinction of the Inner One from Indra and others is declared through such statements as "He is the Self of Indra" and "He is the Self of Vāyu," making identity impossible; and because the grounds for the application of the names "Indra" and so forth, such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), exist in Viṣṇu as well.

Because it belongs to another being (the individual soul) who is dependent on Him, and according to the principle of dependence; and because, through great yoga—as in the Śruti passage, "They call Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni," etc.—and through the conventional usage of the learned, as well as by the principle that "words with other gendered marks [can refer to Viṣṇu] by the power of scripture," there is the possibility of [these terms] applying to Viṣṇu as well. Thus, the one within is Viṣṇu. As for the result, however, the refutation of the previous objection is established. || 7 ||
Oṃ. [The Self is] space, because of its characteristic marks. Oṃ. 8.

The connection [between this section and the previous one] consists either in the extension (*atideśa*) of the previous reasoning after raising a further doubt, or in the form of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises by way of a contrast with the previous case. In the first chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is heard as the answer to the question of Śālāvatya: "What is the goal of this world?"—"Ether," he said, and so forth. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the word "ether" denote the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), or does it denote Viṣṇu? Since the word "ether" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether, the initial conclusion (*prāpta*) is that it refers only to the elemental ether.

Nor is there a contradiction with the *liṅga* (indicative mark) regarding Viṣṇu, because a *liṅga* is weaker than direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Furthermore, one should not suspect that the present discussion does not arise because the established principle—that a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is set aside by an unconditioned *liṅga*—applies here just as it did previously; for that objection is not valid.

Or rather, it is because there is room for a further objection: although words such as "Indra" denote Īśvara according to the principle that the sovereignty and other attributes residing in Indra and others are dependent on Him—since they are obtained through His grace—the word "ākāśa" does not apply to Him. This is because the quality of having cavities (*vivaratva*), which is the ground for the application of the word "ākāśa," does not depend on Him and does not reside in Him, as He is insentient. Furthermore, the probans (*liṅga*) by which the final conclusion was established in the previous case is not the same here, but is instead another.

And thus, although the status of being Vaiṣṇava was previously determined by that inferential mark (liṅga) through the scriptural passages cited in the Commentary, here there is a lack of such certainty; therefore, the prima facie objection (pūrvākṣepa) is that it must be the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) because of the well-established (nirūḍha) use of the term "ether" (ākāśa).

The same applies to what follows. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: "This very *udgītha* is the highest-high (*parovarīyān*); this is the infinite (*ananta*). Because the marks (*liṅga*) of being the highest-high, being the *udgītha*, and being infinite—along with the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating, "That which is superior to the supreme is declared [to be Viṣṇu]," and the scriptural text (*śruti*), "Higher than measure" (*paro mātrayā*)—reside exclusively in Viṣṇu, it is necessary by their force that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) must abandon its worldly conventional meaning and denote Viṣṇu alone. Nor is there an absence of a cause [for this].

Since the *Smṛti* states that "the sky (*nabhas*) gives way to those who breathe" by its own restraint, it is evident that the sentient is dependent on the Lord; how much more so, then, is the insentient? Furthermore, according to common worldly logic, although the quality of being a cavity—which is the etymological basis (*nimitta*) for the word *nabhas*—does not reside in the Lord because it depends on Him as its substrate, it is nonetheless dependent upon Him through His sovereignty over it. Thus, by the principle to be stated later, and because the *Smṛti* declares it to be "endowed with the qualities of all beings," it is established that the word primarily denotes Viṣṇu, as He resides within that [quality].

In this regard, even though it has been stated that "if this space were other [than Viṣṇu], this bliss would not be space," the result of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions consists in the refutation and resolution of the objection that space is other than Viṣṇu. || 8 ||
|| Oṃ, for this very reason, [he is] Prāṇa, Oṃ || 9 ||

In this case as well, the connection [of the topic] arises either through extension (*atideśa*) because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised by way of a contrast with the preceding [section], or in the form of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), or through an investigation according to the sequence of the Vedic text, such as "From space, air" (*ākāśādvāyuḥ*). Regarding the Prāṇa heard in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], in the section beginning "That indeed became Prāṇa," and continuing with "Being the sustainer, he was being sustained," the doubt is whether this Prāṇa is the primary vital air (*mukhyavāyu*) or Viṣṇu.

Since the word *prāṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of the primary vital air (*mukhyavāyu*), even though the view that "prāṇa is indeed the primary vital air" has been refuted here by the previously mentioned logic and by the presence of an unambiguous indicative mark (*niravakāśaliṅga*), there remains the objection that the word *prāṇa* lacks conventional usage in the sense of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the ground for its application—the state of being the cause of life (*jīvanahetutva*) known as *prāṇana*—is found in the primary vital air, which constitutes the body of the wind, just as the potter’s body is the cause of the jar. This is supported by such scriptural and traditional texts as "When he had entered into his *prāṇa*, he arose" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.2) and "That which is attained and that which is abandoned," or according to the method explained in the *Sudhā* commentary, [the relationship is] like that between the potter’s body and the jar.

Alternatively, because the sacrifice also lacks existence as residing in the primary wind—either through the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of perception, or through positive and negative concomitance already understood [elsewhere]—the doubt arises that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not Viṣṇu; thus, as in the previous case, popular usage must be abandoned due to an unconditioned indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "Śrīśca te," since that which was denoted by the word *yuṣmat* (your) [in the previous section] is identified here again by the word *yuṣmat* in the statement "That indeed is Prāṇa," no suspicion arises that these two sections have different meanings. Furthermore, in the section beginning with "Being the supporter," there is the hearing of marks such as immortality in passages like "They call him Death, they call him Immortal. Thus, because of the scriptural statement "That is Prāṇa" and according to the logic applied in the sūtra "Prāṇa is likewise," it belongs to Viṣṇu; for just as the function of air constitutes the body of the primary Prāṇa, so too does the primary Prāṇa [belong to Him].

Because [the breath] is associated with Viṣṇu’s body through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because it is His very life-force, and because even the breath residing in the wind is dependent on Him according to the principle of dependence, and because of its usage in such passages as "the breath of the breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇaḥ*), Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word *prāṇa* through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Furthermore, based on the authority of another scriptural passage cited in the Commentary—"Hrī and Lakṣmī are Your two wives"—it should be understood that *hrī* here is indeed *śrī*.

As for the purpose [of this discussion]: it is the implication of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) by way of His state of full bliss denoted by the term "great enjoyment" (*mahābhoga*), and the resolution thereof. || 9 ||
Oṃ. [The Brahman is] light, because of the mention of its feet. Oṃ. 10.

The connection [of this section] is either by way of a counter-example arising from the objection raised in the previous [section], or by way of the sequence of the Vedic text. In the *Agnisūkta*, it is heard: "My ears fly apart, my sight flies apart; this light placed within the heart—my mind wanders far away with its anxieties; what indeed shall I say? Regarding the light (*jyotis*) mentioned here, there arises a doubt: is it Agni or Viṣṇu? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is Agni.

Because the word "light" (*jyotis*) is conventionally established in the sense of fire, even though it denotes merely that which is opposed to darkness, it cannot apply to anything else here; for this is indicated by the mark of its being situated within the cave of the heart, and because of the proximity of the word "fire" in the phrase "O Agni, you [are] in the darkness. Nor should it be argued that, as in the previous case, the Śruti is set aside by a mark (liṅga) that leaves no other scope, and thus this [interpretation] does not arise; for there is a difference between the two cases. This is because the Śruti concerning Prāṇa lacks the support of a Vāyu-sūkta, whereas this [Śruti concerning Jyotis] is supported by the Agni-sūkta, which serves as its context.

Nor should it be argued that, since the Śruti has scope for Viṣṇu—whether taken as referring to the element (bhūta) by the logic of the "ether" (ākāśa-nyāya) or as referring to a deity (devatā) by the logic of the "inner controller" (antaryāmin-nyāya)—the Sūkta associated with it must likewise refer to Him, and thus those two [the Śruti and the Sūkta] are set aside by the "unconditional" (niravakāśa) marks [of the individual soul]. This is because the marks such as "dwelling in the cave" (guhā-sthatva) also have scope [for other interpretations], and therefore those two [the Śruti and the Sūkta] set aside that [mark].

Even though the systematic classification of hymns—such as "this is an Agni-hymn" or "this is a Vāyu-hymn"—is established by the principle of "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) and so forth when a hymn belongs to Viṣṇu, [the opponent's position] is untenable because, due to the lack of worldly consensus that "this is an Agni-hymn and not a Viṣṇu-hymn," the hymn would otherwise have no scope [for its specific designation]. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Because the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of having a limited majesty—as expressed in passages such as "my ears fly apart"—which is the state of being distant from the ears and so forth, has Viṣṇu alone as its locus according to the Śruti "beyond measure" (*paro mātrayā*), and thus finds no scope elsewhere; because the ground for the application of the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the sense of luminosity exists in Viṣṇu, whereas that which belongs to others is dependent upon Him; because of its usage in such passages as "That is the light of lights" (*tad devā jyotiṣāṃ jyotiḥ*); and because that word "light" belongs to Viṣṇu in the manner to be explained in the passage "of some by light" (*jyotiṣaikeṣām*).

The claim that "this is not the Viṣṇu-sūkta" is based on a lack of knowledge regarding its established renown; therefore, since those two [objections] have scope [only for the ignorant], they are set aside by the indicative mark (liṅga) which has no other scope. By both etymological derivation (yoga) and conventional usage (rūḍhi), the word "light" (jyotis) denotes Viṣṇu alone, and the Sūkta is likewise devoted to Him. As for the result: it consists of the refutation of the objection raised against the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya)—who was described as "hidden in the cave"—by means of the statement "He who knows Him placed in the heart," and its subsequent resolution. || 10 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self is not the object of meditation] because of the mention of meters, we say no; for there is a declaration of the fixing of the mind [upon the Self], and such is seen [in scripture]. Oṃ. (Sūtra 11)

The connection [of this section] arises from the refutation of a previous established doctrine (*pūrvasiddhāntākṣepa*) or from a discrepancy with what preceded (*pūrvavaiṣamya*), which leads to the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In the third chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, there is a doubt regarding the passage: "Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here; Gāyatrī is speech. Is Gāyatrī a meter (*chandas*) consisting of a collection of phonemes, or is it Viṣṇu? The prima facie view is that it is a specific meter, because the word "Gāyatrī" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense.

Nor should it be suspected that, as in the previous case, there would be a contradiction of scripture here as well by means of the marks of Viṣṇu; for there is no purpose in abandoning words well-known to denote Viṣṇu and employing the term "Gāyatrī," which is not so well known.

In the previous case, although the previously established usage [of *jyotis*] was set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the single light, here it is not possible to set aside the multiple scriptural mentions of speech, earth, and so forth—such as "Speech indeed is Gāyatrī" and "This which is the earth"—because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word *gāyatrī* does not apply to Viṣṇu, and its etymological meaning (*yoga*) is secondary. Furthermore, since Gāyatrī is a specific Veda and is eternal, it cannot be subject to dependence on the Lord; thus, the principle of dependence (*tadadhīnatva-nyāya*) does not apply here either. For this very reason, the mention of *jyotis*, which was previously determined to denote Viṣṇu, [is relevant] here in the subsequent sentence: "Now..."

Because of the scriptural statement, "That light which shines beyond heaven," the previous conclusion that the Gāyatrī is Viṣṇu is refuted by its force; for it would be improper to subvert many other scriptural passages [by such an interpretation]. Furthermore, since the word *tejas* (light)—which is a synonym for *jyotis* (light)—is used for the Gāyatrī in the passage, "The Gāyatrī is indeed splendor (*tejas*) and Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*"), it finds its scope there alone. Consequently, by the force of that [usage], it is more logical that even the previously mentioned light is the Gāyatrī itself.

Alternatively, even if Viṣṇu is the subject, because the preceding light is stated to reside in heaven by the Gāyatrī mantra—"The three-footed immortal [light] is in heaven"—and because the light described as being beyond heaven is distinct from that Gāyatrī, and because the previously mentioned light, though it may be Viṣṇu, is not this [present] one—since there is the hearing of its being "seen" (dṛśya) and "heard" (śruta), which contradicts the nature of Viṣṇu who is beyond sight and hearing—it follows that Gāyatrī is not Viṣṇu on account of that scriptural mention of "light. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Furthermore, there is an abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as the scriptural passages concerning the Puruṣa and Brahman: "Then the Person is greater still," "Or rather, this is Brahman," and "He who knows this very Upaniṣad of Brahman"; as well as the agency in singing and protecting—defined as the utterance of the entire Veda—as stated in "He sings and he protects"; the state of having the elements and so forth as His feet, as stated in "All beings are but one foot of Him"; and His status as the supreme of all, as stated in "Nothing surpasses Him."

For it is logical to employ words that are not commonly known for the purpose of meditation based on their possessing the qualities that serve as the grounds for the application of those [well-known] terms; and because it is possible for many words to abandon their well-established meanings through numerous scriptural citations (*śruti*) and indicative marks (*liṅga*).

Based on the statement "He sings and He protects," and because conventional usage is overridden by powerful Vedic etymological application (*śrauta-yoga*), just as the beginningless qualities and so forth are dependent upon the possessor of those qualities (*guṇin*), so too—in view of such Śrutis as "the nature, the individual soul, and karma"—it is possible for even that which is beginningless and eternal to be dependent upon the Lord. Furthermore, by the logic of dependence and through great etymological application (*mahā-yoga*)—since He is indeed designated by all Vedic meters—as well as by Puranic convention, Gāyatrī is Viṣṇu; thus, both the subsequent and the preceding light are He alone.

The difference in instruction—such as being situated in heaven, being beyond heaven, being invisible, and being visible—is justified by the intention to describe the three worlds and seven worlds [respectively], and by the difference in form. Regarding the fruits [of the meditation], there is either the objection and its resolution concerning the identity of the ancient light with Viṣṇu, or the objection and its resolution concerning the Sūtra on "origination and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*), by way of the stated cause of stability in the passage, "For all this is established in it. || 11 ||
|| Oṃ, [the word] *prāṇa* [denotes Brahman], because it is found to follow [as the subject]; oṃ. || 12 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the Supreme Self because of the instruction regarding the speaker's own self, we say no, for there is an abundance of internal (spiritual) connections in this [chapter]. Oṃ. But the instruction is based on scriptural vision, as in the case of Vāmadeva. Oṃ. If it be argued that it is not so because of the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, we say no, because of the threefold nature of meditation; since those [marks] are resorted to [elsewhere], they are applicable here [only in that sense]."

Here, the connection is one of exception (*āpavādika-saṅgati*), because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds by means of the abundance of direct scriptural statements (*śruti*) and indicative marks (*liṅga*), following the logic of the previously established conclusion. In the *Aitareya [Āraṇyaka]*, the term "prāṇa" is heard in many places, such as: "Now these are the glories resting upon the head: sight, hearing, mind, speech, and breath. Regarding this, the doubt is whether the prāṇa is the primary vital air (*mukhya-vāyu*) and so forth, or whether it is Viṣṇu. The prima facie view is that it is the vital air, Indra, or the individual soul (*jīva*), because of the abundance of scriptural statements and indicative marks concerning them. To explain: [The text continues with the supporting evidence for the prima facie view.]

The mention [of the breath] alongside the eye, ear, and so forth; the statements beginning with "they did not injure one another"; the dispute among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); the exiting from and entering into the body; the falling down and rising up of the body; the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), and other such marks of the principal breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), as well as the scriptural mention of "breath" (*prāṇa*) occurring in their company; likewise, the hundred-year lifespan mentioned in the text, "He worshipped him for a hundred years," the mention of the "person" (*puruṣa*) read along with that, and the status of being a "lineage" (*vaṃśa*) toward the eye and other organs as stated in "Breath is the lineage"—these are the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*). [And further: "Indra indeed [slain] Vṛtra..."

The killing of Vṛtra and other such marks—namely, the slaying of Vṛtra, the performance of the Mahāvrata vow, and the state of being unconquered—as well as the scriptural declaration of the word "I" employed by Indra in the passage, "O Ṛṣi, I am indeed Prāṇa"—these numerous scriptural texts and indicative marks are heard [in the context]. And none of these are possible in Viṣṇu. As for the final conclusion (siddhānta):

"This is Brahman, this is Truth"—with these words, one enters that [Brahman] with both feet. Regarding the scriptural passages such as "Brahman entered this Puruṣa," "Aḥ is Brahman," and so forth, as well as those heard in the Śruti such as "The gods lead him forth," "The gods worshipped him as Bhūti," "He is all the Vedas," "For he who shines yonder is indeed Prāṇa," and "By the Bṛhatī metre, starting from ants, the worlds were pervaded by Prāṇa"—these indicate through their respective marks (liṅgas) that he is taught by the gods, is the subject of all the Vedas, resides within the solar orb, is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all, and is all-pervading; this is established by the force of the statements cited in the Commentary and other authoritative texts.

Because Viṣṇu alone is the ultimate goal, as established by the previously cited scriptural passages and others, and because of their abundance; because the previously mentioned scriptural texts and indicative marks (*liṅga*) are applicable elsewhere, being situated within their respective inner rulers (*antaryāmin*); and because the statement "He remains like one indifferent" refers to his external form and thus involves no contradiction.

Even the word *ahaṃ* (I) employed by Indra [in the context of the *prāṇa* discussion] does not denote Viṣṇu as the inner controller of all—either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the word *ahaṃ* used by Vāmadeva in passages such as "I am Manu," or through primary denotation (*mukhyavṛtti*), as in the Smṛti passage "This one is I, you, and that one. Therefore, because the *prāṇa* has Viṣṇu as its ultimate referent, the *prāṇa* is indeed Viṣṇu.
As for the result, this constitutes the refutation and resolution of the objection that the *prāṇa* mentioned in the text "Therefore, the *prāṇa*" is not Viṣṇu. || 12 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the second quarter.

Thus, when it has been established through all the various indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the respective passages that all names contained within the infinite Vedas refer to Viṣṇu, the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of those indicative marks that appear to contradict this is now determined in this chapter (*pāda*). **Sūtra 1:** *Sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt* (Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere). 1. Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere.

|| Oṃ Because the qualities intended [to be attributed to Him] are possible, Oṃ. || Oṃ But because of impossibility, He is not the embodied soul, Oṃ. || Oṃ And because of the designation of action and agent, Oṃ. || Oṃ Because of the distinction of words, Oṃ. || Oṃ And because of Smṛti, Oṃ. || Oṃ If it be argued that He is not [the Supreme Self] because of His having a small abode and because of the designation of that [smallness], we say no, because He is to be meditated upon as such, and because He is like space, Oṃ. || Oṃ If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment [of pleasure and pain], we say no, because of the difference in nature, Oṃ. ||

In these two cases, there is no necessary requirement for a logical connection between the end of the preceding section and the beginning of the subsequent one. However, if such a connection is required, it is an *ākṣepikī* (introductory) connection, arising from the implication of what precedes. In the Aitareya [Āraṇyaka], in the section beginning with "Bādhva says there are four persons," starting with the opening "Of this very one, that [sun] is the chest," and continuing with "For they indeed meditate upon him in the great hymn (*uktha*) by means of the Ṛgveda," etc., after discussing the *uktha*, fire, the *mahāvrata*, earth, sky, wind, space, herbs, trees, moon, and stars, it concludes with "In all beings, they call him alone 'Brahman,'" and so forth.

A certain being residing in all beings is brought forward. Regarding him, there arises a doubt as to whether he is the individual soul (jīva) of the sun, or Viṣṇu, since he is heard of everywhere. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Because of the reference by the word "this" (*etam*) to that very one previously mentioned several times by the term "sun," and because of the statement of the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in his being the essence—having referred to the aforementioned year by the words "of this" (*tasyaitasya*) and then calling it "the essence" (*rasa*)—he refers to the sun; furthermore, because of the citation of the solar mantra, "Citraṃ devānām," and because of the mark that "this" (*etam*) is not specifically stated to be in the sun [but rather in all beings].

[The opponent argues: "It is Āditya alone who is all-pervading. This is because [the text] will later describe him as consisting of the eye, consisting of the ear, and so forth; because there are signs of the individual soul (jīva), such as its connection with the well-known eyes and other organs; because the force of employing the word "beings" (*bhūteṣu*) in the phrase "in these beings" implies his absence elsewhere than in the elements; and because there is the sign of having a small abode (*alpa-oka-stva*). Furthermore, the demonstrative pronoun *etat* ("this") is seen in various places to refer back to what is yet to be described. Thus, it refers to all individual souls (*jīva*), and not to Viṣṇu, because the aforementioned scriptural citations and signs are inapplicable to him.

It would follow [from your position] that because [the individual soul] is identical with all beings, it would experience the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing therein. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since the word *brahman* is well-known in such passages as "They call this very one Brahman" and "That alone is the supreme Brahman of the seers," it refers to Viṣṇu. Because the primary meaning of the word *brahman*—Viṣṇu—is distinct from the secondary meanings such as "caste" (*jāti*), the restrictive particle "this very one" (*etameva*) is appropriately applied. By the force of that restriction, the primary meaning alone must be understood here by the word *brahman*.

This is because of the existence of the marks such as being entirely unheard and so forth, which are stated in the subsequent passage beginning with "He who is ungrasped, unheard, unthought," and because there is supporting evidence from the scriptural designation (samākhyā) in the Smṛti: "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling within the heart of all beings."

Because the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) in passages such as "Prajāpati is indeed the year" refers to Viriñca (Brahmā), and because by the principle of internal guidance (*antarnayanyāya*), the scriptural mention of the Sun is understood as having him as its essence; and because, due to his omnipresence, it is logical for Viṣṇu to abide even in a small place—just as the sky does—the quality of having a "small abode" (*alpaukastva*) is consistent with Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the word "beings" (*bhūta*) is intended for the purpose of such meditation, and since the objection regarding the attainment of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-prāpti*) can be easily resolved through the distinction of specific capacities, the statement "among beings" (*bhūteṣu*) also establishes that [the Lord] resides within the sun.

Since there is no contradiction—given that the nature of being "consisting of the eye" (*cakṣurmaya*) and so forth can also exist in the sense of being the master of the eye and other organs—and since there is no contradiction in the opposing view regarding the all-pervasiveness of either the atomic individual soul (*jīva*) or the sun, Viṣṇu alone is the one referred to everywhere, including in earth and other elements.

The result [of this discussion] is as follows: by the use of the restrictive particle *eva* (only), it is shown that this very [light] consisting of Āditya and so forth is the one [perceived] among the elements (*bhūta*), and not anything else. Thus, there arises an objection to the previous position—that the all-pervasiveness known as "pervasion" (*vyāptatva*), described in the scriptural determination of the prior method in the passage "he saw Brahman spread out"—is untenable because Viṣṇu is perceived as existing elsewhere than among the elements; this constitutes the objection and its subsequent resolution. || 1 ||
Oṃ. The Self [is the cause], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving; Oṃ. 2.
Oṃ, and because of the context, Oṃ.

Here, the connection [of the topic] is by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises due to a discrepancy with the preceding [section]. In the third chapter of the Vājasaneyi [Saṃhitā], it is revealed in scripture: "Whatever he created, he resolved to eat that; indeed, he eats everything—therefore, that is the nature of Aditi. Regarding this, there is a doubt as to whether the eater (*attṛ*) obtained through the statement "he eats everything" is the goddess-mother Aditi or Viṣṇu. The initial position (*prāpta*) is that it must be Aditi alone, because of the scriptural passage beginning with "that is the nature of Aditi" and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being Aditi.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [This is because] the word *savitṛ*, which is a synonym for the word *āditya* and is heard in the scriptural passage under consideration in the *Antaradhikaraṇa*, establishes that it refers to Viṣṇu; whereas although the word *āditya* referred to Viṣṇu in the preceding section, here that is not established, and thus the scriptural statement (*śruti*) lacks any other scope. Or, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—consisting of the nature of being an "eater"—is incompatible with Viṣṇu, who is "non-eating" according to the scriptural text "not eating" (*anaśnan*), both are without scope. Alternatively, even if the scriptural statement has scope by virtue of the logic of the *Antaradhikaraṇa*, it is supported by the indicative mark, which is itself without scope. This is the final position.
