Since the quality of being the "consumer of all" (sarvāttṛtva)—defined as the power of reabsorption, expressed in the phrase "he eats everything"—is established as residing in Viṣṇu alone by such scriptural and traditional texts as "Into whom the world enters at the time of death" and "The creator, the protector, and likewise the consumer," and since the characteristic mark of being Aditi (adititva) and the direct mention of "Aditi" have their scope restricted to Viṣṇu, and furthermore, because the context of Brahman in the passage "In the beginning there was nothing here; this was indeed enveloped by Death" leaves no room for any other, Viṣṇu alone is the "consumer."

The scriptural reference to non-eating will be explained later. However, regarding the fruit [of the definition], since the proponent (siddhāntin) must state either that Aditi’s status as a "limited all-devourer" is established by the force of scripture and indicative marks (*śruti-liṅga*) while Viṣṇu’s is his being the "devourer of all others," resulting in over-extension (*ativyāpti*), or that Aditi alone possesses unlimited all-devouring power, there arises an objection to the *Janmādi-sūtra* and its subsequent resolution. || 2 ||
Oṃ. For the two selves have entered the cave, because of the vision of that [Self]. Oṃ. 3.
|| Oṃ, and because of the qualification, oṃ.

The connection here arises either from the contemplation of the specific nature of being an enjoyer—previously mentioned as the state of being the experiencer of the fruits of karma—or from the emergence of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by way of challenging what was stated before. In the third chapter of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, regarding the scriptural statement, "Two drinking the *ṛta*, having entered the cave in the world of good deeds," there is a doubt concerning the phrase "the two drinking the *ṛta*" and so forth: are they the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), or are they two specific forms of the Lord?

Regarding the phrase "the two drinking," since the dual number heard in the text denotes duality, and since that [duality] is impossible in the case of non-difference, and because the status of being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma is also impossible for one who is free from the bondage of karma; and since, by the logic of the "man with the umbrella" (where the term applies to the whole group), they must be of the same class—namely, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as enjoyers—this being the position reached, we reply: Because the mark of residing in the cave, expressed by the words "having entered the cave," is well-known to belong to Viṣṇu alone through such passages as, "He who knows Him hidden in the cave," and "The ancient one, hidden in the cave, dwelling in the deep."

"That which is the bridge for those performing sacrifices, the imperishable Brahman, the supreme"—this refers to the Brahman characterized by the attribute of supremacy, as heard in the subsequent passage: "the fearless shore for those desiring to cross over. This is established both by the word "Brahman" joined with the qualification of "supremacy" in that subsequent sentence, and by the marks (liṅgas) such as being a "bridge" and "fearlessness," which are confirmed by other scriptural passages such as "This is the bridge, the support."

Because of such Smṛti passages as, "The Self and the Inner Self—Hari alone exists in two forms," the existence of duality is established even for that which is one, through a distinction of form. Furthermore, because the possibility of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action exists—as seen in texts such as, "That Hari eternally drinks what is auspicious; He would never drink what is inauspicious"—the scriptural statement regarding His non-eating is appropriately explained as meaning simply the absence of enjoying what is inauspicious. Thus, the two who drink the *ṛta* are indeed two specific forms of the Lord. As for the result [of this interpretation], however, the refutation and resolution of the objection raised against His being the consumer of all (in the previous section) apply here. The manner of that is stated in the *Candrikā*. **Sūtra 4:** *oṃ antara upapatteḥ oṃ* || 4 || [This concludes the commentary on the sūtra.]

|| Oṃ, and because of the designation of place and so forth, Oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of the mention of a specific bliss, Oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of the mention of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads, Oṃ. || Oṃ, it is not the other, because of non-abiding and impossibility, Oṃ. ||

The connection here arises from the objection raised previously: if the one who is fearless and situated within the eye were different [from the Self], then even the one previously described as fearless would have to be something else. In the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the scripture states: "This person who is seen within the eye—He said, 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the Self situated within the eye is Agni or Viṣṇu. The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is Agni.

"I am that person who is in the sun; I am indeed he"—this statement, made by the fire known as the Gārhapatya regarding its own self's residence in the sun, is due to the fact that the sun and the eye share a single deity, according to such scriptural texts as "The sun, having become the eye... Furthermore, this is because of the abundance of Vedic references to Agni, such as "Then the fires deliberated together. Nor can it be argued that, based on the force of designations such as "He who is here in the person and he who is yonder in the sun, he is one," the word "I" used here refers to Viṣṇu residing in Agni rather than to Agni itself.

It must be stated: [the opponent argues that] through the practice of "I am he" and "I am indeed he," there is a sublation of the conventional designation; and by the force of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "We eat him who performs the expiation for evil deeds," there is also a sublation of the principle of "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) when taking Viṣṇu—who is entirely beyond the world—as the referent. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because immortality and other qualities mentioned in the passage beginning with "This is the immortal" are incompatible with fire, which possesses death and other such attributes—as seen in passages such as "Lightning, rain, the moon, the sun, and fire perish" and "Out of fear of Him, fire burns. Thus, fire cannot be the referent.

Because the words *brahman* and *ātman* have no application to anyone other than Viṣṇu; because of the indicative marks such as the "state of being well-loved" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) and the "attainment of non-attachment" (*asaṅgatvāpādakatva*) mentioned in the passage, "Whatever [liquid], whether clarified butter or water, one pours into this [eye], it goes only to the eyelashes"; because of the context of Brahman established by the statement, "Brahman is Kaṃ, Brahman is Khaṃ"; and because there is no possibility of breaking the context, given that the attainment of Brahman—an indicative mark—is heard in the concluding summary, "He leads them to Brahman," for those who possess this knowledge; and because the word *aham* (I) is employed by Agni... [text continues].

By the principle of the "life-force at the end of the feet" (*pādāntyaprāṇanaya*), since both the repetition (*abhyāsa*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) are also directed toward that [Inner Controller], and because if even Agni were a living being, there would result the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in requiring another inner impelling life-force, Viṣṇu alone is independent and resides in the eye. As for the result: if this one residing in the eye were other than Viṣṇu, then since he himself resides in the sun, even that which was stated as "He who is in the sun" would be that same [other being]; thus, the objection that the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is also something else is raised and resolved. || 4 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord is] the Inner Ruler with respect to the deities and so forth, because His attributes are designated [in those contexts]. Oṃ. 5.
"Oṃ, and it is not the Smārta [doctrine], because there is a description of qualities other than those; Oṃ, and it is the embodied soul, for both [recensions] indeed teach it as distinct."

Here, the connection is by way of an objection (*ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ*), as it is introduced by means of the term "immortality" (*amṛtatva*). In the fifth chapter of the *Vājasaneyi*, it is heard: "This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Regarding this Inner Controller, there arises a doubt: is he either Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) or the individual soul (*jīva*), or is he Viṣṇu? One previous position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) holds that it is Primordial Matter. This is because the state of having the earth and so forth as one's body—as heard in the passage beginning with "He whose body is the earth"—is possible in the case of Primordial Matter, which is the material cause of all things.

The term *śarīra* (body) can also denote the essential nature (*svarūpa*), as seen in such expressions as "the body of the prima facie argument" (*pūrvapakṣasya śarīram*). Furthermore, by such statements as "the cause is pervaded within its effects," it is established that the cause resides within the effect; thus, passages such as "He who dwells in the earth" are also logically consistent. Since cause and effect stand in a relationship of identity through their being both distinct and non-distinct, there is no contradiction between the cause and its residing within [the effect]. Moreover, because the effect is dependent upon the cause, passages such as "He who controls the earth from within" are justified in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).

Alternatively, others hold that it is the individual souls (jīvas) who identify with earth and the other elements who are the respective internal rulers (antaryāmīs), because for those [souls], earth and the rest constitute their gross bodies. Thus, since only primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth are "immortal" in this context, the immortality mentioned by the ancients does not prove that the one situated in the eye is Viṣṇu. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

The attributes mentioned in the passage beginning with "He whom the earth does not know, who from within controls the earth," namely, being unknown by the deities of the earth and so forth, and being internal in the sense of sporting without dependence on anything external, belong exclusively to Viṣṇu according to such scriptural texts as "O Viṣṇu, no one born [knows you]" and "He who is unheard, ungone, unthought, unseen, the inner Person of all beings. Otherwise, since the earth and other elements are insentient (*jaḍa*), the denial of their knowing Him would be redundant; furthermore, the word "whom" (*yam*) would be rendered meaningless.

The term *śarīra* (body) is either derived through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "that which perishes" (*śīryate*), or it is applied figuratively (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) because it is subject to the control of the Lord like a body; for otherwise, passages such as "He who is in the earth" would be difficult to reconcile. Furthermore, since Prakṛti and the individual soul (*jīva*) lack the unique attributes of being composed of the three qualities (*triguṇatva*) and being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), and because there is a designation of difference from the individual soul in the passage, "He who is within the Self, more internal than consciousness, distinct [from it]," the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is indeed Viṣṇu alone, and immortality belongs to him alone. As for the result, however, the resolution of the previous objection applies. || 5 ||
|| Oṃ. [The Brahman] possesses qualities such as invisibility, because of the declaration of its attributes. Oṃ. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ, and because of the distinction and the designation of attributes, it is neither of the other two; oṃ. Oṃ, and because of the presentation of form; oṃ.

The connection here arises from the objection raised against the previously mentioned reason called "invisibility" (adṛśyatva), as stated in the passage, "that which the earth does not know. In the *Atharvaṇa*, beginning with "Two sciences are to be known," and continuing with "Now the higher [science], by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained—[that which is] invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste," and so forth—the doubt is as follows: Is this "Imperishable" (akṣara)—which is heard in scripture as the cause of the universe since "from the Imperishable, this entire world arises," and which possesses qualities such as invisibility—is some form of non-sentient primordial matter (prakṛti), or Brahmā (Viriñci), or Rudra, or rather Viṣṇu?

One prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the source] is insentient primordial matter (*jaḍa-prakṛti*). This is because, by the force of the scriptural illustration "as herbs on the earth," there is no contradiction; and since it is improper to abandon an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the source—consisting in the status of being the material cause as heard in the text "from the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt*)—points to this. Another view is that it is sentient primordial matter (*cit-prakṛti*), because the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) is used in the sense of the Śrī-tattva in the Smṛti passage "The Immutable is called the Imperishable," and because its status as a material cause is possible through its presiding over the material cause.

Regarding the opening statement, "He [taught] the knowledge of Brahman," some hold that the one referred to is Caturmukha (Brahmā) because of the word "Brahman"; others hold it is Rudra because of the hearing of the word "Īśa" (Lord) later on in the phrase "Which of these two is the Lord? Furthermore, words such as "Akṣara" (the Imperishable) do not have their scope restricted to Viṣṇu; for since the Akṣara mentioned in the passage "Higher than the high Imperishable" is designated as the limit of excellence, it follows that this Akṣara is of inferior status and thus cannot be Viṣṇu. For this very reason, the ablative case in the phrase "born from the Akṣara" indicates merely the state of being the cause.

This has been answered: in the view that the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is consciousness, the two ablative cases in the phrase "beyond the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ*) are justified through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); whereas in other positions, they are justified through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because of the attributes belonging to Him—namely, being the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) consisting of the *Ṛg*-veda and so forth, which resides exclusively in Viṣṇu—as evidenced by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Hari is to be known," and "That is knowledge, that is the thought, by which [He is known]"; and because of the presentation of His form in the passage, "When the seer sees the golden-colored one."

Because of scriptural passages such as, "He mixed the mixed [elements] of others," which indicates that the pure form is established solely within that [mixed form] due to its nature as being mixed; because the mention of the syllable as the ultimate limit is not sublated by its being other than Viṣṇu, in accordance with the Smṛti stating, "The three syllables have been declared"; because it is possible for the series beginning with earth and ending with the seen to have as its purport merely the causality [of the syllable]; and because words such as "Brahmā" and "Īśa" have their primary application (mukhyatva) to Viṣṇu alone.

In the case of the insentient (jaḍa), the specific qualification of being "all-knowing" as stated [in the scripture] is inapplicable. Furthermore, because of the designation of Brahman and Rudra as distinct from the Imperishable (akṣara) in the passages, "From that this Brahman, name, form, and food are born," and "When he sees the other, the Lord who is to be enjoyed," the Imperishable—characterized by qualities such as invisibility and declared in scripture to be higher than the high—is indeed Viṣṇu alone. As for the result, however, there is the introduction and its resolution regarding the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) who is endowed with qualities such as invisibility. 6.
Oṃ. Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction in the common term. Oṃ. 7.

"Oṃ. [The opponent argues: 'That which is being remembered must be an inference. Oṃ. [The Sūtra replies: 'Oṃ. It is not so, because of the teaching of its abiding within [the heart] in relation to sound and other [objects]; because such a thing is impossible; and because they study it as being human-like. Oṃ. Oṃ. For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. Oṃ. Jaimini holds that there is no contradiction even with respect to direct perception. Oṃ. Āśmarathya says it is due to manifestation. Oṃ. Bādari says it is due to remembrance. Oṃ. Jaimini says it is due to attainment, for the scripture shows it thus. Oṃ.
And they designate him as "Oṃ" in this [context]. Oṃ.

Here, the connection [of the topic] arises from the implication of omnipresence, which is heard in the middle [of the passage], among the qualities such as being invisible from the front (*prācīnādṛśyatva*) and so forth. In the *Chāndogya*, in the fifth chapter, it says: "One meditates on the Vaiśvānara Self as the immeasurable" (*abhivimānamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaramupāste*); and in the *Vājasaneyi*, in the seventh chapter, in the context of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is that which is within man, by whom this food is digested"; likewise, there is the Vaiśvānara occurring in the *Sūkta*: "The Vaiśvānara, the immortal Agni born of truth" (*vaiśvānaramṛta ājātamagnim*), and so on. Is this Vaiśvānara the physical element (*bhūta*) or its presiding deity (*tadabhimānidevatā*)?

There is a doubt as to whether [the Vaiśvānara] is Viṣṇu or not. For words such as Vaiśvānara and Agni are well-known in common usage as referring specifically to the fire; and because in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad there is heard the scriptural indication (*liṅga*) of being the locus for oblations and having the Gārhapatya and other fires as limbs—as in "In Vaiśvānara that [offering] is placed" and "The heart is the Gārhapatya"—as well as the quality of being a cooker and so forth mentioned in the Kāṇva recension of the Śruti. And if these were to apply primarily to Viṣṇu, there would be a contradiction with worldly convention.

Furthermore, because all knowledge would then result in being Vaiṣṇava, it would be impossible to establish distinctions such as "this is the Agni-knowledge" or "this is another knowledge. Vaiśvānara is either an element or a deity. Nor should one suspect that there is no definitive conclusion that he is simply Agni, on the grounds that the opponent's indications (liṅga), names (samākhyā), and context (prakaraṇa) are more numerous or lack any other scope.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is as follows: Since scripture (*śruti*) is inherently authoritative, even by that much, if the Vaiśvānara who is described as "all-pervading" by the term *abhivimāna*—meaning one whose measure (*māna*) or limit (*maryādā*) has departed on all sides—is not definitively established, then it would be impossible to reach the conclusion desired by the proponent (*siddhāntin*), namely that the previously mentioned all-pervading Imperishable (*akṣara*) is indeed Viṣṇu. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because of the scriptural use of the word "Self" (*ātman*); because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of omnipresence expressed by the term "immeasurable" (*abhivimāna*); because of the traditional designation (*samākhyāna*) in the Smṛti, "I, having become Vaiśvānara"; because this knowledge is studied within the context of Brahman, following the introductory inquiry, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?";

and because of the traditional designation of the Puruṣasūkta, since the text here—by stating "The head itself is the brilliant one" (*mūrdhaiva sutejāḥ*)—implicitly refers to the very limbs such as the head that produce the dualities mentioned in the Puruṣasūkta (e.g., "From his head the sky arose"), and thus there exists evidence that leaves no room for any other interpretation.

Because terms such as *vaiśvānara* and signs such as fire (*agni*) have scope in the Lord (*īśa*) for the purpose of such meditations, and because even those words primarily denoting Viṣṇu must—due to having no other possible referent—be applied elsewhere to establish the conventional usage of "abandonment" (*hāna*) and so forth which depends upon words; and because the systematic arrangement of the various meditations is logically consistent, since through the meditations on fire and so forth, Viṣṇu is manifested within fire and the like, and thus He is to be recollected and attained therein.

Because there is no subverting evidence, Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu; thus, according to the ancient [view], he is that very same [Viṣṇu]. As for the result, however, there are the refutation and its resolution as previously stated. || 7 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the third quarter.

Having thus previously explained the application of all names and marks well-known elsewhere according to the maxim of the breaking of a great wrestler, the application of names and marks well-known in both [the Vedas and other systems] is now undertaken here.
**Oṃ. The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. Oṃ.** (1.3.1)

|| Oṃ, because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated; oṃ. || Oṃ, it is not inference, because of the word "not-that"; oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of the vital breath; oṃ. || Oṃ, because of the designation of difference; oṃ. || Oṃ, because of the context; oṃ. || Oṃ, because of abiding and eating; oṃ. ||

We have already stated that, according to the previous [sūtra], there is no necessary dependence on the context. In the Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad] it is heard: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all vital breaths—know him alone as the one Self. Regarding this abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, there arises a doubt: Is it Viṣṇu, or is it Rudra and the like? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is Rudra, or Pradhāna, or Vāyu, or the individual soul (jīva).

"Rudra indeed is the support of the worlds"; "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me, O Rudra, the destroyer"; "Rudra is the lord of the vital breaths, clad in skins, the wielder of the Pināka bow"; "That which is above the sky, Gārgī, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two—the heaven and the earth—and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—all this is woven to and fro in space alone"; "By the thread of air, O Gautama, indeed, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together."

Because [the word *rudra*] is designated in relation to the three [worlds] in their respective order; and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the state of being born, as in the passage: "He moves within, being born in many ways. Furthermore, although there is the designation of Viṣṇu in the sense that "both the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are woven upon Viṣṇu alone," the designation of Rudra is more powerful due to its being endowed with numerous scriptural texts and indicative marks concerning Rudra. Moreover, the designation of Viṣṇu is sublated by the indicative mark of being born, which has no other possible application.

Nor should it be argued that the mark of Viṣṇu—consisting in being the object of the higher knowledge (paravidyā) as stated in the text, "Now, the other [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained"—is likewise without scope. For, in this way, there could be non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara) without contradicting either [text], since, according to the reasoning previously stated, the mark of Viṣṇu [could apply] to the individual soul, just as the mark of the individual soul [could apply] to Viṣṇu. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows:

Because of the word *ātman* in the phrase "the Self," because of the mark of Viṣṇu in the form of the impossibility of being reached by the liberated in the phrase "this is the bridge to immortality," and because of the absence of words such as "wearing ashes" or "fierce" which are unique to Rudra and others; because the words "Rudra" and so forth occurring in the *Samākhyā* (traditional designation) are shown to belong to Viṣṇu by the Smṛti passage beginning with "because he melts away (*drāvayate*) affliction (*ruj*)," and because even the quality of being "born" belongs to Viṣṇu—on the strength of another Śruti stating "He is unborn, yet He is born in many ways"—since birth can be understood here as a manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).

It should be understood that there are two kinds of knowledge (*vidyā*). Since the subject under discussion is the Supreme Lord (*Īśa*) as the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), and because He is designated as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) in the passage, "When he sees another, the Lord," and because their identity is untenable given the statement of their distinction—namely, that one of them eats the sweet fruit while the other looks on without eating (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)—it follows that Viṣṇu alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

As for the result [of this argument], if the abode of heaven, earth, etc., were something other than Brahman, then the Imperishable (*Akṣara*) characterized by invisibility and other qualities would also be something else; thus, the objection and its resolution are established. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The Self] is the Infinite (bhūman), because it is taught as being superior to the state of serene bliss (samprasāda). Oṃ. 1.
|| Oṃ, and because of the logical consistency with the Dharma, oṃ. ||

"He alone is below, He alone is above; He is behind, He is in front; He is to the south, He is to the north; He alone is all this. "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). "Venerable sir, on what is that Infinite established? "On its own greatness."

The connection [of this section] arises because the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is raised by way of an objection based on the fact that attributes such as omnipresence—heard in the passage beginning with "He alone is below, He is above," etc.—are also heard in the Chāndogya regarding the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, in the passage beginning with "Brahman alone is this immortal one in front; Brahman behind; Brahman to the south," etc. In the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, which is suitable for the inquiry, there is a doubt as to whether the "Plenum" (bhūman) heard in the text, "Verily, what is the Plenum, that is bliss," is the chief vital breath (prāṇa) or Viṣṇu. The prima facie view is that the Plenum is the vital breath.

Having stated, preceded by questions and answers, that name, speech, mind, volition, thought, meditation, consciousness, power, water, fire, ether, memory, hope, and breath each possess a progressively greater degree of excellence, there is no [subsequent] question—such as "Is there something greater than breath?"—nor is there a reply such as "The Plenum (bhūman) is indeed greater than breath. Since the Plenum is therefore distinct from breath, and because the designation "Viṣṇu is indeed greater than the gods" is weaker than the introductory statement "Breath is indeed greater than hope," [the former cannot override the latter].

Because that [interpretation] is sublated. For the mark of departure mentioned in the word "of those whose vital breath has departed" (utkrāntaprāṇān) is incompatible with Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent; and by the principle "Therefore [he is] Prāṇa," the scriptural mention of "Prāṇa" is also incompatible with the view that it refers to the ether of Viṣṇu. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

Because the state of possessing perfect bliss—expressed by the word *sukha* without any qualifying prefix—is declared to be the most supreme among all things such as names; because the attributes such as omnipresence, stated in passages like "He alone is below," are established as residing solely in Brahman according to scriptures such as "The source of universal bliss, beyond all"; and because even the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of Viṣṇu will be mentioned later, making it logical for him to possess the action of departing [from the body].

Prāṇa and Bhūman are indeed Viṣṇu alone; whether by identifying Prāṇa and Bhūman as non-different, or—despite Prāṇa being Vāyu—by distinguishing it from him through the supply of words [from the context] in the question and answer, Bhūman is indeed Viṣṇu. As for the result, the resolution of the objection regarding the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is presented by way of the previously mentioned state of full bliss, which is "happiness. || 2 ||
Oṃ. [Brahman is] the Imperishable, because it supports that which extends to the ends of space. Oṃ. (Sūtra 3)
Oṃ, and that [is so] because of the command; Oṃ; and because of the exclusion of other states; Oṃ.

In the preceding section, the contradiction between omnipresence and departure—both situated within the same context—was resolved; here, however, the contradiction between atomicity and magnitude, which reside within a single statement, is being resolved. This constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*). In the *Aṣyama Brāhmaṇa* of the fifth chapter of the Kāṇva recension, it is heard in the passage beginning, "The Brahmins indeed call this Imperishable (*akṣara*) by the name 'Gāgi'—neither gross, nor atomic, nor short," and so on. Regarding this *akṣara*, there arises a doubt: is it primordial matter (*prakṛti*) or Viṣṇu?

Since the word *akṣara* is used in such passages as "the imperishable which is indefinable" (*yakṣaramanirdeśyam*) with reference to the Śrī-tattva (the principle of Śrī), because the ground for its usage—namely, the state of being indestructible—is present there; and since the support of the moon and other bodies, which is heard in another Vedic text as a quality of the Śrī-tattva in the passage "I bear the Soma of the sacrifice" (*ahaṃ somamāhanasaṃ bibharmi*), is heard here [in the Upaniṣad] in the words "the sun and the moon stand supported by it" (*sūryācandramasau vidhṛtau tiṣṭhataḥ*); and since qualities such as invisibility, mentioned in the passage "invisible, yet seeing" (*adṛśyaṃ draṣṭṛśrutam*), are possible even in the Śrī-tattva according to the Smṛti passage beginning with "ye tvakṣaram" (*ye tvakṣaram...*), it does not eat that.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) is indeed the material nature (*citprakṛti*). For the term "something" (*kiñcana*), which denotes non-eating (*anaśana*), cannot apply to Viṣṇu, who is described as the "Self" (*ātman*) by virtue of being the eater. Furthermore, by the mention of "something," according to the logic of the "cave" (*guhā*), it is also inappropriate for it to refer to the non-eating of the inauspicious. And in the case of the Śrī-tattva (the Goddess Lakṣmī), its status is established by the absence of independent eating and so forth. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Having stated that space itself is woven like warp and woof in that which is called the primordial nature (prakṛti)—which is designated as "that which was, that which is, and that which will be"—the text says, "In this Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, space is woven like warp and woof. This establishes its status as the support of all. Furthermore, because the sign of universal sovereignty—described in the passage beginning with "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī," which possesses excellence in the form of unconditioned jurisdiction and independence—is of unrestricted scope; and because the absence of natural grossness and other qualities, independent of anything else, is described in the passage beginning with "Neither gross nor subtle"; [this Imperishable is established as the Supreme Brahman].

Or rather, because [the term] is a mark (*liṅga*) of qualities such as minuteness and greatness, which are the opposites of grossness and so forth—since [these qualities] reside in Viṣṇu alone according to such scriptural passages as, "He alone supported the seven worlds," "The womb of the world," "The seed of the world," and "They abide in the directions," as well as "Neither gross, nor minute, nor middle-sized, but the middle-sized, the pervasive, and the non-pervasive"; and because the term *akṣara* (the Imperishable) applies to Viṣṇu alone—who is devoid of the fourfold destruction according to the scripture, "Impermanence, loss of the body," etc.—due to the fullness of the grounds for its application; therefore, it is the Imperishable.

Therefore, because of the application of the term "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*), Viṣṇu alone is the Imperishable. As for the scriptural statement regarding non-eating, it is intended to prohibit eating for the sake of subsistence on the elements that constitute the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, qualities such as minuteness and greatness are appropriate because He possesses inconceivable power. Thus, while being the support of all, the fact that He is not supported by anything else serves as a distinguishing mark; one should meditate here that the "Space" mentioned in the Śruti is the Principle of Śrī. Regarding the result, if the Imperishable endowed with invisibility and other attributes were something other than Viṣṇu, then the aforementioned Imperishable would also be so; this constitutes the objection and its resolution according to the method of "Invisibility. (Sūtra 3)
|| Oṃ. He [is Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. Oṃ. || 4 ||

In this context, the connection [of the present discussion] arises from the following objection: since the word *sat* (Being) in the phrase "All this, indeed, was Being alone" (*sadeva*) refers to something other [than Brahman], the status of being the support of all things—stated in the passage "the six abodes" (*sadāyatanāḥ*)—must also reside in that other thing; consequently, the previously mentioned "supporting of everything up to the sky" (*ambarāntadhṛti*) must also belong to that very same thing. In the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagre*), and continuing with "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" a doubt arises as to whether the referent of the term *sat*, which is described as the cause and so forth, is Brahman or rather the *pradhāna* (primordial matter). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the *pradhāna*.

Because of the scriptural hearing of becoming manifold through fire and so forth in the passage, "May I be many," this [desire] is connected only with *pradhāna*, which undergoes transformation. It cannot belong to the Lord, who is changeless, as stated in such scriptural passages as, "He is changeless, imperishable, and pure. Nor should it be argued that what is stated here is merely a multiplicity of His own nature, rather than a multiplicity by way of fire and so forth; for that would contradict the complementary statement, "He created fire. Indeed, it is not logical to effect the creation of fire and other elements after first resolving upon a mere multiplicity of one's own essential nature.

The "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) of the Pradhāna is either secondary—due to its association with the quality of Sattva which is a cause of knowledge, or due to its orientation toward activity, or because the Abhimānin [the ego-principle] acts as the seer. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is this: since it is stated that "It saw," and since the primary sense of seeing is possible, it is improper to accept a secondary sense.

According to the principle of metaphorical attribution (*abhimāninaya*), it is impossible for the primary cause (*pradhāna*) to become manifold through the nature of deities such as Fire (*tejas*) and so forth; furthermore, since becoming manifold in one's essential nature (*svarūpa*) depends upon the creation of those things to be governed (*niyamya*), even if there were an intention to become manifold in essence, the creation of the governed entities like Fire would still be required. This is because, even for a single Lord, multiplicity is possible according to the principle of metaphorical attribution (*guhānayanyāya*), and birth is possible according to the principle stated regarding heaven, earth, and so forth (*dyubhvādinoktanyāya*).

By the mark (liṅga) of being the primary observer and by [the attributes of] being the cause and so forth, that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) is indeed Brahman. However, regarding the result [of the inquiry], there is an objection to the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (janmādi-sūtra) along with its resolution, following the direction stated in the *Candrikā*: since the restrictive particle "only" (eva) in the phrase "Being alone" (sadeva) leads to the perception of Pradhāna itself as the cause, and since that [primacy] is absent in the case of Īśvara, and so forth. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ, [the Self] is the small one, on account of the subsequent [scriptural passages]; Oṃ. || 5 ||

Oṃ. [The Lord is the cause] because of movement and the word [denoting Him]; for thus is the mark seen. Oṃ. And because of the support of this great earth; for He is perceived here. Oṃ. And because of common renown. Oṃ. If it be argued that "He" refers to another on account of subsequent reference, we say no, because of impossibility. Oṃ. If it be argued that it is from what follows, [we reply] that His nature is indeed manifested. Oṃ. And the subsequent reference is for another purpose. Oṃ. If it be argued that this is due to the mention of smallness, that has already been answered. Oṃ.

In this regard, since the passage beginning with "Both heaven and earth in Him" declares that the one residing in the heart-lotus is the substratum of all, there arises a prima facie objection (pūrvapakṣa) based on the challenge: "If He were other than Viṣṇu, then even though it was stated [in the previous section] that 'these creatures have their eternal abode' and so forth, He would nonetheless be something else. This constitutes the connection (saṅgati).

In the first section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "That which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, and within that [palace] is the small ether; that which is within that [ether] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. If they should say to him: "Since this is the small lotus-palace within this city of Brahman, and since there is the small ether within it, what is there that is to be sought, or what indeed is to be desired to be understood? he should reply:

Regarding the doubt as to whether that which resides within the heart-lotus—heard in such passages as, "As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it"—is the element *ākāśa*, the individual soul (*jīva*), or Viṣṇu: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is indeed the element *ākāśa* and not Brahman, because the word *ākāśa*, well-known in its primary sense as the sky, is used here for that which resides within the heart-lotus.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the hearing of the characteristic mark (liṅga) known as being the support of all, this [space] denotes Brahman according to the maxim "Space [denotes Brahman] because of its characteristic mark"; for there is a contradiction with the designation [of the passage], since another Śruti—beginning with "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud"—states that "within it is a subtle cavity, and in that everything is established," thus attributing both the location within the heart-lotus and the status of being the support of all to space itself (the term *suṣira*). Furthermore, if space itself were Brahman, it would be illogical to speak of something residing within it as being the object of search.

Nor can it be argued that, although space is well-known as such, Brahman resides within it and thus exists in the heart-lotus through a traditional succession; for this would be inconsistent with the connection of the sentence. When the question "What is found here? is asked, one should simply say "Brahman is found"; therefore, the statement regarding the equality of the internal heart-space with external space—beginning with "As large as..."—would otherwise be irrelevant. Furthermore, since this would contradict the scriptural mention of a cavity (*suṣira*), it is impossible to maintain the consistency of that passage by asserting that the space described as the support of all in the phrase "as large as... is Brahman itself.

Since it is more logical to state that "both [heaven and earth] are in this" (ubhe 'smin) and so forth—thereby specifying the previously mentioned *dahara-ākāśa* as being equal to the external ether and asserting that heaven, earth, and so on exist within it—it is appropriate that heaven, earth, and the rest reside inside the ether. Therefore, another [teacher] maintains that the ether directly situated within the heart-lotus is what is meant.

Because the word "Self" (ātman) is used in the supplementary passage, "The Self which resides in the small ether is free from evil," and because in the subsequent sentence, "This is its Self," the term "this" (eṣa)—referring back to the individual soul (jīva) introduced by the word "serenity" (samprasāda)—is employed in the masculine gender to designate that [small ether] as the Self, it follows that the passage refers to the individual soul. Furthermore, the characteristic mark of residing within the small ether cannot apply to Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent.

Furthermore, because the part [of Brahman] is complete, even if it were to occupy a small space due to its partiality, it would be impossible for that part of Brahman to be accommodated like the ether on account of its fullness; thus, the application of the passage beginning with "as large as" (*yāvānvā*) is common to both [the individual soul and] the Brahman position. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: by virtue of being situated within the *dahara-ākāśa* (the small ether) located in the heart, it is indeed Brahman itself that resides in the lotus of the heart.

Because of the marks such as being "free from evil" (apahatapāpmatva), "free from old age," "free from death," and "free from sorrow" heard in the subsequent sentence regarding that Self, and because those marks—such as "He has risen above all evils" and "He who eats hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death"—reside in Viṣṇu alone.

Likewise, [the passage] "Day after day they go to this world of Brahman (brahmaloka), yet they do not find it" indicates that it is reached during deep sleep; and because in the statement "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being," that [Being] is heard as an attribute of Brahman according to the logic of the section on "seeing" (īkṣati-nyāya). Furthermore, by the use of the term "world of Brahman" (brahmaloka) for the world of Brahman situated within the heart-lotus, or because Brahman itself is denoted by the word "world" due to its being the support of all, the word "Brahman" is explicitly heard [in the text].

Likewise, because the term *brahmaloka*—which is applied in the passage, "Ara and Ṇya are indeed the two Aṇarvans in the Brahmaloka," to the world that rests upon the nectar-ocean known as Araṇya—is used here for the heart-lotus, there is the hearing of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) indicating that [the heart-lotus] possesses a world resting upon a nectar-ocean. And since that [world] is a quality of Viṣṇu, according to the scriptural text cited in the Commentary: "Ara and Ṇya are indeed the two nectar-oceans," and so forth.

Likewise, [it refers to Viṣṇu] because of the mark (*liṅga*) of being the support of all, heard in the text: "This Self is that bridge, the sustainer, for the non-confusion of these worlds," which concerns that which resides in the heart-lotus; and because that [support-ness] has been determined to be an attribute of Viṣṇu in the *Akṣarādinaya* [section]. Furthermore, it is so because of the designation in the Kāṇva recension of the Śruti: "He who lies within the space (ākāśa) inside the heart, the controller of all," and because that [text] is Vaiṣṇava, since its description of the lordship over all and so forth constitutes the majesty of Viṣṇu.

Likewise, [the passage]—"The small, sinless lotus of the heart, which has become the abode of another, situated in the middle of the city; even there, the small ether, free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon"—is established as referring to Viṣṇu by the well-known designation of the *Taittirīya* [Upaniṣad]. Furthermore, because of the absence of any evidence for [these qualities] residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) or others, attributes such as being "freed from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) cannot possibly belong to them independently, given such statements as: "Others cross over hunger and so forth through His grace."

Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "He moves about there," the possession of true desires and other qualities is predicated of the liberated one alone; moreover, it is impossible for that [liberated state] to reside within the heart-lotus. This is because the word "this" (*eṣa*)—used in the masculine gender in reference to the subject to be enjoined—refers back to the Supreme Light introduced earlier, and since that very Brahman in the form of light is to be determined as Brahman in the statement "Om, the Self, from the context, Om," the injunction here is that this Self resides in the heart-lotus.

Since the principle that He has a small abode everywhere has already been established even in the case of Viṣṇu—because it is logically consistent for one who is full through His inconceivable power (*acintya-śakti*) and so forth to have a small abode—the question "What is there? arises from the thought: "Now that Brahmanhood has been established for the space situated within [the heart] by describing the body and the lotus as the city and the house of Brahman, what kind of thing is that? In response to this question, it is stated that within that heart of Brahman, there exists all this external space, and within it, heaven, earth, and so forth.

Thus, because the statement "as far as space, etc. and so forth is logically consistent with the context of [the Lord] being the support of all, and because the scriptural mention of the "cavity" (suṣira) is justified by the intention that the Lord residing within the cavity is the support of everything—just as a string of jewels is contained within a temple—and because there is no subverting evidence; the result [of this discussion] is the introduction of the doubt regarding the Akṣara (the Imperishable) as the substratum, by way of [showing that] the moon and other things have Him as their support, and its subsequent resolution. || 5 ||
|| Oṃ, and because of its imitation of that [the world], Oṃ. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ, it is also recorded in the Smṛti, Oṃ. ||

In the preceding case, although the word *eṣaḥ* (this) refers to Brahman denoted by the word "light," the masculine gender is appropriate with respect to the Self (*ātman*) which is the object to be enjoined. Here, however, since both words *tat* and *etat* refer to the previously mentioned Lord, the neuter gender would be inappropriate; thus, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt based on its dissimilarity to the previous case.

In the *Kāṭhaka*, it is heard: "Regarding this, they think: 'The supreme bliss is indefinable; how indeed may I know it? Does it shine forth, or does it not shine forth? There arises a doubt as to whether the state of being grasped with favor—the form of being prayed for for the sake of knowledge—belongs to the bliss of the knower (*jñānin*) or to Viṣṇu. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): [it belongs to the knower].

Regarding the phrase “I may know that,” the word *tat* (that) refers back to the bliss mentioned in the first half-verse. Furthermore, because that [bliss] is the bliss of the wise—evidenced by the reference in the preceding verse, “For those wise ones who perceive Him abiding in themselves, theirs is eternal bliss, and not for others,” as indicated by the force of the pronoun *tat* referring to the bliss of the wise already under discussion, and by the word *sukha* (bliss) which serves as a marker of recognition—it possesses the nature of the bliss of the wise. Although the Lord is the subject under discussion in the passage beginning with “The one controller,” there is an intervention [by other topics], and moreover, it is impossible for both [the Lord and the bliss] to be neuter.

Regarding the phrase "of the bliss of the Knower" (*jñānisukhasyaiva*): the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows. Based on the scriptural indicators (*liṅga*) found in such passages as "The sun does not shine there," "Everything shines only after Him who shines," and "By His light all this is illumined"—which respectively indicate that [the object] is not illuminated by the sun and others, is the cause of the illumination of the sun and others, and is the illuminator of the entire universe—these qualities reside exclusively in the Lord (*īśa*), as confirmed by statements such as "The sun does not illuminate That," "I am the radiance and the rays," and "The splendor that resides in the sun."

Since the natural force of the word *tatra* and so forth points back to the immediately preceding phrase “may I know that,” even though the pronoun *tadetad* refers to the Lord (*Īśvara*), one may interpret it favorably as: “How indeed may I know that supreme, indescribable bliss?”—meaning they pray for the sake of knowing it. Thus, when the construction is made such that “that indescribable bliss is this very form of the Self under discussion,” the neuter gender of the words *tat* and *etat* is also justified.

The phrase "the conscious among the conscious" refers to the Lord alone, as He is the subject under discussion due to His proximity. Furthermore, the introduction of the method of the "Unseen" (adṛśyatvanaya) and its resolution are presented by way of the invisibility mentioned in the passage beginning with "But the fruit is indescribable. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ, [the Lord] is known from the word alone, oṃ || 7 ||
Oṃ. But with respect to the heart, [the qualification applies] because the human race has the capacity for it. Oṃ.

In this context, the connection [of the present topic] arises from an objection: since the statement "the Viśvedevas worship [Him]" implies that He is the object of worship, liberation necessarily follows from the knowledge of Him; this, in turn, raises an objection against the claim—stated in the passage "those who perceive Him dwelling within themselves"—that liberation results from the knowledge of Viṣṇu alone. In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, it is stated: "The Person, the size of a thumb, dwells in the middle of the self, the Lord of what has been and what is to be. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Īśāna the primary vital air (Vāyu), or is he Viṣṇu? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is Vāyu.

"Drawing the *prāṇa* upward, he casts the *apāna* downward; the All-Gods (*viśvedevāḥ*) worship him as the dwarf seated in the middle. Because of this scriptural statement, [the Self] is heard to be the regulator of the *prāṇa* and other vital breaths, the one situated in the middle, and the object of worship for all the gods. Furthermore, these attributes are found in the third chapter of the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad]: "In this very way, this *prāṇa* establishes the other *prāṇas*, each separately," and in the fourth chapter of the Vājasaneyi: "This indeed is the child, which is this..."

In the *Śiśubrāhmaṇa*, it is stated: "The middle breath (*madhyamaḥ prāṇaḥ*). Furthermore, from Vedic passages such as "kuvidaṅga namasā," it is understood that [the size] is a property of Vāyu. Moreover, although atomicity (*aṇutva*) is mentioned in the *Akṣaranaya* section regarding Viṣṇu, the measurement of being "only the size of a thumb" heard here cannot apply to Him, because that [atomicity] signifies a lack of any dimension greater than that. Nor can it be justified with reference to the heart, as it cannot withstand logical scrutiny; for if it were merely measured by some thumb or another, there would be no definitive determination, which would render the teaching useless due to the impossibility of its being an object of meditation.

[The opponent argues: "Because the measurement by the thumb of such [beings] as animals and the like is absent, that which resides within them cannot logically be that [Brahman]. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: The term "Vāmana" is established as referring exclusively to Viṣṇu, because of the Vedic revelation of Vāmana—"This one indeed is Vāmani; for he leads all desirable things (*vāmāni*)"—and because of other Śrutis and Smṛtis such as "Upendra, Vāmana, the tall one. Furthermore, according to the maxim that "a word modified in one part remains as if not modified," and through the well-known usage of the learned, the term is established by both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Since it has no application elsewhere, it refers only to Viṣṇu.

Because the quality of being the controller of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is appropriately applied to Hari, the controller of all, according to the logic of the Antaryāmin-Brāhmaṇa; and because another Śruti specifically declares its Vaiṣṇava nature in the passage, "He who leads the nine gods by means of the prāṇas"; and because the term "in the middle" (madhye), through its association with the word "above" (ūrdhva), denotes the middle region, and thus—given the absence of any mention of a "middle person"—its application to Viṣṇu as residing in the middle region is also logical; and because the quality of being worshipped by all the gods is synonymous with being the object of meditation for all beings, which has been established for Him in the Dahara-adhikaraṇa.

Thus, because [the Smṛti] is subject to contradiction by a direct Vedic statement (śruti) that is inherently stronger—being itself devoid of scope while the other is self-evidently powerful—the "thumb-sized" nature is justified either as referring to a specific individual form of that particular thumb, or as a figurative designation (upacāra) applied to the Lord who resides in the heart (the locus) based on the person occupying that place. Furthermore, there is no fault in the scripture, since it has humans as its primary authority even though other living beings possess thumbs. Therefore, this Īśāna is indeed Viṣṇu. The result [of this discussion], however, is the refutation and subsequent resolution of the objection raised against the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* regarding the status of the object of meditation. || 7 ||
Oṃ. Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that] even above that [the world of Brahmā], [liberation is possible], because it is possible. Oṃ. (2.3.8)

Oṃ. If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [bodies]. Oṃ. If it be argued that [the world] originates from the Word (Śabda), we say no, because its origin is from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference. Oṃ. And for this very reason, [the Veda] possesses eternity. Oṃ. And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as shown by scripture and tradition. Oṃ. Jaimini holds that there is no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations [for gods]. Oṃ. And because they exist in the light [of the sun]. Oṃ. But Bādarāyaṇa maintains their existence, for it is indeed so. Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: since it was stated previously that the qualification for dharma pertains to humans, this is now addressed to show that gods and others certainly possess such qualification, even when compared to animals and the like. Regarding the doubt—based on the scriptural statement, "The Viśvedevas worship"—as to whether or not the gods mentioned as worshippers have the qualification for practices such as meditation: the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is that they do not.

If the various deities distinguished by their respective offices were subject to birth and destruction, then—since deities such as Indra would be non-existent both prior to and subsequent to the attainment of the office of Indra and so forth—there would follow the contradiction of ritual acts such as sacrifices consisting of the relinquishment of substances intended for those deities, as well as the invalidation of the eternal Veda which makes known those various deities.

Even if one accepts that they are beginninglessly eternal as a continuous stream by virtue of Indra and others being successively assumed [as their presiding deities], there is no evidence for them having a single name and form; rather, because they possess various names and forms, the lack of authority of the Vedas—which teach a single form—is not avoided. Furthermore, even if such beginningless eternity must necessarily be accepted, those [beings] would lack any desire for liberation as its fruit.

Furthermore, because they lack the qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations that have the status of becoming a Vasu (*vasutva*) as their fruit—since Vasus and others do not possess the qualification for all meditations—and because even regarding those meditations whose fruit is liberation, it is said, "Those devoid of the vision of Brahman have not attained the divine state," and so forth, they lack the qualification for the sake of the knowledge that causes liberation, as their knowledge is already established. As for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Because the gods possess superior intellect and other such qualities, because they are not excluded [from Vedic study] like Śūdras, and because the desire for liberation—the ultimate reality—is possible even for them; and furthermore, although they are subject to birth and destruction, this is established by scriptural statements such as, "Those glorious ones attained the heavenly world where the ancient Sādhyas and gods abide," "The Creator fashioned [the world] as before," and "Just as there is a fixed order in time, so too is the order of the gods and others," as well as by the fact that the authoritative Veda itself cannot otherwise be explained if it were not beginningless and eternal.

Because they are eternal by way of their continuous flow (*pravāha*), and because of the Śruti passage "as before" (*yathāpūrva*) and the Smṛti passage beginning with "without beginning or end" (*anādinidhana*), there is no loss of the authority of the Veda due to the identity of names and forms. Furthermore, although the Madhu-vidyā and others result in fruits such as becoming a Vasu, there is still eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman, because a desire for excellence in the knowledge and liberation of the Vasus and others is possible therein. As for the result, the lack of authority and its resolution regarding the previously mentioned statement "the Viśvedevas worship [it]" are as follows: **Oṃ. The Śūdra is not eligible, because of the hearing of that [word] in disregard, and because of his running toward it; for it is indicated.** (Sūtra 9) The word "Śūdra" here refers to a person of a particular caste, not to one who merely utters the word "śudra. This is because the context concerns the eligibility for Vedic knowledge, and the word "Śūdra" is used in the sense of a specific varṇa. In the story of Jānaśruti, when he heard the word "Śūdra" from the disciples, he was told, "We are attendants of King Janaka, a Śūdra. Since the word "Śūdra" was uttered in disregard of him, and since he subsequently ran toward the presence of the disciples, it is indicated that he was indeed a Śūdra by birth. Therefore, a Śūdra is not eligible for Vedic knowledge. However, this does not contradict the Smṛti which says, "One should teach the three twice-born castes," for that refers to the eligibility of those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*). Moreover, the fact that the Śūdra was excluded from the sacrificial session (*sattra*) is also indicative of his lack of eligibility. This does not, however, contradict the Smṛti rule, "One should teach the three twice-born castes," as that pertains to the eligibility of those who have received initiation (*upanayana*). Furthermore, the Śūdra's exclusion from the sacrificial session (*sattra*) also serves as an indicator of his lack of eligibility. Thus, the conclusion is that a Śūdra is not qualified for the knowledge of Brahman. *Note: The concluding sentence regarding the "fruit" refers to the discussion on the result of the meditation, specifically the scriptural passage "The Viśvedevas worship it," along with the arguments regarding its authority and resolution.* *Note: The final segment of the text is a gloss on the Sūtra, detailing the grounds for the Śūdra's disqualification.* **Oṃ. The Śūdra is not eligible, because of the hearing of that [word] in disregard, and because of his running toward it; for it is indicated.** (Sūtra 9) The word "Śūdra" here signifies a specific caste, not one who merely utters the word "śudra. This is because the context concerns eligibility for Vedic knowledge, and the term "Śūdra" is used in the sense of a particular varṇa. In the account of Jānaśruti, when he heard the word "Śūdra" from the disciples, he was told, "We are the servants of King Janaka, a Śūdra. Since the word "Śūdra" was uttered in disregard of him, and since he subsequently ran toward the disciples, it is indicated that he was a Śūdra by birth. Therefore, a Śūdra is not eligible for Vedic knowledge. This does not, however, contradict the Smṛti which states, "One should teach the three twice-born castes," for that refers to the eligibility of those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*). Moreover, the exclusion of the Śūdra from the sacrificial session (*sattra*) is also indicative of his lack of eligibility. Thus, the conclusion is that a Śūdra is not qualified for the knowledge of Brahman. *Note: The phrase "phalaṃ tu viśvedevā upāsata ityādeḥ" refers to the discussion on the fruit of the meditation, specifically the passage "The Viśvedevas worship [it]," and the subsequent arguments

|| Oṃ, and because of the understanding of his being a Kṣatriya, and because of the indicative mark [found] later with reference to Caitraratha; || Oṃ, because of the reference to the sacraments and because of the statement of their absence; || Oṃ, and because of the engagement [in study] once that absence has been determined; || Oṃ, because of the prohibition against hearing and studying [the Veda], and because of the Smṛti. ||

In this context, the connection is one of exception (*āpavādikī saṅgati*), because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds according to the logic of the previously established conclusion. The doubt is whether or not there is eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) for the *śūdra* and others. The prima facie view is that, because he possesses specific intellect and other such faculties, the *śūdra* also has eligibility for Vedic knowledge, just like the gods and others.

Furthermore, since the injunction for study—"One should initiate him; one should teach him"—is prescribed specifically for the initiated, and since the Śūdra, being uninitiated, is devoid of the right to study, [the term] "one who possesses mere study" (in the third book) refers only to such a person. Moreover, by the address "O Śūdra, you are indeed a Hārita" directed at Pautrāyaṇa—where Raikva is addressed with the word "Śūdra" despite his superior status—and by the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting of Vidura and others' comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas, there must be either initiation and study, or [at least] the capacity for them, even in the case of a Śūdra.

[The opponent’s view is that] there can be acquisition of knowledge of the meaning either through study by one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), or through looking at written texts and so forth by one who does not study, because such knowledge is merely a mental construction. But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Just as the quality of possessing a chariot is mentioned in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*)—"This is a mule-chariot"—and according to the Smṛti, "Where the Veda is, there is a chariot; where there is no chariot, there is no Veda," the chariot is pervaded by the Veda. Since that [chariot] is absent in a Śūdra due to the absence of the Veda, and since it is natural for a Kṣatriya, [the Śūdra lacks the capacity].

Since the status of Pautrāyaṇa as a Kṣatriya is established by that subverting evidence, the conventional meaning of the word "Śūdra" must be abandoned; furthermore, because the subsequent portion of the text mentions his running toward the sage due to the grief born from the swan's disregard—thereby supporting the etymological derivation of "Śūdra" as "one who ran (dru) out of grief (śuca)"—it does not prove that a Śūdra has the qualification [for Vedic study]; thus, there is no qualification for a Śūdra.

Since study depends upon the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and since for a *śūdra* there is an absence of the initiation sacrament according to the Vedic scripture stating, "For a *śūdra*, there is no fire, no sacrifice, and no vows," [the teacher] first ascertained Satyakāma’s non-śūdra status by saying, "Therefore, you are fit to speak of your lineage," and only then performed his initiation.

Because Gautama’s [rule] is operative, it serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of that very nature: "Upon hearing [the Veda], one's ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac; upon reciting it, the tongue is to be cut off; and upon determining its meaning, the heart is to be torn out. Since for a Śūdra, hearing the Veda and so forth are prohibited, he lacks the qualification—which consists in being unprohibited—despite possessing specific intellect and other faculties. Furthermore, it is impossible to determine the meaning even by looking at a written text.

Furthermore, because Vidura and others possessed knowledge produced from previous births, they were distinct from other Śūdras; thus, there is no eligibility for Śūdras regarding Vedic knowledge. As for the result, if one were to argue that a Śūdra has eligibility—just as gods and others do—by the principle of possessing a distinguished intellect and so forth, this would lead to a contradiction with scriptural texts that prohibit such eligibility. Consequently, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position holds that the general statement regarding the human eligibility of the scripture is contradicted by authoritative evidence. In the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, there is no contradiction, because the general statement refers to those other than Śūdras. Om. On account of action, Om. 10.

In this context, there is a connection as a counter-example arising from the doubt that the word *vajra* does not denote Viṣṇu through its etymological function (*yogavṛtti*), because—as in the previous case with the word *śūdra*—no established etymological derivation is found for it within the remainder of the sentence. A doubt arises in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Whatever exists here in this entire world, having issued forth, vibrates by means of Prāṇa; a great terror, a raised thunderbolt (*vajra*). Those who know this become immortal. Is the *vajra* mentioned here the weapon of Indra, or is it Viṣṇu? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the weapon of Indra.

Because the word *vajra* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that [Indra] context; because, as in the previous case, there is no established etymological derivation (*yoga*) for Viṣṇu in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*); and because the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "it is called *vajra* because of its warding off" is weaker than the direct scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the *vajra*.

Furthermore, if one were to abandon the established conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and accept Viṣṇu on the basis of etymological derivation (*yogikatayā*), then since such a derivation could easily be asserted for other meanings as well, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of no fixed relationship between word and meaning. Moreover, there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being "upraised" (*udyatatva*); and since this term is well-known in the sense of a weapon in Smṛti texts such as "those with upraised arms bearing weapons" (*udyatāyudhadordaṇḍāḥ*) and in Śruti texts such as "with that Indra raised the thunderbolt" (*tenendro vajramudayacchat*), the indicative marks and the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) override the marks of Brahman, such as being the cause of liberation through knowledge. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: [the term refers to Indra].

The entire world vibrates by means of *prāṇa*—that is, it trembles with *prāṇa* as its cause. Since the quality of being the impeller of all movement belongs to Viṣṇu alone, as established by such scriptural and traditional texts as "For who indeed could breathe, who could live? (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.4.1), this term has no application to anyone other than Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the scriptural mention of the *vajra* (thunderbolt) finds its scope in Viṣṇu because of its non-literal application to others as stated in Smṛti—which serves to corroborate the Śruti—and because of its usage in the statement, "Of weapons, I am the *vajra*" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 10.28). Since the Smṛti is the author of that etymological application (*yoga*), the fault of lack of restriction does not arise.

And since the word *udyata*—which has the *liṅga* (indicative mark) of being preceded by the prefix *ut*—can denote Viṣṇu as well, insofar as its form signifies "one who possesses exalted effort," [the prima facie view is] that "this *vajra* is indeed Viṣṇu. The purpose [of this discussion], however, is the implication that Viṣṇu is the cause of liberation through knowledge, and the resolution thereof. || 10 ||
|| Oṃ, because of the vision of light, oṃ || 11 ||

Here, as in the previous case, because the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds by abandoning the well-known meaning of the word "light" (*jyotis*)—established in scripture as "Viṣṇu alone is the light"—due to an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that leaves no room for other interpretations, the connection (*saṅgati*) is one of exception (*āpavādikī*). In the sixth chapter of the Kāṇva recension of the Śruti, there is the doubt regarding the "light" mentioned in the passage, "This one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart": is it the individual soul (*jīva*) or Brahman? The prima facie view is that it is the individual soul.

"Being the same [in both states], he wanders through both worlds. "This person, when being born, entering into a body, becomes united with evils; when departing, dying, he leaves the evils behind"—because there is an abundance of characteristics of the individual soul (jīva), such as wandering through worlds dependent upon karma.

Furthermore, in response to the question, "What is the light of this person? the text states, "By the light of the sun alone he sits," and so forth, thereby describing how the sun, moon, fire, speech, and the self each serve as the cause of knowledge for the one following them upon the setting of the preceding one. Then, in response to the question, "Which is the self?", it is said, "This which [is perceived] here. Since that which was described as having the nature of the lights of the sun and others is shown by such passages as "The sun does not shine there" to be incapable of being Viṣṇu, it necessarily follows that it must be the individual soul (jīva).

If the term "Self" were taken to refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman), then because the nature of being the light of the Self—which is devoid of setting and so forth—belongs to the individual soul (jīva) at all times, the restrictive particle "only" in passages such as "by the light of the sun alone" would be inappropriate. This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Because the scripture states, "Viṣṇu alone is light; Viṣṇu alone is Brahman," the word *jyotis* (light) refers exclusively to Viṣṇu. Since this term is heard in the opening, "The light within the heart," and in the conclusion, "In this regard, this person is self-luminous (*svayaṃ jyotiḥ*"), the entire passage is determined to refer to Viṣṇu by virtue of being situated between these two. Consequently, the marks belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) found therein are accommodated as referring to Hari, by interpreting them as having an implied causative sense (*antarṇīta-ṇyartha*). Furthermore, the movement through the two worlds is possible only for the Lord acting independently, taking the individual soul along with Him.

Even though the Lord, denoted by the word "Self," is light, the restriction "by the sun alone" is appropriate for the purpose of making known the predominance of external light for the individual soul (jīva); thus, this light is indeed manifold. As for the result, however, there is the introduction of the Sūtra "The Light has feet" (*jyotiścaraṇa*) by way of its being placed within the heart, as well as its resolution. || 11 ||
Oṃ. Space [is distinct from Brahman], because it is designated as being something other than that, and so forth. Oṃ. 12.

In this context, because immortality—which was heard in reference to the previously mentioned light in the passage, "Having moved about outside the nest as immortality"—is here heard in reference to the ether in the statement, "That is immortality," and because that [ether] is different [from the previous light], there is an "implied" connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) since the previously mentioned [light] is also implied by the mention of the sun. In the *Chāndogya*, in the final section, regarding the ether heard in the passage, "Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman, that is immortality," there arises the doubt: is this the well-known unevolved ether (*avyākṛtākāśa*), or is it Brahman?

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: because the two particles *vai* and *nāma* have well-known meanings, and because in the case of the passage "Ākāśa, indeed, is called..."—wherein there is a connection with the subject as "Ākāśa is indeed well-known"—or in the case of the connection with the predicate as "the sustainer of name and form," it is well-known that Ākāśa is the sustainer of name and form; furthermore, since in common worldly usage only space (*avakāśa*) is known to be the sustainer of name and form by providing them room through its own nature, whereas the Lord (*īśa*) is not so known.

"This space is indeed the ether (ākāśa)"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: In the statement "that which is between those two," since that which exists apart from name and form has been described as being entirely within the scope of words and so forth, its nature as a name is thus explained; furthermore, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of being devoid of both manifest and unmanifest forms is established by such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as "from which words turn back" and "formless and touchless," as well as by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as "He is nameless because He is not well-known" and "He is formless because He is devoid of the elements. Since these attributes belong exclusively to Viṣṇu, [the ether is He].

This ether is indeed Viṣṇu alone; for there is evidence from the word *brahman* in the phrase "That is Brahman," and from the indicative mark of immortality in the phrase "That is immortal. Furthermore, the two particles used in their well-known senses—such as in the Śruti text "He said, 'It is Ākāśa'"—are well-established in referring to Viṣṇu both by his essential nature, as in the Śruti "One [Lord] supported all the worlds," and as the sustainer of names and forms. Since Vedic usage is internal and must be accepted within the Veda, it cannot be sublated; thus, this Ākāśa is Viṣṇu.

The result [of this section], however, is the refutation of the *dyubhvādi-nyāya* (the principle of heaven, earth, etc. by way of establishing the Brahman’s status as the substratum of all—which is characterized by being the bearer of name-and-form—and its subsequent reconciliation. Although it was stated in the sūtra *talliṅgāt* that the conventional worldly usage [of the word "name"] must be abandoned due to an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that leaves no room for another interpretation, this section is commenced again because of a specific doubt arising from the two words "vai" and "nāma. || 12 ||
|| Oṃ. On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure, Oṃ. || 13 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from a doubt based on the difference from the preceding case: either because, although the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) could refer to the Lord (*Īśa*) there due to its well-known Vedic usage, such a possibility is absent here; or because, while the ether—being insentient—cannot be associated with the marks of the Lord (*īśaliṅga*) as being distinct from Him, it might be possible here to interpret those marks as belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) as distinct from the Lord; thus, the doubt arises through a contrast with the previous instance.

In the *Kaṇva-śruti*, in the eighth chapter, there occurs the following: "Having rejoiced and wandered about in this state of serene repose (*samprasāda*), and having seen both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he hastens back again according to his method and according to his source, to his own nature alone. Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it, for this person (*puruṣa*) is unattached. Regarding this passage from the *Śruti* which mentions "his own nature" and so forth, a doubt arises as to whether it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Lord (*īśvara*).

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is the individual soul (*jīva*), because in the world, the status of being the "seer from time immemorial" (*svanādi-draṣṭṛtva*) is well-known to belong only to the living soul.
