This is because, even in the absence of Vedic renown, worldly renown is to be accepted within the Veda; furthermore, since the Lord is bodiless, He cannot logically possess the status of being a "seer from time immemorial. Moreover, the mark of Brahman consisting of "detachment" (*asaṅgatva*) is compatible with the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*) as well, through its non-difference from the Lord. However, the attribute of the individual soul—namely, being a "seer from time immemorial"—is incompatible with the pure consciousness of Brahman.

Furthermore, since the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) has been stated in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, the proponent (*siddhāntin*) would be unable to assert that the attributes [of the soul] belong to the Lord if he intended their non-difference. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because the quality of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*), mentioned in the scripture "for this [Self] is unattached" (*asaṅgo hyayam*), is a unique attribute of the Lord alone—as seen in passages such as "unattached and intangible" (*asaṅgam asparśam*); because dream-objects and the like are real according to the principle to be stated later in the sūtra "He declares the creation in the intermediate state to be real" (*sandhye sṛṣṭim āha hi*); and because the Lord is omniscient according to the scripture "He who is all-knowing" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*), it is possible for the Lord to be the primary knower of dream-objects and the like in their entirety.

Because of the mention of difference in the two contexts of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and departure (*utkrānti*)—namely, "embraced by the intelligent Self" (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*) and "mounted upon the intelligent Self" (*prājñenātmanā anvārūḍhaḥ*)—it is impossible that the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) is not heard [in scripture]. Furthermore, since in the Sūtra "In deep sleep and in attaining [the state of] union" (*svāpyayasampattyoḥ*), the context of deep sleep is stated to refer even to liberation (*mukti*), difference exists as something pertaining to liberation and is therefore real. Thus, the objection regarding the lack of connection with the quality of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*) raised against the statement in the section on the Imperishable (*akṣaranaya*) that Viṣṇu alone is the object of the word "Self" (*sva*), and its resolution, [are explained here]. 13.
Oṃ. [The Lord is Brahman] because of such words as "Lord" and so forth. Oṃ. 14.

In this context, the introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) arises from the doubt that the "unattached one" (*asaṅga*) mentioned in the verse "the unattached does not cling" might be someone other than the Lord; therefore, the question is raised: "Is he indeed the same as the previous one? In the sixth chapter of the Kāṇva recension of the Śruti, there is a doubt regarding the "Brāhmaṇa" heard in the passage: "This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa"—is this Brāhmaṇa Viriñca (Brahmā) or the Lord (Īśa)? The prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that this Brāhmaṇa is indeed Viriñca.

Regarding the phrase "This indeed is that great unborn Self" (*sa vā eṣa mahān aja ātmā*): although the word *aja* (unborn) can apply to Viriñca (Brahmā) through its etymological derivation (*yoga*)—as he is born from the Lord who is denoted by the letter 'A'—and through its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and although it could also apply to the Lord (Viṣṇu) through the etymology "born from the Lord" (*īśena jāyate*) and the conventional usage found in the *Mahābhārata* statement "Therefore I am remembered as the Unborn," nevertheless, because [the term] has no application to Viṣṇu who is devoid of caste, and because it occurs in conjunction with the word *brāhmaṇa* which is conventionally established for the Brahmin caste, this [term *aja*] leads exclusively to Viriñca. Furthermore, the word *mahat* (great) refers to the presiding deity of the principle of *mahat* (*mahattattva*) according to the logic of the "presiding deity" (*abhimāninayanyāya*).

Viriñca alone [is the referent] because of his being joined [with these attributes], and because the term *ātman* also applies to him; for it is stated that "the self is Viriñca, the benevolent one," and since the usage "the Great Self is higher than the intellect" establishes that the word is conventionally rooted (*rūḍha*) in Viriñca. As for the marks of Brahman mentioned in the passage beginning with "the controller of all," they are compatible with Viriñca through non-difference from Īśvara, by setting aside both [conflicting claims], just as in the previous prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is because a single coherent syntactical unity is possible through non-difference, as in the passage: "The names Hari, Viriñca, and Hara are used for the purposes of maintenance and so forth."

Furthermore, it is impossible to assume that the passage intends both [meanings] simultaneously due to the resulting split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because the marks such as "mastery over all" mentioned in passages like "the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all," are Viṣṇu's alone—based on scriptural texts such as "the lord of immortality" and "the seven half-embryos"—[the term *akṣara* refers to him].

Because the term *brāhmaṇa* has scope through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "that which is reached or known by the *brahman*, i.e., the Veda," and because the scriptural statement regarding the Unborn (*aja-śruti*) likewise has scope, it is improper to accept non-difference by subverting both, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasañjaka*), and because it is contradicted by such statements as, "From Him these were born: the universe and Hiraṇyagarbha. Furthermore, since the Smṛti is consistent when understood in reference to the form of the Lord residing within each [individual], this Brāhmaṇa is indeed Viṣṇu himself.

However, the objection is that the fruit [of knowledge] intended for Viṣṇu in the sūtras concerning the desire to know and so forth—namely, His eternal majesty—is inappropriate; this is followed by its resolution. || 14 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fourth quarter (pāda).

Thus, having established in the first three quarters the coordination (*samanvaya*) of words found in scriptural passages that indicate other qualities—such as being the cause and being composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—which are connected to that [Brahman], here, for the sake of establishing the perfection of all attributes denoted by the term "Brahman," the coordination of those words consisting of names and marks (*liṅga*) that are well-known elsewhere is now stated, as their turn has arrived. **Sūtra 1:** *Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is inferential according to some, we say no; because [the Self] is apprehended as presented in the allegory of the body, and Scripture shows this.* *Oṃ.* 1. If it be argued that [the Self] is inferential according to some, we say no; because [the Self] is apprehended as presented in the allegory of the body, and Scripture shows this. *Oṃ.* The opponent argues: In the passage beginning with "Two birds...," the individual self (*jīva*) is understood from the context, while the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is merely inferred based on the mention of the Lord's qualities. Therefore, the term "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the individual self, not the Supreme Self. This is not so. The word "Self" here refers to the Supreme Self, because it is apprehended as the subject of the allegory of the body. Just as in the allegory of the chariot, the body is designated as the "chariot," so too here the body is designated as the "tree. The individual self is the "eater" (*bhoktṛ*), and the Supreme Self is the "Witness" (*sākṣin*). Furthermore, Scripture explicitly shows this distinction in passages such as: "The one who knows both these [souls] as seated in the same tree... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and "Two birds... are companions, inseparable friends" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6). Thus, the term "Self" denotes the Supreme Self. *Note: The provided text contains the opening of the fourth pāda of the Brahmasūtra, specifically Sūtra 1, which addresses the interpretation of the "Self" in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.*

|| Oṃ, but it is subtle because it is worthy of that; oṃ || || Oṃ, it is purposeful because it is dependent on that; oṃ || || Oṃ, and because there is no statement that it is an object of knowledge; oṃ || || Oṃ, if it is argued that [the text] says so, we say no, for it refers to the wise one; oṃ || || Oṃ, because of the context; oṃ || || Oṃ, and thus there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone; oṃ || || Oṃ, and as in the case of the "Great One" (mahat); oṃ || || Oṃ, like the cup, because there is no distinction; oṃ ||

In this context, the connection with the preceding section should be understood as arising from the following doubt: if the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and others—which denote the ultimate limit (*parāvadhi*) and the lowest state (*avaratva*)—were to refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), there would be a contradiction with the previously established status of being the Lord of all (*sarveśvaratva*). Regarding such passages as "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great One; the Person is beyond the Unmanifest," "But the living beings alone are subject to suffering," "Others enter [into] a womb," and "Those two are bound by cause and effect," the doubt arises whether the primary meaning of the terms heard—such as "the Unmanifest," "suffering," "bound," and "lower"—is the individual soul and so forth under discussion, or the Lord (*īśvara*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: Brahman is not indeed the source-nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth, because words such as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and others are well-known to refer to those [entities] alone; furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for their denoting Viṣṇu. Moreover, even if those words do not denote the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and so on, if they were applied to it, there would be no distinction, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all words could be used for everything, resulting in a lack of systematic order.

Furthermore, in the case of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), since it is implied as the limit superior (*parāvadhi*) by its connection with the fifth case-ending, it would entail a state of inferiority; moreover, qualities such as the soul’s (*jīva*) possession of knowledge and suffering are incompatible with Viṣṇu due to scriptural authorities such as, "No one is seen equal to you, nor anyone superior," and "He is without blemish, without fault," as well as due to the contradiction with the previously mentioned status of being the sovereign lord of all. Finally, there is the hearing of the term "Great" (*mahat*) in the Unmanifest in passages such as, "And the Pradhāna stands pervading the Great," which is determined to refer to the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) because it possesses the characteristics of that principle.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Because Viṣṇu is denotable by all words such as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and so forth, according to scriptural passages such as "All names enter into Him"; and because of Vedic and Smṛti usage such as "the unmanifest, immovable, and tranquil" and "by this living self"; and because the grounds for the application of terms like "unmanifest"—namely, subtlety, being the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so on—are primary in the Lord (*īśa*) according to texts such as "That which is subtle and supreme is to be known," these terms are primarily applied to Him.

Although the words *mahat* and *camasa* are well-known to denote the principle of *mahat-tattva* and sacrificial vessels respectively, just as the terms *Viṣṇu* and *head* are established as primary in such passages as "the great, all-pervading Self" (*mahāntaṃ vibhumātmānam*) and "this is that head; for this is the cup with its opening downward" (*idaṃ tacchiraḥ eṣa hyarvāgbilaścamasaḥ*) due to the predominance of their etymological grounds (*pravṛttinimitta*), so too, even though words such as *avyakta* are well-known elsewhere, they are appropriately understood as primary when applied to the Lord (*Īśa*).

"Know Him alone as the Self; abandon other words"—since this statement declares that the Lord alone is to be known by one seeking liberation, while no other is so declared, it follows that the Veda is directed toward the knowledge of the Lord alone. Furthermore, although inferiority, suffering, and the like do not apply to the Lord, they are nonetheless dependent upon Him; thus, on the ground of His sovereignty (*svātantrya*), it is logically consistent for the Lord to be designated by fifth-case forms expressing "limitation" (such as *parasmāt*) or by terms such as "suffering" (*duḥkhin*).

Furthermore, since even the state of being greater than the Great (mahat) is possible for Him who is beyond everything, Hari alone is the primary referent of words such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta). The result [of this discussion] is the refutation of the objection regarding the coordination of all words mentioned in the *Samanvaya* Sūtra, and its subsequent resolution. || 1 ||
|| Oṃ. But because it begins with light; for thus some [scriptures] record. Oṃ. || 2 ||
|| Oṃ, and because of the instruction regarding meditative construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth; oṃ.

In the preceding section, the consistency of terms such as "from the senses" (*indriyebhyaḥ*) and so forth—which denote established deities and their respective sequences—was explained. Here, however, that same consistency is stated for terms which denote rites to be performed (*sādhya-rūpa-karma*) and their sequences; this constitutes the connection with what preceded. Regarding the scriptural statement, "Every spring, one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," there arises a doubt: do the words "Jyotis" and so forth heard therein denote Viṣṇu, or do they denote other things such as ritual acts? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they denote ritual acts and the like, because those terms are well-known in the context of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others.

Furthermore, if one abandons the established usage and asserts that [the term *jyotis*] denotes Brahman, there would be a loss of the performance of the prescribed ritual, because there would be no other means to establish the ritual, its constituent parts, their sequence, the deities, the time, or the qualified performer. Moreover, it is untenable to claim that these terms function in the context of the ritual and so forth—just as they did previously—by virtue of their connection with the Lord (*īśa*) denoted by the word *jyotis*, since this would entail the necessity of resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for anything other than the Lord.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for these [words] and because the absence of conventional usage would entail the absence of the perfection of qualities (*guṇapūrti*), only *yoga* (etymological derivation) remains as the denotation; moreover, conventional usage regarding the object of action (*karman*) is more powerful than even that. Also, for the sake of establishing that [Brahman] is denotable by all words, if the constituent parts of words such as "light" (*jyotis*) were to refer to Brahman, it would be impossible for the whole [word] to refer to it, and thus *yoga* would be untenable. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): [it is as follows].

By stating, "They praised Him for a hundred years; therefore, they call Him 'the Hundred-versed One' (Śatarcin), though He is truly this [Viṣṇu]," and so forth, the text first establishes that certain terms such as "Śatarcin" refer to Viṣṇu through both *mahāyoga* (etymological derivation) and *vidvad-rūḍhi* (conventional usage among the learned). Finally, by declaring, "All these Ṛg-verses, all the Vedas, all sounds, are but one utterance—namely, Prāṇa [Viṣṇu]"—it affirms that the primary meaning of all words resides in Viṣṇu. Thus, even a term like "madhu" (honey), which commonly refers to honey or the like, [is shown to apply to Him].

Without abandoning conventional usage and without contradicting it—just as in passages such as "This sun is the honey of the gods," where words like *madhu* (honey) are stated with the sense of *mahāyoga* (great etymological derivation) for the purpose of meditation—there is no failure to establish the intended meaning because one accepts that terms such as *jyotis* (light) refer to the Lord through *mahāyoga* and other modes of derivation, while leaving intact their conventional usage elsewhere.

Having accepted that the individual components [of the compound] refer to something else, and having admitted that the whole refers to the Lord (Īśa), since the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is possible—namely, that Hari alone is the primary meaning of words such as "light" (*jyotis*) because the world, woven and stretched out, arises from that light—the result remains exactly as before. || 2 ||
Oṃ. [The Vaiśeṣika doctrine] is not [to be accepted], even because of the inclusion of the number [of categories], because of their diversity, and because of the excess [of categories]. Oṃ. 3.
|| Oṃ: Breath and the others [are the five], because of the remainder of the sentence. Oṃ. || Oṃ: For some, light [is the fifth], since food is not mentioned. Oṃ. ||

In the previous instance, it was stated that although the basis for the application of words such as *jyotis* (light) is not well-known [in its primary sense], that which is obtained through etymological derivation (*yoga*) exists there even if it is not commonly known. Here, however, it is stated that for the word *pañcajana* and others, that very meaning is indeed well-known in reference to the Lord; this constitutes the logical connection. In the sixth chapter of the Kāṇva recension of the Śruti: "The gods worship that light of lights, the immortal life; in which the five groups of five people and space are established."

The doubt arises as to whether the term "five people" (*pañcajana*) refers to the primary meaning of words such as "people" (*jana*) and so forth—referring to the one who, being wise and immortal, thinks of himself as the immortal Brahman according to the Śruti—"I am indeed that immortal Brahman"—or whether it refers to those things denoted by the words "prāṇa," "eye," "ear," "mind," and "speech" mentioned in the remainder of the passage in the genitive case, or rather to the specific forms indicated by those respective words in the accusative case. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the five people are none other than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest, because the word "people" denotes a plurality of distinct entities.

Furthermore, it is impossible for [the Self] to be the Lord (īśa) because that would contradict the statement "one only, without a second. Even in the case of a king who has brought many people under his control, we do not observe the use of plural terms [to refer to him]; thus, the principle of subordination (*tadadhīnatva*) does not apply here either. Although the general rule that "one cannot be many" might be set aside in the phrase "in the cave" (*guhām*) due to the contradiction posed by its being situated within a cave, there is no such contradiction here; therefore, that principle also finds no application. This is because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self" (*ātmā*) in the phrase "that very Self" (*tam evātmānam*).

[The opponent argues: Since that which is eternal is Brahman, it is illogical for the five classes of beings dependent upon it, as well as the ether, to be Brahman, because the relationship between a substratum and its superstratum cannot exist between two identical entities. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Because the supplementary passage—"the life-breath of the life-breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, the mind of the mind"—is heard in the genitive case, it contains marks of Viṣṇu such as being the controller of the life-breath and so forth; therefore, they are of the nature of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, these [beings] possess primacy both verbally and in meaning relative to the life-breath and others indicated by the genitive case.

Because of the previously stated reasons—such as being denotable by all words beginning with "tāvā etāḥ" (as in the passage "nāmāni sarvāṇi..."), and being knowable by those seeking liberation—even though [Brahman] is one, it possesses manifold forms; thus, by the power of specific distinctions that serve as substitutes for difference, there is the possibility of the relationship of container and contained between the nature of the body designated as "pañcajana" and so forth, and that which is indicated by the word "yasmin" (in whom). This is because the number five is possible through such a representation of differentiation.

Even though the form called "food" (anna) is not heard in the supplementary passage of the Kāṇva recension—as it is in the Mādhyandina recension—it is nonetheless fivefold when taken together with the previously mentioned light (jyotis). Therefore, the "five people" (pañcajanāḥ) in the supplementary passage are specifically the elements (bhūta-rūpa-viśeṣāḥ) denoted by the words "prāṇa" and so forth, which appear in the accusative case. In this section (pāda), the result is everywhere the same as before. || 3 ||
And [Brahman is the cause] because it is designated as such in the case of ether and the other elements, just as has been stated. Om. 4.

The connection [of this section] arises from the suspicion of a discrepancy with the previous [section], based on the objection that while a relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) is possible—as seen in such instances as "Time was always present" (*kālassadāsīt*)—a relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa-bhāva*) is never observed [between Time and Being], and is therefore untenable. In the *Taittirīya* Upaniṣad, within the *Brahmavallī*, regarding the passage beginning "From the Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced; from space, air," there arises a doubt: do the words "space" and so forth, which are heard as effects and causes, primarily denote Viṣṇu, or do they denote the elemental ether and so forth? As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Regarding the statement "it is not born, it does not die," and so forth: since Brahman is not an effect (*akārya*), the notion of being an effect is inherently contradictory; therefore, its own status as an effect is all the more impossible. Furthermore, even the relation of cause and effect in the form of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is contradictory in a single entity. Even though a son is dependent upon his father, the word "born" (*jāta*) is not observed to apply to him [in the sense of being produced], and thus the logic of dependence does not apply here. Moreover, because the Vedic text "all names... must necessarily be restricted in scope, and because it would otherwise result in the non-establishment of the birth of ether (*ākāśa*) and other elements, words such as "ether" denote something else entirely. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Since Viṣṇu alone possesses forms that act as the controllers of ether and the rest—as established by such scriptural texts as "He who dwells in the ether"—and since these forms residing in ether and so forth are manifold, there is the possibility of a relationship of cause and effect in the form of a manifestor and the manifested (*vyañjaka-vyaṅgya-bhāva*) during the production of air and the other elements, whether through the sequence of manifestation and non-manifestation or through the principle of priority and posteriority. Furthermore, because there is no subverting evidence, it is impossible to restrict the scriptural statement "names... and so forth; thus, the previously mentioned proofs remain valid.

Furthermore, since the conventional usage [of these terms] elsewhere has been accepted according to the method stated by Jyotir-nātha, and because there is no lack of proof for the origination of ether and the rest, Hari alone is the primary referent of words such as "ether" (ākāśa). || 4 ||
Oṃ, from complete attraction; oṃ. 5.

|| Oṃ, because of the designation of the world; oṃ. || Oṃ, if it be argued that this is due to the characteristics of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, that has already been explained; oṃ. || Oṃ, but Jaimini [holds it to be] for another purpose, on account of both the question and the answer, and likewise some [scriptural passages] also; oṃ. || Oṃ, because of the connection of the sentences; oṃ. || Oṃ, Āśmarathya [thinks it is] a sign of the fulfillment of the initial proposition; oṃ. || Oṃ, Auḍulomi [thinks it is] because of the state of one who is about to depart; oṃ. || Oṃ, Kāśakṛtsna [thinks it is] because of the abiding [of the Self]; oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: if it is admitted that words such as "space" (*ākāśa*) have conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) elsewhere as well, then their primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) would be equal for the Lord and elsewhere, just as in the case of words like "dice" (*akṣa*). The doubt is whether the primary status of all words for both the Lord and others is equal, or whether it is greater for the Lord and lesser elsewhere. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Just as words like "dice," which denote multiple meanings, have equal primary status in multiple places, so too all words should have equal primary status for the Lord and elsewhere.

Otherwise, there would be the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) of the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) applies only to inferiority elsewhere; for if primacy were restricted solely to the Lord due to its abundance therein, it would follow that the term is not well-known in the world at large. Furthermore, since the human goal is accomplished through the knowledge of the Lord alone, the usage of words toward ritual acts, deities, and so forth—which would have to be secondary functions—would result in futility for one seeking liberation who desires no other fruit. Moreover, it is not logical to claim that the abundance [of the quality] resides in those [other things] rather than in the Lord, because the cause of the word's function exists in other things as well.

Nor can it be argued that, according to the principle of dependence (*tadadhīnatva*), just as the dependence on the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived in the passage, "When the soul leaves one branch, then that branch withers," and the dependence on air is perceived in the passage, "For all worlds are led by air," both of these [the individual soul and air] would likewise have to be accepted as primary denotations (*mukhyavācyatva*) like the Lord (*īśvara*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

The primary denotation (*mukhyatā*) of words is indeed greater in Brahman than elsewhere; for while it may be inferior elsewhere—just as with conventional (*rūḍhi*) and etymological (*yoga*) meanings, or even with secondary (*gauṇa*) and indicative (*lakṣaṇā*) meanings—in the case of the Lord (*Īśa*), even where convention exists, there is a gradation possible between the conventions of the learned and the ignorant, and between ordinary etymology and great etymology (*mahāyoga*). Consequently, those [words] which reside in Viṣṇu by way of the supreme primary function (*paramamukhyavṛtti*) through both great etymology and the convention of the learned, are drawn away from other [objects] and employed in their primary sense there.

For just as for children there is the perception of a lion in a painted image, so for people there is the occurrence of linguistic usage (*śabda-vyavahāra*) regarding one thing based on what is well-known in another; because the application of Vedic usage to ritual action (*karman*) and the like is possible solely for the purpose of knowing Īśvara, by way of [action] being the support of the deities of the rites and so forth; and because the independence heard in relation to the individual soul (*jīva*) and others is established as residing in their Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), as proven in the "Prāṇa" section at the end of the first chapter. As for the result: it is the objection to the restriction stated in the *Samanvaya* Sūtra—that Viṣṇu alone is the primary meaning of all words—and its resolution. || 5 ||
Oṃ. And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. Oṃ. 6.

|| Oṃ, and because of the teaching of covetousness, oṃ. || Oṃ, and directly from both [scriptures], there is manifoldness, oṃ. || Oṃ, because of self-making through transformation, oṃ. || Oṃ, for the source is also sung [in scripture], oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: "It was previously stated that for all words, their primary function (*adhika-vṛtti*) refers to Viṣṇu, while elsewhere it is secondary (*hīna*). However, this is incorrect because it is impossible for feminine nouns to have a primary function [referring to Viṣṇu]; how, then, can there be any consideration of 'superiority'? The doubt is as follows: regarding words such as *prakṛti* (nature) and others mentioned in passages like "This indeed is the nature, the non-evolute," are they denotative of Viṣṇu or denotative of something else? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they denote something else, because they are well-known to refer to other things and because they are feminine in gender.

Because womanhood is absent in the Supreme Person; for, by the prohibition of womanhood in the passage, "One should not speak of him as a woman with speech," it is also untenable that womanhood consists in a particular form. Although a neuter word such as *brahman* might be appropriate here merely for the sake of grammatical correctness—as in the case of words like *kalatra*—it is not so here, because there is no basis for such an interpretation. Furthermore, the phrase "all names" admits of a restricted application.

Even in the case of a husband who has brought his wife under his control, we do not observe the use of the word *bhāryā* (wife) [to refer to him]; therefore, since one must admit that the femininity residing in another is dependent upon the Lord, the application of that word (*bhāryā*) to the Lord on the basis of the principle of dependence is likewise untenable. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: In such scriptural passages as, "Alas! All names indeed designate this very Person," the Lord's status as the denotable object of all words without exception is stated in general; furthermore, the analogy of the river and the ocean is employed [to illustrate this].

For in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti" and "Prakṛti is indeed Vāsanā; thus Your will is called infinite," will (icchā) is denoted by the word *prakṛti*; and since that [will] is stated to be the very nature of the Lord in the Śruti passage, "He is the contemplation, He is the impetus," and so forth, and because it is explicitly denoted by the word *prakṛti* in the text, "This is woman, this is man, this is *prakṛti*."

Having entered that primordial nature (prakṛti) and transformed it through the form of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, He draws out His own self in manifold ways as its controller; thus, because this is possible through yoga, and because the Śruti passage "the source of all beings" (yadbhūtayoniṃ) uses the word *yoni* to denote the state of being female—defined as the immediate cause of birth—Lord Hari alone is the primary referent of all feminine nouns such as *prakṛti*. 6.
Oṃ. By this, all [the cases] have been explained, have been explained. Oṃ. 7.

Here, the connection [of this section] arises from the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) due to its dissimilarity with what preceded. Regarding such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*), there is a doubt: do words such as "non-existent" (*asat*), "void" (*śūnya*), and so forth, belong to those who maintain the Lord (*Īśa*) or to others? As for the prima facie view: it is logical that the previously mentioned form of "femininity" (*strītva*) [is the basis for the word *asan*], because it does not involve the loss of a specific form; however, a basis for the application of "non-existence" (*asat*) and so on—such as the state of being negatable—is not logical, because it would entail the loss of a specific form.

Since that which is non-existent (*asat*) lacks an essential nature (*niḥsvarūpa*), there can be no regulation of it; consequently, because it is impossible for it to be dependent upon the Lord, the principle of dependence (*tadadhīnanyāya*) does not apply to it either. Therefore, words such as *asat* and so forth denote something else [than the Lord]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Even though well-known states such as emptiness (*śūnyatva*) do not reside in the Lord, since the application of the term is possible through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) stated in Smṛti texts such as "He makes [the world] empty" (*śamūnaṃ kurute*), and since even the non-existent can be regulated by its very state of non-existence, and because there is the aforementioned proof of its dependence [on the Lord], Hari alone is the primary referent (*mukhyārtha*) of words such as *asat* and *śūnya*. The result [of this interpretation] has already been stated. || 7 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the first quarter of the second chapter.

Since the contradictions to the previously stated reconciliation (*samanvaya*) are resolved here, there is a logical connection (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between this chapter and the preceding one. By means of the four quarters (*pāda*), there is a sequential refutation—through the subversion of words at their endings and beginnings—of those [objections] that proceed like a horse and so forth, consisting of arguments based on reasoning, objections regarding established consensus, and contradictions with scriptural statements supported by reasoning. Because it possesses four forms, the contradiction with *smṛti* (tradition) is refuted in the first quarter. **Sūtra 1:** "If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for other *smṛtis*, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other [Vedic] *smṛtis*. (1)
Oṃ, and because others are not perceived, Oṃ. Oṃ, by this, Yoga is refuted, Oṃ.

There arises a doubt as to whether the Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe, which was previously stated through the reconciliation of the Śrutis, is logical or not. The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that it is not logical. This is because [the claim of Viṣṇu’s authorship] contradicts all the Śruti and Smṛti texts, such as those of the Sāṅkhyas and Kāpilas, which teach that Śiva and others are the creators. Furthermore, these [Smṛtis] possess greater authority due to their being endowed with the quality of reliability (*āpti*), since they were not composed by Śiva and others who are renowned for their omniscience and other virtues; whereas the Śruti, being impersonal (*apauruṣeya*), lacks a personal source and is therefore weak.

In the systems of Kaṇāda and others, although the Śruti possesses a firm foundation because it was spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*), the Smṛtis are stronger due to their clarity of meaning and their being supported by reasoning. Consequently, since they do not possess equal strength, and because a contradiction between them would render any option (*vikalpa*) regarding the reality weak, sublation by the Śruti is untenable. Furthermore, there is no contradiction based on differences of place and so forth, as such non-contradiction is appropriate given that the various texts in the Śruti and elsewhere declare the respective [deities] to be the creator of all. Thus, according to the principle of contradiction in the *Pūrvatantra*—"But when there is contradiction, [the Smṛti] is not to be relied upon"—the Smṛtis...

The position that [the *Pāñcarātra*] possesses authority because it is rooted in the *Śruti* is refuted here by the statement that those [other] *Smṛtis* are sublated due to their contradiction with the *Śruti*. However, there is a distinction here, as these *Smṛtis* are rooted in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Śiva and others. Therefore, since the *Śruti* texts must be interpreted in accordance with those respective *Smṛtis* as having Śiva and others as their authors, they lack authority when contradicted by the *Smṛtis* of the Buddhists, the Jains, and so forth. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the *Pāñcarātra* and other *Smṛtis* were composed by Viṣṇu and others who are the most omniscient, and because they are in agreement with what is stated in the *Śruti*, they possess authority through that corroboration.

Furthermore, because [the Veda] is more powerful due to its quality of expressing its meaning with absolute clarity, it sublates those [Smṛtis]. Even when performing the means prescribed in the Smṛtis of the Śaivas and others, there is a discrepancy regarding the results, as the results described as such are not perceived through direct perception. Since they also lack the status of being spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*), the non-Vedic Smṛtis are invalid. Therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe is established through the consistent interpretation of the Śruti.

Although it was stated in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* that the meaning of the Veda must be determined solely by means of the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth, this [sūtra] is commenced again because of the doubt that even those [other criteria] might be interpreted here in conformity with them. In the *Śāstrayoni-nyāya*, having accepted the authority of the Smṛtis regarding matters whose fruits are perceptible, the objection arose that their authority should likewise apply to the fact of the universe's causality; in response, it was stated that they possess no authority there, based on such passages as "One who does not know the Veda... (*nāvedavit*).

However, it should be understood that here the lack of authority is stated on account of contradiction with the very result of perception; therefore, this [section] does not have its meaning already established [by the previous]. As for the "result" (phala), throughout this chapter it consists everywhere in the objection to the status of being the creator of the universe as stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, and the resolution thereof. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The world] is not [identical with Brahman] because it has different characteristics; and its being so [i.e., being Brahman] is known from scripture. Oṃ. (Sūtra 2)
|| Oṃ, but it is indeed perceived, oṃ. ||

Here, because of the doubt that if the Smṛtis were invalid due to their failure to correspond with their results (*phala-visaṃvāda*), then for that very reason the Śruti and the Śrauta-smṛtis would also be invalid, there is an introductory connection (*apavādikī saṅgati*). The doubt is whether the Śruti and the Śrauta-smṛti are authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or not.

Regarding the performance of the *kārīrī* sacrifice and others as prescribed in such injunctions as "one desiring rain should sacrifice with the *kārīrī*," there arises a discrepancy between the result and the expectation—such as rain not falling when desired. Consequently, just as in the case of a forgotten recollection, the Veda (*śruti*) would be non-authoritative despite its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), or else its very authorlessness would be denied. Thus, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that both the Vedic revelation and the traditional law (*smṛti*) are not authoritative. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The remainder of the argument follows: Even if a person who has previously experienced a certain thing fails to remember it at the time of performing an action due to distraction or other causes, and thus acts contrary to their memory, this does not prove that the original experience was invalid; rather, it indicates a lapse in memory. Similarly, even if a person desiring rain performs the *kārīrī* sacrifice and rain does not fall, this failure does not negate the validity of the Vedic injunction itself. Therefore, the Veda remains authoritative. Furthermore, the fact that a person may fail to remember a specific detail does not invalidate the general rule. Consequently, the Veda is indeed authoritative, and its authorlessness is maintained. This concludes the section.

Because the Veda is authorless—according to such statements as "by speech, which is eternal and multiform," and by the reasoning set forth in the Commentary regarding the systems of the gods and others—and because the Smṛti based on the Śruti follows that same principle, it is free from any suspicion of defect and thus possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge like a witness.

Furthermore, regarding authority (*prāmāṇya*), since the objects of the Veda are stated to be unsuitable for the senses in passages such as "Neither the eye nor the ear," they are to be known through their own inherent nature without depending on corroboration. Consequently, a sublation consisting of a discrepancy with the result is not established for specific qualified practitioners, as the results are indeed observed. Moreover, any occasional discrepancy regarding the result can be explained as being caused by defects in the agent or other factors. Since it is accepted that the authority of the Smṛtis is known precisely through their correspondence with those [Vedic texts], the Śruti and the Śrauta-smṛtis are indeed authoritative, owing to their distinction from those [Smṛtis] that lack such correspondence. || 2 ||
|| Oṃ. But there is a designation of the presiding deity, because of distinction and following after; oṃ. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and it is also perceived; Oṃ.

In the preceding section, the contradiction with mere reasoning known as "inconsistency" (*visaṃvāda*) was refuted. Here, the contradiction with firm reasoning—arising from the scripture's causing one to deviate from the perceived meaning—is being refuted; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). The doubt is whether such scriptural passages as "The earth spoke," "The waters spoke," and "That fire indeed [spoke]" are authoritative or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the scripture which asserts the speakerhood of the earth and other elements at the beginning of time is not authoritative.

The argument that "clay does not speak because it is insentient or because it is clay, like [commonly] agreed-upon clay" is invalid, as its meaning contradicts reason; for it is impossible for that which is insentient and devoid of organs of action to possess agency, the status of a seer, and so forth. Furthermore, since there is no sublation by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*)—whether one takes as the subject (pakṣa) the clay currently serving as a cause, or merely what is established for the opponent—the Veda is not non-authoritative. Consequently, according to the Jaiminīya principle that "other [Vedic passages] are likewise [authoritative] because of their similarity to those [accepted parts]," the entire Veda is also authoritative.

Regarding the point that [the Veda] lacks authority: the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows. Since the Veda is eternal according to the direction previously stated, it is impossible for it to be non-authoritative when its defects have not even been suspected; furthermore, it is impossible for an insentient entity to possess the capacity for speech and so forth. Therefore, because both the Veda’s status as authoritative and its status as a speaker are inexplicable without something else, that which makes them possible must be postulated. By the inexplicability of both these points, there is established—through such scriptural statements as “The deities presiding over the earth and other elements are of celebrated power,” as well as through the direct perception of great beings—an intelligent being who possesses such presiding agency (*abhimānin*).

Since [the Lord's] possession of a body and other attributes necessary for being a speaker and so forth has been established—thereby removing the objection based on our non-perception of such things—and since He possesses the power of invisibility (*antardhāna-śakti*) and so on; and since, by the principle of dependence upon that [presiding deity], words such as "clay" primarily denote the deities presiding over them because the causal basis for the application of those terms (such as "clay-ness") residing in clay and the like is dependent upon that [deity]; and since there is no contradiction with reason in accepting that the speakers and others denoted by words like "clay" are indeed deities, the Veda is indeed authoritative (*pramāṇa*). Thus ends section 3.
"Oṃ. If it be said that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [the scripture] is a mere negation. Oṃ. (4)

Oṃ. [The Sāṃkhya doctrine is] "inconsistent" because, on account of the merging [of the effect into the cause], the same undesirable consequence would apply [to the cause as well]. Oṃ. [This is not so] because there exists an illustrative example. Oṃ. And because of the defects in their own position. Oṃ. If it is argued that "the reasoning may be inferred otherwise because of the instability of reasoning," even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation. Oṃ. By this, those who do not accept [the authority of the Vedas] are also explained. Oṃ.

Here, the connection [of the topic] arises from a doubt raised by means of the logic of the previously established conclusion (*pūrvasiddhāntanyāya*): if, for the sake of avoiding contradiction with scripture and reasoning, words such as "clay" are shown to have other meanings, then what need is there to mention that words such as "non-existent" (*asad*) in the passage "Being alone, my dear... must likewise have other meanings in order to avoid contradiction with scripture and reasoning? The doubt is as follows: Is the Vedic text beginning with "From which indeed... (*yato vā*), which declares Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe, authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not authoritative.

The universal prior non-existence (*viśvaprāgabhāva*) at the time of dissolution is the cause of the universe, because it exists in the immediately preceding moment in a manner that is both necessary and not otherwise established, just like [accepted causes]. When its causality is thus established through reasoning, combined with the scriptural text—"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadevedamagra āsīt*)—which refers to the universal prior non-existence denoted by the word "non-existent" (*asat*), it follows that the disputed entities are non-existent during dissolution, because they are entities, like any effect. Since the existence of any entity whatsoever is unestablished at the time of dissolution, and given the rule that every effect must have an agent, it is established by elimination that [the cause] is indeed the non-existent (*asat*).

Because of the parsimony [of the principle] resulting from the postulation of God and so forth based on scriptural passages such as "He made the mind," it follows that even the material cause—the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva)—is itself the agent. This is because [the opponent's view] contradicts the reasoning that establishes prior non-existence as the agent; furthermore, since the instrumental case ending denoting agency is observed even in the case of insentient things in expressions such as "one stands by means of a tree," there is no logical inconsistency in accepting that non-existence possesses agency.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues] that the world is indeed without an agent, like a falling riverbank, because it is an effect, like a jar; or else it must have a living being as its agent, like curds and so forth, or an insentient entity as its agent, and so on—on account of such arguments combined with scriptural passages such as "This arose from nothing," which contradict [the position of an intelligent creator]. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: Since the agency of Viṣṇu is intended to consist in his possession of knowledge, will, and other such qualities, it does not merely consist in being the possessor of the instrumental case (tṛtīyā-yogitvamātra). Moreover, since [agency] is negated only in its essential nature (svarūpataḥ), there is no contradiction in its existence [when understood as the aforementioned qualities].

Because, according to the rule that upon the destruction of an effect only its cause remains, it is logical that at the time of dissolution (pralaya) only pure existence (bhāvamātra) remains. Furthermore, the arising of that which remains as such—being under dispute—is dependent on existence, because it possesses the quality of having an origin. This is because [the opponent's view] is contradicted by such arguments establishing the existence of being at the time of dissolution, such as: "The disputed destruction has a remainder, because it is a destruction, like a commonly accepted one."

Because the argument for existence (*bhāvatva*) is flawed—being countered by opposing arguments (*satpratipakṣita*) according to the direction already stated, and being subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) at the time of dissolution—and because the view that only non-existence remains at the end of the cosmic cycle lacks scriptural authority; and because, although dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*) is unstable, the validity of our position is possible when supported by the scripture (*āgama*) regarding God’s authorship; and because [theories] such as causelessness or the individual soul (*jīva*) being the cause are refuted precisely by the aforementioned reasoning which opposes them; and because scriptures such as "Non-being (*asat*)," etc., refer to God according to the principle stated in "By this, all [such passages] are explained"—therefore, the knowledge derived from the scriptures concerning Viṣṇu’s authorship is indeed authoritative. || 4 ||

|| Oṃ. If it be argued that there is no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] because of the attainment of the state of being an enjoyer, [we reply] "it would be so, as in the case of the world. Oṃ. || 5 ||

Previously, having accepted the non-existence of Brahman, the agency of non-existence itself was suspected. Here, however, having accepted its existence according to the aforementioned direction, the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is also raised as a doubt; this is the connection [between the two sections]. The doubt is whether the universal agency—stated through the harmonization of such scriptural texts as "Viṣṇu alone is the agent"—is logical or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is not logical.

Because of the scriptural statement, “In the highest imperishable, all become one,” there is oneness with the liberated; since no otherness is perceived in anything else, oneness must have existed previously, and because [the individual soul] is non-different from the transmigrating soul, this contradicts the reasoning based on non-difference established by scripture. Nor is it improper to use the suffix *cvī*—which denotes the attainment of a state not previously possessed—even if there was oneness previously, because the prior existence of difference is admitted, and the suffix is justified as signifying the cessation of that [difference].

And thus, regarding the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), that identity is possible either by abandoning the contradictory attributes of being the creator of all versus being a limited creator, through the soul’s similarity to the Lord, or by abandoning the attributes of the soul, through its similarity to the Lord. In the first case, it is impossible for Viṣṇu to be the creator of all; in the latter case, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Because of the scriptural teaching of oneness—in the subsequent passage, "The stainless one attains the supreme divine equality," as well as in other passages such as, "As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that"—and because there is no instance observed anywhere of an absolute non-difference occurring later for one who was previously distinct, it is established that the intent is oneness in liberation or the oneness of the individual soul (jīva); thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe is logical. || 5 ||
Oṃ. Its non-difference [from Brahman] follows from the words concerning "origination" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. Oṃ. 6.

|| Oṃ, and because it is perceived when there is existence, oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of the existence of what follows, oṃ. || Oṃ, if it be argued that it is not so because of the designation of non-existence, we say no, because of another attribute, on account of the remainder of the sentence, oṃ. || Oṃ, because of reasoning and another scriptural word, oṃ. || Oṃ, and like a cloth, oṃ. || Oṃ, as in the case of the vital breaths and so forth, oṃ. ||

In the preceding section, the doubt that the Lord is not the creator of the universe at all was set aside. Here, however, having accepted that status as established by scripture, the doubt is removed that such agency is dependent on other means and possesses a nature subject to external control; this is the logical connection (*saṅgati*). The doubt is whether the independent agency of Viṣṇu as stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra* is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is not logical.

The creation of the Mahat and other principles requires an independent instrument distinct from the agent, because it is a creation, like the creation of a cloth; this is contradicted by many such arguments. Furthermore, it contradicts the scriptural statement, "He was born from water, from earth, and from essence," which mentions water and other independent instruments. If [the Sāṅkhya claims] there is no dependence on those [instruments] because they are created by Īśvara, then there would likewise be no dependence on other instruments subordinate to Īśvara. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

The independent agency of Viṣṇu is indeed logical, because the Śruti passage, "What was the support? What was the instrument? implies the necessity of such means as a support; likewise, the Śruti passage, "There was neither non-existence nor existence," states the absence of such means as the primary elements (bhūtas) at the time of creation.

Furthermore, because it contradicts other scriptural passages that establish the existence of a creator being for those two [the earth and the mountain], and because it is untenable to imply their existence in their own right, that scripture is intended merely to deny their independence. This is because it is contradicted by the previously mentioned negative inferences (*vyatirekānumāna*), such as: "The creation under dispute does not depend on any means other than its agent, because, while having an agent other than that which is dependent, it is a creation," and so forth.

Just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth lack independence because they have entered into the Lord, the instruments [of action] are determined to be non-independent due to their entry into the Lord, as established by the *Smṛti* text: "Having entered into both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. Furthermore, there is no perception through authoritative means such as *Śruti* of any instrument other than the Agent; for passages such as "From the waters... are not in conflict [with this], since texts like "Substance, action, and time... intend to show that these are merely subordinate instruments. Moreover, even for the Lord, when creating out of sport (*līlā*), the employment of other instruments is possible.
|| Oṃ. Because of the designation as another, there would follow the defects of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. Oṃ. || 7 ||

|| Oṃ, but [the Lord is] greater, because of the teaching of difference; oṃ. || Oṃ, and like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is impossible; oṃ. || Oṃ, if it be argued that it is not so because of the observation of withdrawal [of the world], [we reply] no, as in the case of the increase of milk; oṃ. || Oṃ, even among gods and others in the world; oṃ. || Oṃ, there would follow the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being transformed, or else the contradiction of the scriptural texts declaring its partlessness; oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that the lack of independence of living beings (*jīva*) regarding breath and so forth, mentioned previously, is untenable because we experience the independent agency of living beings. Regarding the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*), the doubt is whether the intended independent agency belongs to Viṣṇu alone or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Because of the scriptural statement, “From the individual soul (jīva) all beings arise,” and because this is corroborated by the experience of independent agency such as “I am doing this,” and by the reasoning that “the jīva is the agent because it is conscious, like the Lord (Īśvara) accepted by the Siddhāntin,” the claim that Viṣṇu alone is the independent agent is contradicted; furthermore, since the jīva’s status as the agent in the case of a jar and other such objects is established, it is logical—by the principle of parsimony (lāghava)—that the jīva alone is the agent even in the case of the great elements and so forth, whereas the Lord, being unfit [for direct perception], would never be perceived.

One [view] holds that it is not tenable for Him to be the agent, because if His fitness [to be an agent] were asserted on the grounds that hearing and so forth would otherwise be useless, then since He exists always and everywhere, His non-existence would be ascertained through the non-perception of what is fit—given that He is not perceived here and now—and thus the postulation of His authorship is struck down by the fault of complexity (*gaurava*). Another [view], however, maintains: Since the status of being the agent of the great principle (*mahat*) and so forth contradicts experience in the case of a living being (*jīva*), let the Lord (*Īśvara*) be the agent there; but He is not the agent even of jars and the like, because it is simpler to postulate that these have only the living being as their agent, as established by experience.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Since it is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) alone to be an independent agent—given that its failure to accomplish its own welfare is a matter of common experience—and since activity in acts such as pulling up a blade of grass would be contradicted by experience (if the soul were active either with its entire capacity or only partially) and by the scriptural text, "This [Self] is eternal and partless," such activity is untenable. Furthermore, because the Lord (*īśvara*), though always present everywhere, may not be perceived due to the power of concealment—as is the case with gods or even *piśācas*—the scriptural statement, "From the [Supreme] Soul they arise," is appropriately understood as referring to the Lord, supported by the mark of its being a novel teaching (*apūrvatā*).

Furthermore, because the experience of independent agency on the part of the Cārvāka—like his notion of the inert body’s independence—is an error regarding the soul which is dependent upon God, and because [the soul], despite being endowed with consciousness, lacks independence like a stone and such, the soul is not an independent agent; thus, due to this counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), the reason is unproven (*aprayojaka*), and because of the absence of independence, the soul is not [an independent agent].

Since the independence of the Lord of all knowledge regarding jars and the like, as well as His status as the independent agent regarding the great elements (mahat) and so forth, is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since this complexity (*gaurava*) is not a defect, both of the aforementioned prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) are untenable; therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu alone is the agent. As for the result: in the preceding and subsequent positions, there is respectively the impossibility and the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition, and their resolution is found in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). || 7 ||
Oṃ. But it must be accepted on the authority of scripture, because [the knowledge of Brahman] is rooted in the Word. Oṃ. (2.1.3)

Oṃ. And likewise in the case of the Self, for [the world] is manifold; Oṃ. And because of the defects in its own position; Oṃ. And it is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture]; Oṃ. If it be said "no, because of the absence of organs," that has already been answered; Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that the defect of "the consequence of total involvement" (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) and so forth would apply to the Lord as well, just as it does to the individual soul (*jīva*), even though He is the agent. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the agent of all things is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because Viṣṇu’s engagement in even a minor action, such as the taking up of a blade of grass, would entail the consequence of total involvement, it would result in the fallacy of Him being non-omniscient (*aprekṣāvat*).

If [the Lord] were to act only partially, it would contradict such partless scriptural texts as "not here, not there, not this" (*neha nānā*); furthermore, since no distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord could be established, that same defect would apply to the Lord himself. Moreover, there is no basis for imagining that this defect applies to the Lord alone, and because of the scriptural statement, "It has neither eyes nor ears, neither hands nor feet," He lacks the instruments such as hearing. Therefore, Viṣṇu’s agency is untenable. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because in common worldly usage, such as in the expressions "he who is contradictory," "non-contradictory," "Manu," or "non-Manu," the Lord is said to possess contradictory attributes without contradiction; because He is accessible solely through scripture and thus lies beyond the scope of dry logic, He cannot be sublated by it; and because of scriptural texts such as "The ancient Person possesses manifold powers," Viṣṇu possesses a power that effects the impossible and eternally encompasses all objects, thereby resolving even that which contradicts reason.

And since there is an absence of any previously mentioned [defects] in the individual soul (jīva), the Lord is distinguished from it; because the previously cited scripture beginning with "He has no effect or instrument" refers to the material body (prākṛta), and because He possesses a body endowed with limbs such as hands consisting of qualities like knowledge and bliss, His status as the creator is logical. In the *Śāstrayoni* section, it was stated that dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*) is not a means of proof; here, the distinction is that it is not a means of sublation (*bādhaka*). || 8 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord] does not [act] because He has a purpose. Oṃ. 9.
|| Oṃ, but as in the world, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport; oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: previously, the contradiction with reason regarding the aspect of the cause (*hetumukha*) was refuted; here, however, the contradiction with the firm reasoning regarding the aspect of the result (*phalamukha*) is being eliminated. For if Viṣṇu were to have a specific purpose in view, he would be subject to incompleteness, and such a being—like Caitra or others—would be incapable of being the creator of all; yet if no purpose were in view, it would be impossible for a conscious and discerning being to engage in activity at all, and since there would be no fruit born of compassion, it would be illogical to say that he acts out of compassion. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because the scripture states, "This is the very nature of the Lord," the creation of the universe and other such acts are the very nature of the Lord; and because, even in the absence of a stated purpose for what is natural—such as the blinking of an eye—it is observed that there is no need for a fruit, and just like the effortless movement of a fingertip, the creation of the universe and so forth are logically established as being accomplished by the Lord without effort; and because, although there is an absence of a fruit for Himself arising from compassion, there exists the welfare of others, it is fitting that the creation of the universe and other acts are of the nature of divine play (līlā). || 9 ||
|| Oṃ. There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He has regard for [the karma of beings]; for thus Scripture shows. Oṃ || 10 ||

|| Oṃ. If it be argued that [the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no, because [karma] is beginningless. Oṃ. And this is both logical and observed. Oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: here, the contradiction with reasoning regarding the result in the form of the purpose for others mentioned in the previous method is being refuted. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is logical or not. The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is not logical.

If Viṣṇu were to act with the aim of some ulterior purpose, then, since he would be independent of those various individual karmas, there would arise the fault of partiality and cruelty in bestowing happiness, suffering, and so forth, by way of distribution, without any cause. If, on the other hand, he bestowed fruits in dependence upon karma, then since the karmas themselves would be dependent upon him, there would again arise partiality and the like in his causing good and evil deeds to be performed without any cause. If he were not dependent on Viṣṇu, then, because he would depend on karmas that are themselves independent, his sovereignty would be lost.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Even though Viṣṇu bestows fruits in accordance with each respective action, since actions are beginningless by way of their continuous flow, he causes subsequent meritorious and other types of actions to be performed in dependence upon each preceding action of that person, and thereby grants the fruit. Thus, there is no lack of a cause for his directing the performance of actions through such differentiation. Furthermore, because actions themselves are dependent on Him—as stated in the Śruti, "For He alone causes one to perform good deeds"—the charge of His lack of independence does not arise.

Furthermore, although [the Lord] has the power to act otherwise due to His independence, He does not do so because He would thereby incur partiality in the bestowing of fruits in relation to those [beings]. Moreover, since He transcends injunctions and prohibitions—which do not establish the authority of the Vedas that teach that dharma and the like are the causes of results—and because He, like the individual soul (*jīva*) who possesses such [qualities], would be the cause of sin (*pratyavāya*); and finally, because being "in accordance with their respective beginningless capacities" is precisely the meaning of the word "equal," this does not contradict the noble quality of universal equality expressed in the statement, "I am equal toward all beings."

Furthermore, because it is stated as a fault in such scriptural passages as, "Whether one performs merit or even sin, one does not become a sinner by that much alone," it is logical that Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all is free from fault. || 10 ||
Oṃ, and because all dharmas arise [from the Tathāgata], Oṃ. 11.

Thus, in the previous systems, it was stated that there is no contradiction with reason regarding each individual quality—such as being the creator, the sustainer, and so forth—and the absence of each corresponding defect. However, because this is a concluding summary, the connection here is that [the attributes] apply "everywhere. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s possession of the aforementioned fullness of qualities and freedom from defects is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not logical. This is because it contradicts reasoning: "Viṣṇu does not possess fullness of qualities through freedom from defects, because he is a conscious being (*caitanya*), like Caitra and others"; otherwise, if defects were absent, the very nature of being a "quality" would not exist. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Brahman eternally possesses all excellent qualities because, while desiring them, He is capable of possessing them, just like a person who is honored [and strives for excellence]. Brahman eternally abandons all defects because, while desiring to abandon them, He is capable of doing so. Since the state of being full of flawless qualities is established by such scriptural texts as "The qualities heard in the Lord are even mutually contradictory," which are supported by these logical arguments, and since the agency of a conscious being [as a mere cause] is not the determining factor, it is logical that Viṣṇu is full of flawless qualities. Furthermore, there is no lack of proof regarding the qualifying attributes in these two logical arguments.

This is because that [agency] is inferred precisely from the fact of being a sentient being (prekṣāvattva), and because the qualified object [the Self] is established according to the principle of "But from Scripture" (Śrutestu). The purpose [of this section], however, is the objection to and the resolution of the matter stated in the Chapter on Concordance (Samanvayādhyāya). || 11 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the second quarter.

And because others are not perceived—since this is an expansion of the reasons stated in the *Guṇasūtra* according to the method of the *Smṛti*, its connection with the preceding section is either through the statement "contradiction with established doctrine (*samaya*) is addressed here," or by the direction previously mentioned. Since there are two types of established doctrines according to the *Smṛti* beginning with "Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, and so forth," and since those who follow reason (*haituka*) are more powerful due to their reliance on logical proof, they are refuted first:
**"And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, [the Veda] is not based on inference."** (Sūtra 1.1.3) *oṃ* || 1 ||

Oṃ, and because of [the nature of] activity, Oṃ. Oṃ, if it is argued that it is like milk and water, then even there, Oṃ. Oṃ, and because of the non-existence of distinction and due to independence, Oṃ.

There is a doubt as to whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of all things, as stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, is logical or not. The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) view is that it is not logical. This is because the cause of the universe is established by such inferences as: "The effects beginning with Mahat are produced by an independent cause, or produced by a cause of their own class, because they are effects, like a jar"; and "Pradhāna is the cause of the universe and possesses the agency consisting of independent activity, because it is a real entity, like water and so forth," or "because it undergoes transformation independently, like milk, due to its being a substance. Thus, [the opponent argues] on the basis of independence.

This is because it is contradicted by the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṅkhya, which seeks to establish that *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the agent. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the first inference is refuted by the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); and the latter two are countered by opposing arguments (*satpratipakṣatva*), such as: "The Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest do not possess independent activity because they are insentient, or rather, they are created by a sentient being because they are effects, like a jar. etc.

"O Gārgī, by the command of this very Imperishable, the eastern rivers flow," "By this indeed does the cream of milk come into being," and "Nothing is done without you"—from such scriptural passages, as well as because the example of the movement of water and so forth toward a conscious agent is flawed due to the deficiency of the probandum, the theory of a purely non-conscious creator is unauthentic and contradicted by valid means of knowledge.

Since the doctrine that teaches that [Brahman is the cause] is itself subject to refutation, its contradiction [by other means of knowledge] is of no consequence; therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe, as stated through the harmony of the Śruti, is established. The result here, however, throughout [this section], concerns the refutation and resolution of objections regarding the agency described in the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādy-asya yataḥ). || 1 ||

In this context, it is appropriate to first refute the agency of the insentient—whether as a solitary entity or as one possessing the attributes of God—by means of scripture and inference. The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that since those two [scripture and inference] are not authoritative, the agency of the body alone is established, and thus God is not the agent. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world is logical or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is not logical; for even without God, the production of subsequent effects from preceding causes is possible, and in some cases the production of an effect is explained by inherent nature alone, just as the production of intoxication occurs from certain substances.

Since there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned scripture and inference due to the absence of validity in anything other than direct perception, and since we accept that if scripture and the like were invalid—on the grounds that we do not admit the existence of imperceptible entities such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—then merit and so forth would simply not exist, this [consequence] is acceptable to us.

"How can there be a Lord? How much less can there be His authorship? And how much less can there be His independence?"—this contradicts the doctrine of the Cārvākas. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): since the Cārvāka scripture lacks authority regarding anything beyond the senses, and because it does not apply to unperceivable objects, to that which is unperceivable, or to that which is not attained; and because, according to the maxim "Scripture is purposeful regarding what is not [otherwise] attained," it cannot have such things as its subject matter; and because the non-existence of *dharma* and so forth is not accessible to the senses; therefore, the inference that "dharma and the like do not exist, because they are not perceived by direct perception" is [invalid].

Furthermore, because you do not accept [the Vedas] as authoritative, and because there is no means for understanding the non-existence of dharma, adharma, and so forth, it is impossible for those [Vedas] to be an object [of knowledge]; moreover, there would be an absence of any purpose such as dharma, heaven, or liberation.

Since objects such as wealth can be acquired through other means like commerce, there is no result in the form of benefiting the world by teaching the absence of dharma and so forth; for if one were to know that dharma and the like do not exist, one would only encounter harm through mutual violence and the like for the sake of others’ wealth and women. Thus, because the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) are absent, his doctrine is flawed. Furthermore, the claim that it could still be a scripture despite the absence of these two is contradictory; therefore, his wicked doctrine is utterly ineffective, and it is logical that Viṣṇu alone is the Creator. || 3 ||
