Regarding this, what was stated previously—that because the doctrine of the "foolish" (durmati) is contradictory due to its emptiness of objects and so forth, the Lord (Īśa) must be the creator—is not correct. The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that it contradicts the Sāṅkhya system, which holds that the Puruṣa possesses objects and the like as subordinate factors. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe is logical or not. The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is not logical.

Even though it is impossible for the purely insentient (*jaḍa*) to possess agency (*kartṛtva*) in the form of spontaneous activity, since in the world we observe that the body alone—through its connection with the *jīva*—engages in activities such as carrying stones, there is no contradiction in accepting that the primary agent is *pradhāna* (primordial matter) qualified by the attributes of the *jīva*. This is established by the inference: "The activity of *pradhāna* is subservient to the *jīva* and brought about by a sentient being, because it is an activity, like the activity of carrying stones. Thus, there is no obstacle to this position. However, this contradicts the Sāṅkhya doctrine which holds that *pradhāna* is the primary agent subservient to the *puruṣa* (spirit). As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): [the following follows...]

By the previously cited scripture beginning with "Nothing whatsoever is done by anyone else than You," the dependence of even the body's activity upon the Lord is established. Furthermore, since it is impossible for the worldly and investigative consensus—which recognizes the soul as the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and the body as its adjunct (*aṅga*)—to be consistent with the theory that the primary agency belongs to the Pradhāna (primordial matter) having the soul as its quality, such a view lacks scriptural authority. Moreover, even those [scriptures] purporting to teach such a meaning are considered of poor intellect and thus do not contradict the stated position. Therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu alone possesses agency. || 4 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that the defect—the impossibility of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*)—does not apply because it is accepted here that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the principal (*aṅgin*). The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not logical.

Following the direction previously stated, by means of the example of the carrying of stones and so forth—which shows that the soul’s agency is subordinate to the body—one may employ the following inference: "The activity of the *pradhāna* under dispute is dependent upon a soul whose agency is subordinate [to matter], because it is an activity [of a non-intelligent entity] like the activity of carrying stones. By this inference, since there is no purpose for a Lord (*īśvara*) in the spontaneous activity of the *pradhāna*—which is already dominated by the *puruṣa* (soul)—the [Lord's] status as an agent is remote. Furthermore, because the previously cited scripture is disregarded due to its contradiction with reason, there is a conflict with the Sāṅkhya doctrine which holds that the *puruṣa* is primary.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Even if one were to infer otherwise than the previous position—that the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses the capacity for activity even without a body—it would follow that the body is useless if it has such capacity; whereas if it lacks such capacity, then even if its activity is for the sake of connecting with a body, the status of the soul as the primary agent (*aṅgin*) is untenable because the soul alone lacks the power [to act]. If it is argued that the connection with *prakṛti* (primordial matter) provides the capacity in that case, then even regarding the activity of connecting with *prakṛti*, the same logic would apply, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Because there is no beginning [to saṃsāra], it is entirely impossible for one who is already liberated to engage in activity; therefore, since the connection with a body must be brought about by an independent Lord alone, the same logic applies even to activities such as bringing stones. Thus, because the corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) lacks the property to be proven (sādhyahīna), the inference is flawed. Furthermore, since there is no proof for the stated position, it lacks scriptural authority (aprāmāṇika). On the other hand, by accepting an independent Lord, everything becomes consistent. Therefore, Viṣṇu’s status as the agent is logical. The distinction here is that while in the previous verse the agency of the individual soul (jīva)—which was established through scripture and reasoning—was refuted, in this verse the agency of the soul as established by the [materialist] doctrine (samaya) is refuted. || 5 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that the fault stated regarding the atheistic position does not apply to the view of those who affirm God (Īśvara), due to the difference from the previous case. Here, the doubt is whether the previously mentioned infinite qualities of Viṣṇu are logical or not. The prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are not logical.

Since the Lord and the Self, as substances, necessarily possess the five general qualities known as number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction—which are useful for their agency—as well as the three specific qualities of knowledge, desire, and effort, and since there is no evidence for any quality beyond these eight, they cannot possess fourteen qualities like the individual soul; thus, the claim that they possess infinite qualities is dismissed from afar due to its contradiction with the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The remainder of the text follows: ...For the Lord, who is the cause of all effects, there must be a substratum for His qualities such as omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. Furthermore, because He is the creator of all things, He must possess qualities such as the power to produce effects simultaneously in all places and times, the power to create diverse effects from a single material, and the power to sustain the world through His will. Moreover, since He is the object of the devotion of those seeking liberation, He must possess qualities such as supreme compassion and the capacity to bestow grace. Therefore, it is established that the Lord possesses infinite qualities, which are distinct from the eight qualities mentioned above and are not limited by the categories of the Vaiśeṣika school. Thus, the claim that He has only eight qualities is refuted. This concludes the section on the qualities of the Lord. Now, regarding the nature of the Lord’s body... [and so on].

Since the Vaiśeṣikas speak inconsistently, their doctrine—which teaches an unauthoritative method—is in contradiction with the meaning already stated; therefore, it is correct that [the Lord] possesses infinite qualities. To explain: as for what was said—that the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth is not the non-inherent cause of the dimension of a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and so forth, but rather that the dimensions of two atoms and a dyad do not exist [as causes], but only the numbers two and three residing therein—this is incorrect.

For it is logical that dimension (parimāṇa) residing in atoms and so forth is of the same nature as that residing in dyads and so forth; even though there is a difference in kind between the "shortness" (hrasvatva) of what resides in a dyad and the "atomicity" (aṇutva) of what resides in an atom, it is still logical for accumulation (pracaya) alone—just as in the case of number—to be the cause.

Regarding the dimensions "atomic," "large," "long," and "short," there is no evidence for such intermediate species; rather, since all things possess relative minuteness and largeness, and since it is logical that visibility or invisibility depends upon a particular observer, there is no risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Likewise, because a cloth distinct from the conjunctions of the intended threads is not perceived, conjunction among the threads cannot be the cause with respect to that cloth; thus, the theory of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is untenable.

Likewise, if God is accepted as the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) on the grounds that His will is eternal, then even during the dissolution (pralaya), when that will exists, there would be no production of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and other effects because of the absence of atomic motion; this would result in a deviation (vyabhicāra) from the rule. Furthermore, since there is an absence of such effects at other times as well, it follows that they would never arise. If, on the other hand, His will is non-eternal, then for its production, there must be dependence upon another instance of His will; this leads to an infinite regress (anavasthā) through a series of unproven entities. If no such dependence is admitted, then just as in the case of dissolution, His will would not be the cause in other instances either. Therefore, the view that He is an efficient cause is also untenable.

Likewise, having accepted the distinctness of qualities (*guṇa*), the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), and so forth, if one further accepts a separate inherence (*samavāya*) as the object of specific cognition and the like, then because that [inherence] would likewise require another, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Consequently, since inherence is untenable, even the "inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—defined by the characteristic "that wherein the effect inheres when it arises"—is untenable; thus, the creation of the universe is illogical. Similarly, dissolution (*laya*) is also not tenable according to that doctrine.

Furthermore, since the inherent causes—the atoms—and the efficient cause—God—are eternal, the production of effects would necessarily occur at all times. Moreover, the eternity of atoms is untenable even in their own system, as it contradicts the inference that "atoms are non-eternal because they possess color and other qualities, like a jar. Otherwise, it would follow that cloth and other such things are also eternal. In our own established doctrine, however, there is no such fallacy, as the reason is qualified by the attribute of being material (bhautikatva).

Furthermore, one should consider that his view is flawed because it is censured in the *Mahābhārata* by the Lord in the form of a jackal, who stated that devotion to *anvīkṣikī*, the science of logic, is useless, and declared that such attachment to the science of logic is the cause for rebirth as a jackal. As for the result, it concerns the refutation of the objection regarding the possession of complete qualities mentioned in the preceding chapter. || 6 ||

Thus, having refuted the theory of the composition of atoms (*paramāṇu-ārambhavāda*), the theory of their accumulation (*tatpuñjavāda*) which has been presented is now refuted; this is the connection. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the universe is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not logical.

Since the entire world, which exists in the form of matter, consciousness, sensation, perception, and mental formations, is in ultimate reality merely an aggregate of atoms as its cause, the cognition of jars and so forth is established by that alone; therefore, the postulation of a transformation of atoms and of a "whole" (avayavin) composed of them is redundant. Furthermore, since existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), if an existing entity were permanent, it would produce other bodies of the same class, such as jars, and from those [two], likewise [others]—thus [the series would continue for] a single moment.

Thus, because of the occurrence of endless effects, or because existence—defined as the capacity for causal efficiency—is otherwise inexplicable, one might argue by means of inference that "whatever exists is momentary, just like a lamp and so forth, and these entities exist. Since this aforementioned collection of effects can arise solely through time, karma, and causes, there is no need for an *īśvara* (God); furthermore, since the authority of scripture (*āgama*) is not accepted [by the opponent], there is no proof [for such a God]. It is on the grounds of such arguments, according to the views of the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, that [the position] is contradicted. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

The statement of those two [the Vaiśeṣikas] is untenable because their doctrine is flawed; thus, the contradiction they present is irrelevant and ineffective as a reason. Therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu is the creator. To explain: first of all, the claim that a jar or the like is merely an aggregate of atoms caused by atoms, and that there is no other such thing as an "unreal" entity, is incorrect.

If [the aggregate] were caused by a single atom, it would be untenable because it would contradict the claim that it arises from a "collection" (*samudāya*). Even in the position that it is caused by multiple atoms, if one says it is "caused by multiple atoms joined together," there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the collection exists when there is a joining, and the joining exists when there is a collection. Furthermore, if one says it is "caused by multiple atoms existing separately," then since those atoms would always exist, the collection would also necessarily exist eternally; this contradicts the accepted doctrine that the dissolution of the collection consists in its destruction.

Now, if you think that because the number of oneness residing in sparse atoms is accepted as the referent of the word "collection," even though that number is eternal, its cognition and linguistic usage [occur] only through being manifested by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

[Opponent: "Because [the cognition of a collection] depends on the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—namely, 'this and that'—and because that [cognition] is caused by proximity, when [the world] dissolves, atoms lack proximity; thus, due to the absence of that [proximity], there is an absence of the cognition and linguistic usage based upon it, and therefore dissolution is established. [Reply: That is not so. Since both the object and the self are momentary, it is impossible for the collection of atoms, the relative cognition, the cognition of that collection, and the linguistic usage to share a single object or a single substratum. Consequently, it would follow that the cognition and linguistic usage regarding a collection could never possibly occur.

Furthermore, in your own view, since you admit that atoms possess the inherent nature of producing similar effects, it is impossible for conjoined atoms to arise from those that are sparse. Moreover, regarding the doctrine of momentariness, because production and destruction at every moment are untenable—as indicated by the two sūtras beginning with "asati" and "pratisaṅkhyā"—momentariness itself is also illogical.

Furthermore, because [the theory of momentariness] is flawed according to the previously mentioned *arthāpatti* and the direction stated in the Sūtra "and in both ways" (*ubhayathā ca*), and because the inference is subject to the fallacy of *prakaraṇasama* as indicated by the phrase "and in space" (*ākāśe ca*), and because it is sublated by the recognition "this is that very same thing," momentariness lacks any basis in valid cognition. || 7 ||

This is because there is a contradiction with the view of the Śūnyavādins, who hold that since the Vedas and other sources are not authoritative, such [an entity] lacks scriptural warrant. Furthermore, by accepting the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), the faults stated against all [other] positions cannot be avoided. Because it is understood from the scriptures cited in the Bhāṣya—such as "Whomever I desire, him I make fierce"—that Śiva is dependent [on other factors], and because Śiva is bodiless; and because at the time of dissolution all elements have dissolved, there would be no substratum such as earth at the time of creation, making agency impossible; and because the entire collection of causal instruments must be directly presided over by effort, it would follow that [Śiva] would possess a perishable body and experience suffering and the like.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that all the Vedas are in harmony with Viṣṇu—on the grounds that He possesses, according to the method taught by the Śruti, eternal and manifold powers regarding all objects, and possesses a body consisting of knowledge, bliss, and so forth—and because there is a lack of evidence for Śiva’s status as the creator, that doctrine is flawed; thus, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator is established. By this same logic, the doctrines of the Śākta, Saura, Skānda, and Gāṇapatya schools are also refuted. || 11 ||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: although the doctrine of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimata*) was previously refuted, it is here refuted again due to a specific defect. The doubt is whether the Viśvakartṛtva (the status of being the creator of the universe) attributed to Viṣṇu is logical or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not logical; for in the Śrutis and other sources, the status of being the creator of the universe is heard to belong to Śakti alone, who is endowed with the quality of omniscience. Thus, there is a contradiction with the doctrine of the Possessor of Power. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Since the birth of offspring from a woman alone who is not favored by a man is impossible, and since Śakti alone cannot be the cause of the universe starting with Brahmā, it follows that she is the mother of the world only when favored by Śiva. Even in the Madhyama-Vāma view, because [Śakti] lacks the means such as knowledge (jñāna) necessary for her own origination, she cannot act as a favorer; thus, knowledge and other qualities must be admitted for her. Furthermore, even in the Aṇu-Vāma view, the admission of Śakti is redundant for the production of the universe by such a Śiva alone. Moreover, all three views are contradicted by the Śrutis and other authorities. Therefore, Viṣṇu’s status as the agent is correct. || 12 ||

In the investigation of the *adhibhūta* (the elemental), the *adhidaiva* (the divine), the *paramātman* (the Supreme Self), and the *jīva* (the individual self), first the investigation of the *adhibhūta* and *adhidaiva* is undertaken according to the maxim of the needle and the kettle (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*). Here, by the term *viyat* (ether/space), both the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and its presiding deity are intended. The doubt arises whether ether is subject to origination or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not subject to origination.

This is supported by the experience of ether’s non-origination, by the reasoning—"Ether is unoriginated because it is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), like the [Supreme] Self"—and by the powerful scriptural testimony of its beginninglessness, such as "This ether is indeed beginningless," which outweighs the argument based on the plurality of scriptural passages concerning origination.

Because that [non-origination] is established. For, since the scriptural statement regarding its origination—"ether was produced"—is not authoritative as it contradicts this [doctrine of non-origination], it is also improper to describe the scriptural statements on non-origination as being merely figurative. This is because in passages such as "it is neither born nor dies," words expressing non-origination have their primary sense; and since a dual nature (of both being and non-being) without a cause is impossible, the primary sense is what is logical here as well. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that ether possesses origination, because there is an abundance of scriptural statements regarding its origination, such as "from the Self, ether was produced."

Nor is there any contradiction with other scriptural passages (śruti). Since the elements designated as "ether" (viyat)—namely, the elemental ether and its presiding deities—can undergo origination in the form of acquiring specific attributes dependent on another [Brahman], those scriptural texts concerning their origination possess greater authority. This is because they have a wider scope, encompassing all such cases, and because they are supported by the inference: "Ether possesses origination, because it has limited power, like a jar."

Because it is logically untenable otherwise, and because the scriptural statement regarding beginninglessness—though frequent—is weak due to its limited scope and impossibility of being applied literally to past entities, it is proper to interpret it figuratively; furthermore, since it is established by scripture that "Prāṇa, Śraddhā, and Ākāśa arise part by part," the single term denoting non-origination applies to Viriñca and Brahmā just as the word "Brahman" does [to Viṣṇu], and because it would contradict the proposition [of the Upanishads] that "He created all this," as stated in: "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone."

Because of the contradiction with the abundance of previously cited scriptural texts on origination (such as "From this, space was produced"), it is logical that the relationship between ether and Brahman as primary and secondary [respectively] is appropriate. In this manner, the birth of primordial matter (prakṛti), the individual soul, consciousness, time, the Vedas, the great principle (mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and so forth—consisting in the attainment of specific qualities dependent upon another—should also be understood as described. As for the result, however, there is the refutation and resolution of the objection regarding the Lord's authorship of the entire universe. || 1 ||
Oṃ. By this, Mātariśvan is explained. Oṃ. 2.

Here, the connection [of the topic] is established either by the scriptural sequence beginning with "from space, air" (*ākāśādvāyuḥ*), or by the extension of the previously stated reasoning. Although the word "air" (*vāyu*) includes both the primary elemental air and those who preside over it—both primary and secondary—it is the primary air alone that is the subject of this inquiry, because it is the primary air that serves as the cause for dispute. The doubt here in this context is whether air possesses an origin, characterized by the attainment of specific qualities dependent on another, or whether it does not possess an origin. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not possess an origin, based on the scripture: "Fire, water, and earth, as well as space—these are non-eternal; but air, indeed, is eternal."

Nor can there be any room for objection on the grounds that this [text] has a figurative meaning, just as the scriptural statement regarding the non-origination of space does; for if air were subject to birth just like space, it would be impossible to state that air is eternal prior to the non-origination of fire, water, and earth. Nor can it be argued that because the words "space" and so forth refer only to the elements, the specific mention of the eternity of air—which is eternally existent by its own nature—follows from the impossibility of stating air's eternity prior to the non-origination of the elements.

Because there is no reason to accept [the elements] as mere material entities (*bhūtamātra*); because the Śruti, by specifically stating that Vāyu alone is conscious—namely, "Fire, water, earth, and space: these are insentient; Vāyu indeed is conscious"—excludes the possibility of possessing the eternal nature common to all individual souls (*jīva*); because [Vāyu] is the object of worship for all the gods as stated in the mantra "O, where indeed..."; and because the Śruti states that Vāyu is devoid of rising and setting—"He neither rises nor sets."

[Objection: Air is not subject to birth because it is supremely eternal and supremely conscious, like the Lord (Īśvara), and so forth, according to such reasoning. Likewise, even though air possesses many reasons pervaded by eternality, its being subject to birth would contradict experience. [Reply: The established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: Air is indeed subject to birth in the form of attaining a specific state dependent on another, namely its connection with a body. This is because of scriptural texts concerning its origin, such as "The vital breath (prāṇa) [arose] from air," and so forth; because of the reasoning regarding its limited power; and because of the hearing of such a state of being produced.

For this [jīva] also, like Īśvara, there would be the consequence of lacking such a nature of birth, and because it would entail the fallacy of their contradictory independence. Nor is there any contradiction with the aforementioned Śrutis and other authorities; for all of that is consistent when intended as the eternality of knowledge distinct from its own essential nature (svarūpa). As for the fruit [of the practice], however, it is as before. || 2 ||
|| Oṃ, but the non-existence of that which exists is not possible, because it is logically untenable; oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt: "Just as there is the birth of things such as the sky, which are otherwise impossible to be born, let there likewise be a birth for Īśvara. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu, who is described as the creator of all, possesses birth or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that he indeed possesses birth, because of the scriptural hearing of his birth in the passage, "From the non-existent, the existent was born," where the word "existent" refers to Īśvara. Nor can it be argued that this contradicts scriptural texts concerning his beginninglessness, such as, "He is neither born nor does he die."

This is because the scriptural statement regarding "birth" can be consistently explained as referring to the attainment of specific qualities dependent on another, while the statement regarding its own nature refers to beginninglessness; otherwise, the same logic would apply to the previously mentioned conscious primordial matter (*cit-prakṛti*) and so forth, as there is no difference in their being beginningless in relation to their bodies. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Although the Lord is equal to the nature of consciousness (*cit-prakṛti*) due to the beginninglessness of bodies and so forth, because He is independent and because it is logically untenable for the non-existent to be a cause—given the Śruti, "the existent was born from the existent"—and because the Śruti, "Brahman indeed was the non-existent; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the existent," intends to show that Vāyu is produced by the Lord, Viṣṇu does not possess an origination consisting in the attainment of specific qualities dependent on another. As for the result [of this discussion], however, it concerns the refutation and resolution of the objection regarding His being the creator of the entire universe. || 3 ||
|| Oṃ, [the self] consists of light, for thus it says; Oṃ. || 4 ||

Thus, when it is established that the Lord and the non-Lord possess birth and non-birth respectively, and when—by the aforementioned reasoning—it is proven that light and so forth are produced by the Lord, then its birth from something else elsewhere is also established.

The connection [of this section] is stated as "it is said, 'no'. There is a doubt: does the elemental deity of fire arise from the deity of air, just as [the deity of air arises] from Īśvara, or does it arise directly from Īśvara? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it arises from air alone, based on the scriptural text, "From air, fire. It must be replied that this [text] refers merely to air being a door (an instrument). For if [Īśvara] were capable of creating even without that [air], the door would be useless; but if He were incapable, then the status of being born from air would follow independently [of His will].

Because of the scriptural statement, "He created that fire," it is logical that fire is born from both Īśvara and Vāyu; furthermore, if it were held to originate from Īśvara alone, it would lack authority due to its contradiction with the aforementioned scripture. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: fire possesses birth independently from Īśvara alone, because of the scriptural statement, "He created that fire."

Even for the Lord, who is capable of creating without depending on anything else, the creation of the element fire and its deity through the medium of the element air and its deity—designated by the word "vāyu"—is possible as a mere sport (*līlā*). Since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) against the scriptural statement "From air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*) being taken in a secondary sense (*dvaramātra*), there is no contradiction [with other texts]. In the theory that [air] is the cause, although the word "vāyu" is primary when applied to the Lord, and thus the fact that the element fire and its deity are born from Him is established, the doubt that they might likewise be born from the element air and its deity is set aside; this is the distinction.

In the doctrine of non-difference (*tadananya-naya*), the logical consequence that other means of realization (*sādhana*) lack independence has been refuted; however, it should be understood that here [in this system], such dependence is established by scripture (*śruti*). As for the fruit (*phala*), it is as before. || 4 ||
Oṃ, the waters, Oṃ. 5.

The connection here is that, immediately following the discussion of fire (*tejas*), the specific cause of water is now being considered. Furthermore, the connection concerns whether the elemental water and its presiding deity arise independently—like Īśvara and others—or from the elemental fire and its presiding deity. Based on the scriptural statement, "From fire, water [arose]," it is initially concluded that they arise from the elemental fire and its presiding deity. Nor does this contradict the scriptural text: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it created the waters."

[The opponent argues: "By the reasoning that water produced from fire is seen in the case of sweat—namely, 'water is produced from fire because it possesses the nature of water, like sweat and so forth'—and by the concordant and powerful Vedic scripture, 'From that [fire], indeed, waters were born,' this [other] scripture is sublated and thus lacks authority. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: According to the scriptural statement, "He emitted those waters," the birth of the elements of fire and their presiding deities also occurs from the Lord alone.

Regarding the scriptural statement that water arises from fire, such as "He created all this" and "Viṣṇu is indeed the creator of everything," [the text] is intended merely as a means (dvāra), because the word "all" occurring in such Śruti and Smṛti passages has its primary meaning in Viṣṇu, because no other entity possesses inherent power, and because, according to the previously stated direction, He resides therein and thus produces earth and the rest. || 5 ||
Oṃ. [The prāṇa] is the earth, because of its specific function, its form, and other reasons such as the difference in scriptural passages. Oṃ. (Sūtra 6)

Since the status of being a door (dvāratva) is established by the reasoning already stated, the specific point under consideration here is: through what particular door [does the transition occur]? This constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*). The doubt is as follows: Are the waters the door for the Lord’s creation of food, or are they the door for the creation of earth? Since the two scriptural passages—"The waters thought" (*āpa aikṣanta*) and "They created food" (*tā annamasṛjanta*), and "From the waters, earth" (*adbhyaḥ pṛthivī*)—have mutually contradictory meanings that leave no room for alternative interpretations, and since there is no means of deciding between them, the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that neither of them serves as the door.

Because of the scriptural mention of "food" (anna) in such passages as "From water, food is produced" and "They created food," which—by gaining the merit of having well-known meanings—must be understood as referring to the commonly known food rather than the earth; for this is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being born from rain, as seen in the statement, "Wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant. Furthermore, since it would contradict the scriptural text "From plants, food [arises]," it is impossible to understand the word *pṛthu* as referring to anything other than the earth.

Because of the contradiction with the aforementioned scriptural statements, it is untenable that water serves as the medium (*dvāra*) in both cases; because it would entail numerous unwarranted assumptions, it is also untenable that food is produced from both [water and fire]; and because this would necessitate abandoning the primary meaning [of the texts], it is likewise untenable that food is produced from water through a succession of steps. Thus, the two scriptural passages appear to be without authority. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since the scriptures, being of non-human origin and thus free from defects, cannot possibly lack authority, one must necessarily accept some other meaning [for the texts].

Because of the scriptural statement, "They created food," in the preceding passage; because of the subsequent statements, "It created fire" and "It created water," followed by the hearing of the phrase, "Of those [waters], making each threefold"; because this constitutes a context concerning the elements (*bhūta*); because of the hearing of the black form in the words, "That which is black is of food"; and because that [blackness] possesses the characteristic mark of earth according to the Smṛti, "The earth is black by its very nature."

Because the word *anna* (food) refers to the earth, based on both indicative marks (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), as well as the Vedic usage: "Water and earth are food" (*āpaśca pṛthivī cānnam*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the indicative mark because the word *anna* in the two sentences beginning with "Wherever it rains" (*yatra kva ca varṣati*), although denoting the earth, can—by necessity and through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—be understood as referring to that which consists of earth, just as in the passage "Fire is the food" (*tejo 'śitam*) it is understood as referring to that which consists of fire; thus, water serves as the instrument specifically for the birth of the earth.
As for the result, however, the objection and resolution concern the fact that [Brahman] is the direct cause of everything by means of other entities. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ, but it is from that very meditation on Him, because of His characteristic marks, that He [is the cause], oṃ. || 7 ||

Having thus stated that there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding birth in relation to the *adhibhūta*, *adhidaiva*, and *janman*, the connection [of this section] is that it now states the absence of contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding their dissolution (*laya*). Since it has been established that the *adhibhūta* and *adhidaiva* elements under discussion, such as ether (*viyat*) and so forth, dissolve because they possess the quality of being born, a doubt arises as to whether the agent of that dissolution is Rudra or Viṣṇu. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it must be Rudra alone, because he is universally renowned as the destroyer. "Rudra [is... [the text continues].

Furthermore, in the Śruti passage "Viśāntaka" (the Destroyer of the Universe), the term *antaka* denotes his status as the annihilator. As for the scriptural texts regarding Viṣṇu’s role as the annihilator—such as "that into which they enter when they depart" and "to whom the world goes at the time of death"—these lack authority because they contradict the Śruti concerning Rudra’s status as the annihilator, which is supported by reasoning such as: "Viṣṇu is not the slayer, because he is the progenitor and the protector, like a father and so forth. For this very reason, the claim that Rudra acts as the instrument for Viṣṇu’s annihilation is also untenable. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Viṣṇu alone is the agent of the dissolution of all things. This is because, in the Śruti passage beginning with "By meditating upon Him," the fact that even the beginningless [world] is dependent on Viṣṇu implies—by the logic of *kaimutya* (how much more so)—that the dissolution of the world, which has a beginning, is likewise dependent on Him. Furthermore, this is clearly perceived in various Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as: "He to whom the world goes at the time of the final transition, He is our Hari"; "He who dissolves all this"; and "The creator, the protector, and the destroyer—He alone is Hari."

The scriptural text regarding Rudra’s role as the destroyer, such as the Smṛti passage beginning with "The Lord is merely the instrumental cause," refers to Rudra being the instrument (*dvāratva*) in only certain instances of destruction. As for the logical argument: since the failure of fathers and others to kill [their children] is caused by the defect of attachment (*mamatā-doṣa*), rather than being caused by their status as fathers, this defect does not apply to Hari, who is faultless and distinct from the world; thus, the argument is irrelevant. The purpose [of this discussion], however, is the refutation and resolution of the objection raised against the quality of being the destroyer as stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra*. 7.
|| Oṃ, but here the sequence is established by way of reversal; Oṃ || 8 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the inquiry as to by what sequence the dissolution of everything is accomplished. The doubt is whether the elements of the manifest world (*adhibhūta*) dissolve in accordance with the order of their birth or in reverse order. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is precisely according to the order of birth; for there is an abundance of scriptural texts regarding sequential dissolution, such as: "It is produced in sequence and dissolved in sequence," "Its origin and dissolution are in sequence," and "Its production and dissolution are indeed in sequence."

As for the statement that dissolution occurs out of order (*vyutkramāt*), this is because such a scriptural teaching is sublated by the more powerful scriptural teaching of sequential dissolution, which is generally observed in the world and supported by reasoning. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that they dissolve precisely out of order, based on the unambiguous scriptural teaching of dissolution: "And dissolution is out of order. As for the scriptural teachings regarding sequential dissolution, [it is said]: "Two kinds of sequence are taught: namely, out-of-order (*vyutkrama*) and in-order (*anukrama*)."

Because the Śruti passage, "One [element] at creation and another at dissolution," etc., allows for even a reversal of order by treating it as a valid sequence; because in the world, the destruction of earlier-born things is caused by a lack of capacity; and because here, according to Smṛti such as "Since the former [elements] belong to Viṣṇu," the dissolution of earlier-born things later on is possible due to their increased capacity, the previously stated reasoning is not decisive, and thus there is no sublation of the Śruti regarding the reversed order.

As for the result: since there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning dissolution (laya-śruti), one or the other would lack authority; and because that would lead to a loss of confidence in other [scriptures] as well, Viṣṇu’s status as the destroyer and so forth would not be established. Therefore, the objection and its resolution [are presented]. || 8 ||
|| Oṃ. If it be argued that consciousness and the mind [arise] in succession within the interval because of their respective signs, we say no, because there is no distinction. Oṃ. 9 ||
But the designation [of the Self] as "moving and non-moving" must be figurative, based on its dependence on those [bodies], because it exists when they exist. Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is established by the removal of any suspicion regarding an exception to the previously stated rule that dissolution occurs in reverse order. The doubt is as follows: do all the elements under discussion dissolve in reverse order, or do some dissolve in the regular order? As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

Regarding the statement "and from the mind, consciousness," since the principles of the heard [Veda] and the mental consciousness arise in that sequence, their dissolution occurs in that very same order, according to the scriptural teaching: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self of knowledge. Therefore, it is not correct to argue that in the phrase "and from the mind, consciousness," the words "mind" and "consciousness" do not refer to the *tattvas* (principles), but rather refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and cognition (*avabodha*), while other [principles] dissolve out of order except for the mental consciousness-principle.

Because these two terms refer primarily to the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*vijñāna*), they must be taken in their primary sense, as it is improper to abandon the primary meaning. As for the statement that "dissolution occurs out of order," the scriptural teaching regarding the dissolution of everything out of order is set aside by the scriptural teaching of the sequential dissolution of the mind and the intellect. This is because the former is supported by the reasoning that it follows worldly observation—where some things are seen to dissolve in sequence and others out of sequence. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because the terms *manas* and *vijñāna* are observed to be used respectively for the internal organ (*antarendriya*) and the principle of consciousness (*vijñānatattva*), they lack the status of denoting the mere principle [of the mind] alone; thus, they would apply primarily even to the sense organs and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the expression "the consciousness of the mind" (*manaso vijñānam*), this contradicts the Smṛti which states: "The principle of consciousness (*vijñānatattva*) arose from the Great One (Mahat) and from the Four-faced One (Brahmā)."

Because it is impossible for them to have reality as their object, and because they refer respectively to the internal organ and the cognition produced by it, there is no specific evidence regarding the order of the arising and dissolution of the mind (*manas*) and the individual consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, since the scripture states that "all this arises in sequence and dissolves out of sequence," and because of the teaching on the dissolution of everything out of sequence, all [elements] dissolve precisely in reverse order. As for the result, however, since there would be a lack of authority due to the contradiction between the two scriptural passages, the previously mentioned objection regarding the creatorship and destroyerhood [of Brahman] is resolved through their harmonization. || 9 ||
|| Oṃ. The Self [is not produced], because it is not heard [to be so] in scripture, and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. Oṃ. || 10 ||

Since the Śruti has thus stated that everything other than Brahman undergoes dissolution through a process of inversion, a doubt arises as to whether Brahman itself might likewise be subject to such dissolution. Consequently, there is a connection [between this section and the preceding one]. The doubt concerns whether Viṣṇu, who is the subject under discussion as the agent of the creation and dissolution of all things, is subject to dissolution known as the destruction of the body or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that he too is dissolved, based on the text: "Having dissolved all this, he merges into internal darkness"; thus, it is concluded that he dissolves. However, the Śruti passage, "The eternal among the non-eternal," is sublated by the aforementioned Śruti supported by reasoning, namely: "Viṣṇu is subject to dissolution because he is sentient, like the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor can the Śruti regarding dissolution be interpreted as meaning "being concealed," for there is no basis for such an interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "But [it is] impossible": although it was stated there that the Lord does not originate by virtue of His own independence, it was argued that the assumption of a body for the sake of *līlā* (divine play) is logically possible. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Viṣṇu does not possess dissolution known as the destruction of the body, because there is a lack of evidence [for such a thing].

Regarding the statement "it dissolves into the mind" (*manasi līyate*), the *Śruti* says: "That which was covered by the unreal, non-existent [Tamas]" (*tucchenābhvapihitam yadāsīt*). In this passage, having first stated the dissolution of everything in the words "neither being nor non-being existed" (*nāsadāsīt*), it then describes the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) with the words "Tamas existed" (*tama āsīt*), and further speaks of the concealment of Brahman and its subsequent manifestation. This is confirmed by another *Śruti*, the *Paiṅgi-śruti*, which states: "Dissolved in Tamas, one perceives Nature (*prakṛti*), the Person (*puruṣa*), and Time; no one perceives Him. Thus, the term "concealed" (*apihita*) carries this meaning. Otherwise, the verse "The Eternal among the eternals... (*nityo nityānām*) would be contradicted.

This is because it would contradict numerous scriptural passages on eternity, such as "He is eternal, devoid of qualities, and all-pervading. Furthermore, reasoning that contradicts scripture lacks authority. As for the result, however, since dissolution into Brahman precludes creation and so forth, there is an objection regarding that [result] which is here resolved. 10.
Oṃ. [The Self] is indeed a knower for this very reason. Oṃ. (11)
|| Oṃ, and because of reasoning, oṃ. ||

Thus, having conducted a brief investigation into the elements (*adhibhūta*) and so forth according to the maxim of the needle and the kettle (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*), there is now a transition: up to the end of this chapter, an extensive investigation into the individual soul (*jīva*) is undertaken. The doubt is as follows: does the individual soul have an origin, or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not have an origin.

Because the eternity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by the scriptural text, "Of the eternal, the eternal," where the word "eternal" ending in the genitive case denotes the eternity of the souls; and because that scriptural statement of the soul's eternity is supported by reasoning—namely, that no cause for the production of the soul's essential nature (*svarūpa*) is perceived, and thus it is devoid of a cause—and thereby sublates the scriptural passage regarding its origination, such as "All these [souls] emerge from the conscious Self. Nor should it be argued that, just as ether and the other elements undergo birth in the form of the acquisition of specific qualities dependent on another despite being devoid of a cause for the production of their essential nature, the same applies to the soul.

If the scriptural statement regarding birth were intended to mean such an origination [of the individual soul], then the scriptural statement regarding non-origination would also logically be intended to mean the absence of that [origination] in the case of the individual soul and ether, just as it is in the case of Brahman; for it is improper to assume multiple meanings for a single term. And thus, the previously mentioned objection—that there remains a contradiction with those [scriptures]—is raised here once again. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

"These very conscious selves, being indestructible, enter the supreme light; they arise as indeed indestructible. Thus, although there is no origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) in its own essential nature because that nature is indestructible, the scriptural texts concerning its origination and non-origination are not in conflict. This is because the text regarding origination refers to the attainment of specific states dependent on others through the origination of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), while the text regarding non-origination refers to the essential nature of those very adjuncts. Therefore, by having different scopes, there is no contradiction between them.

Since there is no scriptural statement regarding the origination of Brahman in the form of the acquisition of a specific state dependent on another, the scriptural statements of its non-origination may indeed intend its absence [of such change]. However, because such scriptural statements of non-origination exist for the individual soul (jīva) and others, it is improper to claim that they intend its absence; furthermore, it is more logical to accept multiple meanings [for the term "origination"]. Therefore, the individual soul possesses such an origination known as its connection with a body. As for the result [of this discussion], it concerns the objection and resolution regarding [Brahman's] being the creator of all things. || 11 ||
Oṃ, [the teaching] on the departure, the going, and the returning. Oṃ. 12.

|| Oṃ, and by its own nature, in the two subsequent [sūtras], oṃ. || Oṃ, if it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural teaching [to the contrary], we say no, on account of the context of the other [sūtra], oṃ. || Oṃ, and on account of the words "self" and "own," oṃ. || Oṃ, there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood, oṃ. || Oṃ, if it be argued that this is due to a difference in location, we say no, because of our own admission; for [it is said to reside] in the heart, oṃ. || Oṃ, or rather, on account of its qualities, as in the world, oṃ.

Since origination and non-origination have been considered with respect to the *jīva* as the subject (*dharmī*), here the atomicity and magnitude—which are its attributes (*dharma*)—are considered; this constitutes the logical connection (*saṅgati*). The doubt is whether the *jīva* under discussion is all-pervading (*vyāpta*) or atomic (*aṇu*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is all-pervading. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the pervasion of the Self: "By pervasion, the consciousness of the Self [is established], and [the Selves] are without qualities" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6), where the plural ending indicates the pervasion of many Selves. Furthermore, since the general rule that plurality is based on difference has no exception here—as there is none in cases such as "the two who drink the Truth" (Ṛgveda)—this passage refers to the individual *jīvas*.

Regarding the scriptural text stating that "this self is indeed minute" (*aṇu*), since the doctrine of the soul's minuteness is untenable—because if it were minute, it would be impossible for it to have knowledge of touch and so forth in relation to the entire body, and because the view that its knowledge of touch and so forth arises from having the same dimensions as the body is vitiated by the fault stated in the principle "on account of impossibility in one" (*naikasminnasambhavāt*)—it is established that this scripture lacks authority when it contradicts more powerful scriptures, owing to its being supported by the reasoning consisting in the soul's knowledge of touch and so forth throughout all bodies.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of touch and so forth is possible through partial pervasion (*aṃśavyāpti*), and thus the reasoning [of total pervasion] is irrelevant; for since the parts would be sentient, it would be impossible for many of them to achieve unanimity simultaneously, which would lead to the consequence of the body being torn apart by contradictory actions, or else result in the body being entirely inactive. This is because pervasion must be of the whole nature (*svarūpavyāpti*) alone. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: The individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic (*aṇu*), because of its possession of departure and motion, as stated in the Śruti: "Having departed from this body, he goes to that world; from that world, he comes back to this world," just like a bird. As for their [the soul's] pervasion, it is not observed in the case of space and other such things.

Because it is impossible for [the soul] to be pervaded by those [qualities], and because [if it were so] the consequence would be its impermanence and other such defects, a middle-sized dimension is refuted; thus, atomicity alone is established. This is also supported by the Śruti text: "For this Self is atomic" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1). As for the Śruti text "The selves are indeed all-pervading" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13), that refers to Viṣṇu, as it occurs within a section concerning Viṣṇu who creates this world. Furthermore, because of the word "Self" heard in the supplementary passage "for this Self has risen above the power of measurement," and because of the indicative mark of being immeasurable, the plural number is justified according to the principle of the "cave-dweller" (guhā-naya) [where the singular is used for the plural]. Therefore, that text is devoted to Viṣṇu.

Just as a drop of sandalwood paste situated in one part of the body pervades the entire body through its own parts, so too, since the individual soul (jīva) is properly located in the region of the heart according to the scriptural statement "This Self [is indeed] in the heart," it is possible for sensory cognitions such as touch to arise through the pervasion of its essential parts throughout the whole body; thus, this reasoning is not without purpose. As for the result, however, there is the refutation and resolution of objections regarding the harmony of the scriptures. 12.
Oṃ. There is a distinction, just as in the case of fragrance; and thus it shows. Oṃ. 13.

In this context, the connection with the previous objection is as follows: if the individual soul (*jīva*) were atomic (*aṇu*), then it would be impossible for a yogi to possess multiple forms. The doubt is whether the soul is of a single form or of multiple forms. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is of a single form, because of the scriptural text: "He is one-fold, not seven-fold. Furthermore, this is supported by reasoning: although multiplicity of forms is possible through the power of yoga by means of a plurality of bodies within a non-material self, such multiplicity is impossible in an atom.

The claim that [the Lord] possesses many forms even through parts as small as an atom is untenable, because it contradicts the scriptural testimony of His being partless, namely, "He is eternal and without parts. As for the argument that a yogi might possess manifold forms—just like drinking the ocean—through a power that accomplishes the impossible, this is incorrect, as it would result in the yogi attaining equality with the Lord. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding manifoldness, such as "He is fivefold" or "He is sevenfold," is sublated by the reasoned scriptural testimony of His being of a single form. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Even though the individual soul (jīva) lacks parts, its possession of manifold forms is possible through a division into parts like fragrance, by virtue of a power dependent upon the grace of the Lord—whose inconceivable power is attained through yoga. Thus, the individual soul is multiform. As for the scriptural texts concerning its uniformity, they refer to the identity of its essential nature (svarūpa). Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness refer to its lack of distinct parts. As for the result [of this knowledge], it is as previously stated. 13.
Oṃ. Because of the separate instruction. Oṃ. 14.
Oṃ. But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that [name], just as in the case of the "wise one" (the Self). Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that, because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are one, the power of the soul does not depend upon the Lord. The doubt is whether the soul is different from the Lord or non-different. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they are non-different, because of the scriptural statement of the identity of the soul and the Supreme in such passages as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), where the two terms are understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is further supported by the fact that the opening of the passage is "One only, without a second," its conclusion is "That thou art," it is repeated nine times as "That thou art, That thou art," and because the oneness [of the Self] is not known through any other means of knowledge, it constitutes something previously unknown (*apūrva*).

"The delay for him lasts only so long" is because [liberation] possesses a fruit; because of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating, "by which what was unheard becomes heard"; and because it is established through analogies such as that of the clay vessel. Furthermore, because it is endowed with the six marks of interpretive intent (tātparya-liṅga), it is more numerous [in its authority]. Thus, the Śruti passages such as "Two birds... are not authoritative [as proving duality]; otherwise, there would follow the consequence that the Śrutis concerning oneness would be rendered devoid of subject matter. This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

"The distinction scripture (*bheda-śruti*)—stating, "The Supreme is distinct from the multitude of individual souls (*jīva-saṅgha*), inconceivable, supreme, and full; for the multitude of individual souls is incomplete"—is more powerful due to its status as a foundational authority (*upajīvya*). This is because it is supported by reasoning such as the fact that two things cannot occupy the same substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*) when they possess contradictory attributes (such as being full versus incomplete). As stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "The difference of one's own self from the Supreme Lord, who is known through scripture, is perceived. How can oneness be asserted in the face of this contradiction with direct experience? Thus, due to its foundational nature, the scripture of distinction possesses greater force.

Because it contradicts that [scriptural testimony] and contradicts direct experience, because the definition of the two words [tattvamasi] would be secondary if the word *tat* alone were taken in a figurative sense, and because it is logical that "That art thou" and similar passages mean "You are similar to Him" by virtue of possessing qualities such as knowledge and bliss similar to His—therefore, they cannot have identity as their primary purport. Furthermore, since the introductory and other indicators (*upakrama*, etc. establish the intended meaning only when it is not contradicted by other means of knowledge, and because it has been explained otherwise elsewhere, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*). || 14 ||
Oṃ. And because [the self] is manifested as far as the body extends, there is no fault, since that is what is seen. Oṃ. 15.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised by the statement, "Therefore, one should desire liberation from bondage," which implies that liberation follows immediately after the previously mentioned beginningless bondage. The doubt is as follows: Is the individual soul (*jīva*) eternal or non-eternal? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is non-eternal. This is because of the scriptural text, "O Brahman, he attains dissolution" (*brahmaṇi layam abhyupaiti*). Furthermore, it is because of the logical argument that since the birth of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is mentioned in the passage "He is indeed born," the birth of the reflection must necessarily follow; and because there is an invariable rule that whatever possesses birth is subject to destruction.

Furthermore, there is no grounds for the assumption that, although the limiting adjunct (upādhi) known as the body is subject to birth, there exists some other limiting adjunct of the individual soul (jīva) that is beginningless and eternal. The scriptural passage beginning with "He [is endowed] with beginningless merit" (so 'nādinā puṇyena), which speaks of the infinity resulting from the soul's connection with beginningless karma, is intended to establish the beginninglessness of the soul; it is not authoritative because it contradicts the scriptural texts regarding the soul's non-eternality supported by reasoning. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

Because the Śruti and Smṛti passages such as, "The Supreme is eternal; the individual soul (jīva) is eternal; pleasure and pain are non-eternal," would otherwise be inexplicable, an eternal and beginningless limiting adjunct (upādhi) must necessarily be postulated. Furthermore, from statements such as, "The limiting adjunct of the jīva is said to be twofold," it follows that since the adjunct of the essential nature (svarūpopādhi) is eternal and beginningless, the proximity of the adjuncts of the all-pervading Lord (bimbeśa) is likewise so; thus, the jīva is eternally beginningless. As for the scriptural texts concerning dissolution (laya), they refer to external adjuncts. || 15 ||
|| Oṃ. But because of the possibility of manifestation for that which already exists, like virility and so forth; oṃ. || 16 ||
|| Oṃ. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other. Oṃ. ||

In the preceding section, in the first sūtra concerning distinct substrates (*pṛthag-adhikaraṇa*), the teaching that one should desire liberation from bondage through that very [means] was established. Here, however, the connection is that the state of having those qualities as its essence (*tad-guṇa-sāratva*), as stated in the second sūtra of that same section, is now being established. The doubt is whether the individual soul (*jīva*) has the nature of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, or not. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it does not have the nature of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, because of such scriptural passages as, "When he is freed from suffering, he becomes blissful," and because its nature as knowledge, bliss, and so forth is not perceived at present.

Even while the "I" (aham) appears as the individual soul (jīva), it is illogical to claim that its true nature—consisting of bliss and so forth—is unperceived due to some obstruction; for there is no absence of knowledge, nor is there any other positive entity acting as an obstruction to that knowledge. Furthermore, the body and such cannot act as obstructions, because they serve merely as the locus for experience in the form of the perception of pleasure and pain. Moreover, if the soul were already of the nature of bliss and so forth, any effort toward liberation would be rendered useless.

The scriptural passages such as "Consciousness is the Self" and "That is Bliss," when confronted with the reasoning of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and other scriptural texts concerning bliss and so forth, are not authoritative [as they appear]. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as consisting of knowledge and so forth is declared by such Śruti and Smṛti texts as "The Supreme Self is eternal bliss, eternal knowledge, and eternal power" and "The gods possess eternal bliss, knowledge, and power."

Since the designation of difference—such as that the soul becomes blissful through the subsequent manifestation of its masculinity and other qualities that were unmanifest in childhood—is established in the Śruti and other scriptures, and since the non-acceptance of an obscuration for that which is of the nature of bliss and so forth would entail the consequence of its being perceived eternally; and since non-perception is logically accounted for by the necessity of accepting a specific power of obscuration, and because effort toward perfect manifestation is thus possible, this individual soul (jīva) consists of knowledge and the like. Consequently, there is no failure in the interpretation of the Śruti passage "Thus, O gods" (*evaṃ surāḥ*) through the supply of ellipsis and other such means. || 16 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord] is the agent, because the scripture has a purpose. Oṃ. (Sūtra 17)

Oṃ, because of the teaching on his dwelling, Oṃ. Oṃ, because of appropriation, Oṃ. Oṃ, and because of designation; if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the instruction regarding action, Oṃ. Oṃ, as in the case of perception, there is no fixed rule, Oṃ. Oṃ, because of the reversal of capacity, Oṃ. Oṃ, and because of the absence of meditative absorption, Oṃ. Oṃ, and just as a carpenter acts in both ways, Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: "Let there be the manifestation of bliss (*ānanda*) and other qualities that already exist [in the self], but not of agency (*kartṛtva*), because that [agency] is never absent [from the Self]. The doubt is as follows: Is the individual soul (*jīva*) an agent or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not an agent. This is because of the scriptural text, "There is no other agent" (*nānyaḥ kartā*), and because it is simpler (*lāghava*) to accept that the Lord alone possesses agency. Furthermore, in the sūtra *itaravyapadeśāt* (1.1.17) and others, by the mention of "failing to perform what is beneficial" (*hitākaraṇa*), the agency of the individual soul is negated.

Nor should it be argued that even if independent agency is denied by the Śruti and the Sūtras, let there be dependent agency; for although the power of agency may be dependent, if it were to take the form of being subject to God through the payment of wages and so forth—just as a carpenter is dependent on the person who commissions a palace—the Śruti, which states "He makes the Self subject to Himself," would be contradicted. Furthermore, if the activity were dependent on God like a wooden puppet, then agency would ultimately amount to non-agency, and like that puppet, the self would be unfit for injunctions and prohibitions.

Thus, because there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts on non-agency (*akartṛtva*) that are supported by reasoning, the scriptural text regarding the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*), namely "whatever action one performs, that one attains," is authoritative. This is established through reasoning in the form of the "otherwise-untenability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the meaningfulness of the scripture consisting of injunctions and prohibitions—which would otherwise be purposeless for the insentient, the Lord, and the liberated—and through the observation of the performance of practices that serve as means for liberation and other goals; furthermore, it is established by direct perception through the hearing of the individual soul's agency in acts such as meditation (*upāsanā*) in passages like "one should meditate upon the Self alone as the world."

Because of the two reasons—having incomplete power and having unfulfilled desires—and because its dependence is established by the Śruti text, "He is the agent and the cause," it is accepted that the individual soul possesses a dependent agency characterized by having its activity subject to the Lord, like a wooden doll. Thus, there is no contradiction with the previously cited Śruti and Smṛti texts. Furthermore, since it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the capacity for agency dependent on another is the very basis for being subject to injunctions and prohibitions, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Therefore, the individual soul is the agent. || 17 ||
Oṃ. [The soul] is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of diversity, and also because otherwise it is taught by some as being the state of a fisherman, a kitava, and so forth. Oṃ. 18.

Oṃ. From the color of the mantra, Oṃ. Oṃ. It is also recorded in Smṛti, Oṃ. Oṃ. Not so with the Supreme, like light and so forth, Oṃ. Oṃ. And they remember it, Oṃ. Oṃ. Permission and avoidance are due to connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth, Oṃ. Oṃ. And because of non-extension, there is no confusion, Oṃ. Oṃ. And it is merely a reflection, Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is established here that between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who were mentioned previously, there exists a relationship characterized by the status of the dependent and the supported; this is based on the scriptural statement, "But [the soul is] from Him" (*parāt tu tacchruteḥ*). The doubt is whether the individual soul can be determined to be a part (*aṃśa*) of the Lord or not a part (*anaṃśa*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it cannot be so determined. For instance, a determination of its being a part is not possible.

"The individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed portions (*aṃśas*)"—this is the scriptural statement regarding their being portions. Since it is stated that they are "indeed portions," there is no specific authority for an option (*vikalpa*) as in the case of rice and barley; nor is there an option established by differences of place, time, and so forth, as in the case of the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Therefore, the two scriptural passages do not constitute a contradiction. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: A son or other [dependent] is indeed a portion of the father or other [protector], because he is to be nourished by him like a child, because he is contained within him by having been conceived in his womb, because he depends upon him for subsistence, or because he is related to him as a subordinate entity. Thus, while being inferior to him, he is a portion of him by virtue of possessing some degree of similarity to him.

For, having introduced the subject with "This is indeed a part of the Supreme," the text states, "They designate him variously—as father, as son, as brother"—thus expressing various types of relationships; likewise, through the two scriptural passages stating both difference and non-difference—"The Supreme is one, the individual soul (jīva) is another" and "Brahman is the slaves, Brahman is the gamblers"—it is established that the status of being a part is twofold, since these statements would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, from the mantra-text "All beings are but a foot of Him" and the Smṛti passage "A portion of My very Self is in the world of living beings," it is logical to conclude that the scriptural texts denying [the soul] being a part merely intend to deny that the soul is a part consisting of the essential nature [of the Lord].

Just as there is a distinction between the two portions of light—the one presiding over the fire at the end of time (Kālāgni) and the one presiding over a firefly—based on their being the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the essential portion (*svarūpāṃśa*) respectively, as established by Smṛti and other texts cited in the Bhāṣya such as "These are the portions and parts of the Person" (*ete svāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ*); and just as there is a distinction between the two portions of the sun—the one presiding over its radiance and the one presiding over its reflection—based on whether they possess independence of activity or not, and based on the presence or absence of full power; and just as there is a distinction between the individual souls (jīvas) who are the incarnations of the Lord (such as Matsya) and the Lord Himself, based on whether they are reflections of the Lord or the Lord Himself, even though there is no difference in their being portions of the Lord—so too, because of the lack of equality [between the jīva and the Lord], this is indeed the means of valid knowledge that resolves the contradiction between the two Śrutis. || 17 ||
Oṃ. [The soul is] not [perceived] because of the restriction of being invisible. Oṃ. 19.

Oṃ. And it is the same even in the case of the Abhindhya and others; Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul] is limited by the span of a thumb, we say no, because of its being contained within [the body]; Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised by the refutation of the previous argument—that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection—on the grounds that there is no equality between the *jīva* and the source of descent (the Lord). The doubt is as follows: Is the *jīva* a reflection of the Lord, or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not. This is because of scriptural texts denying the relationship of original and reflection, such as: "There is no relation, nor is the *jīva* dependent on the Supreme"; and because [the *jīva*] possesses diversity—such as being a god, demon, human, or animal—just like a jar or other objects; and because of the logical conclusion that the *jīvas* are not reflections of a single [source].

The scriptural statement, "He became the counterpart of every form" (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva*), is not authoritative because it contradicts prior scriptural passages supported by reason. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Even though the original object (*bimba*) is of a single nature, the diversity of the reflected image (*pratibimba*)—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is logically possible due to the diversity of the beginningless adjuncts (*upādhi*) of its own nature, such as ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and so forth. Thus, the soul is the reflection according to the scripture "He became the counterpart of every form. The other scriptural passage stating that there is no connection is intended to negate the status of being a reflection based on the dependence upon distinct adjuncts. Here, for each respective view, the objection to the consistency [of the scriptures] and its resolution must be stated regarding the results.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fourth quarter.
Oṃ, likewise the vital breaths, Oṃ. 1.
|| Oṃ, because a secondary sense is impossible, oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of conformity with the initial proposition, oṃ. ||

The connection with what precedes has already been stated. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) have an origin or not; the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they do not, because of the scriptural text regarding their beginninglessness: "In the beginning, the vital breaths alone were this. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural text, "He created all this," for that general statement is set aside by the specific earlier scriptural text, which is more authoritative due to its lack of an intervening generality and its specific nature.

Nor is there a contradiction with the specific scriptural statement: "From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the senses. For the claim that the scripture is invalid—on the grounds that it contradicts the Smṛti statement "the senses have no material cause" and the reasoning that they thus lack a material cause—is refuted. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: The birth of the vital breaths is established by specific scriptural texts such as "He created the prāṇa," "He [created] the prāṇas," and "From this [Brahman] is born the prāṇa," which are supported by the general scriptural text "He [created] all this," as well as by the reasoning already stated in the section on ether (viyat)—namely, that [the prāṇas] possess limited power and so forth. Thus, their birth is proven.

"Because of the Smṛti statement, 'These [prāṇas] are eternal by virtue of their subtlety,' although they possess beginninglessness due to their subtle form and lack of material cause, there is no sublation of the scriptural texts on beginninglessness or of logical reasoning, because at the time of creation there exists an accumulation of parts such as the elements; therefore, the prāṇas have an origin. Here too, for each section (*adhikaraṇa*), the results of the prima facie and final positions are as previously stated. (1)
Oṃ. That [Brahman] is the cause, because of the Vedic revelation; Oṃ. (Sūtra 2)

Here, the connection [of this section] arises from the justification that the mind is born from within the primary vital breath (*prāṇa*). Regarding the doubt as to whether the mind possesses birth or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not. This is because of the scriptural text: "The mind is eternal due to its beginninglessness; for no person exists without a mind, while other [senses] are non-eternal. Since this text, having stated the non-eternality of the other senses, specifically declares the eternity of the mind, it constitutes a specific revelation (*viśeṣa-śruti*); therefore, any contradiction with this would be untenable. Furthermore, it is improper to argue that the mind's birth is established by the force of Vedic texts on creation, just as in the previous case [of the breath], because such an argument is logically inconsistent.

Furthermore, if the mind (*manas*) were to have a beginning, it would follow that the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which is rooted in it, would also have a beginning; thus, the scriptural statement regarding its birth would be devoid of authority. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Since the mind’s birth is established by a specific scriptural statement—namely, "the mind and all the sense organs"—which mentions the birth of the mind separately from the sense organs; and since the Smṛti text "because of slight accumulation" does not contradict its beginninglessness (given that this slight accumulation is merely a cause for minor growth), thereby supporting such scriptural passages as "the mind is eternal"; and because there is no possibility of the bondage [of the self] having a beginning; therefore, the mind indeed possesses origination.
|| Oṃ, because speech is preceded by that [Oṃ]. || 3 ||

Here, the connection [of this section] arises from the refutation and subsequent establishment of the view that the mind is born within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
