There is a doubt as to whether the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) has an origin or not; the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it does not. This is based on the scripture: "Speech indeed is eternal, for it is not produced; for in this [speech], the Veda remains" (*vāgvāva nityā...*), and by the reasoning stated in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), which describes its being the locus of the Veda in the form of the capacity for the eternal utterance of the Vedas. Furthermore, the claim that the scriptural texts regarding birth and non-birth refer respectively to the subtle form and the grossly developed form—thereby avoiding contradiction with the aforementioned scripture—is also refuted.

It has already been refuted that the word *vāk* (speech) refers to the Veda rather than the sense organ, because for one who is capable of constantly reciting the Veda, the accumulation [of merit] would be useless; furthermore, by the very statement that it is based on the Veda (*śruti*), it is established that the word *vāk* pertains to the Veda. Therefore, the scriptural passage regarding the birth of speech, "And all the sense organs," is not authoritative [for proving the origin of the sense organs]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the scripture states, "Mind alone is the prior form, speech is the subsequent form," speech is heard to have mind as its cause.

Furthermore, because the word *vāk* (speech) [in the context of] "one speaks with speech" (*vācā vyāharati*)—by virtue of the force of the preceding sentence, by the authority of another Śruti passage stating "from the mind alone speech is produced, and from speech comes utterance," and because it refers to the sense organ (*indriya*)—the Śruti's declaration of its eternity is justified through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), intending merely the proximity of the eternal Veda, as supported by the Smṛti: "The eternity of the organ of speech consists in its proximity to the Śruti and its fitness. This is also because the metaphor serves the purpose of establishing the capacity for its utterance. Thus, according to the Śruti on birth, the organ of speech is indeed subject to origination. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because the sevenfold course has been specified, Oṃ. (Sūtra 4)
Oṃ. But since [the hands and other limbs] are situated [in the body], it is not thus. Oṃ.

The inquiry into birth was undertaken by relying on the fact that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) possess the nature of being subjects (*dharmin*). The connection [of this section] is that the inquiry into birth is undertaken by relying on the attributes (*dharma*) of number and form. Regarding the doubt as to whether there are seven vital breaths or twelve—resulting in the conclusion that there is no definitive determination—or whether there is a determination that there are twelve: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no definitive determination. This is because of two scriptural passages conveying contradictory numbers: "Seven vital breaths come forth" and "These vital breaths are twelve—the twelve months, the twelve Ādityas."

Nor should it be argued that even though there are twelve breaths (*prāṇas*), the scriptural mention of seven is consistent with the logic of the fifty [elements]. This is because the assertion of sevenfoldness is untenable in the absence of a limiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Furthermore, since there is no reason for mentioning five along with these [seven], their absence is understood. Moreover, the scriptural mention of sevenfoldness is more authoritative due to the following reasoning: based on the Smṛti statement, "There are exactly seven Maruts externally, and likewise seven breaths within the self," the number of the presiding deities (*abhimānin*) is seven; and by the rule that the number of the presiding deity and the object presided over must be equal, the objects they preside over are also sevenfold. Thus, the scriptural testimony of sevenfoldness prevails.

The scriptural statement regarding the number twelve is also more authoritative because it is supported by the reasoning previously mentioned and by the supplementary passage stating "twelve months" and so forth; for, since the deities mentioned in that supplementary passage—such as the twelve Ādityas—are the presiding deities of the sense organs as well, the mention of "twelve months" and so on is made with the intention that those very deities are the presiding deities of the sense organs. This is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Even though there are twelve vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the statement that they are "sevenfold, deposited in the cave" is justified by the intention to specify those limited by the nature of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), as mentioned in the supplementary passage. Thus, the mention of seven—namely, the ear, eye, skin, tongue, nose, mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—is appropriate. Since speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals differ in their nature as organs of action (*karmendriya*), they are not included in the recitation alongside the [seven] in the scriptural mention of "seven"; therefore, it is impossible to suspect the non-existence of the others based on that alone. Consequently, the determination is simply that there are twelve, according to the scriptural statement of twelve. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ, and the atoms, Oṃ || 5 ||

In the preceding section, the number of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) was investigated; here, their dimension is considered—this is the connection. When the doubt arises whether the *prāṇas* are atomic or all-pervasive, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are all-pervasive, because of the scriptural text stating their pervasiveness: "Like an eye stretched out in the sky. By mentioning the pervasiveness of the eye as an illustrative example for this pervasiveness, [the text supports the prima facie view].

Furthermore, because of its strength—evidenced by the logical possibility of hearing and seeing from afar, as well as remembering—and because it renders even that which is very firm into an object of perception, the scriptural statement regarding minuteness, "He sees with atoms," is not authoritative, as it is sublated by the more powerful scriptural statements concerning pervasiveness. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

For instance, because the scripture states, "Just as the light of the minute eye is pervasive, even so is the light of this person pervasive; for this person is indeed minute," and because the statement regarding the atom-like size of the Self is authoritative due to its being supported by the illustration of the eye and its status as a specific scriptural teaching, it establishes minuteness and so forth. Furthermore, although the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are minute by their very nature, their pervasiveness through their fiery essence (*tejas*) explains how they are capable of hearing and seeing from a distance.

For it is possible that even the scriptural statement regarding the general pervasiveness of the vital breaths (prāṇas) intends their capacity for manifestation rather than their actual spatial pervasion; furthermore, if the prāṇas were pervasive by their very nature, it would follow that everything would be directly perceived [by them], which would result in the impossibility of deep sleep. Therefore, the prāṇas are atomic (aṇavaḥ). || 5 ||
Oṃ, and he is the most excellent, Oṃ. 6.
Oṃ. [The individual self] is not the vital air or its functions, because it is taught separately.

The connection [of this section] is that, immediately after the inquiry into the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), there follows an inquiry into their impeller. Regarding the doubt as to whether the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is born or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not so. This is because of the scriptural text, "This breath does not rise," and because of the reasoning supported by the statement in Smṛti, "That which is its attainment and its abandonment is likewise birth and death," which establishes that since it bestows birth and death upon all, it cannot itself be subject to birth and so forth; thus, this scriptural passage possesses greater authority than the texts concerning mere origination, such as "He created the vital breaths."

Furthermore, the scriptural mention of birth for the term *prāṇa*—as in the passage beginning, "In the vital air and in the external wind"—is also consistent with its denoting things such as the vital breath. Nor is this point already covered by the sūtra, "By this, Mātariśvan is explained," because although that [sūtra] speaks of the birth of the external and primary wind, here [the discussion concerns] the internal *prāṇa* and so forth, which is not appropriate there; for that [internal *prāṇa*] is the cause of the birth and death of all beings.

The objection arises from the further doubt that it is impossible for such [a thing] to engage in activity for the sake of producing a cause of suffering. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: because the scripture states, "Indeed, this one remains subtle and emerges in a gross form," there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning birth and non-birth, since they refer to the fact that the vital breath (prāṇa) does not arise from its own nature nor from the body and so forth.

Because the word *prāṇa* occurring in the passage concerning birth is shown—by its separate mention in the remainder of that very text, namely, "From *prāṇa* come faith, ether, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, food, and from food, strength, austerity, mantras, and action"—to refer to the primary *prāṇa* rather than to fire (*ceṣṭā*) and so forth, the primary *prāṇa* is indeed born. Although it is impossible for it to have an origin other than itself by its own nature, its birth from Viṣṇu, who possesses supreme majesty, is established because the scripture itself states, "together with *prāṇa*" (*saprāṇam*). Thus, its birth is logically consistent. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ. But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. Oṃ. || 7 ||
Oṃ. And because it is not something produced, there is no fault; for thus the scripture shows. Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: the birth of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) mentioned previously is here challenged on the basis of its independence in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, the doubt is whether the principal vital breath is independent or dependent. The initial position is that it is independent, based on the scriptural text: "The vital breath does not depend on anything."

Because of the statement in the Smṛti, “By depending on whom His activities [are performed],” etc., she possesses the greatness of being the impeller of the entire universe; because she is endowed with the reasoning that she has no other support; and because of her superiority, as evidenced by the Śruti stating her dependence, “Prāṇa is situated under the control of another. Precisely due to the contradiction between this and the Śruti and reasoning regarding independence, the previously mentioned Śrutis concerning her birth lack authority. Furthermore, since the Śruti, “She arises in a gross form,” is appropriately explained as referring to the assumption of a *līlā-vigraha* (sportive body), the previously mentioned reasoning that her birth is illogical is refuted.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: The principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is dependent on another, because it is heard in scripture that, together with the senses such as sight, it likewise remains under the control of Him (the Lord), as stated: "For all this indeed rests only upon the Supreme—the vital breath and the vital breath. Furthermore, this [scriptural statement] possesses greater force because it is supported by the reasoning expressed in the statement, "Since there cannot be two Lords," which demonstrates the impossibility of a duality of lords.

And regarding the scriptural statement and logical reasoning that "all this is under the control of Prāṇa" and "Prāṇa stands under the control of another," these refer to his being a subordinate lord; for passages such as "the word 'Lord' may apply to him" are intended to mean that he is a subordinate lord who is not the supreme Lord.

Even though the term "Lord" (Īśvara) is applied equally to the eye and other organs, the status of being a subordinate lord (avāntareśvaratva) is established for the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) due to the difference between the presence and absence of activity during deep sleep; because in the absence of the individual soul's effort, there is observed a distinction between the functioning and non-functioning of the eyes and so forth, as well as between their being employed by an agent and not being so employed, according to the Śruti passage beginning with, "All these indeed are instruments" (*tāni ha vā etāni sarvāṇi karaṇāni*). Furthermore, its inclusion [in the category of the Lord] following the sūtra "He is the supervisor" (*so'dhyakṣaḥ*) will be explained in that very context. **Sūtra:** "The fivefold function is designated like that of the mind. (Oṃ pañcavṛttirmanovadvayapadiśyate Oṃ) || 8 ||

The connection [of this section] is that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are brought into proximity by the context of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), are here being investigated. When there arises a doubt as to whether these five—the *prāṇa* and the rest—can be determined as being either servants of the principal breath or its very nature, the initial position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they cannot, because of the scriptural statement regarding their servitude: "All these are indeed servants of the principal one."

This is because the scriptural passage beginning with, "This Prāṇa places the other prāṇas each separately," and the Smṛti passage beginning with, "All [the functions] such as Prāṇa, Apāna, and so forth," are more authoritative due to their being supported by reasoning—namely, that they act according to His command. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding their being His very nature, "The prāṇas and others are indeed the forms of the Principal One," is also more authoritative because it is supported by the reasoning that establishes their nature as His own, namely, that they possess His manifest, excellent qualities.

Furthermore, it is heard in such passages as, "The apāna is established in the anus and the generative organ; the prāṇa itself is established in the eyes, ears, mouth, and nose," that these [organs] possess distinct qualities. For this is not appropriate for servants, because the relationship of master and servant cannot exist between them. Since a choice between alternatives is impossible regarding a real entity, the two scriptural statements would be contradictory in meaning and thus lack authority. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

Furthermore, because the Śruti passage beginning with "Then this [Prāṇa] proceeds with five functions" describes the Mukhya-prāṇa as having five servants and five forms by means of the mind and the sense organs, there is no lack of authority in the two Śrutis due to their compatibility with reason, as both types of descriptions are accepted separately. Moreover, regarding the possession of excellent qualities by the individual [servants] mentioned after introducing them as "the other prāṇas," [it is said]: "The five primary forms are full of all qualities."

"His other five servants, beginning with Prāṇa, are also said to possess good qualities. According to this Śruti, since the relationship between master and servant is established through the gradation of the essential nature and its servants, there is no contradiction. Having introduced the other prāṇas as "servants" with the words "the other prāṇas," the fact that they are explicitly stated to possess good qualities in the passage beginning with "the anus and the generative organ are apāna" is also appropriate for the servants; thus, the prāṇas and others can indeed be determined in two ways. || 9 ||
|| Oṃ, and it is atomic; Oṃ. || 9 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt: "Let the Prāṇa also be all-pervading (vibhu), in order to possess the superior good qualities of being the impeller of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, as previously described. Regarding the doubt whether the Prāṇa is all-pervading or atomic, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is all-pervading. This is because of the scriptural statement of pervasion, such as "The Prāṇas indeed are below," and because of the reasoning based on its being the pervader of the entire universe as stated in Smṛti, such as "Since it stands pervading the entire world"; these are stronger than the scriptural statement of atomicity, "The Prāṇa is indeed atomic. Thus, the declaration of its pervasion prevails.

Nor is [the designation of] Vaiṣṇava thus subject to the charge of having a limited scope (sāvakāśa), because in another scriptural passage—"The Great One is the chief vital air (mukhyaprāṇa); by him the moving and the unmoving are pervaded"—the pervasiveness of the chief vital air is clearly perceived. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: By such scriptural texts as "This vital air is minute and named Great," the distinction between minuteness and greatness is stated according to the difference between the vital air residing within the body and that which exists outside the body. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding minuteness—"The chief vital air is indeed minute; when it departs, it departs through the channels" (nāḍībhiḥ)—is more authoritative because it is supported by the logical reason of its movement through the channels. || 9 ||
|| Oṃ. But the presiding [deities] over light and so forth [are the gods], because of the scriptural teaching; oṃ. || 10 ||
|| Oṃ, because [the self] possesses breath, like sound; oṃ. || Oṃ, and because it is eternal; oṃ. ||

Having defined the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), the connection [of this section] is that it is now considered with respect to which among them the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) belongs. Regarding the doubt as to whether the sense organs, such as the eye, are instruments of the individual soul (*jīva*) or instruments of Brahman, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are instruments of the individual soul. This is because the scriptural statement, "They call the vital breaths the instruments of the individual soul," is supported by the reasoning that they are experienced as being under the control of the individual soul; thus, the claim of being instruments of the individual soul prevails over the scriptural statement regarding their being instruments of Brahman. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

By the scriptural passage beginning with "He who dwells in the eye," it is stated that the sense organs such as the eye have Brahman as their substrate; likewise, by the passage beginning with "He who dwells in fire," it is stated that [Brahman] is the impeller of the elements such as fire, and thus, by the force of reasoning, even the eyes and other organs which are parts thereof are directed by Brahman. Furthermore, by the scriptural passage beginning with "He who dwells in the vital breath" (prāṇa), and by the force of reasoning that [Brahman] is the impeller of the vital breath which impels all the senses, the sense organs themselves have Brahman as their cause. Even though they are directed by the primary Lord, [it is not the case that...].

Because of the Smṛti statement, "It is primary with respect to the individual soul (jīva)," it is logical that the sense organs function as instruments for the jīva. As for the scriptural texts stating that the sense organs are instruments of the jīva—such as the Śruti passage, "For he shows [objects] by means of this self, by means of the eye," and the Smṛti passage, "By means of the instruments, Brahman, the Cause"—these are intended to mean merely that Brahman causes the jīva to perform actions such as seeing through the eyes and other organs which are Brahman's own instruments; they do not imply that the organs belong to the jīva. This is like saying that Caitra’s axe is the instrument of Maitra; it expresses only the status of being a means for an action toward the jīva.

Alternatively, because the connection between the individual soul (jīva) and the instruments is beginningless and eternal according to the Śruti text, "Indeed, it is not separated from the instruments," the intention may be to refer to the soul's instruments figuratively—just as one might speak of an axe belonging to Caitra as belonging to Maitra when it has been in use with him for a long time. Furthermore, the experience of being under the control of the soul is also appropriate insofar as it is based on egoistic identification (ābhimānika). || 10 ||
Oṃ. Those [organs] are the sense-faculties, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the "best" one. Oṃ. 11.
|| Oṃ, because of the scriptural teaching of difference, oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of the distinctness [of their characteristics], oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following objection: it was previously stated that the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is not an instrument with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*); however, since that breath is also an organ (*indriya*), it too should be an instrument with respect to the soul. Regarding this, the doubt is whether the previously mentioned nature of being an organ applies to all the vital breaths or only to the twelve organs other than the primary breath. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it applies to all of them, because of the general scriptural statement that "the vital breaths indeed are the organs."

Although that [the vital breath] is common to all, it possesses the logical reasoning of moving toward this [body], and thus it is more powerful than even the specific scriptural statement, "They say there are only twelve sense organs. Furthermore, it is difficult to establish the status of the sense organs for only twelve; for it is impossible to exclude the sense-organ status of any one among those thirteen, since all are equally subject to the Lord's power. The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that, with the exception of the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), only the twelve possess the status of sense organs.

This is because of specific scriptural statements such as, "They say there are exactly twelve sense organs; however, the primary vital breath (prāṇa) is not a sense organ," whereas general scriptural passages characterized by the reasoning of "moving toward this" can possibly have as their subject matter everything other than the primary vital breath. Furthermore, the primary vital breath is not identical to the eyes and other [senses].

This [distinction] is established because of his equality with the Lord (Īśvara) as the controller of all vital breaths endowed with mobility and as the agent and instigator of all actions, whereas such qualities are absent in the eyes and other organs; for this is proven by scriptural texts such as, "Indeed, when the senses have become fluid," and "Remaining steady, the chief vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) acts and causes others to act. Furthermore, although he is subject to the Lord like the other vital breaths, he differs from them because, unlike the other vital breaths, he does not depend on the effort of the individual soul (jīva) to be under the Lord's control. || 11 ||
|| Oṃ. But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching; Oṃ. || 12 ||

Since the creation of objects such as the body depends upon the process of *trivṛtkaraṇa*—the mixing of the three elements beginning with earth—that process is a quality of Viṣṇu according to scriptural texts such as, "This divinity [made] these three divinities... Therefore, the creation of the phenomenal world of names and forms, including the body, is by Viṣṇu alone, not by Viriñca (Brahmā). As for the scripture supported by the previously mentioned reasoning, it refers to secondary creation (*avāntarasṛṣṭi*) in accordance with the Smṛti text: "Brahmā and the others are his subordinates. || 12 ||
Oṃ. Flesh and so forth belong to the earth; as it is according to the word [of scripture], so it is for the other two elements as well. Oṃ. 13.
|| Oṃ, but because of its preeminence, it is designated by that; it is designated by that. Oṃ. ||

Previously, the body and so forth were stated to have an agent; here, however, the material cause (*upādāna*) is being discussed, which constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). Regarding the term "form" (*mūrti*), there arises a doubt as to whether the body under discussion is composed of water, or of earth, or of fire, or of all three elements combined. One prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the body is composed of water, based on the observation that meat and other substances produce satisfaction (*tṛpti*), supported by the reasoning of its capacity to satisfy, and by the Vedic scripture stating, "The body is water. Another view is that it is composed of earth, based on the observation of hardness, smell, and so forth, supported by the Vedic scripture stating, "The body is earth."

Another [teacher] maintains that the body is composed of fire (*taijasa*), based on the reasoning of the observation of heat and such scriptural passages as, "Having arisen from the oblations offered to the divine source of fire, he becomes a body of gold. However, the position that the body consists of the three elements (*bhūtatrayātmaka*), although found in such texts as, "These three deities, having reached the person," is untenable because it contradicts specific statements such as, "Water alone is the body. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: although the body has multiple elements as its material cause (*prakṛti*), specific designations are justified by reference to the particular conjunction with each respective element.

"Whatever is solid is earth; whatever is liquid is water; whatever is hot is fire"—from this Vedic scripture, it follows that the body is indeed composed of multiple elements as its material cause. || 13 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
The second chapter is completed.
Now begins the third chapter.

Thus, in the first chapter, the meaning of the word *brahman* as it occurs in the *jijñāsā-sūtra* was established as an accomplished entity (*siddha-rūpa*) through the methods of consistency (*samanvaya*) and non-contradiction (*avirodha*). Now, in the subsequent two chapters, the meaning of the remaining words, beginning with *jijñāsā*, is being determined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya-rūpa*). Consequently, the sequence of these two pairs of chapters—preceding and succeeding—is established by their respective natures as investigations into the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished.

In this regard, the connection between the chapters (*adhyāya-saṅgati*) is as follows: with respect to the fruit denoted by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), the third chapter here consists of an inquiry into the means (*sādhana-vicāra*), because detachment (*vairāgya*), devotion (*bhakti*), meditation (*upāsanā*), and immediate knowledge (*aparokṣa-jñāna*)—which were mentioned by the words "then" (*atha*) and "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*)—serve as its causes. Furthermore, the sequence of the sections (*pāda*) should be understood, since each preceding one serves as the cause for each succeeding one. **Sūtra 1:** *Oṃ tadantarapratipattau saṃpariṣvaktaḥ praśnanirūpaṇābhyām Oṃ.* (Upon entering the next state, he departs enveloped [by the elements], according to the question and the explanation. *Note: The provided text contains a portion of the first Sūtra of the third chapter of the Brahma-Sūtras.*

The series of reflections previously stated by the authors of the *Candrikā* has not been mentioned here by me; however, it is now clearly set forth for the delight of the virtuous. Now, the following inquiry arises: Are the means to liberation—such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, which are denoted by the words "therefore" (*atha*) and others in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*—to be practiced, or are they not to be practiced? To determine this, one must consider whether, at the time of death, the individual soul (*jīva*) is entirely separated from the elements (*bhūta*) or not. To that end, one must further consider whether there exists any authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) or purpose (*prayojana*) for the non-separation from the elements, or whether such evidence and purpose do exist.

If the first position is held, then since liberation (*mokṣa*) would consist solely in the separation from all elements, liberation would be accomplished effortlessly through natural death alone; thus, no means of practice would be required. If the latter [position] is held, then even though liberation consists in the separation from the elements, because that does not occur at the time of natural death, the means for the sake of liberation must indeed be practiced; this constitutes the relationship between the result and its cause. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): no means of practice is required.

Even without that [separate departure], liberation is established as the release from the elements by means of death itself—which consists in the cessation of all elements—according to the Smṛti: "Death is the cessation of the elements," and by the Smṛti: "Liberation is release from them. Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence for the elements accompanying the deceased soul; once they have fulfilled their purpose by providing the body and its experiences, they have no further need [to follow]. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta):

By the force of the statement regarding the soul as indicated by water in the question and answer—"Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, water comes to be called 'man'?"—and by the authority of such scriptural evidence as "Endowed with the elements, he goes to the next world and this world," since there is a purpose for the elements in the sense of effecting the formation of a body, and because it is understood that the elements accompany the soul, there is no total separation from the elements at death; thus, [the opponent argues] that the cessation of the elements occurs only when there is a memory [of the world], as in the Smṛti passage: "At the time of death, he leaves him."

Thus, because the traditional authority (smṛti) refers to a partial aspect [of the means], the practice of the means must indeed be performed for the sake of liberation in that form; however, regarding the fruit, the objection to and resolution of the means mentioned in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* [are to be understood]. || 1 ||
Oṃ. But because it consists of those [qualities] and because of their abundance, Oṃ. 2.

Even though the existence of a single elemental state (*ekabhūtagati*) has been established by the force of the previously mentioned arguments and so forth, since a single element cannot initiate a body and is thus not the efficient cause, there arises the objection: "Death itself is liberation; what is the use of practicing the means [to it]? This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). The inquiry is whether, upon embracing the deceased soul, only water departs or all the elements do so. For that purpose, the question is whether the word *āpaḥ* (water) found in the passage concerning the questions and so forth refers to a single element or to multiple elements.

Regarding that point: there is no reason for the word *āpaḥ* (waters) to refer to multiple elements, and it is not logical for the word *āpaḥ* to have such a meaning; rather, it would be the opposite. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since in the initial question and so forth, only water is heard to proceed by means of the word *āpaḥ*, and since there is no reason for the word *āpaḥ* to refer to multiple elements—and because it would result in the undesirable conclusion that "the elements become human-speeched" [if other elements were meant]—it is improper to hear the word *āpaḥ* used in a specific sense [for others]; therefore, only water proceeds, not the other elements. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Since the elements are indeed mixed, as stated in the Śruti, and because the meaning "the elements are human speech" is obtained through the word *āpaḥ* (waters) itself—which denotes the nature of the elements—then even though all elements are mixed, the designation [of the self] by that term is justified by the aforementioned principle: namely, that among all the elements present in all bodies, such as those composed of earth, water alone is predominant due to its greater abundance. Thus, it is said that "all the elements go [with him]. As for the result, however, it consists solely in the refutation and resolution of objections regarding the performance of the means. || 2 ||
|| Oṃ, and because of the departure of the vital breaths, oṃ || 3 ||

In the preceding section, the movement of the elements was established by implication through the statement regarding the movement of water consisting of those elements; here, that movement is specifically proven by means of inference. Thus is the connection. Now, the inquiry arises as to whether the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) mentioned in the word "atha" and so forth are unnecessary or necessary. For that purpose, it must be determined whether the elements under discussion move along with the individual soul (*jīva*) or not. And for that purpose, it must be determined whether there is a specific means of knowledge [to prove this] or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
according to the direction stated previously, the movement of the elements is established by implication from the movement of water consisting of those elements. This is the conclusion.

Because that [movement] depends upon specific pride (*māna*), and since such pride is not perceived here, the proof that "they do not go" is not necessary. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: the elements (*bhūtāni*) indeed go along with the living soul (*jīva*), because they are invariably concomitant with those who travel together.

Whatever is invariably concomitant with that which moves together [with something else] is itself a mover together with it; for example, an object invariably concomitant with one who accompanies a king is itself a companion of the king. Since such a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the form of an inference exists, the elements (*bhūtāni*) necessarily possess movement along with the living self (*jīva*). This is because the qualification of the reason (*hetu*) is established by the scriptural statement, "Indeed, where the elements are, there are the instruments (*karaṇāni*)," and by the declaration in the scripture, "These are never separated.
Thus, the probans (*sādhana*) is necessary. || 3 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul does not go to Brahman] because of the scriptural mention of its going to Agni and others, we say no, because that is figurative. Oṃ. (Sūtra 4)

The connection [of this section] is that the non-establishment of the reason stated previously is being refuted here. Now, the inquiry is whether the means of attainment mentioned by the word "etcetera" (ādi) is to be performed or not to be performed. For that purpose, the question is whether the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) under discussion depart together with the individual soul (*jīva*), or do they not depart? For that purpose, the question is whether the scriptural statement regarding the departure of the vital breaths to Agni and so forth refers to the departure of the breaths in their entirety as a whole, or whether it refers to their departure part by part. For that purpose, the question is whether there is no basis for such a partial division and there is a sublation [of the alternative], or whether the opposite is the case.

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), however, is as follows: "When this person has died, speech goes into fire, breath into the wind, the eye into the sun," and so forth; because of such scriptural statements regarding the departure of the vital functions (prāṇas) such as speech toward their corresponding deities (adhidaiva) like fire, there is no departure together with the individual soul (jīva).

It is untenable [to claim that the elements go with the soul] because they do not depart part by part along with the soul; because there is no authority for the phrase "in another portion as the presiding deity" (adhidaiva); because at every death there would be a departure of the portions, leading to the consequence that all [elements] would depart over time; and because if the elements were to go to the destination of the presiding deities along with the vital breaths, yet not go there with the soul—since the soul does not go there with them—then in either case, it would follow that there is no absolute inseparability between the elements and the vital breaths. Thus, [the theory] is illogical.

The view that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart along with the living self (*jīva*), and therefore no spiritual practice (*sādhana*) need be performed, is incorrect. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: According to the Smṛti text, "O Brahman, at the death of a person... it is established by the Smṛti statement, "At the time of death, he leaves him behind," that the departure of the vital breaths occurs only partially to both [the self and the elements]. Since there is no absolute separation between the elements and the vital breaths, the vital breaths and the elements indeed go along with the living self; thus, spiritual practice must be performed. || 4 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul is not eternal] because it is not heard of in the first [chapter], we say no; for it is precisely those [scriptural passages] which establish it on the basis of logical consistency. Oṃ. (Sūtra 5)

The connection [of this section] is as follows: since it was previously argued that the mention of fire (*agni*) and so forth was figurative (*bhākta*), here the argument is made that the mention of faith (*śraddhā*) is likewise figurative. Now, the inquiry is whether the means denoted by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is to be practiced or not to be practiced.

For that purpose, there arises the question of whether there is a departure of the elements together with the individual soul (jīva) or not. To that end, regarding the word *śraddhā* (faith) heard at the beginning of the passage—"In this very fire, the deities offer faith"—does it refer merely to that which is joined with faith, or does it refer to the soul joined with both faith and water? For that purpose, must the concluding statement—"Thus, in the fifth oblation, the waters become human"—be interpreted in accordance with the opening statement, or is it the reverse?

In this regard, is the opening statement (*upakrama*) more powerful, or the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*)? In the first case, since the opening statement must be taken according to its literal meaning, the concluding statement must be interpreted in conformity with it; thus, because the question and answer would not apply to the departure of the elements (*bhūtagati*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) results in the conclusion that there is no simultaneous departure of the elements, and therefore no means of attainment (*sādhana*) need be practiced.

In the final view (*siddhānta*), however, because the concluding summary must conform to the word "self" (*ātman*), the word "faith" (*śraddhā*) found in the opening passage must be interpreted accordingly; thus, by the force of the question and answer, it is established that the result is that the movement of the elements together [with the self] is the means to be practiced. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is that there is no movement of the elements together with the individual soul (*jīva*).

In the Śruti passage beginning with "In that very [fire]," since the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.4) records the oblation of the one who desires heaven—specifically the one accompanied by *śraddhā* (faith)—into the first fire called *dvya*, there is no mention of the departure of the elements (*bhūtagati*). Otherwise, there would be the contingency of having to state "the elements" [instead]. Nor is it correct to claim that the word *śraddhā* refers to the elements because it contradicts the word *āpaḥ* (waters) found in the concluding portion;

for the opening statement (*upakrama*) is more authoritative due to its lack of contradiction at the time of its occurrence and its priority of presentation, and thus the conclusion must be interpreted in accordance with it. As for the final established position (*siddhānta*):

Although the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) does not come first, because it takes the form of an explanation of the opening (*upakrama*), it possesses greater force through the logical connection of the meaning as occurring first; thus, in accordance with that [conclusion], the opening must be explained. Consequently, it is appropriate that the word *śraddhā* found therein refers—by means of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication)—to the living being endowed with faith, water, and the self. Therefore, there is a simultaneous departure of all beings. Here, the detailed exposition establishing the superiority of the conclusion by refuting the claim of the superiority of the first [the opening] as stated by the "moderns" (*navīna*) is to be understood from the *Upasaṃhāravijaya* composed by the venerable teacher (*gurupāda*). || 5 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul does not exist] because it is not mentioned [in the texts], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices and other such rites are known [to exist]. Oṃ. 6.

Thus, there is an internal connection (*antarasaṅgati*) because a doubt arises here by way of challenging the two means of knowledge—the scriptural statement regarding the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the inference based on the movement of the senses—which were determined in the previous section. The primary inquiry in the preceding section was this: do the elements (*bhūta*) that constitute the body depart along with the individual soul (*jīva*), or do they not? To that end, the question is whether the two arguments previously mentioned—the scriptural statement concerning the soul's purpose and the inference from the departure of the vital breaths—are or are not effective in establishing the departure of the elements.

For that purpose, between these two [scriptural passages], which is stronger: the non-hearing of the elements in a restrictive sense, or the opposite? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the hearing of the departure of the elements occurs even through the statement of their "going" by implication (*arthāt*), based on the mention of the "going" of the self in the context of the question and its exposition—just like [the statement] "Speech goes into fire" (*agniṃ vāgapyeti*) and so forth—the non-hearing of the elements in a restrictive sense is indeed stronger.

Since even the specific scriptural teaching regarding the nature of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) serves to establish the Vedic meaning only when there is a hearing of that distinction, and since those two [the breath and the self] cannot establish it in the absence of a scriptural statement regarding their perceptible movement, the elements do not depart together; thus, this means of accomplishment is not to be practiced. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Just as even the eating of poor food is still considered "eating," it is logical that even a hearing [of the scriptures] that is merely nominal (ārthika) is still "hearing. According to the previously mentioned direction, because these two possess the force of being supported by the means of knowledge that apprehend the pervasion and the probans (*vyāpti-liṅga*), they act as obstacles to the general absence of hearing; furthermore, they themselves establish the objective reality of the matter. This is also evident from the direct scriptural statement: "Then indeed, why does he not abandon the sacrificer? It is the elements alone that go with the elements, through the elements he eats, through the elements he is born, and through the elements he moves."

In this regard, although the word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is heard in the scripture, since it is established by the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori) that others besides him—namely, those who perform the ritual acts—are likewise not separated from the elements (*bhūta*), it follows as a practical means to be implemented that the elements indeed depart along with the living soul (*jīva*). Thus ends [the discussion of] verse 6.
|| Oṃ. Or [the worship of the devotee] is based on devotion, because he does not know the Self; for thus the scripture shows. Oṃ. || 7 ||

The connection [of this section] with the preceding one arises from the following doubt: the statement made previously—that all living beings are never separated from the elements (*bhūta*)—is untenable; for since liberation is heard of as being brought about by action (*karman*), if that very liberation were to lack the non-separation from the elements, the principle of *kaimutya* (the argumentum ad absurdum) would not apply. Here, the inquiry is whether the means to liberation, such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, mentioned by the word "now" (*atha*) and others, need be practiced by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) or not. To that end, the question is whether the immortality (*amṛtatva*) heard of through action in passages such as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" is primary or merely figurative.

Regarding that purpose, the question is whether there exists an obstacle to its being primary or not. In the first case (if there is no obstacle), liberation can be obtained from other means as well; therefore, detachment (*vairāgya*) and the like need not be practiced. In the latter case (if there is an obstacle), they must be practiced; such is the relationship between the result and the means. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The means consisting of detachment and so forth need not be practiced, because even without them, liberation is established through action alone—which is easily performed—according to scriptural texts such as "one attains [it] even thereby. Nor is the immortality mentioned in the scripture merely figurative, for there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) to that effect. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

In passages such as "He who knows this thus becomes immortal," it is stated that the status of true immortality belongs primarily to the knower of the Self alone and not to anyone else. Since this statement constitutes a subverting factor (*bādhaka*)—in the form of a conflict with an unrestricted scriptural declaration (*niravakāśa-śruti*)—it necessarily follows that the scriptural texts concerning water and so forth must have a figurative meaning (*gauṇārtha*). Consequently, since liberation cannot be attained through any other means, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) must indeed employ detachment (*vairāgya*) and other such qualities as the means for achieving that goal.

The manner in which the scriptural statement has a secondary (gauṇa) sense is as follows: by such scriptural passages as, "The soma-drinker indeed becomes immortal for as long as Indra, for as long as Manu," the immortality of one who performs optional (kāmya) rites is shown to be merely temporary; whereas for the seeker who performs non-optional (akāmya) rites, there is immortality known as liberation through the gateway of knowledge. This is because the supplementary portion of the text, "We have reached the light, we have found the gods," states that they "desired to know Brahman, the Light" (*jyotiḥ*), and because it is stated [in the Sūtras], "Because of the state of being thus at the time of departing" (*utkramiṣyata evaṃ bhāvāt*). Furthermore, this is supported by the Sūtra: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse."

Furthermore, because it will be explained later, for the wise person who performs action without desire, immortality (*amṛtatva*)—which consists in the manifestation of a specific portion of the bliss of liberation according to the direction stated in such passages as "But the Agnihotra and so forth are indeed for that purpose alone, for that is seen"—is to be understood in this manner. As for the result, however, there is the resolution of the objection regarding the performance of the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) mentioned by the word *atha* and others. || 7 ||
Oṃ. At the end of the performed [actions], one who possesses residual karma [ascends], as is seen from scripture and from memory. Oṃ. 8.

In the preceding section, it was stated that the attainment of immortality as a fruit born of ritual action (*karma*) is figurative (*bhākta*). Here, however, the connection is that it is being stated that the production of fruits such as heaven from ritual action is figurative only by way of a "portion" (*bhāga*), and not in its entirety. In this context, the inquiry is whether the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should perform [the means] such as detachment (*vairāgya*) mentioned by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), or whether they should not. For that purpose, the question is whether there is the complete enjoyment of the binding ritual action in heaven and other realms, or only a partial enjoyment.

For that purpose, the question arises whether there exists a partial enjoyment of karma or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: based on such statements as "A living being is bound by karma," since there is no evidence for the postulation of a partial enjoyment of that binding *kāmya*-karma which has gone to heaven and so forth along with the individual soul, total enjoyment is possible; and even if one were to accept the return from heaven due to a remainder of karma after enjoying it through experience, the exhaustion of all karma would still be possible through a second repetition of this process.

If there were an absence of the seed of bondage, bondage would cease of its own accord; thus, one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) would have no need for the practice of detachment (vairāgya). However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: Based on the Śruti text, "Then, by the remainder [of his works], he returns to this world," and the Smṛti text, "Possessing the residual traces of what was experienced," it is stated that even for one who has gone to heaven, some karma accompanies him according to his fitness. Since he returns only while still possessing a remainder of karma, and since the necessity of performing further karma is indicated by the rule "at least ten [must be present]"—which implies the performance of no small amount of work—it follows that because karma is not exhausted entirely through experience, the practice of detachment and so forth is indeed necessary. || 8 ||
Oṃ, as it was, and not otherwise; Oṃ. 9.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: since it was previously stated that "one who possesses latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) departs," a doubt arises as to whether one returns exactly as one came or by another path; this doubt is what is being resolved here. The inquiry is whether the detachment (*vairāgya*) mentioned in the preceding words is something to be practiced or not. For that purpose, the question is whether the return is by the very same mode of departure or otherwise. For that purpose, the question is whether hearing about the path is useful for the return or not. In the first case (if it is useful), because the return is by the very path already present in the mind, there is an absence of afflictions (*kleśa*) during the return; therefore, there is no need for detachment regarding the karma that causes those [afflictions]. In the latter case (if it is not useful), however, because the return occurs in another way [independently of the path], [detachment is required].

Because of the affliction caused by traveling on an unfamiliar path, detachment from its causes is necessary; this is the relationship between the cause and the result (*phala-phalibhāva*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since there is no reason for returning via an unfamiliar path by abandoning the familiar one, and because it would contradict the scriptural statement, "He returns by the same way he came," the return must be by the very path of the journey; therefore, detachment and the like are not required. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Since the soul lacks independence in its movement, the recollection of that [path] is not applicable to the return; for the *Bhāṣya* states, "From smoke to the cloud," and the scripture (*śruti*) indicates that the return occurs along the path of departure only as far as the ether (*ākāśa*), while it is stated that from there onwards the process is otherwise. Furthermore, since the scripture says "as they went" (*yathetam*), it is logical to accept that the return occurs by some mode of movement different from the one used in the departure. Thus, the return is indeed different from the manner of going; this is the point regarding dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 9 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul] is different because of its movement, we say no; for Kārṣṇājini holds that this is meant for the purpose of merging into That. Oṃ. 10.
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the scriptural injunctions] would be purposeless, we say no, because they depend upon that. Oṃ. But Bādari maintains that it is only good and evil deeds."

Thus, since the establishment of the path of going and returning has been accomplished, the determination of its means is now undertaken; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). Now, the inquiry is whether detachment from optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) mentioned in the opening words is necessary or not. For that purpose, it must be determined whether the "going and returning" is the fruit of conduct (*caraṇa*) or the fruit of optional rites. For that purpose, one must determine whether, in the scriptural passage, "Those here whose conduct (*caraṇa*) was pleasant enter a pleasant womb," the word *caraṇa* refers to the practice of ritual auxiliaries (*karmāṅgācāra*) or to the rites themselves (*karman*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The going and returning is indeed the fruit of conduct (*caraṇa*), not the fruit of ritual action (*karman*). This is because the scripture concerning conduct states that going and returning is the fruit of conduct. Conduct itself is not merely ritual action; for if it were, it would result in its own redundancy in light of the scriptural statement, "As one acts, as one conducts oneself," and the traditional law (*smṛti*) which says, "Conduct is declared to be the purifier by virtue of being an auxiliary to ritual action."

Since those who perform sacrifices and other rites are the subject under discussion, it is possible for them to be referred to by such expressions as "those who [perform] sacrifices" and so forth; thus, even without the word *caraṇa*, there is the possibility of the term being used as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for their actions (*karman*). Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement in passages such as, "Those who here in the village worship with sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts—they pass into smoke," which describes the cycle of going and returning as the fruit of sacrifices and the like. For even there, by the prefix *upa* in the verb *upāsate*—which signifies proximity—the term *caraṇa* is understood as referring to conduct proximate to the performance of ritual action.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: The going and coming, which are the fruits of actions known as merit and demerit, indeed exist. This is because the going and so forth are understood to be the fruits of action from the Śruti text, "The deluded, considering sacrifice and works of public utility to be the highest, know no other good," and from the Smṛti text, "The knowers of the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin... and so on. By the force of these [texts], the scriptural mention of "conduct" (*caraṇa*)—through a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*)—refers to sacrifices and the like; yet, since those who perform sacrifices possess beauty and so forth precisely through their beautiful conduct and the like, [the term "conduct"] functions as an indicator (*sūcaka*).

Because the term *caraṇa* can have a meaningful application—given that the scriptural injunction "practice dharma" (*dharmaṃ carata*) is supported by the usage "they practice dharma" (*dharmaṃ carataḥ*)—it follows that the term *caraṇa* refers specifically to sacrifices and the like. Therefore, to assume a different meaning for the scriptural passage "those who [live] in villages... is without authority. Furthermore, this would contradict the designation [of the path], namely: "Now, those who win worlds through sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity enter into smoke. Thus, one must cultivate detachment toward ritual acts performed for the sake of desire. || 10 ||
"Oṃ, it is also heard that even those who perform prohibited acts [attain liberation], Oṃ. 11.
Oṃ. By means of self-restraint, others experience ascent and descent, because their course is seen [in scripture]. Oṃ. And they remember [it]. Oṃ.

There is a connection [of this section] because of the doubt that, according to the direction stated above, states such as going [to other worlds] are the fruit of karma known as merit (*puṇya*), but not the fruit of karma known as sin (*pāpa*). Now, the inquiry is whether the dispassion (*vairāgya*) mentioned by the word "then" (*atha*) pertains only to optional meritorious karma, or also to sin and so forth. For that purpose, the question is whether the suffering of traveling on the aforementioned paths and so on—which is presented as the fruit of karma called merit and sin—belongs only to those who have performed meritorious deeds, or also to those who have not performed meritorious deeds.

For that purpose, [the question is]: is the going and returning prompted by the fear of sin (*pratyavāya*), the desire for results (*phala-kāmanā*), and so forth, or is it prompted solely by karma? For that purpose, [the further question is]: is there any evidence for the going and so forth of those who have committed no merit (*apuṇyakṛt*) even when they are devoid of fear and the like, or is there not? In the first case (if there is no evidence), the going and so forth belong only to those who have performed merit and possess the fear of sin and the like; in the latter case (if there is evidence), however, the result belongs to both—the performers of merit and the performers of non-merit. Such is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The suffering of going and so forth belongs only to those who perform meritorious deeds, not to those who do not; for the latter possess the fear of transgression (*pratyavāya*). According to the maxim, "One who is afraid falls from the tree," it is observed that only those possessed by fear experience the suffering of falling and the like. Furthermore, because they possess the desire for fruits, the going and so forth belong only to those who perform meritorious deeds with a specific motive. For the Śruti states: "He who, thinking himself wise, desires desires, is born again and again among those very objects through his desires"—thus, it is said that only those with desire return.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of fear and an absence of desire, those who have performed the *aniṣṭhā* rites do not experience the suffering of returning [to rebirth] and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the possession of fear and the like is not the cause of suffering such as falling, but rather that karma alone is the cause; for there is no evidence (*kalpaka*) to support such a claim.

Furthermore, for those who do not perform merit and instead commit evil—just like those who perform merit—the suffering consisting of the temporary obstruction of desires and the like is absent, and because of the abundance of enjoyments such as garlands, sandalwood, and women, the mere suffering of future rebirth and so forth is rendered insignificant; thus, it might be argued that detachment and the like need not be cultivated there. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since the *Śruti* states, "Those here who have performed good deeds and those who have performed evil deeds, having experienced the results of their good [deeds], return," the return of others—as well as those who perform merit—is declared. Likewise...

In the Śruti cited in the Bhāṣya, "All these doers of evil fall into Saṃyamana," and in Smṛtis such as "The sinners go [there]," it is stated that for those other than the doers of merit, there is the great misfortune of eternal hell and so forth. Therefore, even for all those who are ignorant of the Lord, the suffering of returning [to this world] and so on certainly exists; thus, the two reasons—[the absence of the state of being a Bhava-yukta and the absence of the desire for results]—are ineffective. One who is not afraid and is devoid of desire for rewards must cultivate an even greater degree of detachment toward worldly objects, observing how even poison that has been consumed causes death. || 11 ||
Oṃ, even seven times, Oṃ. 12.

In the preceding section, the statement that those who hate Hari dwell eternally in hell was deemed improper, because it was objected that such [eternity] is contradicted by the scriptural statement, "As many as fourteen Indras," which indicates its non-eternality. Thus, there is a thematic connection through this objection. Now, the inquiry is whether the extreme detachment resulting from hatred toward the Lord and so forth, mentioned in the word *atha*, is not necessary or whether it is indeed necessary. For that purpose, one must consider whether the hell described as the fruit of such actions involves a return [to worldly existence] or not. And for that purpose, whether hell is singular or manifold. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Since there is no evidence for a specific division of hells, and because it is stated in passages such as "from one up to fourteen Indras" that [the duration] is non-eternal, hell for those who hate the Blessed One consists merely of a return [to rebirth]. Nor should it be argued that, given the understanding of eternality from the Smṛti text, "For those submerged in great darkness, there is never any emergence," a single hell could be both eternal and non-eternal depending on the individual; for this would contradict such statements as, "He made hell empty."

Therefore, it is not necessary to possess an extraordinary degree of detachment (*vairāgya*) toward hatred for the Lord. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because the *Smṛti* cited in the Commentary—beginning with "Raurava and Mahāraurava"—predominantly describes the expansion of transient hells (*anityanaraka*) alongside the two eternal hells (*nityanaraka*); and because the passage beginning with "as many as fourteen Indras" is appropriately understood as referring to transient hells; one should understand that the hell resulting from hatred for the Lord is indeed devoid of return, and thus one must cultivate an extraordinary degree of detachment toward it. || 12 ||
|| Oṃ And even there, because it is a function of that [Brahman], there is no contradiction. Oṃ || 13 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: "Let there be the experience of eternal or non-eternal hells for the two types of practitioners who perform prohibited acts (*aniṣiddhakārin*); even so, detachment (*vairāgya*) toward those causes is not necessary, because they do not possess the nature of suffering (*duḥkha-svarūpa*). Now, the inquiry is whether detachment regarding sin and the like, as mentioned by the word *atha*, should or should not be cultivated; for that purpose, one must determine whether hell—which is the fruit of such acts—is of the nature of non-suffering or of the nature of suffering.

For that purpose, it must be considered whether it follows that the Lord who impels [beings] to hell experiences suffering because hell is characterized by suffering, or not. For that purpose, one must ask: what is "experience" (*bhoga*)? Is it merely the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of suffering, or is it specifically the state of inferiority and so forth produced by that [suffering]? The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the very direct perception of suffering constitutes the nature of experiencing it, if the inhabitant of hell were suffering, it would follow that the omniscient Lord who impels him would experience suffering in the form of being a witness to that suffering; therefore, hell is not of the nature of suffering [for the Lord].

If it were argued that there is no Lord, nor one who impels Him, because such a view contradicts the scriptural passage cited in the Bhāṣya stating that "He impels everything," and therefore one need not cultivate detachment—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: According to the Smṛti, "The very state of being low or high is designated as the experience (*bhoga*) of suffering and so forth. Since the term "experience" refers precisely to states such as lowness, and since even though He is the impeller of the sufferer, His non-existence within Hari—who is changeless and possesses inconceivable power—is established by Śruti and Smṛti through the text, "He is not a partaker of suffering," [it follows that] regarding the suffering of the denizens of hell...
Since there is no sublation [of this fact], one should cultivate detachment toward hell, thinking, "It is truly full of suffering. || 13 ||
"But because knowledge and action are the subjects under discussion [in the preceding context]. || 14 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: "Is it improper to speak of the suffering of hell and so forth for the sake of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*), since even without that [teaching], living beings can independently, by their own will, abandon or undertake those courses of rebirth (*gati*) which are the fruits of such actions? Now, the inquiry is whether dispassion toward meritorious action (*kāmyakarman*), as mentioned in the word *atha*, is necessary or not. To determine this, the question is whether living beings possess independence regarding their courses of rebirth and so forth, or not.

For that purpose, regarding the Śruti passage: "Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths, they become these small, mixed creatures," is there a reference here to the two paths consisting of the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna, or rather to knowledge and ritual action? As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

In the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the two previously mentioned paths—the path of the gods and so forth—are referred to in the two statements, "They attain the light" and "They attain the smoke. By stating that beings do not travel by either one alone, the independence of the elements (bhūtas) regarding their movement is understood. This is because it would be illogical to say that they do not travel on a path that is beyond the scope of human effort. Furthermore, although the lack of independence of the individual soul (jīva) was stated in passages such as "Because of the designation of another," etc., its independence remains possible only as being dependent upon the Lord (Īśvara).

If it is argued that living beings possess independence even regarding the attainment of their destination, then this is equally true regarding the independence of the means [to that end]. Furthermore, the objection regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) applies here as well. Thus, since independence lies in the destination itself, according to the maxim, "When the root is secured, one has no desire to go to the tip of the branch," what is the use of detachment from optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), given that independence resides in the fruit? The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they attain the light (*arciḥ*); whereas those who in the village perform sacrifices, works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*)," and so forth.

Regarding the passage, "Those who worship [saying] 'It has been given' [follow] the smoke," although there is no distinction in the fact that both knowledge and action were previously introduced, and that the paths beginning with the path of the gods (devayāna) and their respective means—knowledge and action—were likewise introduced, it is said: "Two paths have been proclaimed: the path of knowledge and the path of action."

"One who is devoid of that [discipline] goes in three ways: as an animal, or to hell, or to darkness"—by this name of a Smṛti cited in the Bhāṣya, and by the reference in the subsequent sentence, "of these two, namely knowledge and action," it is established that the independence of living beings pertains only to the means (*sādhana*), not to the fruit (*phala*). Since there is an absence of such independence regarding the fruit, and since the Lord grants independence in that regard only by accepting that the scriptures—such as those concerning injunctions—are not rendered purposeless due to the existence of injunctions regarding the means, there is no possibility of attributing independence to the fruit itself. Therefore, detachment from desire and the like is indeed necessary for the optional rites (*kāmya*). || 14 ||
Oṃ. It is not [the case that the self exists] in the third [state], because it is not perceived there in that way. Oṃ. 15.

|| Oṃ, and it is also recorded in common worldly usage, Oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of being seen, Oṃ. || Oṃ, in the third [chapter], there is the inclusion of the term "sound" for that which arises from sorrow, Oṃ. || Oṃ, and because of remembrance, Oṃ.

Here, the connection [of the topic] arises from the consideration of the nature of *tamas* (darkness) previously mentioned in the verse, "The animal realm or hell is *tamas*. Now, the inquiry concerns whether one should cultivate an intense detachment toward the *tamas* that is the fruit of hating the Lord, as stated by the word "atha," or not. For that purpose, it must be considered whether *tamas* is a mixture of pleasure and pain like other hells, or whether its essential nature is exclusively suffering. For that purpose again, it must be considered whether suffering is invariably concomitant with pleasure, or not.

To that end, the question is whether there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the means of knowledge that apprehends the pervasion—that "wherever there is suffering, there is pleasure"—regarding darkness, or whether such a proof does exist. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Regarding the pervasion that "where there is suffering, there is pleasure," although universal pleasure and suffering are imperceptible because they transcend the senses, their apprehension is possible through the traditional teaching (smṛti) stated in the Bhāṣya: "Where there is suffering, there is pleasure. Thus, since pleasure is established by inference even in darkness accompanied by suffering—just as in other hells—and no subverting evidence is observed, one should cultivate detachment toward that darkness which is not significantly worse than other hells. However, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: [The rest of the passage continues with the refutation of this view.]

Since it is understood from scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that darkness is invariably associated with suffering—given the traditional teaching that "where there is suffering" [refers to hell]—it follows that darkness necessarily pertains to the other hells; therefore, one must cultivate detachment toward it. For instance, darkness does not persist as pleasure, for the scripture says, "For here there is only suffering," and the tradition says, "For those submerged in the blinding darkness, there is not even a trace of happiness."

The direct perception of the four-faced Brahmā, established by the Smṛti cited in the Bhāṣya beginning with "By the grace of Nārāyaṇa," is more powerful than that established by Smṛti such as "Just as a king [acts] toward one who is very dear. Furthermore, there is the following inference: those who disagree [with this] are not possessed of suffering, because they are not non-objects of the Lord's will; for whatever is not an object of the Lord's will is not so [as it appears], just as a hare is not possessed of horns. Nor is there a lack of proof (asiddhi) [for the reason].

These [beings] are not desired by the Lord to be happy because they are disagreeable; for whatever is disagreeable to someone is not desired by that person to be happy, just as an opponent of a king is not desired by the king to be happy—this is established through such inference. Furthermore, their disagreeableness is established simply from the fact of being hated. Likewise, there is the *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on the impossibility of another explanation, since one understands from the hearing of the nature of *tamas* in Smṛti texts such as "Tamas is said to be threefold," that the listeners undergo a fainting fit produced by an excess of pain born of hearing. || 15 ||
|| Oṃ. [The soul] attains the state of having that as its own nature, because it is logical; oṃ. || 16 ||

Let there indeed be detachment (*vairāgya*) toward the cause of suffering and its fruit when they are undesirable; however, [one might object] that it is not appropriate toward optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and their fruits, because they are causes of happiness and are themselves of the nature of happiness. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) arising from such a doubt. Now, the inquiry is whether the detachment from optional rites and so forth mentioned by the word "atha" is proper or improper. For that purpose, the question is whether ritual action is a cause of great happiness or not.

For that purpose, regarding the state of becoming smoke and so forth—heard in such passages as "having become smoke, he becomes a cloud"—in the case of those performing ritual acts (*karmiṇaḥ*) during their journey to heaven and other realms: does this state consist in either identity with the deity of smoke and so forth or reaching that place, or rather does it consist in similarity and the like? For that purpose, is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in "he becomes smoke" and so forth primary, or is it of the nature of similarity and the like? For that purpose, is the coreferentiality in "he becomes smoke" and so forth primary, or is it figurative (*gauṇa*) by way of similarity and the like?

Regarding whether there is an obstacle to that end or not: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows. The state of becoming smoke and so forth is for the sake of either attaining identity with the deity or attaining the deity’s own station. Since there is no obstacle to abandoning the primary meaning of the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and since the deities—by virtue of their affection and other qualities—are capable of granting even their own station, which is to be attained through knowledge, there is no impossibility of the ritualist attaining that station; and because it is a cause of happiness, there is no detachment from ritual action. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

In the world, because one thing is observed to become another, yet it is impossible for a ritual performer who is absolutely distinct [from the deity] to attain identity with that deity; and because, since that state (the state of the deity) is to be reached by the qualified practitioners through knowledge alone, it is impossible for many performers of rituals to simultaneously occupy a single state—given that it would be illogical for many to attain one and the same state—the literal sense of the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) must necessarily be abandoned. Therefore, the attainment of the state of smoke and so forth, as stated in the Smṛti passage beginning with "But upon reaching that, there is indeed movement," refers either to similarity with the deity or to entering into that [deity].

Or rather, [the word "not"] refers to the identity of the locus; thus, because it is not a cause of great bliss, it is appropriate to have detachment toward both the ritual action for desired ends and its fruit. || 16 ||
Oṃ, not after a very long time, because of the distinction; Oṃ. 17.

In the preceding section, the state of being smoke and so forth for the performer of ritual action (*karmī*) was considered; here, however, the consideration is whether the arrival [of that state] occurs after some time. Alternatively, the connection [between sections] arises from the doubt: "Even if the performer of action attains the nature of the deities, since that [state] lasts for a long duration and possesses great happiness, one might not develop detachment (*vairāgya*) toward ritual action. Here, the inquiry is whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to have detachment toward optional ritual action (*kāmyakarman*), as indicated by the word "then" (*atha*). For that purpose, the question is: is that [attainment of the nature of the deities] a cause of great happiness, or is it not?

Regarding whether there is a fixed time for the journey back or not: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows. Since there is no fixed time—such as "one must arrive at exactly this much time upon the return"—and since the scriptures state that during the return one reaches many places (as in the passage beginning, "He returns by the same path through space"), and because there is no reason to return quickly by abandoning the great bliss obtained through the nature of those respective deities, it is not proper to cultivate detachment from karma while remaining in the intermediate region until the end of the kalpa, which is the cause for obtaining such bliss.
