In the preceding [section], those who were under discussion—the qualified persons for meditation—were considered: do they not have the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) as their limit, or do they indeed have that as their limit? For that purpose, there is an inquiry: does the inference establishing a qualified person superior to the vital breath contradict the scriptural text, "The vital breath is indeed greater than all; nothing is greater than the vital breath," or does it not? For that purpose, there is an inquiry: can the word "all" (*sarva*) in the scripture, while primarily referring to the Supreme Self, also possess a restricted application by referring to other qualified persons? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

In the passage "Prāṇa indeed [is] for all," if the word "all" were taken in its unrestricted sense, it would follow that the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) possesses unqualified supremacy over everything; since two distinct entities cannot both possess such supreme status, one must assert the non-difference of Prāṇa from Viṣṇu, who is established by Śruti and other means as the sole possessor of supremacy over all. However, because this would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of denying the difference between the vital breath and the Supreme Self—which is established by numerous authorities cited in the Bhāṣya in passages such as "like the eye, etc."—the word "all" must necessarily be understood in a restricted sense, referring to something other than those [entities].

Since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against restricting [the scope] by means of a sense other than [merely] excluding specific qualified persons (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), it follows that the inference—"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is joined with a superior qualified person, because it is a qualified person, like Name (*nāma*) and so forth"—acts as a subverter of that scriptural passage. Because this inference remains unsubverted, a qualified person superior even to the vital breath is established; thus, the qualified persons for meditation do not have the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) as their limit. As for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): [it is as follows].

Although the word "all" (sarva) has its scope restricted to something other than the Lord by the force of multiple means of knowledge, this inference is invalid because it is sublated by the statements of the Bhāṣya found in various places—such as "like the eye and so forth"—and by the Bhāṣya statements yet to be cited beginning with "For the supremacy belongs to the gods," which are intent on establishing that Hari alone is superior to the vital breath; and furthermore, it is sublated by the previously mentioned Śruti, which contains the word "all" with a restricted scope, conforming to those [Bhāṣya] statements and referring exclusively to those other than the Lord. Thus, the inference lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge.

The meditators (upāsakas) are indeed those whose [meditation] is limited to the vital breath (prāṇa). However, the result is the justification for the statement that the synthesis of all qualities pertains to the meditation on Brahman. || 21 ||
|| Oṃ. The exchange [of attributes] distinguishes [the two], for it is like the other cases; oṃ. || 22 ||

In the preceding section, it was stated that since Prāṇa alone is Hiraṇyagarbha, it is appropriate for him to possess the collection of all attributes previously mentioned; however, that statement is incorrect. This is because, as he is the highest of all, there is no other being superior to him who could be his object of worship. Alternatively, the connection [of this section] is as follows: having defined the qualified aspirant for meditation in the previous part, the object of meditation is now defined here. The doubt is whether Viṣṇu—who was introduced in the preceding section as being superior to Prāṇa—is indeed superior to Prāṇa, or not.

To that end, there arises an inquiry in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: following the passage beginning with "Prāṇa is indeed greater than hope," and continuing from above Prāṇa with "But truth alone is what must be sought to be known," is this one called Truth—the supreme among all—non-different from Prāṇa, or is He different, namely Viṣṇu? For this purpose, the question is whether there exists a distinction between the section on Prāṇa and the section on Truth, or not. As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

In this context, just as there is a distinction between the fifteen sections beginning with Name and ending with Breath through the form of questions and answers—such as the question, "Is there anything greater than Breath? and the answer, "Truth, indeed, is greater than Breath"—there is no such distinction here between the section on Breath and the section on Truth. Since there is no difference between Breath and Truth, Viṣṇu, who is the referent of the word "Truth," is not superior to Breath.

Nor can there be an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a question and answer that would differentiate the two contexts, because there is no evidence for such an assumption. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): after stating that the one who speaks of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is an "exalted speaker" (*ativādī*) by virtue of speaking of an exalted thing—via the passage, "He, indeed, seeing thus, thinking thus, and knowing thus, becomes an exalted speaker"—the text subsequently says, "But he indeed is an exalted speaker who speaks with the Truth. By using the word "but" (*tu*), it declares that the speaker of the Truth is an exalted speaker even more so than the speaker of the vital breath.

The objection—that because of the exclusion [of others], the indicative mark, the supplying of ellipses in the question and answer, the interruption of the context, and the Smṛti statement "For Viṣṇu is the highest among the gods," the word *tu* (but) does not imply the supplying [of Viṣṇu] as "Viṣṇu, whose name is Truth, is higher than Prāṇa"—is refuted by the method of the *bhūman* section, since such an objection would be fallacious due to the scriptural hearing of distinctions even in a reality devoid of difference, as will be explained in the passages beginning with "But knowledge indeed" and "But thought indeed. The manner of this refutation is clear in the *Candrikā*.
The justification for meditating on [the Self] as "Self" is stated in the passage beginning with, "But the fruit consists of bliss and so forth."
|| Oṃ, for that very [Self] is indeed [the subject of] "Truth" and so forth, Oṃ. || 23 ||

The connection here is due to the specific consideration regarding Viṣṇu’s superiority over Prāṇa, as previously stated. Having established that Viṣṇu alone, denoted by the term *Satya*, is superior to the aforementioned Prāṇa, the inquiry now arises: "Are there many others who are also superior? To that end, the question is whether the nine entities listed after *Satya*—namely, *Vijñāna*, *Mati*, *Śraddhā*, *Niṣṭhā*, *Kṛti*, *Sukha*, *Bhūman*, *Ahaṃkāra*, and *Ātman*—are distinct from *Satya* and from one another, or whether they are non-different. For this purpose, the inquiry is whether there is any evidence for their non-difference or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Since there is no evidence for the non-difference of [the qualities] beginning with Truth (satya) and ending with the Self (ātman), and since their difference is more logical according to the principle of distinct words, it follows that there are many superior entities starting from Breath (prāṇa) and including Truth and the rest. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: If [the qualities] beginning with Consciousness (vijñāna) were different from those beginning with Truth, then the statement of Consciousness and the rest in response to the question, "Venerable Sir, I desire to know Truth," and so forth, would result in an inconsistency. By the force of the fact that this [statement] cannot be otherwise explained, the phrase "Venerable Sir, I desire to know Truth" must be understood as having the intent of desiring to know the quality of Truth; thus, the mention of Consciousness is made because it is invariably concomitant (avinābhūta) with Truth.

Likewise, in the passage "O Blessed One, I desire to know consciousness (*vijñāna*)," since all [attributes] are logically established as non-different because they are intended to express qualities inseparable from consciousness when there is a desire to know the qualities of consciousness; and because of Smṛti texts such as "Truth and the rest, ending with 'I', are its qualities," they are non-different. Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is superior to Prāṇa. || 23 ||
Oṃ. Elsewhere [the rule regarding the non-mention of the name] is due to desire, and in that case it is also due to the [absence of mention of the] abodes and so forth. Oṃ. 24.
Oṃ. There is no omission [of the subsidiary rites] because of their being performed with reverence. Oṃ. Because of the mention of their presence [in the text]. Oṃ.

If it were thus stated that everything beginning with *satya* is Viṣṇu, then since Śrī would also possess the status of an eligible candidate (*adhikāritva*), she too would have to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*) after *prāṇa*. Consequently, there arises the objection that the statement regarding the range of eligible candidates ending with *prāṇa* would be incorrect; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). Here, the inquiry is whether Śrī—who is brought into proximity by *prāṇa* and Viṣṇu—is an eligible candidate for meditation or not. For that purpose, the question is whether she is bound [by the conditions of eligibility] or not.

For that purpose, [it must be considered] whether Sītā’s dwelling on earth and so forth was merely a "birth" and the like—consisting of the soul's union with a body—or rather, it was a "manifestation" (prādurbhāva) and the like. For that purpose, [it must be considered] whether Śrī’s worship of the Lord was for the sake of being released from the bondage of karma and the like which causes birth and so forth, or rather, it was for the sake of an excellence of unconditioned devotion, as if she were already liberated. For that purpose, [it must be considered] whether there exists any basis for conceiving it as being caused by devotion, or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), however, is as follows:

In passages such as, "That which was worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Bhava, by the goddess Śrī, and by the Sāttvata sages," the worship of the Blessed One by Śrī herself is heard. And this worship, like that of others, is for the purpose of liberation from bondage through the mediation of pleasing the Blessed One; for if she were already one who had accomplished her purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*), such worship would be inappropriate. Furthermore, there is no evidence to suggest it is caused by an excess of devotion. Otherwise, even for the Sāttvatas and others, that worship would not have that [liberation] as its purpose.

And thus, because by the power of that [divine will] Śrī appears in the form of Sītā, Rukmiṇī, and others, and because her concealment and so forth consist of the assumption and abandonment of bodies dependent on karma—thereby making her known to be bound like other individual souls—and because she is virtuous while being bound, Śrī is indeed qualified for meditation. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: [The established conclusion: Even though she possesses a body subject to karma, she is not bound; rather, she is the supreme sovereign who, out of compassion for the world, assumes various forms such as Sītā and Rukmiṇī through her own divine power. Therefore, she is not a mere subordinate subject of meditation, but is the very object of worship. This is because her "bondage" is merely a display of her sovereignty, intended to manifest her grace toward the world, and not a state of subjection to karma as it pertains to other individual souls. Thus, she remains the supreme authority.

By the force of the scriptural passages cited in the commentary beginning with *sarvāyatana*, it is understood that [Śrī] is eternally liberated due to her eternal connection with the Lord and His preeminent grace. By virtue of that, it is understood that her dwelling on earth and so forth are merely manifestations (*prādurbhāva*) caused solely by her own will under the direction of the Lord's will, and thus lack the nature of bodily union or the like dependent upon karma. Furthermore, based on the Smṛti passage, "Just as Śrī, though eternally liberated... and because worship is conceived as being caused by an excellence of devotion, Śrī is not a [limited] qualified aspirant (*adhikārin*). The result, however, is the establishment that for practitioners, [the state of liberation] lasts until the end of their vital breaths. || 24 ||

|| Oṃ. There is a restrictive rule for the purpose of determining that [the fruit]; for when those [auxiliaries] are seen, there is no obstruction to the separate [attainment of the fruit]. Oṃ. || 25 ||

In the preceding section, it was stated that even in the absence of results, there is no lapse in the worship of Śrī due to the necessity of performing it with reverence; however, the connection [of the present topic] arises from the doubt: "In that case, since those who have not yet achieved their purpose lack results, would there not be a total lapse of all forms of worship, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth? Here, the inquiry is whether the threefold worship—consisting of hearing, reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)—should be performed individually or collectively. To determine this, it must be examined whether there is any fruit for each of these three types of worship or not.

For that purpose, there arises the question: do the three [means] have no utility in being the means to that [vision], or do they? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Meditation (*upāsana*) is indeed for the sake of seeing the Lord, according to the scriptural text, "He is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*). And since that [seeing] is accomplished either through hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*) or through meditation alone (*nididhyāsana*), there is no evidence for its being accomplished by all three together. The scriptural text, "He is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," is also consistent with the injunction of optional alternative means.

Furthermore, there is no utility for the triad [of hearing, reflection, and meditation]. It is not tenable to claim that hearing is useful for making known what was unknown, reflection for producing a restrictive discipline (*niyama*) regarding that, and meditation for producing direct perception (*dṛśi*). Thus, since all three would have distinct results, it is illogical to enjoin the triad with the purpose of attaining direct perception. And so, in the absence of utility for either the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or its application, as regards direct perception—

[The opponent argues: Since there is no fruit due to the absence of the three being accomplished together, the meditation on the whole should not be performed. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: In the scripture stating, "One should see [the Self] through the mind," all three are enjoined with the purpose of seeing; and since there is no word indicating an option (*vikalpa*), it is understood that they function as a means through conjunction (*samuccaya*). Therefore, the triad must indeed be performed as the cause for the fruit consisting of the vision of the Self. Nor should one suspect a lack of utility.

Although meditation alone is the cause for [attaining] direct realization (*darśana*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are useful because they accomplish the removal of the obstacles—namely ignorance, doubt, and error—which are required for the arising of vision. As for the result, it is the establishment of the triad mentioned in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*. || 25 ||
Oṃ. For it has been said that this is indeed like a gift. Oṃ. 26.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: either because once the primary duty has been established, its subsidiary (aṅga) is now being defined here; or because while the fruit of the triad of hearing and so forth was previously stated, here their subsidiary is being stated; or because while the subsidiary of meditation—namely, hearing and reflection—was stated as the cause for the vision [of Brahman], here the subsidiary of all three is being stated. Here, the inquiry is whether the triad of hearing and so forth under discussion is a cause for knowledge when performed in any manner whatsoever, or only when accompanied by the teacher’s instruction preceded by devotion.

To that end, there is no proof that such [knowledge] possesses the quality of being a cause for the fruit by virtue of being endowed with the instruction of a Guru; rather, there exist subverting arguments such as contradiction with Śruti, and indeed the opposite. This is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

This is not so, because there is no evidence that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means lead to vision (*dṛśi*) only when conjoined with the teacher’s instruction; on the contrary, since the scripture [states] "It is to be seen," it prescribes the triad of hearing and the rest specifically for the purpose of the object to be seen (*dṛśya*). Furthermore, if knowledge were dependent upon the grace of the teacher, it would follow that liberation—even for one who possesses knowledge—would likewise be dependent upon him. This would entail the possibility that liberation might sometimes fail to occur due to the teacher’s displeasure. Moreover, there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) in the form of the refutation stated [in the Sūtra]: "There is no such restriction for all. Therefore, [the opponent's view is untenable].

However, it may be argued that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are the cause of knowledge only when they are accompanied by the teacher’s instruction; yet, the teacher’s displeasure is not an obstacle to liberation. If that were the case, then even the teacher’s instruction would be of no avail for knowledge. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: hearing and so forth are the cause of knowledge only when they are endowed with the auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) of the teacher’s instruction given out of affection, and not by themselves alone.

This is because the scripture, stating "A person who has a teacher knows," reveals that knowledge is dependent upon the grace of the guru; therefore, without that [grace], knowledge is not established through mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Smṛti*: "Whatever one endowed with perfect characteristics and a well-pleased mind may give to a disciple becomes true; there is no doubt about this. And: "Whatever even a guru might give when his heart is not exceedingly pleased, that does not become true; therefore, the guru should always be worshipped."

Nor does the scriptural contradiction regarding the "drinking of the substance" (*dravyapāna*) constitute a sublation [of this view]. This is because hearing and so forth are the primary means [to knowledge], whereas the gift to the teacher is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) thereof; just as the extraction of *soma* juice—though it depends on firmly pressing the stalks—is a subsidiary part of the study of the *Soma* chapter, so too, although knowledge depends on the gift to the teacher, it is logically consistent that the gift is a subsidiary part of the hearing and other means which are the causes of knowledge.

Furthermore, although there is no injunction establishing the subsidiary (*aṅga*) as being of equal status with the primary means of accomplishment, the offering (*pradāna*) is nonetheless permitted by the scriptural mention of the substance, since it is established either through firm custom—such as the pressing of the *muṣṭi*—or through another scriptural statement. Nor should it be argued that the occasional absence of knowledge due to anger, or the absence of liberation for the knower, constitutes a sublation; for since knowledge and liberation are ordained by the Lord (*Īśvara*), their non-existence is impossible.

Furthermore, the curse of the Guru is effective as a cause for the diminution of knowledge and other virtues, according to the Smṛti passage beginning with "Even for the knower, upon the curse of the Guru," and so forth; thus its purposefulness is established. As for the result, it is the support of the dependence on the Guru, which was stated in the verse: "But the fruit [arises] from the commonality of the object of the others. || 26 ||
|| Oṃ, because of the abundance of the liṅgas; for that is more powerful, and that too, oṃ. || 27 ||

The connection (*saṅgati*) here is established because, in the context of the relationship between the previously mentioned subordinate member (*aṅga*) and the principal member (*aṅgin*), the strength of the subordinate member is now being proven. Here, there is an inquiry as to whether the two means—namely, the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, and the gift to the teacher (*gurupradāna*) which is its subordinate member—are of equal strength, or whether one of them is stronger. To that end, the inquiry is whether the equality of humanity (*puruṣatva*) establishes an equality between the efforts of the teacher and the student, or not. Furthermore, regarding the conclusion that one of them is stronger, the inquiry is whether the student’s effort is stronger, or the teacher’s gift is stronger.

Regarding that matter, there is no proof for the superiority of *pradāna* (the act of bestowing), while there is indeed a refutation—or rather, the opposite. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): since there is no refutation [for the superiority of *pradāna*] and there is an absence of proof, *pradāna* is not superior; rather, it is only hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth that are the primary means, because even if the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) were to establish the superiority of *pradāna*, it would entail the consequence of the procedure being sublated by the direct scriptural statement (*āmnāna*), and it would further entail the consequence of rendering hearing and the rest purposeless. Therefore, due to the absence of refutation and the absence of proof, *pradāna* is not superior. On the contrary, hearing and the rest alone are the primary means.

Or, let it be granted that there is no difference in strength between the teacher and the disciple because they are equally human; thus, both the bestowal by the teacher and the effort of the disciple would be equal. For there is no distinction whatsoever even when a difference in degree exists. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: equality is not tenable. While they may be equal in being human, just as they differ in the roles of teacher and disciple, their respective efforts can also vary in degree; therefore, mere humanity is not the determining factor. When a difference in degree does exist, it has been stated that the bestowal itself possesses greater weight, because of the presence of supporting evidence in the form of a plurality of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

For although violence (*hiṃsā*) possesses the power to produce sin, sacrificial violence is seen to produce merit through the force of its constituent procedures (*itikartavyatā*), such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), anointing (*añjana*), and circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*). Just as those procedures possess predominance (*prābalya*) in that context, here too there is no risk of destroying the status of [the gift] as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) due to the predominance of the act of giving. Furthermore, since hearing and so forth are also necessary—both by the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) and by the traditional law (*smṛti*) "the grace of the guru is powerful"—there is no futility in them, and thus there is no subverting obstacle (*bādhaka*).

The abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga*) is evident in the commentaries and other works. As for the result, it consists in the corroboration of the previously stated point of doctrine—that hearing and so forth, together with their attendant procedures (*setikartavyatva*), serve as causes for knowledge. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that in some cases a teacher might not be required, which would render the aforementioned [position] untenable. || 27 ||
Oṃ. A prior conceptualization may arise from the context, as in the case of ritual action and mental [action]. Oṃ. 28.
|| Oṃ And because of extension, oṃ ||

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it was stated that "the grace of whom is powerful," and here that Guru is being considered. Here, the inquiry is whether the Guru under discussion is restricted to one previously obtained, or whether another may also be accepted. For that purpose, the investigation is whether there is no reason for abandoning the previous one and there is a subverting factor (bādhaka), or whether the opposite is the case. Likewise, regarding the position that another may be accepted, the question is whether he can be anyone at all, or whether he must be one who is not inferior to the previous one and is indeed a bestower of complete grace. As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

For the acceptance of a guru is indeed for the sake of attaining spiritual merit (*śubha*). Since that [merit] will be attained through the very guru previously received, there is no reason to abandon him; furthermore, there is the subverting argument consisting of the scriptural hearing of the fault: "One who abandons the guru and the mantra shall go to the Raurava hell. Therefore, it is the previously received guru alone [who is to be followed], and no other should be accepted. Moreover, on the view that another may also be accepted, since there would be no regulating factor, it would follow that just anyone could be chosen. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

For the acceptance of a teacher (*guruparigraha*) is not merely for the sake of obtaining some small measure of merit, but rather for the sake of obtaining all the merit appropriate to oneself that one requires. If the teacher previously accepted is incapable [of providing this], then another teacher must also be accepted, because there exists the capacity—characterized by the intent to bestow complete grace—to fulfill the need for what was not obtained from the former. Furthermore, he too must not be just anyone, but one who is not inferior to oneself and who is indeed a bestower of complete grace.

If that [teacher] is equal [to one's own teacher], there is an option as to whether he should be accepted with the prior permission [of the former teacher] or not—just as in the case of two meditations yielding equal results—but it is not a rule that he must necessarily be accepted. If he is superior, he should be accepted even without the prior permission. This is because the entire aforementioned point is established by the *smṛti* stating, "A superior one is obtained from the previous," and the *smṛti* stating, "Someone [obtains] complete favor," and because in the *śruti* passage, "Worship Brahman," the previous teacher himself is shown to authorize the acceptance of someone equal to or superior to himself.

Nor is there a contradiction with the statement regarding faults; for that [statement] has scope because it refers to the acceptance of what is inferior, refers to useless acceptance, and refers to the absence of prior authorization. As for the result: it is the support of the point stated under the verse "itaretu" (II.27)—namely, that meditation on the qualities and so forth must be performed according to the method taught by the omniscient Guru. || 28 ||
Oṃ, but knowledge alone [is the means], because of the definitive determination; Oṃ. 29.
Oṃ, and also from seeing, oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: since it has not been determined by the statement regarding the cause being a "light means" (*laghūpāya*) that the worship whose procedure consists of the offering of the Guru, along with its distinctions of fruit, qualification, and object of meditation, is a cause of liberation, all that was previously stated is like a painting on a wall (i.e., baseless). Here, the inquiry is whether the practice of hearing and so forth, which is the subject under discussion, is not to be performed or is indeed to be performed. For that purpose, the question is whether a determination that such practice is a cause of liberation through the medium of knowledge is possible or not.

Regarding that matter, there arises the inquiry as to whether the description—given in the passage beginning with “or figurative” (*bhāktaṃ vā*)—of the statements concerning karma being the cause [of liberation] as being merely figurative (in the sense of being an indirect cause of liberation) is improper or proper. For that purpose, one must consider whether there exists any sublation of the understanding that karma is a direct cause of liberation, as conveyed by the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the phrase “by action alone” (*karmaṇaiva*). Furthermore, in the view that determines karma to be a cause of liberation through the medium of knowledge, is this solely by way of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), or also by way of immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*)? In passages such as, "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," although the restrictive particle (*eva*) may have its scope in the manner to be explained later, there is no subverting authority that would negate the understanding—derived from the instrumental case-ending—that action is the direct cause of liberation (denoted by the word *saṃsiddhi*). This is because statements such as, "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," merely establish that knowledge is a cause of liberation, and thus do not negate the status of action as a cause of liberation.

And thus, since the power of those statements which teach that [knowledge] is the direct cause of liberation—being free from any contradiction—establishes that action (*karman*) is also a direct cause of liberation, it is improper to describe the causality of action toward liberation as merely figurative (as done in the third chapter, first section, under the sutra *bhāktaṃ vā'nātmavittvāt*). Since the statement "there is no other path," which expresses a cause with exclusive restriction, is stronger than the statement regarding ritual action (*karman*), it directly negates that action is the cause [of liberation]. Consequently, even in passages such as "by action alone," the way in which action serves as a cause for liberation must be described—according to the previously stated method—as being only indirect. Thus, because it can be determined from the context that meditation (*upāsanā*) is the cause of liberation by means of knowledge (*jñāna*), meditation is indeed what must be performed.

Even knowledge, which serves as the means, is not merely indirect; rather, by the force of such scriptural statements as "upon seeing Him, one is liberated," the Śruti regarding the "knower" (vidvān) also refers to direct perception. Thus, since there is the hearing that even direct knowledge [is required], the triad of hearing and the other [means] must indeed be performed. Furthermore, the Smṛti [which speaks of liberation upon hearing] is also restrictive in nature, as will be refuted later. As for the result, it has already been established as previously stated. || 29 ||
|| Oṃ. And because of the superior strength of direct Vedic revelation and other means, there is no sublation. Oṃ. || 30 ||

If the Śruti is more authoritative because it possesses exclusivity (*sāvadhāraṇatva*), then there arises a connection [of this section] due to the doubt that the Smṛti is likewise authoritative because it is the word of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*). Here, liberation—which was introduced in the preceding section as the fruit of knowledge—is examined: is it accomplished through ritual action (*karman*) or is it accomplished through knowledge (*jñāna*)? For that purpose, the inquiry is whether the Smṛti statement, "by action alone," is more powerful than the Śruti statement, "there is no other path," or not.

Is the restriction "by action alone" (*karmaṇaiva*) for that purpose without scope, or does it have scope? For that purpose, is there no basis for providing scope, or is there? The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Liberation is accomplished by action, because of the Smṛti text stating "by action. Nor should it be said that the Smṛti is weak because it is sublated by a Śruti text containing a restriction; for the Smṛti itself also contains a restriction. Nor can it be argued that [the Śruti] has scope because it excludes non-connection (i.e., it means "liberation is attained *only* by action"), since there is no basis for such a construction.

Nor should it be argued that when there is a conflict with Śruti, Smṛti is weak while Śruti alone possesses authority—this being established in the *Pūrvatantra* by the rule "In case of conflict, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded"—because that [rule] applies only to the position that Smṛti derives its authority from being rooted in Śruti. However, since the authority of the Smṛti "by action alone" is accepted precisely because it is the word of the Lord (Bhagavat), it possesses greater force due to its being the speech of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) and its use of an exclusive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); thus, it sublates the Śruti concerning knowledge (*vidyā*). The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Liberation is to be accomplished by knowledge alone, not by ritual action. This is because, regarding its being accomplished by knowledge, there exist powerful scriptural texts (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), logical arguments (*upapatti*), and traditional codes (*smṛti*); for the *śruti* possesses greater authority due to its being endowed with an exclusive determination that leaves no room for alternative interpretations. Likewise, even for Indra, who had performed many rituals, there is the powerful indicative mark of his prayer for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) for the sake of liberation in the form of bliss unmixed with suffering, as established by the *śruti*: "Indra [performed] horse-sacrifices."

Nevertheless, it is logically established that the eternal goal of man cannot be achieved by means of ritual action (*karman*), which is determined to have a fruit characterized by origination and destruction. This is because the scriptural statement, "Nothing that is uncreated is attained by means of what is created," is both authoritative and flawless; and because the Smṛti text, "One is bound by action," being the word of the Lord and endowed with sound reasoning, possesses great force.

Thus, because there exist many powerful arguments establishing that liberation is to be accomplished through knowledge (*jñāna-sādhya*), the restrictive determination "by action alone" (*karmaṇaiva*)—along with the statement "they have attained perfection through action"—is merely an exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavacchedaka*) and thus has its scope limited. Therefore, this Smṛti lacks authority for establishing that [liberation] is to be accomplished by action. Its purpose, however, is to support the necessity of performing meditation (*upāsanā*). || 30 ||
Oṃ. [The proof of the existence of the Lord] is established from the presence of the fourfold logical reasons, beginning with the "concomitant" (anubandha), etc. Oṃ. 31.

Regarding the phrase "and because of [the mention of] vision" (*darśanācca*): since "vision" was previously determined in the preceding section (*pūrva-naya*) to be the cause of liberation and is thus the subject under discussion, its being accomplished through devotion (*bhakti*) and other means is stated here; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). The inquiry is whether the vision under discussion arises merely from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—accompanied by the granting [of grace]—without devotion and the rest, or not. For that purpose, the question is whether the meditation (*upāsana*), which is the cause of vision, leads to the final result even if it occurs without devotion and the rest. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

"Vision [of the Lord] will occur through mere hearing and so forth, even when conjoined with giving, provided they are devoid of devotion and the like. This is because, according to Smṛti texts such as "One who is endowed with the correct characteristics," there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished through the grace of the Guru. Nor is it logical to claim that meditation itself is impossible for one devoid of devotion and the like; for such meditation can occur even through hatred. And it is not tenable to say that meditation accompanied by hatred does not culminate in its fruit.

Regarding the statement in the Seventh Skandha, "The kings such as the Caidya [Śiśupāla] and others [attained liberation] through hatred," this refers to the memory of liberation for those who meditated even with hatred. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: vision [of the Lord] does not arise from worship accompanied by ritual offerings when it is devoid of devotion and the like; rather, it arises only from that which is endowed with devotion and the rest.

For even the worship of the Lord, if devoid of devotion and other such qualities, is not a cause for the goals of human life, but rather a cause of misfortune; this is established by numerous authorities cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna*, beginning with the statement: "The claim that liberation arises from hatred and so forth contradicts the words of the Śruti. Furthermore, since worship that culminates in the fruit, as well as the grace of the Guru, are achieved only through devotion and the like—this being established by such passages as: "Nevertheless, one may obtain the grace of the Guru through the perfection of qualities such as devotion, which are established from time immemorial"—it follows that devotion and the rest are indispensable.

As for the statement beginning with "the Caidya and others [were saved] through hatred," this is justified because it refers to those who are naturally devoted. The result, however, is the establishment of the efficacy of the description of the Lord's majesty found in the preceding section concerning devotion. || 31 ||
Oṃ. And it is seen that [the difference] is like the difference between various cognitions; this has been stated. Oṃ. 32.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: since it has been stated that devotion and so forth are necessary for the vision [of the Lord], the gradations within that vision are now being determined. The inquiry is whether the vision of the Lord, which is the cause of liberation under discussion, is of a single mode or of multiple modes. To that end, the question is whether scriptural statements such as "Upon seeing Him alone, one is liberated" and "Through devotion one comes to know Me" mean that knowledge of a single uniform nature is the cause for all [liberated souls], or not.

Regarding this matter, there is a doubt as to whether or not there exists any basis for the claim that the knowledge which is the cause of liberation for all is of a single uniform nature. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The knowledge that is the cause of liberation for all is indeed of a single uniform nature. This is because the scripture, in the passage "Having seen Him alone," declares that liberation occurs through the knowledge of all without distinction. Furthermore, in the passage, "By devotion one comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what My extent is; then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter," it is shown that complete knowledge arises for all through devotion and other such means.

For it is remembered in the *Gītā* that liberation is attained through complete knowledge alone. Nor can the *Śruti* and other texts be interpreted as referring to something specific [other than full knowledge], because there is no basis for such an assumption. Furthermore, the gradation in the meditations (*upāsana*) which cause knowledge cannot serve as such a basis; for even among those possessing various kinds of means, the equality of the goal may occur—as is seen, for example, among farmers—thereby rendering that gradation irrelevant to the final result.

If knowledge possessed specific variations of degree—being either deficient or superior—then because the *Smṛti* states in the verse beginning with "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*) that liberation is attained through complete knowledge alone, it would follow that those lacking such knowledge could not attain liberation; this would result in the subversion of the established principle stated as "there is no restriction for all" (*aniyamaḥ sarveṣām*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: the vision of the Lord by qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*) indeed takes many forms. Since the means of worship (*upāsana*) leading to that vision is diverse, a corresponding diversity in the knowledge produced by it is necessarily required, for the fruit conforms to its cause.

Nor is that [diversity] rendered irrelevant by the possibility of another explanation; for since the diversity of knowledge is established by such scriptural texts as, "The internal seer, the external seer," and so forth, the uniformity of all [knowledges] is sublated, and thus the diversity of meditations is explained through that [diversity of knowledge]. It is improper to postulate [this] based merely on the occasional analogy of a farmer's vision. Nor does the fault of the consequence that no one would attain liberation arise.

For, by the Smṛti statement, "Indeed, upon seeing the incarnations," liberation is understood to be attained by qualified aspirants through knowledge that has reached varying degrees of excellence; and by the Smṛti statement, "by devotion," it is either justified as referring generally to knowledge concerning all objects as the cause of liberation, or specifically as referring to the qualified aspirant in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha. As for the result, it is the justification of the gradations of liberation mentioned in the verse beginning with "yāvat. || 32 ||

Oṃ. [The soul does not become the body] even on account of similarity, because it is perceived [as distinct], just as death [is distinct from the living]; for there is no falling into the world [of the body]. Oṃ. 33.

The connection [of this section] is established by the determination that the diversity observed regarding the vision of the Blessed Lord is due to the fact that it is the vision of the *bimba* (the original form) alone that is the cause of liberation. Here, the inquiry is whether the vision of the Blessed Lord under discussion—which is the cause of liberation—has as its object any form whatsoever, or specifically the *bimba* form. For that purpose, the question is whether, if only the vision of a form were the cause of liberation, the uniformity of the forms of the Blessed Lord as determined in the section beginning with "Not even from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*) would be compromised, or not.

Likewise, there arises the question: if any form whatsoever were the cause of liberation, would that [liberation] result in futility or not? The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: If one were to accept that one particular form possesses the power to grant liberation while another does not, then the equality of all forms—which was stated in the scriptural passage, "The Supreme is not characterized by dual attributes even from the standpoint of location, for He is everywhere"—would be contradicted. Consequently, the knowledge of any form whatsoever must indeed be the cause of liberation.

Furthermore, if the perception of the universal (*sāmānya*) were the cause of liberation, it would follow that the perception of that [particular] is fruitless, which is not tenable. Therefore, since liberation itself is its fruit, the perception of the universal is also indeed a cause of liberation. Moreover, if one were to argue that some knowledge of form is a cause of liberation while other [knowledge] is not, then there would be the undesirable consequence of violating the stated rule, namely that even the knowledge of the reflected image (*bimba*) would be a cause of liberation in some cases and not in others. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: just as...

Although there is no difference in the nature of death among those who have died, liberation occurs immediately after a specific type of death; likewise, although the forms of the Lord are equal, the knowledge of a specific form of the Lord—according to the Lord’s own resolve—is the cause of liberation, not the knowledge of just any form. For scripture states that even though the Lord is equal [to all], He liberates one only upon the vision of His own specific form (the *bimba*). Nor is the vision of the general [form] thus rendered fruitless.

"Because people [act] from the perception of the universal," according to this Smṛti, there is no such [undesirable] consequence regarding the perception of the reflection, as that [Smṛti] pertains to conceptualization (vikalpa) in perception; however, the result is the establishment of the necessity of meditating upon the original object (bimba). || 33 ||
|| Oṃ. And by the subsequent [scriptural] statement, the sound has that same nature; but because of its abundance, there is a connection. Oṃ. || 34 ||

The connection [of this section] is established because the independence of devotion (*bhakti*), which was previously mentioned as the cause of seeing, is here set aside. The inquiry is whether the vision under discussion arises through the power of devotion or through the power of the Lord (*īśvara*). For that purpose, the question is whether the scriptural text, "Devotion alone reveals Him," intends the independence of devotion, or whether it intends devotion to be the instrument for the agent, the Lord, in granting the vision.

Therefore, there is no grounds for assuming that devotion (*bhakti*) is intended here as an instrument (*karaṇa*); rather, it is logical that the specific mention of "devotion alone" is intended in its primary sense. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): since there is no basis for interpreting the scriptural hearing of devotion’s agency in the passage "Devotion alone reveals Him" as being intended to denote instrumentality, and because it would be unjustified to single out devotion alone among existing other means due to a lack of supporting reason, devotion alone—without depending on the grace of the Lord and by its own power—brings about the direct perception of the Blessed One.

"He gives [it]"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). However, if the agency of seeing belongs to devotion alone, there arises a contradiction because the *Atharva-śruti* states: "But for that wise one who strives by these means, this Self enters the abode of Brahman. Here, for the sake of that person who strives for the purpose of vision through these means such as teaching and so forth, the Supreme Self, being pleased, enters the wind—the abode of Brahman—and becomes manifest to him. Thus, by accepting that the Lord, when pleased by means such as devotion, is Himself the giver of His own direct perception, there would otherwise be a contradiction.

Because of the scriptural statement, "Devotion alone [attains Him]," and because devotion cannot logically be the agent (kartṛ), it must be understood as the instrument (karaṇa); thus, since devotion is the most prominent among the means, it is appropriate to specify it by saying "devotion alone. Furthermore, since it has been stated in the first chapter that all words such as "devotion" have their primary application (samanvaya) in the Blessed Lord, it is logical—by the principle of the section on primordial matter (prakṛti-naya)—that the word "devotion," even in its feminine gender, primarily refers to Viṣṇu according to scripture.

Based on the authority of such Smṛti passages as "Viṣṇu is the supreme one established in devotion," the direct realization (aparokṣajñāna) of Him arises through the power of the Lord, who has been propitiated by beginningless devotion. As for the result, it is the establishment of His unmanifest nature (avyaktatva), as stated in the verse: "That [Self] is indeed unmanifest. || 34 ||
|| Oṃ. [The self is one] because of its existence in a single body. Oṃ. || 35 ||

The statement that beginningless devotion (*anādibhakti*) is the cause of being seen [by the Lord] is improper; for, according to the direction of the arguments in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts regarding the sūtra "From a particular station" (*sthānaviśeṣāt*), it is impossible for [the Lord's grace] to depend on a fitness consisting of the attainment of beginningless devotion and so forth. With this intention, the objection is raised, which provides the connection [to the present topic]. Here, the inquiry is whether or not there is a dependence on beginningless fitness with regard to the meditation under discussion and the like. For that purpose, the question is whether such fitness can possibly be beginningless or whether it cannot.

For that purpose, it must be considered whether the parts (aṃśa) of the Lord arise in their own essential nature or not. For that purpose, it must be considered whether there is difference (bheda) between the part and the whole (aṃśin) or non-difference (abheda). For that purpose, it must be considered whether there is no proof for non-difference and there is a sublation (bādhaka) [of it], or whether the opposite is the case. As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

Since there is no evidence proving the non-difference between a part and the whole, and on the contrary, because there exists a subverting argument in the form of the undesirable consequence that one would not perceive differences in knowledge, pleasure, pain, and so forth—just as one does not perceive such differences between Caitra and Maitra—their difference is necessary. Consequently, even if the whole, such as Indra, is beginningless, it is possible for a part such as Arjuna to arise by way of its own nature; thus, since parts like Arjuna are beginningless, their fitness for those attributes must also be beginningless, which is impossible if [the whole] were beginningless.

It is not the case that there is no requirement for beginningless fitness (*anādi-yogyatā*) in practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: In the view that the part (*aṃśa*) has its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), since there would be an absence of prior karma performed by that [part] which brings about its body, it would follow that liberation is impossible; thus, a body caused by karma is untenable. Consequently, as there is no other alternative, and because of the Smṛti text stating, "But the fires were born separately as parts of him through his very karma," one must necessarily admit that the parts, such as Arjuna and others, abide in bodies acquired through the karma of the whole (*aṃśin*). Furthermore, this is because the relationship between a part and the whole would be impossible if they were distinct entities.

Because the persistence of the soul in a body acquired through desire would otherwise be inexplicable; because the fruit of the primary means of attainment, such as meditation (*upāsanā*), residing in the whole (*aṃśin*) is experienced even partially by the part (*aṃśa*); and because there is no sublation—since the non-experience of limited knowledge, pleasure, and so forth is rendered possible by the will of the Lord through contact with humans, the eating of material food, and the like, which would otherwise be inexplicable—the part and the whole are non-different. Furthermore, since it is impossible for a part that is non-different from the beginningless [whole] to have its own nature produced anew.

Since that [nature] is also beginningless, it is possible for the capacity that constitutes its property (*dharma*) to be likewise beginningless; thus, there exists dependence on beginningless capacity in practices such as meditation (*upāsana*). As for the result, however, there is no risk of an absence of regulation—such as the contingency of even those devoid of capacity engaging in meditation—due to this [requirement of capacity]. || 35 ||
Oṃ. For the limbs are bound [to the Upaniṣads], not to the branches [of the Vedas] for each Veda; Oṃ. 36.
|| Oṃ, or there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and so forth; oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: whereas in the preceding portion meditation was taught for the deities such as Indra and others according to their respective fitness, here the meditation on the Lord, who is the subject at hand, is being discussed. Herein lies the inquiry: should the meditation on the Lord, who is the subject at hand, be performed alone, or should it be accompanied by the meditation on the deities who are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of Brahman? To that end, the question is whether there exists any indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) regarding whether the prohibition of other worship found in passages such as "Know Him alone as one" and "One should not worship another deity" applies in every respect, or only in terms of predominance.

Likewise, for one who worships another deity, should all the qualities perceived in one [deity] be meditated upon by all, or only those appropriate to each? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the worship and adoration of other deities are prohibited in such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti* and *smṛti*) as "Know Him alone as the One," and since there is no evidence that this prohibition applies only to independent worship and so forth, one should perform the worship of the Lord alone. Even if the worship of a deity is performed, the worship of all deities must be conducted by attributing to them the very qualities perceived in one [deity].

This is because deities and so forth are seen to be objects of worship everywhere, and because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since the presentation of deities in the Vedas serves the purpose of worship—according to the maxim that "there is no purpose for study [otherwise]"—and since their mention in the Vedas would otherwise be futile in the absence of such worship, there exists a supporting proof in the form of the "unaccountability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) of that mention. Therefore, by that very fact, passages such as "him alone" (*tameva*) must necessarily be understood as primarily intended to prohibit worship.

Since there is no contradiction between them, the worship of the Lord should be performed precisely by means of the practice of worshipping other deities as well. Even regarding the worship of other deities, according to Smṛti texts such as "Because of equality, or because of superiority," since the gods possess a hierarchy of high and low status, the qualities of the superior should not be meditated upon in relation to those who are inferior; rather, one should meditate only on those qualities appropriate to each. Just as all words denoting the Lord do not apply everywhere but only to what is appropriate, so too, the qualities of the inferior should not be meditated upon in relation to the superior.

Just as there is meditation upon mantras that describe lower deities by treating them as if they were higher ones, so too worship (upāsana) for the sake of specific results must be performed only by those of the highest qualification, not by everyone; this is because of the Smṛti passage beginning with "of the deities who are limbs of worship. The result [of this argument] is the establishment of the meaningfulness of those portions of the Veda that describe deities. || 36 ||
Oṃ. Just as the ritual act (*kratu*) is superior, so too does [the scripture] show; Oṃ. (Sūtra 37)

In the preceding section, it was stated that the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhṛti*) need not be performed by everyone, because its fruit is unattainable by all in the context of deity-worship. Now, a doubt arises: "In that case, the meditation on the quality of 'the Great' (*bhūma*) should also not be performed by everyone, since unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśaya-bhūmatva*) cannot be attained by anyone. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*). Here, regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "That which is the Great" (*yo vai bhūmā*), the inquiry is whether the quality of the Great is to be meditated upon by all or not. To determine this, the question is whether such meditation is purposeless or indeed purposeful.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Just as the qualities such as "supporting" (*sambhṛti*) and so forth are not to be meditated upon by everyone because the fruit of such meditation—namely, the attainment of all things—is impossible for all, so too the state of "plenitude" (*bhūmatva*), which consists of unsurpassed fullness, is not something desired to be attained by anyone due to their incapacity; thus, being purposeless, plenitude is not to be meditated upon by all. Even though it serves as a qualification for the knowledge and bliss that are to be meditated upon by all, plenitude is not to be meditated upon by all, because, like the "having joy as its head" (*priyaśirastva*) and so forth, it is useless and lacks practical utility regarding the fruit. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

"Indeed, the Infinite (Bhūman) alone is the supreme deity to be worshipped"—from this scriptural statement, it is understood that the attainment of the desired fruit occurs only when the Infinite is worshipped in conjunction with all its attributes, such as knowledge and bliss; otherwise, it does not. Thus, since the worship of the attribute of Infinity in the form "Knowledge is the Infinite" and "Bliss is the Infinite" serves as the cause for obtaining the intended result, the state of being Infinite must be worshipped by all, just as a sacrifice consists of the initiation, the Prāyaṇīya, the three Savanas, and the Avabhṛtha.

Since success is achieved only through persistence in all sacrifices, whereas otherwise there is failure, it is superior and must therefore be performed by everyone; thus, the result [of this practice] is the justification for the meditation on transcendental qualities, as stated in the sūtra: "But the fruit [arises] from the description of what is to be done" (3.3.42). || 37 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord is] manifold because of the distinction between sound and the other [objects of sense]. Oṃ. 38.

The connection [of this section] arises either because there is here a consideration of the specific details of what was previously stated in general, or because of the following doubt: if the state of being "plurality" (*bhūmatva*) were to be the object of worship for all [aspirants], would it not result in the collapse of the gradations mentioned in the passage beginning with "as far as" (*yāvat*)? Here, the inquiry concerns whether the subject under discussion—the state of being plurality—is perceived by the qualified aspirants in a uniform manner or in various forms. To that end, the question is whether, if it were perceived in various forms, that perception would be erroneous or not.

For that reason, the state of being "much" (*bhūman*) is of a single form alone; even a manifold form is not possible. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: since gradation is impossible and untenable within the state of *bhūman*, which consists of unsurpassed fullness, it must be of a single form. Furthermore, although it is of a single form, because it appears with gradation during the stages of hearing, reflection, and immediate intuition (*aparokṣajñāna*), it would follow that hearing and the other means are false cognitions; therefore, it is more reasonable that it is perceived as having a single form. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Just as there is a gradation in the infinity of past years, months, fortnights, days, ghaṭikās, and so forth, here too, since a gradation is possible within the state of "abundance" (bhūmatva), and because such infinities exist both in the qualities of the Lord and in the Lord Himself, the abundance manifests in various degrees according to each individual's qualification. Since it would follow that the cognition during hearing, reflection, and direct realization is erroneous if one were to perceive only "that much" without perceiving the full extent, it is perceived in its manifold forms; thus, it is indeed manifold that is perceived by those qualified for it.

That which is to be meditated upon is determined according to the specific fruit each individual seeks to attain; as for that fruit, it has been previously explained through its various gradations. 38.
Oṃ. Conceptual construction [is superior] because its fruit is distinguished. Oṃ. 39.

The connection [between the sections] is as follows: a specific rule was stated previously regarding the meditation on qualities (*guṇopāsti*), whereas here it is stated regarding the meditation on forms (*rūpopāsti*). Here, the inquiry is whether there is a restrictive rule that the worship of the Lord must not be performed with a form distinct from the original image (*bimba*), or whether it is a matter of option—whether it should or should not be performed. For that purpose, one must determine whether there is no fruit for such worship, or whether there is. And for that purpose, one must determine whether the fruit of that worship is liberation (*mokṣa*) or something else. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Since meditation performed by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) cannot result in any fruit other than liberation, and since—as stated in the passage beginning with "Not even from similarity, because [the reflection] is perceived"—liberation is achieved through the worship of the Archetype (bimba), it is illogical for meditation on anything other than the Archetype to yield the fruit of liberation; furthermore, such meditation would be fruitless and, on the contrary, would obstruct the worship of the Archetype which is essential for liberation. Therefore, meditation on Nṛsiṃha and others distinct from the Archetype must certainly not be performed. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows:

Although lay followers (upāsakas) desire liberation, the worship of the image (bimba-upāsanā) is effective as a means to that end; because it results in the removal of the sins required [for liberation], it is fruitful. Therefore, one who desires such a result should perform the worship of Nṛsiṃha and others. However, for one who is capable of destroying sin through intense worship of their own [internal] image alone, it need not be performed. This is an optional alternative based on qualification (vyavasthita-vikalpa), like the rule regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, according to the Smṛti text beginning with "For the sake of liberation, that which is suitable for oneself... The purpose [of this discussion] is to establish the efficacy of the texts that expound upon Nṛsiṃha and other deities. || 39 ||
Oṃ. Optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or they may not, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason. Oṃ. 40.

The connection [of this section] arises either from the following doubt: "If the worship of Nṛsiṃha and other forms must be performed because it has liberation as its useful fruit, then the worship of optional forms and so forth must also be performed, since they too are useful for that end"; or else, from the demonstration that the worship of optional forms and so forth is optional, just like the worship of Nṛsiṃha and others. Here, the inquiry is whether the worship directed toward the forms and qualities of the Lord—which are the means to fulfill desires—is also mandatory or optional. To that end, the consideration is whether or not there exists a reason—such as its utility for liberation—for its necessity.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the accomplishment of knowledge and so forth occurs even without wealth and the like, and because the worship of that form of the Lord—which acquires wealth and so forth—along with its qualities and other attributes, is useful for knowledge by way of providing a livelihood and such, there is a necessary desire for wealth; therefore, the worship of the desirable forms of the Lord and so forth is indeed mandatory. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Since even those destitute of wealth, houses, gardens, and fields are seen to acquire knowledge—and since there is no fixed rule that knowledge arises only through wealth and the like, which would render such means useless for the meditation that causes liberation—and furthermore, because those qualified for it (the *adhikārin*) possess the desire for liberation and thus lack the desire for wealth and other worldly things, the following is established as an option based on the distinction of the qualified person (*adhikāribheda*): either meditations with specific desires (*kāmyopāsana*) should not be performed by seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), while they may be performed by others; or else, even by a seeker of liberation, such meditation should not be performed for the sake of wealth and the like, but rather for the sake of pleasing the Lord—this being an option determined by the difference in the resulting fruit (*phalabheda*).

The rule that [this must be] performed as a necessary duty (avaśyaka) is based on the Smṛti passage beginning with "For whoever... (Yasya yasya hi). As for the result, it is the justification for the description of the torments of hell and so forth, which have as their fruit the detachment (vairāgya) mentioned in the Chapter on Detachment (Vairāgyapāda). || 40 ||
Oṃ. Just as there is the state of being supported within the limbs, Oṃ. 41.
Oṃ, and because of the disciples, Oṃ. Oṃ, because of the summary, Oṃ. Oṃ, and because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities, Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: although the worship for specific desires (*kāmyopāsti*) was previously established as something to be performed because there exists a qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*), here, since such a qualified person does not exist for the worship of the deities residing in the limbs [of the Lord], it might be considered not to be performed. Here, the inquiry is whether the meditation (*upāsana*) concerning deities such as Brahmā and others—who reside in the limbs of the Blessed Lord—is something that ought to be performed or not.

For that purpose, it must be determined whether the mention in the Śruti of the deities as being dependent on the limbs, the injunction for such meditation (*upāsana*), and the hearing of common attributes are capable of establishing that such meditation is an obligatory duty (*kārya*), or rather they are not. For that purpose, it must be determined whether that meditation is without a qualified agent (*niradhikārika*) or with a qualified agent (*sādhikārika*). For that purpose, it must be determined whether there exists anything that establishes a qualified agent, or whether there is not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Such meditation is not an obligatory duty, because there is no reason [for its necessity].

Nor can it be argued that because the Śruti states, "Brahmā is in the head, Rudra in the forehead," and so forth—indicating that the gods reside within the limbs—the description of them must be taken as being for the purpose of meditation (upāsanā), according to the maxim "there is no purpose [for stating what is already known]," and thus the statement cannot be explained otherwise. This is not the case.

It must be stated that the scriptural injunction, "In whichever limb of the Supreme He is to be meditated upon, He is to be thought of in exactly that way," as well as the teaching that "the qualities of the Supreme are common [to all] and are to be gathered by the seeker of liberation who perceives reality"—namely, the hearing of the Lord's qualities such as the eyes being the abode of the sun and so forth—along with the equality of qualities such as knowledge and bliss, constitute the reason for the practice of such meditation.

If such worship were open to all qualified persons (*sarvādhikārika*), the restrictive rule of meditating on the four qualities beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*)—as stated in the sūtra *ānandādayaḥ*—would be violated. For attributes such as having Brahman as the head (*brahmāśritaśiraskatva*) are not qualifiers of Bliss and the other qualities in the same way that "vastness" (*bhūmatva*) is; if they were, it would contradict the previously established restriction. Furthermore, that worship cannot be restricted to the gods alone, as there is no evidence for such a limitation. Indeed, there is no scriptural statement such as "these gods should worship [it]" corresponding to the phrase "Brahmā [is] the head," in the same way that there is a statement "the king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" where the word "king" serves as a qualification.

Even in the absence of such a specific injunction, if one were to postulate a specific qualified person (adhikārī), there would be a contradiction with the logic stated in the Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasaṃgraha, namely, "because there is no difference in the injunctions" (*codanādyaviśeṣāt*). Therefore, since such meditation would be without a qualified person, the mention of it in the Śruti and so forth—being itself purposeless—would not be capable of establishing that such meditation is something to be performed. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that such meditation is indeed something to be performed. Nor is there an absence of a reason, because the mention of it in the Śruti and the resulting *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of explaining it otherwise) serve as the impellers for its performance. Furthermore, the defect of being without a qualified person does not apply.

For the Śruti states, "By means of their limbs, the gods are indeed to be released [from the body]," and because it is heard that the fruit of meditating on qualities such as having the head resting upon Brahmā, the forehead resting upon Rudra, and the eyes resting upon Sūrya is the attainment of the highest station; and since that [station] is to be attained by the gods, it is appropriate—upon considering the nature of the fruit—to assume that the gods themselves possess the qualification for this meditation, just as in the Madhu-vidyā. The purpose of this [discussion], however, is to establish the meaningfulness of that specific meditation. || 41 ||
Or rather, it is not so, because of the scriptural statement regarding their coexistence. 42.
Oṃ, and from seeing [the Tathāgata], Oṃ.

The connection here is that what was previously stated is now supported by means of a specific reason. Here, the inquiry is whether the meditation on the qualities of the Lord—such as His being the creator and so forth, which are based upon Brahman—should be performed or not. For that purpose, the question is whether the non-mention of such meditation in all the Vedic branches is inexplicable except on the grounds that it should not be performed, or whether it is explicable otherwise. For that purpose, the further question is whether there exists any basis for an alternative explanation or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): [it is as follows].

Such meditation is not necessarily mandatory because it is not mentioned in all recensions (*śākhā*). If it were mandatory, it would follow that it must coexist with the meditations found in every recension. Here, the fact that it is not mentioned everywhere is logically untenable unless it is non-mandatory; thus, it leads to that very conclusion. However, the established position (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The full argument continues: Even if a meditation is not mentioned in a particular recension, it may still be performed by one who has studied another recension where it is prescribed. Furthermore, since the injunction to perform the sacrifice itself implies the performance of its constituent parts, the meditation—being an integral part—is included even if not explicitly stated. Moreover, the mention of meditations in specific contexts (such as the *udgītha*) indicates they are intended for those performing the ritual acts associated with those contexts. Therefore, while meditations are indeed to be performed, they are not universally obligatory across all recensions; rather, they are to be practiced according to the specific context and the particular recension studied by the practitioner. Thus, there is no contradiction.

In every respect, if there were an absence of being an effect (*kāryatva*), it would follow that the statement regarding it [the Supreme] in certain instances would be purposeless. This is because the Śruti, in passages such as "He is Truth, Knowledge, the form of Supreme Bliss," speaks of the fourfold qualities beginning with Knowledge; and since it is stated that the worship of Him by means of these and other superior qualities is the prerogative of the Devas alone, such worship is not mentioned as applicable everywhere. Furthermore, since the alternative explanation—that He is not an effect for anyone—is untenable, worship in that manner must indeed be an effect. As for the result, it is the corroboration of the previously stated objects of knowledge (*prameya*). || 42 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fourth quarter. Om. "The human goal [is attained] from this [knowledge], because of the scriptural statement," so says Bādarāyaṇa. Om. (1)

|| Oṃ: Because it is a supplement, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases; thus Jaimini [maintains]. || Oṃ: Because of the observation of customary practice. || Oṃ: Because of the scriptural statement to that effect. || Oṃ: Because of the act of simultaneous grasping. || Oṃ: Because of the injunction for one who possesses that [knowledge]. || Oṃ: And because of the restrictive rule. || Oṃ: But because of the teaching of something additional, Bādarāyaṇa’s view is thus, for such is seen there. || Oṃ: But the scriptural vision is equal. || Oṃ: ||

The connection of this [section] with the preceding section is that the greatness of the knowledge accomplished through the meditations taught in the previous section is stated here. Here, the inquiry is whether this knowledge is a cause for liberation alone, or whether it is also a cause for other human goals such as heaven and so forth. For that purpose, the question is whether there is any evidence for the latter or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Knowledge is not a cause even for human goals other than liberation, because one who desires liberation has no desire for those [other goals]. Even if a desire were present—as in the case of Saubhari and others—there is no evidence that knowledge is the cause of those [goals].

This is because it contradicts other scriptural passages that establish the causality of action, as well as those texts demonstrating the nature of action itself—for instance, the scripture stating, "It is action alone, whether pertaining to the divine or the human, that takes hold of the body; there is no other cause therein. Furthermore, scripture declares that action alone is the cause of fruits other than liberation, and that action is subordinate to knowledge (*jñāna*)—as seen in the passage "Whatever [is performed] with knowledge"—by virtue of its capacity to impart excellence to the fruit produced by action when that action is performed by one possessing knowledge.

For this very reason, there is no room for the suspicion that knowledge and action possess equal status as causes with respect to [attaining] heaven and the like. Likewise, because the Smṛti states, "The gods did not even drink [the Soma]," and because we observe the performance of ritual action by the gods who possess knowledge in the passage, "The gods worshipped the sacrifice with the sacrifice," it follows that if knowledge alone were the cause of all superior goals, such [action] would be untenable; thus, one might infer that action alone is the cause. Furthermore, this is precisely the position accepted by the teacher Jaimini.

Nor should it be suspected that the conduct of the wise is merely a pastime like that of the liberated, for the Śruti states, "The knower of Brahman should perform actions prescribed for all time," thereby enjoining action even for the wise. Furthermore, what is enjoined cannot be a mere pastime. Moreover, in the latter half of the verse, "Even while performing actions here," it is stated that "evil action does not cling to you" who act in this manner; thus, because the scripture declares that there is sin in the non-performance of action even for the wise, [their conduct must be understood as obligatory].

Since the conduct of a knower cannot be considered mere sport (*līlā*), and because it would contradict the conduct prescribed by the Śrutis as well as the doctrine of Jaimini, passages such as "Whatever world one contemplates with the mind... and so forth—which aim to show that knowledge is the cause of all human goals—are like the statement regarding wealth and other things that serve as means to the ritual acts for heaven, where it is said, "They shall attain heaven through wealth, body, and home," even though these are mentioned as primary only in a secondary sense.

This [passage] should be understood as being intent on stating that knowledge is predominant over the residual portion of ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*); it does not, however, directly intend to establish that knowledge is subordinate to ritual action because it is the cause of all human goals. This is because there is no evidence that would allow for such a subordination, and because it will be stated later in the section on praise that knowledge alone is capable of securing liberation regardless of whether rituals have been performed or left undone; furthermore, since knowledge possesses a superior efficacy, it is illogical for it to be subordinate to ritual action. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Although action cannot be subordinate to knowledge because it does not produce an excellence in knowledge, there is scriptural authority stating, "From knowledge alone comes heaven; from knowledge alone comes liberation.
