Since this scripture declares that the fruits such as heaven are attained through knowledge alone, and since it is heard that action produces an excellence in the fruit born of knowledge and is thus subordinate to knowledge, [the text says]: "The worlds won by the Rājasūya and increased by the Aśvamedha..."

By the statement of the *Mahābhārata*, "O highly fortunate one, pray [speak]," and by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the observation of the superior results obtained by Yudhiṣṭhira and others through sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, it is understood that knowledge alone is the cause of all purposes. Furthermore, since ritual action functions as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to knowledge by imparting excellence to the fruit produced by knowledge, and since this is the view of Bādarāyaṇa, those scriptural passages which appear to state that action is the cause must be interpreted as meaning that action is subordinate to the knowledge that is its cause. Thus, there is no contradiction; for [the text says]: "Whichever world..."

By the force of such statements and because it is the opinion of Bādarāyaṇa, knowledge is indeed the cause of all human goals other than liberation. Nor is there a contradiction between the views of Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa, for there is no conflict due to the difference in the qualified aspirants—whether divine or human. As for the result, however, it is an intensified engagement in the pursuit of knowledge and so forth. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The rule] is not universal. Oṃ. 2.
Oṃ, the division is like that of a hundred; Oṃ. Oṃ, for one who possesses merely the study; Oṃ.

In the preceding section, it was stated that since all human goals are attained through knowledge, the qualification for such knowledge does not belong to all knowers, but rather to the superior ones; even among them, only those who are unimpeded. Here, the connection is that it is now stated that there is no qualification for knowledge for everyone. The inquiry is whether or not there is a qualification for everyone regarding the knowledge under discussion in the previous section as the cause of all human goals. For that purpose, the question is whether the classification of persons need not be accepted, or whether it is worthy of acceptance.

Is the desire for that [result] and so forth alone the determining factor for qualification (*adhikāra*), or is something else also required? Is the desire for that result and so forth the cause of qualification, or is it not? As for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Since the principle that "one who is desirous, capable, and learned is entitled" establishes that the desire for the fruit is the primary requirement—and because there is no other factor that serves as a cause for entitlement—such factors as the desire for liberation (which consists of a state free from suffering and full of bliss), the capacity for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, and the requisite learning are possible and present in everyone. Thus, since all possess the common causal factor of desire, it is improper and groundless to accept a division of persons such that only some have the entitlement and others do not.

If there were no eligibility for some, it would follow that others would also lack it, leading to the undesirable conclusion that knowledge (*jñāna*) would have no qualified practitioners at all; therefore, everyone possesses the eligibility for knowledge. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

since there exists another qualifying factor—namely, the state of having studied the entirety of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) and fruits according to one's capacity—a requirement proven by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "One should recite the Vedas, then study their meanings, and then, having investigated them, realize Brahman," and "Indeed, one who is not a Vaiṣṇava has no eligibility even for the Veda," mere desire (*arthitva*) and so forth are not the sole determining factors.

Furthermore, although all possess the same status as deities according to the direction stated in the Smṛti, "And there is no liberation for the gods," the division of persons is justified because the qualification for Soma belongs only to the one hundred and one [deities] who exceed the two Brahmans—the higher and the lower—and not to others; thus, not everyone has the qualification for knowledge. The result, however, is the establishment of the superiority of knowledge over ritual action. || 2 ||
Oṃ. [The meditations] are not [restricted to specific stages] because there is no distinction. Oṃ. 3.

Previously, it was stated that the qualification for knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) belongs only to some; here, however, the connection [of this section] is established by demonstrating that even among those [qualified], the full qualification does not belong to all. The inquiry is whether the qualification for knowledge under discussion is of one kind for all beings, such as the gods and others, or of various kinds. To that end, the question is whether the gradation of vision mentioned in the sūtra, "And because a difference in vision is seen" (*prajñāntarapṛthaktvadṛṣṭiśca*), can be accounted for by a diversity in the capacities of the qualified persons even without a diversity in their qualifications, or not.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the previously mentioned gradation of knowledge among qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*) is established solely by their varying degrees of capacity, and because there is no evidence for otherwise, there is no qualification for the various forms [of practice]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Because the varying degrees of capacity among qualified aspirants are the cause for the varying degrees of qualification, in the absence of such variation in capacity, there is likewise an absence of any gradation in capacity itself.

Since the previously mentioned gradations of knowledge must be accounted for through the very gradations of eligibility (*adhikāra*) based on the degree to which one relies [on the scriptures], and since this would otherwise be inexplicable, as well as by the scriptural passage cited in the *Bhāṣya*—"Now, the means for achieving the goals of man"—it follows that eligibility is of various kinds; thus, the complete eligibility belongs only to the best of gods and not to others. The result, however, is the establishment of the excellence of knowledge. || 3 ||
Or rather, there is inference for the sake of praise. Oṃ. 4.

Oṃ. And some [hold that the life-stages] may be chosen according to one's own desire. Oṃ. And there is the suppression [of the former by the latter]. Oṃ. But the state of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) is indeed mentioned in the sacred texts. Oṃ. Jaimini [holds that it is] a mere reference, because there is no injunction and because [the text] actually censures it. Oṃ. It is to be performed, Bādarāyaṇa maintains, on account of the scriptural statement of their equality. Oṃ. Or rather, it is an injunction, like the wearing [of the sacrificial cord]. Oṃ. If it be argued that it is merely a commendatory statement because of its connection with other matters, we say no, because it conveys something not previously established. Oṃ. And because of the word expressing existence. Oṃ. If it be argued that they are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitation, we say no, because of the specific qualification. Oṃ.

Oṃ; and likewise, because of the connection with a single sentence. Oṃ; for this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth. Oṃ; and there is dependence on everything, because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and the like, as in the case of the horse. Oṃ; one should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth, because even though that is so, those [virtues] must necessarily be practiced as they are auxiliary to that [knowledge], due to the injunction regarding them. Oṃ; and there is permission to eat all kinds of food in the event of the loss of life, because that is seen [in scripture]. Oṃ; and because there is no sublation. Oṃ; it is also recorded in Smṛti. Oṃ; and from this [scriptural evidence], there is no license for acting according to one's own will. Oṃ.
Oṃ, and because it is enjoined, the duties of the stages of life are also [to be performed]. Oṃ, and as being auxiliary [to knowledge]. Oṃ.

Thus, since the distinction among qualified persons (*adhikāribheda*) has been established in the preceding section, the present connection (*saṅgati*) is that the non-contradiction of the three types of statements with mutually contradictory meanings is now described according to the distinction among these three types of qualified persons. Here, the inquiry is whether there is any difference for one who possesses the knowledge under discussion based on right conduct (*sadācāra*) or misconduct (*durācāra*), or whether there is not.

For that purpose, there arises the inquiry: does the statement, "By what would he be a Brahmin? He would be such by being exactly as he is," intend to enjoin the performance of desired conduct for the knower alone, or does it intend the mandatory performance of all good conduct and so forth? In this regard, the investigation concerns whether or not there exists a sublation—consisting of the violation of the rule that knowledge is the cause of liberation, and the doctrine of the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya)—should a distinction arise in the case of the knower through his engagement in virtuous activity and the like.

For that purpose, it must be determined whether the improper conduct (*asatpravṛtti*) of a knower (*jñānin*) is a cause for the arising of an obstacle to the very nature of liberation, or rather a cause for the arising of an obstacle to the excellence of the bliss contained within liberation. To that end, one must consider whether the statement in the Śruti—"Even if one who knows thus were to eat everything, he remains exactly so"—is inappropriate or appropriate given the existence of a specific distinction, such as the obstruction of the excellence of bliss, resulting from improper conduct and the like. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

There is no distinction for the knower (*jñānin*) between right and wrong conduct, because in the Śruti passage, "He is a Brāhmaṇa," the optative suffix of the injunction regarding conduct as one pleases is prescribed by the word *iti* with reference to the knower in general. Since there is likewise no specific injunction for the knower regarding right and wrong conduct, it would follow that even the defining characteristic of being far removed from all injunctions would apply to the knower. Nor is it tenable to argue that this sentence does not intend to enjoin conduct as one pleases for the knower in general, but rather for a specific type of knower.

Because there is no reason to assume that a general statement intends a specific one. And thus, not only is the lack of restriction inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the injunction regarding the conduct of those who desire [liberation], but also because of the scriptural hearing of the lack of restriction regarding acting according to one's own will, namely: "By him, it is exactly in this way. Now, it might be argued that it is not tenable for this sentence to have as its purport an injunction for the conduct of one's own will for every knower in general.

In accordance with such scriptural injunctions as, "Having risen in the morning, one should then perform the twilight worship," this statement—being of the nature of a prohibition (as it consists in the absence of a positive injunction) and taking the form of prohibitions such as, "A Brahmin must not be killed"—is free from the constraints of injunctions and the like; thus, its dedication to the constant practice of all good conduct according to rule has been described by the supreme authority, the teacher Jaimini. Likewise: "But that man who should be delighted only in the Self, satisfied with the Self..."

And by the Smṛti passage, "He who is content in the Self alone has no duty to perform," it follows that one who finds delight in the Self—having attained the bliss caused by the vision of the Supreme Self—and who is content in the Self alone for the very reason of possessing contentment caused by the Supreme Self, and who is satisfied with the Self—having attained the sense of sufficiency regarding sense-objects through the grace of the Supreme Self—for such a person there is no duty to perform; according to this statement, and by the force of the supplementary clause implying that he is not one who is prohibited from non-performance due to inequality, and in accordance with the teachings of the Śruti and other sources, [this applies] even among those who follow the path of conduct (*ācāra*).

If it is argued: "Since the teacher Bādarāyaṇa has described the state of being devoted to the conduct of desire in the form 'for some there is conduct [of desire], for others there is non-conduct,' and since this pertains to both meanings, how can one maintain that it has the single meaning of being an injunction and thereby claim that there is no distinction even regarding the conduct of a knower as he pleases?"—it is not so. For if that were the case, the passage would result in being merely a miscellaneous narrative (*pāriplava*), which would entail the consequence of its lack of authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Furthermore, let us grant that there is no distinction [between the knower and others] due to the absence of a means of proof; however, such a distinction will arise from the presence of a means of proof regarding the specific case. To explain: if there were a distinction for the knower based on right and wrong conduct, then, because knowledge whose power is blunted by wrong conduct would lose its status as a cause of liberation, the established rule of liberation—stated as "there is no restriction for all"—would be violated.

If knowledge conjoined with right action were to become the cause of liberation, it would contradict the statement, "But it is knowledge alone [that causes liberation], because of the definitive determination. Furthermore, if the liberation of a knower were not obstructed by wrong action, then it would follow that even one who merely desires to know (the seeker) would not have their knowledge obstructed by such actions; this would result in the futility of the entire section on dispassion (*vairāgyapāda*). Nor is it tenable to argue that right action and the like do not operate upon the very nature of liberation, but rather operate upon the manifestation of an excellence of bliss in liberation and the removal of its obstructions.

If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural passage permitting the consumption of all kinds of food by the man of knowledge (*jñānin*), because in that context, even regarding the eating of all food, it is stated without distinction. Furthermore, there is no grounds for assuming that the passage has another subject matter. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Even though the statement "By what means could there be any distinction for the knower (jñānin) through right or wrong conduct? is understood as referring to the knower alone, it is intended merely as praise of the knower; nevertheless, because the definition of the Lord as being "far removed from all injunctions" would result in the undesirable consequence that He is not the Lord (anīśa), it must be taken as having the nature of an injunction. Furthermore, according to the method stated by Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa, it has the purpose of enjoining the performance of all good conduct.

In the midst of all this, the claim that [the scripture] is merely intent on the non-performance of certain dharmas—that is, its intent is the injunction for acting according to one's own will—is untenable. This is because there is no contradiction with the Gaupavana Śruti, which states: "Human beings are governed by injunctions; the gods are indeed ungoverned; Brahmā alone is governed by his own will," and with Smṛti texts such as: "The activity of Brahmā proceeds solely by his own will, though he is impelled by injunctions. These passages establish a systematic distinction among the qualified agents—namely humans, gods, and Viriñca (Brahmā)—thereby showing that the scripture does not contradict itself.
Because there is no authority for the word of one who merely possesses knowledge and acts according to his own whims; and because the liberation of a knower is not obstructed by his improper conduct.

By the Śruti text, "Moving at will, consuming at will," it is established that even for a knower (*jñānin*), the *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) that has begun to bear fruit is subject to destruction by knowledge once a portion of it has been experienced; this is confirmed by the Śruti, "Beholding the Self, having destroyed both merit and sin," and is further established by the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori). Consequently, there is no fixed rule regarding the timing of liberation, which constitutes a breach of the previously stated rules. This is because the injunction for instruction is prescribed specifically for those endowed with qualities such as being an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward), as seen in the text: "He who shall speak this supreme secret among the *ūrdhvaretas*."

Since the obstruction [to liberation] is known through the occurrence of improper activity even when knowledge exists, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that mere knowledge alone produces the nature of liberation; thus: "Even while seeing this Self, one might perform action without reflection."

Since there is no subverting argument—such as the consequence of having to accept the doctrine of the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*)—even though there is a requirement for right conduct and the avoidance of wrong conduct as auxiliary factors for the sake of the excellence of bliss in liberation, as established by the force of such statements as "When one attains the supreme excellence of bliss that is well-restrained within the self"; and since the scriptural passage regarding the permission of all food (*sarvānnānumati*) has its scope limited to the occasion of the imminent departure of life (*prāṇatyāga*), as indicated by the marks mentioned in the Commentaries and other sources; [therefore, the doctrine of exclusive knowledge remains unrefuted].

Furthermore, it is argued that for a person of knowledge (*jñānin*), acting according to their own will is possible because there is no obstacle to not performing what is prohibited, or because there is no authority for performing it, or because there is no prohibitive authority, or because there is no obstacle to performing it. The first two [alternatives] are not tenable, because they are unproven. Nor is the third, because of the scriptural statement: "Seeing thus, one should not act according to desire," and because of the statement: "One who knows the past and future is capable of uplifting the three worlds."

Furthermore, there is a prohibitive scriptural and traditional (smṛti) injunction stating: "Even one such as this should not abandon Vedic or Smārta conduct. Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because of the existence of a subverting factor consisting of the diminution of bliss, according to the smṛti: "Bliss diminishes through improper action. Therefore, there certainly exists a distinction for the knower (jñānin) consisting of the diminution of power and bliss resulting from good and evil activities. As for the result, it is the support of the majesty of knowledge, which effects liberation even when improper conduct occurs. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ, but in every way they alone [are the cause], because of both marks; oṃ || 5 ||

Oṃ, and he demonstrates non-overpowering; Oṃ. Oṃ, and moreover, that is seen even in the interval; Oṃ. Oṃ, it is also recorded in Smṛti; Oṃ. Oṃ, and there is special favor; Oṃ. Oṃ, therefore the other is superior, also because of the indicative mark; Oṃ. Oṃ, but for one who has become that [state], there is the state of being that, according to Jaimini also, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of that form; Oṃ.

Regarding the phrase "because it was specified in the preceding [section]," the connection is as follows: it is stated here that knowledge is attained only by those qualified persons characterized as inferior, middling, and superior who were under discussion, and not by others. Here, the inquiry is whether this knowledge can be attained even by the unqualified, or only by those qualified as mentioned. To determine this, the question is whether there is any basis for the claim that it is attainable only by the qualified, or if there is not.

Likewise, even in the view that [objects] are attainable through fitness (*yogya-prāpyatva*), one must consider whether there is the production of fitness for those [objects] by overcoming their unfitness through great effort, or not. For that purpose, one must determine whether that unfitness is the non-nature (*asvabhāva*) of those objects or their nature (*svabhāva*). And for that purpose, one must determine whether there is any evidence for its non-overcoming if it were their nature, or whether such evidence exists. As for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Since there is no evidence for the claim that [knowledge] belongs only to those who are qualified, and since we observe that even those unqualified for the Vedas attain the Veda through effort, it follows that even the unqualified can indeed attain knowledge through effort. Even on the view that knowledge is attainable only by the qualified, we see that the unqualified can become Brahmins once their lack of qualification has been overcome. One should not suspect that being a Kṣatriya is non-inherent while being unqualified is inherent and thus cannot be removed even by effort; for there is no proof for such inherent status.

Furthermore, if [the attainment of knowledge] were inherent, it would follow that it must produce its corresponding fruit according to one's nature, just as in the case of the seeds of *yava* or *kalam* rice. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: even when there is great enthusiasm regarding place, time, attendance upon a guru, and so forth, those who are unfit do not attain knowledge; rather, it is only those who are fit who do so.

Although the instruction from the Four-faced One (Brahmā) was the same for both Indra and Virocana, they did not attain perfect knowledge; on the contrary, they attained a perverted understanding. This is clarified by the fact that, despite being eligible for liberation, Indra and others attained such knowledge as indicated by signs such as the acquisition of wisdom. Since this is established in texts such as "Ṛṇve vīra ugram" (*He hears the fierce [Indra]...*), and because such a result would otherwise be inexplicable, it is understood that the grace which causes such knowledge exists only in those who are fit for liberation.

Nor is it logical to claim that even for those who are unfit, fitness may arise through the suppression of unfitness by means of great effort; for unfitness is their very nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence, since both scripture and tradition explicitly state this: the Śruti says, "The gods [attain] divine prosperity alone," and the Smṛti says, "The Asuras [attain] through their own asuric nature," thereby clearly teaching that non-suppression is indeed their inherent nature.

Likewise, by the restrictive scripture stating, "The Asuras do not [possess] the divine, nor do the Devas possess the Asura [nature]," by the scripture stating that "the form of the Asuras is not divine" which indicates they lack that nature, by the scripture stating that "the Devas worshipped Him as Bhūti" which shows that through their mutual contrary modes of worship, the Devas and Asuras obtain respectively correct and contrary fruits, by the doctrine of Ācārya Jaimini which establishes that the Devas, Asuras, and humans possess the inherent natures of divinity and so forth, and by the scripture stating, "The Devas are indeed the younger, while the Asuras are the elder," [it is said]: "I do not know."

Thus, by the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the prohibition against entering the crowd, one understands from the existence of results corresponding to those respective natures that unfitness (*ayogyatā*) and so forth are indeed intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and are not overcome. As for the result, it is the establishment that liberation is attainable through mere fitness (*yogyatā*) alone. || 5 ||
Oṃ. And [the expiation] does not apply even to one who holds an office, because of the inference of a fall [from his status] due to its incompatibility [with such a position]. Oṃ. 6.

"Oṃ. Some say that even when preceded by another [rite], it is like the pacification of a state; so it has been said. Oṃ. But outside [the village], it is in both ways, according to Smṛti and custom. Oṃ."

Previously, it was stated that knowledge is unattainable by those who are unfit; here, however, it is said that even among the fit, it is attained only by those devoid of longing for states such as divinity, and not by all. Alternatively, there is a connection with what follows because of the doubt that the previously mentioned status of being a deity and so forth cannot be natural, since scripture declares it to be achievable through effort—thereby implying its non-naturalness. Since the deities were the subject of the preceding section, the relevant inquiry is whether the state of being a deity is attainable by those other than gods, or by gods alone.

Regarding that purpose—the attainment of that state—is there or is there not an obstacle to the performance of desire and effort? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: By the force of such scriptural statements as, "A person established in his own duty attains the status of Viriñca after a hundred births," and "Through oblations at the offering of the swift Viṣṇu, may you know the Rudra-nature and the greatness of Rudra," it is understood that the status of Viriñca and so forth is achievable through effort. Since divinity and the like are not innate—unlike consciousness and other such qualities—they can be attained through all efforts.

Because sentience and its inherent nature are universally accepted as possible, and because there is no obstacle to the desire and effort required for attaining the status of a deity and so forth; otherwise, even the desire and effort for knowledge, devotion, and the like would not exist. What need is there to say more? Not only would the status of a deity be attainable by others besides the gods, but even the sovereignty of the Lord (Bhagavat) would be attainable through effort. However, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is this: neither the status of a deity nor the sovereignty of the Lord is attainable, precisely because the desire and effort directed toward them are impossible.

One who desires a status such as that of Brahmā and the like is cast down by gods and others, because of the impossibility of attaining that status despite the desire for it, just as one who desires the rank of a king [is punished]. One who exerts effort toward the status of a god and the like falls, because of exerting effort toward an unattainable ascent, just like one intent on climbing an unsuitable tree; thus, the undesirable consequence is understood through inference. Nor is the qualification "unattainability" unestablished, since corporeality and the like are not inherent [to the self] in the same way that consciousness is.

Since the statement, "The states of being a god, an asura, a human, and so forth, belong to living beings by their very nature," makes it known that these are inherent to their own-being (*svabhāva*), and since the statement, "Desiring something auspicious elsewhere, one may fall [into other states] without contradiction," makes it known that there is an absence of misfortune when there is a desire for knowledge and the like, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument. As for the result, just like the state of a deity, knowledge too is to be attained only by those who are fit; thus is the previously stated point established. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ. "Because the scripture declares the fruit for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya. Oṃ. || 7 ||

"Oṃ, [the study of the Veda] is for the sake of officiating at sacrifices, according to Auḍulomi, for it is for that purpose that one is hired. Oṃ. "Oṃ, there is an injunction for another auxiliary effort; this is the third [kind of injunction], pertaining to one who already possesses [the primary qualification], like the injunctions regarding the beginning of the ritual. Oṃ.

In the preceding section, the nature (*itthambhāva*) of knowledge was described; here, however, the manner in which it produces its fruit (*phalaniṣpādanaprakāra*) is stated—this is the connection (*saṃgati*). The inquiry is whether the knowledge under discussion produces its fruit only for the deities presiding over the principles (*tattvābhimānidevas*), or for living beings (*prajās*) as well. For that purpose, [the question is]: in the case of a fruit produced by action, is it only the status of being the instigating agent (*prayojakakartṛtva*) that is the determinant, or is even the mere status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) sufficient? Is there no reason [to support] the position that "even the status of being the agent [is sufficient]," and is there a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), or is the opposite true?

To that end, even in the position that agency (*kartṛtva*) is also a motivator (*prayojaka*), one must consider whether it is necessary for the fruit to be identical to that of the motivating agent, or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): since there is no evidence to restrict agency when it acts as a motivator, it must necessarily be stated that the fruit is indeed equal to the fruit of the master (*svāmin*). However, this contradicts the Śruti passage, "For the master enjoys the fruit, not one who performs the action without being the master," and also contradicts the opinion of Ātreya-Ācārya.

In the world, even though a craftsman or similar agent is dependent on an instigator (*prayojaka*), since no fruit produced by the action is seen [to accrue to the instigator], and because there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) such as contradiction with scripture (*śruti*) and the like, and because there is an absence of any proving evidence (*sādhaka*), the status of being an agent does not belong to the instigator. Rather, it belongs to the ownership consisting of the agency of the instigator. For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of knowledge arising from hearing and so forth performed by the subjects accrues only to the gods who impel all the senses and other faculties, and not to the subjects themselves. As for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): [The text continues: ...the fruit of the action is indeed for the one who possesses the agency of the instigator. This is established by the scriptural statement: "He who dwells in the breath (*prāṇa*) and is within the breath," and so forth, which shows that the Self is the inner controller of all. Furthermore, the Smṛti states: "The Lord, dwelling in the heart of all beings, by His majesty causes them to revolve, as if mounted on a machine. Thus, the agency of the instigator is proven both by scripture and by reasoning. Reasoning is as follows: the fruit of an action must accrue to the one who possesses the ownership of the agency; this is observed in the world, where the owner of the field reaps the harvest produced by the laborer working in the field. Moreover, the scripture declares: "Whatever he does with desire, that alone he attains. And the Smṛti says: "Whatever state he remembers at the time of death, to that state he goes, O son of Kuntī, having become its nature. Therefore, it is established that the fruit of the action belongs to the one who possesses the agency of the instigator. Thus ends the section on the agency of the instigator. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the body is the agent. The opponent argues: "The body alone is the agent, because it is the body that performs actions such as walking and running, and because the scripture speaks of the 'body of action' (*karmakāya*). To this we reply: No, the body is not the agent, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). Agency requires sentience, as is seen in the case of a person. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The self (*ātman*) is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower. And the Smṛti says: "The body is not the agent; the agent is the one within. Therefore, the body is not the agent. Nor is the sense-organ the agent, because it is merely an instrument, like an axe. Nor is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) the agent, because it is a mere modification of air. Nor is the mind (*manas*) the agent, because it is a tool for thought. Therefore, the Self alone is the agent. This is confirmed by the scripture: "The Self is the witness, the knower, the solitary one. And the Smṛti says: "The Self is the witness of all. Thus, the Self is the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the body is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "The intellect is the agent, because the scripture says: 'The intellect is the cause of bondage and liberation,' and because it is the intellect that discriminates between right and wrong. To this we reply: No, the intellect is not the agent, because it is an instrument. Just as an axe is an instrument for a woodcutter, so the intellect is an instrument for the Self. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Self is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower. If the intellect were the seer, it would be called the "seer of the intellect," but it is not so called. Therefore, the Self is the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the intellect is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "The ego-sense is the agent, because it is the ego-sense that thinks 'I am the doer,' and because it is the ego-sense that identifies itself with the body. To this we reply: No, the ego-sense is not the agent, because it is a product of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is like the false notion of a snake in a rope. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Self is pure, beyond the ego-sense. And the Smṛti says: "The ego-sense is born of darkness (*tamas*). Therefore, the ego-sense is not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the ego-sense is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the mind (*manas*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "The mind is the agent, because it is the mind that desires and resolves, and because the scripture speaks of the 'mind-made body' (*manomaya-kāya*). To this we reply: No, the mind is not the agent, because it is an instrument of thought. It is like a charioteer driving a chariot. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The mind is the instrument of thought. And the Smṛti says: "The mind is the cause of bondage and liberation. Therefore, the mind is not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the mind is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "The vital breath is the agent, because it is the vital breath that moves the body, and because the scripture speaks of the 'five-fold vital breath' as the agent. To this we reply: No, the vital breath is not the agent, because it is a modification of air. It is like the wind moving a tree. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The vital breath is the instrument of movement. And the Smṛti says: "The vital breath is the cause of life and death. Therefore, the vital breath is not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the vital breath is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the elements (*bhūta*) are the agent. The opponent argues: "The elements are the agent, because they produce the body, and because the scripture speaks of the 'elemental body' (*bhautika-kāya*). To this we reply: No, the elements are not the agent, because they are insentient. They are like clay producing a pot. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Self is the witness of the elements. And the Smṛti says: "The elements are the instruments of the Self. Therefore, the elements are not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the elements are the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the agent. The opponent argues: "The atoms are the agent, because they combine to form the body, and because the scripture speaks of the 'atomic soul' (*aṇu-jīva*). To this we reply: No, the atoms are not the agent, because they are eternal and partless. They cannot act. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Self is all-pervading. And the Smṛti says: "The atoms are the cause of the world. Therefore, the atoms are not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that the atoms are the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "Primordial matter is the agent, because it undergoes transformation, and because the scripture speaks of the 'self-born' (*svayambhū*). To this we reply: No, primordial matter is not the agent, because it is insentient. It is like a wheel turning by itself. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Self is the witness of primordial matter. And the Smṛti says: "Primordial matter is the cause of creation and dissolution. Therefore, primordial matter is not the agent. This concludes the section on the refutation of the theory that primordial matter is the agent. Now begins the section on the refutation of the theory that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the agent. The opponent argues: "The Lord is the agent, because He is omnipotent, and because the scripture speaks of Him as the 'creator of all'. To this we reply: No, the Lord is not the agent in the sense of being a performer of actions, because He is eternally free from action. He is the witness of all agents. Furthermore, the scripture says: "The Lord is the witness, the knower, the solitary one. And the Smṛti says: "The Lord is the cause of

Although it is understood through the Śruti text "For he is the master," the Smṛti text "That which is greater than that is declared for the gods," and the opinion of Ātreya, that the presiding deities of the principles (tattva-abhimāni-devas) possess full ownership over the fruit [of actions] by virtue of being the instigating agents (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) in the hearing and other acts performed by living beings; nevertheless, in the case of activities such as the imparting of knowledge ordained by the Śruti text "for the gods," they are employed merely as auxiliary factors (*sahakāritvena*) for the sake of bestowing grace so that knowledge may arise in living beings.

Furthermore, since results are observed even for those born as householders who were taken along as assistants by the patron (gṛhapati) such as Vaideha in a sacrificial session (sattra), there exists for subjects (prajā) as well a fruit produced by knowledge, which is caused by their agency. As for the fruit, however, it has been stated that there is no fixed rule; thus, this concludes the justification for the rule regarding liberation. || 7 ||
|| Oṃ. But because of the totality [of the means], there is the conclusion with the householder. Oṃ. || 8 ||
Oṃ. [The rule] regarding silence applies to others as well, because of the instruction [given to them]. Oṃ.

The connection [between the sections] is as follows: in the preceding section, it was stated that the gods possess the fullness of fruit; here, however, it is stated that they possess the fullness of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*). Here, among wise men distinguished by their various stages of life (*āśrama*), the inquiry is whether the householder (*gṛhastha*) or the ascetic (*yati*) is superior in liberation. For that purpose, the question is whether the capacity for the performance of all ritual actions is the determining factor for superiority in liberation, or whether it is simply the practice of means for a long duration.

To that end, regarding the superiority of the ascetic (*yati*) in liberation, there arises the question: Is there a contradiction with such statements as "Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher," which conclude that liberation belongs to the householder, or is there not? To resolve this, one must determine whether that [statement] refers to human beings or to deities. To that end, is there no evidence supporting its application to deities and is there a subverting argument [against it], or is the opposite the case? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since those residing in other stages of life (*āśrama*) lack the capacity for all virtuous acts, whereas householders alone possess that capacity, and since that capacity is the determining factor for superiority, the householder alone is superior, not the ascetic.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, at the end of the eighth chapter, where—beginning with the words "Having studied the Veda in the family of the teacher"—the conclusion is made regarding the householder alone, stating that he "attains the world of Brahman and does not return again," thereby indicating that the intent is that the householder alone possesses the highest status regarding liberation; for there is no basis for interpreting this statement as referring to a deity.

Nor can their status as primary householders (*mukhya-gṛhin*) be established merely by their possessing all the duties of a householder. For if that were so, it would follow—contrary to the position of the Siddhāntin—that householders who achieve perfection with haste are inferior to ascetics who achieve perfection without haste; and furthermore, it would result in the undesirable conclusion that gods possess no superiority over human ascetics regarding liberation. The Siddhānta, however, is as follows:

Although a householder possesses the eligibility for all virtuous acts (*satkarma*), because he lacks the discipline of such constant practice, the liberation attainable by him is subject to a long duration. This is because of the scriptural statement: "Householders achieve liberation with speed, and ascetics [achieve it] with even greater speed," which indicates that the means for liberation are accomplished over time. Furthermore, since the liberation of an ascetic is achieved through practices requiring a longer period than the liberation of a householder, the ascetic alone is superior in regard to liberation, not the householder. Nor does this contradict the *Chāndogya* passage.

For in the Śruti passage beginning with "All these indeed are householders," the gods alone are described as the primary householders by virtue of possessing all the duties of a householder; thus, in the Chāndogya statement as well, it follows by the principle of the primary and the secondary (*mukhyāmukhyanyāya*) that it refers to the gods as the primary householders. Nor is there any subverting objection that this would imply the absence of any superiority for the gods over human ascetics regarding liberation.

For it is stated in the Śruti, "All these are indeed ascetics" (*kṛtsnā hyete yatayaḥ*), that the status of possessing all the duties of an ascetic is also attributed [to the householder]; and likewise, because the Śruti "The gods alone are students" (*devā eva brahmacāriṇaḥ*) declares that he possesses the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*), his superiority even over the ascetic is established. As for the result, by stating this superiority for those qualified for knowledge, the greatness of knowledge itself is vindicated. Regarding the commentary (*ṭīkā*), the reason for not presenting the doubt as to whether the householder or the ascetic is superior is clearly explained in the *Bhāvadīpa*: the intention is that since the method of the prima facie and final positions can be inferred by the students themselves, there was no need to state another doubt. || 8 ||
Oṃ. [The soul] does not manifest itself, because it follows [the body]. Oṃ. 9.

If it is argued that there is a superiority among those qualified for knowledge (jñānādhikārin) because the instruction for some qualified seekers might be given with full disclosure due to the greater fruitfulness in accomplishing knowledge, then the connection [of this section] is established by such a doubt. The inquiry is whether the instruction regarding indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), which is a cause for attaining direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), should be performed with full disclosure or not. To that end, the question is whether there exists a proof for disclosure and no counter-argument against it, or the reverse. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

One might argue that instruction should be given through public proclamation, because by standing in places such as assembly halls or squares, knowledge can arise for many who are fit for the realization of truth; and since this results in a greater fruit, it constitutes a supporting factor (*sādhaka*) while lacking any contradicting factor (*bādhaka*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: if instruction were given through public proclamation, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those unfit to receive it would grasp the meaning of what was taught, just as those who are fit do.

Furthermore, since the instruction of the unqualified is prohibited by such Vedic texts as "May we not be among the thieves" (*mā nastenebhyaḥ*), and because it is established that such instruction is a cause of misfortune, whereas for the qualified alone it is a cause for the arising of knowledge and a cause for the excellence of its fruit, the instruction must be given without disclosure [of one's own spiritual status]. The result, however, is the justification for the excellence of knowledge. || 9 ||
|| Oṃ. [The fruit] belongs to this life, provided there is no obstruction; for that is observed. Oṃ. || 10 ||

In the preceding section, the statement regarding the nature of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) as being "extremely secret" was inappropriate; this is because that [indirect knowledge] lacks the capacity to produce direct perception (*dṛṣṭi*), due to its deviation from the fruit which is direct perception. The connection [of the present section] lies in the removal of this doubt. Here, the inquiry is whether there is a rule that the direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*)—which is the goal to be accomplished by the indirect knowledge under discussion—is produced only at the time of the completion of the means, or whether there is no such rule and it may occur in another birth.

For that purpose, [the question is]: does its non-arising in that birth result in its never arising at all, or not? For that purpose, [the question is]: is there no rule-governing principle (*aniyamakalpaka*), or is there one? As for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

If immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) does not arise despite the completion of the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), then—just as heavenly bliss does not arise despite the completion of the means such as sacrifice because of the impossibility of experiencing such bliss within the limits of that very body due to the absence of the necessary cause—here too, since there is no powerful cause [to prevent it], there would be no basis for inferring that its non-arising in this life implies its arising in another birth; consequently, the result would be that it never arises at all. Therefore, immediate knowledge must arise in that very same life. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Just as when the fruit of a sacrifice—Heaven—is not produced upon the birth resulting from the completion of the means (*sādhana*), there is no possibility of experience limited by that body because the cause for such experience is absent; so too here, since the cause consisting of the obstruction of *prārabdha*-karma exists when knowledge does not arise in that body, there is no fixed rule that it must arise in that very birth or that its non-arising in that birth necessitates its arising in another birth. Nor is there a lack of scriptural authority (*kalpaka*) for this, because it is understood from scripture thus: "Having heard of the Self and having meditated with a mature intellect, one may indeed obtain the vision of the Supreme even in this world.
The purpose [of this discussion], however, is to establish that hearing and the other means are causes of knowledge. || 10 ||
Oṃ. Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is ascertained; because that state is ascertained. Oṃ. 11.

Just as in the previous case there was no fixed rule that knowledge belongs only to this life, so too there is no fixed rule that the fruit of liberation occurs only immediately after the fall of that body; thus, because of this proof, there is a connection [to the present topic]. Here, regarding liberation—which is to be accomplished by the knowledge under discussion—the inquiry proceeds as before: is there a fixed rule that liberation occurs only after the fall of the very body in which the knowledge arose, or is there no such rule? In this manner, the sequence of reflections, along with the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusions (*siddhānta*), are to be understood.

The distinction, however, is as follows: regarding the uncertainty—whether the arising of knowledge occurs in the present birth, which is complete with the means for knowledge, or whether its arising occurs in another birth—the doubt arises as to why there is no such postulating factor here [in the present life] when there is an absence of such factors that cause obstruction to the *prārabdha* (commenced karma). In response to this specific doubt, the fact that the certainty of liberation for one established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*)—expressed in the text "one established in Brahman attains immortality"—would otherwise be inexplicable, as well as the scriptural statement "the knower attains immortality," serve as the basis for postulating the absence and presence of those obstructing factors that cause such uncertainty.
The resolution: "But the fruit is not restricted"—this is the justification for what was stated. || 11 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Nyāyamuktāvalī composed by the venerable Yati Rāghavendra.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

In the previous [chapter], by the word "fruit" (*phala*) in the aphorism "Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation," it was indicated that liberation alone is the primary fruit of knowledge, while other results are incidental. That primary fruit is elaborated upon in this chapter. Since liberation—which is fourfold, distinguished by the destruction of karma, departure [from the body], the path [to higher worlds], and experience—is realized sequentially, the author will explain all of these in order across the four quarters (*pāda*). First, in the first quarter, he states the fruit known as the destruction of karma. Therein, through seven methods (*nyāya*), the means which is absolutely necessary is investigated.
Oṃ. There is repetition [of the means], because of the repeated instruction. Oṃ. (1)
Oṃ, and from the Liṅga, Oṃ.

Regarding the phrase "pertaining to this world" (*aihika*), the inquiry here is whether the hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices under discussion are to be performed only once or must be repeated. For that purpose, the question is whether the injunction for hearing and so forth culminates in performance only once—like the injunction for the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice—or whether it requires repetition—like the injunction for threshing. For that purpose, the question is whether knowledge arises from performing hearing and so forth only once or not. And for that purpose, the question is whether ease of accomplishment is a merit of knowledge, or rather, difficulty of accomplishment alone is its merit.

For that purpose, the question arises whether there exists or does not exist a conception of the difficulty [of the practice] as a merit. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth should be performed only once, like the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and others; for since the arising of knowledge is possible by that much alone, the injunction regarding hearing and so forth culminates in performance only once. Nor should it be argued: "Why should this not be like the injunction 'one threshes the rice' (*vrīhīnavahanti*), which, because the fruit consisting of the removal of the husks is not accomplished by a single performance, culminates in the repetition of the threshing"? [The response to this objection follows:]... (text continues)

If that were the case, it would follow that knowledge lacks the quality of being easily accomplished (*suśakatva*), which consists in its being obtainable through the performance of the means only once. Nor can it be argued that difficulty in accomplishment is itself a merit for knowledge, as there is no evidence (*kalpaka*) for such a claim. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means must be repeated, just like threshing (*avaghāta*). For just as the removal of the husk is not seen to result from threshing performed only once, so too the arising of knowledge is not seen to result from hearing and the rest performed only once; therefore, the injunction for these [means], like the injunction for threshing, culminates in their repetition.

Nor does the admission that knowledge is to be accomplished through the repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth entail the loss of its quality of being easily attainable; for in the case of knowledge which is the cause of a great fruit, difficulty itself is a merit. Nor is there a lack of justification for admitting that knowledge is to be accomplished by the repetition of hearing and so forth on the grounds that its difficulty is a merit; rather, such repetition is inferred from the fact that Uddālaka taught the truth—beginning with "That very one is the subtle essence" (*sa eṣo 'ṇimā*)—nine times to Śvetaketu when he was in his sixth year of eligibility, as this would otherwise be inexplicable. Otherwise, it would follow that he should have given the instruction only once.

Likewise, in the *Bhṛguvallī* of the *Taittirīya*, the Śruti states: "To him he said this: 'Food, breath, eye, ear, mind, and speech. With the intention that Bhṛgu should perform hearing, reflection, and meditation once again upon the very objects consisting of food and so forth—since he had previously asked, "Teach me, O Venerable One, Brahman"—Varuṇa spoke these words: "Seek to know that."

Furthermore, because there is the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) in the form of the necessity of reflecting upon what has been heard—such as the Smṛti statement, "One should listen constantly"—which leads to the inference of the repetition of listening, reflection, and meditation; and because the result, such as that mentioned in the passage beginning with "the result is [attained] in this life," establishes that the intended acts of listening and so forth are causes of knowledge. || 1 ||
"Oṃ! They indeed approach [the teaching] with the thought 'It is the Self,' and they cause others to grasp it so. || 2 ||

The connection [of this section] is established by the fact that, whereas it was previously stated that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means must be repeated for the sake of knowledge, here it is proven that meditation (*dhyāna*) on that very selfhood—which is designated as "lordship" (*svāmitva*)—is necessary. Here, the inquiry is whether the instruction regarding the meditation on the selfhood under discussion is to be performed constantly or not. For that purpose, the question is whether the extreme familiarity with the lordship consisting of selfhood acts as an obstacle to its meditation and so forth, or not. And for that purpose, the question is whether there exists any factor that precludes such an obstacle, or not.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The meditation (*dhyāna*) and instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the Self need not be performed constantly, because that [Self], whose nature is that of the Lord (*svāmin*), is eternally established. Since it is already well-known, its constant presence in every mind renders meditation and instruction useless; for it is precisely the state of being unknown that necessitates instruction. Furthermore, there is no basis for the claim that meditation and instruction must necessarily be performed even for that which is already well-known. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

By such statements as, "The meditation 'I am the Self' must be performed in every way by those seeking liberation," and through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the instruction for meditating on Viṣṇu as the Self is a cause of liberation. Since the necessity of performing meditations for the sake of liberation cannot be established merely through their being well-known or unknown, it follows that the meditation on the Self as the Self and the instruction thereof must indeed be performed constantly and in every way. As for the result, it is the establishment of the logicality of the great purport (*mahātātparya*) of the Vedas residing in [Viṣṇu] as the Sovereign. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Not in a symbol, for he is not that; Oṃ. 3.

The connection [of this section] arises because the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is raised here by way of challenging the previously mentioned meditation on [the Self as] lordship. In the seventh [chapter], there is an inquiry regarding whether the objects of meditation—such as Name, Speech, and so forth, referred to by words like "Name" and "Speech" in passages such as "One meditates on Name as Brahman" and "One meditates on Speech as Brahman"—are to be meditated upon as non-different from Brahman, or rather as being located within it. For that purpose, the question is whether the scriptural text "Name is Brahman" and so forth intends to express identity, or whether it intends to express their location therein in the form "Name [is] Brahman."

For that purpose, is even false worship a cause for the goals of human life, or is it only true worship? The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is as follows: Name, speech, and so forth are to be meditated upon as Brahman, because the scripture teaches the meditation on their identity through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the passage, "Name is Brahman. If it is argued: "But since the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established in the Sūtra 'Because of the separate teaching' (B.S. 1.1.17), the identity of Name and Brahman must be false," we say no.

In the previous section, since being well-known or unknown was not a determining factor, and since the object of meditation is the cause for achieving the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), just as in the case of meditating on the Self (*ātman*), the reality or unreality of the object to be meditated upon is likewise irrelevant. This is because such meditation is possible due to the possession of results mentioned in the supplementary scriptural passages (*vākyaśeṣa*), such as: "As long as he has not reached that [world], he moves about there according to his will. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

"Those that are insentient, unreal, and unfit [for worship] are not to be worshipped, because of the absence of fruit and because of the opposite [result]"—by this *Saṃkarṣaṇa-sūtra* and by the statements cited in the *Anuvyākhyāna*, it is stated that false worship is either fruitless or yields a contrary result; thus, since false worship does not lead to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), such worship should not be performed. Furthermore, on the strength of the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "From Name up to Prāṇa," one must perform worship by remaining in the state of [the respective entity] as being Brahman, and not by identifying with it as a single unity.
As for the result, it is the support of the previously mentioned meditation on the Self. || 3 ||
Oṃ. Brahman is the cause because of its excellence. Oṃ. 4.

The connection [of this section] with the preceding one is established by proving the necessity of meditating on Brahman-hood (*brahmatva*) here, which was the subject under discussion in the previous section as "Name-Brahman" (*nāmabrahma*). Here, the inquiry is whether this Brahman-hood, being the subject at hand, is to be meditated upon always and in every way, or not. For that purpose, the question is whether there exists a reason for meditating upon it in such a manner, or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: meditation on that which is designated as "Brahman-hood" should not be performed always and in every way. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Since the quality of being Brahman includes all other qualities within itself, since it consists in the Lord’s own excellence and thus is superior to the other qualities, and since meditation upon it is a cause of a particular delight in the Lord—just like meditation upon His being the Self—and because liberation would not be accomplished in the absence of this meditation, one must always and in every way meditate upon Him as Brahman. Furthermore, since that [quality of Brahman] is expressed specifically through the qualification "the Self-Brahman" (Ātma-brahma), one should understand that there is no violation of the rule regarding the meditation on the four qualities.
"But the fruit is greater than the earth"—this is the justification for what was stated. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ. And the notions of Āditya and so forth [are to be applied] to the limbs, because it is logical; oṃ. || 5 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: since it was stated in the preceding section that Brahman-hood—which serves as a qualification—is to be meditated upon, one might suspect that *ātmatva* (the state of being the Self) likewise should not be meditated upon, just like the state of being supported by the limbs [of the body]. Here, regarding what was stated in the sūtra "As the support exists in the limbs" (*aṅgeṣu yathāśrayabhāvaḥ*)—namely, that the meditation on the deities as being supported by their respective limbs of origin is to be performed by the deities themselves—the inquiry is whether this is to be done by the deities always and in every way, or whether it is to be done only occasionally. To resolve this, the question is whether there is any specific reason for it to be done in that manner, or whether there is none.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: Even though other qualities exist, since there is no specific reason—just as in the case of meditating on Brahman—to always meditate specifically on the quality of being a limb of one's own respective substratum, and because the deities such as Sūrya do not permanently reside in the limbs of the Lord due to their movement through various locations for the purpose of illuminating the world and so forth, such meditation would be a false meditation due to that constant absence from the limbs of the Lord.

And because it would not yield the desired fruit, worship should not be performed in that manner. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: According to the Smṛti text, "The limbs of Viṣṇu must be meditated upon by the gods," entry into the limbs of the Blessed Lord is necessary for the liberation of the gods; and since that [liberation] cannot be accomplished without the constant practice of such meditation on His qualities.

Because there exists the cause consisting of entry into the Lord’s body, and because there is no possibility of false worship—since [the deity] eternally resides within the parts of the Lord in another form—the deities must always perform worship everywhere in this manner: with the Sun by virtue of having the eye as their own substratum; with the Moon by virtue of having the mind as their substratum; and with Brahmā by virtue of having the head as their substratum. As for the result, it is precisely the support of the practice of identifying with the Self (ātmatvopāsana); for even though there exists a relationship of substratum and superstratum, there is the objection that the relationship of master and servant would likewise result in being non-worshipable, and this [text] serves to dispel that doubt. || 5 ||
Oṃ. He is seated because of the possibility [of it]; Oṃ. 6.

Oṃ, and because of meditation, Oṃ. Oṃ, and with reference to immovability, Oṃ. Oṃ, and they remember, Oṃ. Oṃ, wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], there [is the same result], because there is no distinction, Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] is established because, after previously describing meditation (*upāsanā*) in a general manner, the specific procedure is now explained following a distinction between meditation (*dhyāna*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*). In the sixth chapter of the *Gītā*, it was stated that "having sat upon a seat, one should practice yoga," whereby the seat and other requirements are mentioned as ancillaries to meditation. The inquiry is whether these are necessary or not. To that end, the question is: is the fixing of the mind on Hari, which is useful for meditation, appropriate without a seat, or is it not appropriate? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Since the worship of the Lord as the cause of vision is accomplished merely by fixing the mind on Hari, a formal seat is not mandatory. Nor should it be argued that fixing the mind on Hari is impossible without a seat; for that is possible even through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and other means. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering invalid injunctions such as, "Viṣṇu should be constantly remembered."

If, on the grounds that the instruction regarding the seat and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable, their necessity were established, then—on the grounds that statements such as "on the mountain peak," "by the riverbank," and "having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*" would otherwise be inexplicable—the restriction of place and other factors would also necessarily be required. However, this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Although the fixing of the mind upon Hari may occur through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and other means by virtue of the absence of mental distraction, the *Smṛti* states: "If the body is motionless, there will also be no movement of the mind. From this, it is understood that the absence of mental distraction is also dependent upon the immobility of the body. Furthermore, since bodily immobility is possible only through a specific posture (*āsana*), and based on the authority of the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "The body, head, and neck should be held straight," a seat is indeed indispensable for the purpose of properly fixing the mind upon the Lord as a requisite for meditation.

Nor does the necessity of a seat contradict the injunction for constant meditation (*upāsana*), despite the apparent contradiction between constant meditation and the necessity of sitting. Regarding the necessity of a seat, there is no conflict with the scriptural injunction for meditation based on the Smṛti statement, "He should be remembered constantly," because meditation is twofold—consisting of remembrance (*smaraṇa*) and contemplation (*dhyāna*). Since meditation in the form of remembrance is to be performed constantly, there is no contradiction even if a rule regarding the seat applies there; however, for meditation in the form of occasional contemplation, the necessity of the seat remains uncontradicted. For this very reason, the instruction concerning the seat and other requisites is not purposeless.

Nor does this entail the necessity of specific locations and so forth; for these lack the utility for meditation that postures (āsana) and the like possess, or the utility for knowledge that hearing (śravaṇa) and the like possess. Furthermore, regarding Smṛti texts such as "one should resort to that very place," the point is that whatever location ensures one-pointedness of meditation is to be accepted, rather than a restrictive rule concerning mountain peaks and the like. The purpose [of the mention of location] is simply to justify the instruction on postures and other such requirements. || 6 ||
|| Oṃ, until the final departure; for even there, it is seen. Oṃ. || 7 ||

In the preceding section, it was stated that while a specific seat (*āsana*) is necessary because of its particular nature, specific locations and so forth are not necessary due to the absence of such particularity. Similarly here, there arises the following connection: since the doubt may arise that the meditation under discussion in the sūtra "And from meditation" (*dhyānācca*) extends only up to knowledge and not beyond it to liberation—because no further distinction is produced by meditation once liberation is attained—the inquiry is as follows: regarding the meditation under discussion in the phrase "and from meditation," is it necessary only up to the point of knowledge, or is it also necessary up to the point of liberation?

Is there, for that purpose—that is, for the sake of knowledge—a reason to perform until liberation what has been prescribed, or is there not? For that purpose, does an excellence of bliss in liberation arise through means other than meditation, or only through meditation itself? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the increase of bliss in liberation can occur through other means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, apart from meditation, there is no reason to perform until liberation what has been prescribed for the sake of knowledge; therefore, meditation need not be practiced until liberation. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

In the *Gītā*, it is stated: "For him who has ascended to yoga, tranquility (*śama*) is said to be the means. By declaring that for one who has ascended to yoga—that is, for one possessing immediate realization (*aparokṣajñānin*)—tranquility, which is meditation (*dhyāna*), is the cause of supreme bliss, we understand from this that meditation is primarily the cause of the increase of bliss. Furthermore, based on the scriptural injunction, "One should meditate upon the syllable *Oṃ* until the end of life," and by the principle of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument) expressed in the scripture, "Even the liberated ones worship this," it follows that meditation must indeed be practiced until liberation is attained.

The justification for the gradations mentioned in such passages as "But the fruit lasts as long as the office" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.32) is as follows: otherwise, since there would be no fruit of meditation for those possessing knowledge at the time of liberation, it would follow that there is no gradation [in liberation]. || 7 ||
Oṃ. Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging of future karma and the destruction of past karma, because of the scriptural declaration of both. Oṃ. (2.1.8)

Oṃ. For the other [karmas] as well, there is likewise non-attachment; however, upon death [the remainder is exhausted]. Oṃ. But only those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed, for that is the limit. Oṃ. But the Agnihotra and other rites are for the sake of that very [attainment], because of scriptural indication. Oṃ. According to some, there is exhaustion of both types by means of knowledge. Oṃ. For it is said, "Whatever [is performed] through knowledge. Oṃ. But having exhausted the others by experience, one then attains [union]. Oṃ.

Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, the nature of liberation known as the destruction of karma (*karmakṣaya*) is now stated here; this is the contextual connection (*avasara-saṅgati*). [This is indicated by the phrase: "Thus, liberation is the fruit."

The doubt is whether liberation from the previously mentioned knowledge is untenable. For that purpose, there is the consideration of whether the destruction and so forth of the karmas—both preceding and following knowledge—which are obstacles to liberation, is untenable or tenable. For that purpose, there is the consideration of whether there is a sublation (bādhaka) in accepting such destruction and so forth, or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): in the sūtra "Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation" (*evaṃ muktiphalāniyamaḥ*), it was stated that liberation indeed occurs through knowledge when there is an absence of obstruction caused by karma; however, that statement is untenable.

Because it is impossible for those past actions that have been performed—which act as obstacles—to cease [merely] before or after the arising of knowledge. Therefore, is there the cessation of past actions through experience (*bhoga*), or is there their destruction by knowledge—like cotton by fire—and the non-clinging (*alepa*) of future actions? Regarding the first alternative: does their experience occur in that very same body, or in another body? Even regarding the latter: is it sequentially, or simultaneously through a multiplication of bodies (*kāyavyūha*) within a single birth? The first [alternative] is not tenable, because there exist actions whose fruits require many bodies. The second is also not tenable.

If that were the case, knowledge separated by a long period of time would—like a withered seed—fail to be a cause for liberation. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because such [karmas] ripen at indefinite places and times; and even if one were to accept that through the power of yoga these [karmas] result in experience at only one specific place and time, it would follow that there is an absence of experience due to the efficacy of yoga. Furthermore, since other karmas can arise during those periods of experiencing [the results], [liberation] would never be completed.

Nor does the knower not act, because that would contradict the statement in the *Gītā*: "Indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action. Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because that would contradict the *Smṛti* text: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of aeons if it has not been experienced. For if karma were destroyed by knowledge alone, liberation would necessarily follow immediately after the arising of that knowledge.

Furthermore, if the merit of past actions were destroyed by knowledge, there would be a contradiction with the statement regarding the utility of knowledge in the sūtra, "And there is a need for all [works], because of the scriptural texts concerning sacrifice and so forth" (BS 3.4.26). Moreover, if future [actions] do not adhere, there would be a contradiction with the reason for the excellence of bliss stated in the section on praise. By this very logic, the statement in the eleventh adhikaraṇa of the Vairāgyapāda—that those who perform sacrifices and so forth, as well as those who hate Hari, attain darkness—is also untenable.

This is because, prior to or after the filling of hatred, there is no possibility of the destruction or non-clinging of virtuous actions, whether through their fruition or through the filling of hatred. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: even though the exhaustion of actions occurs through fruition, liberation through knowledge is indeed logical even when there is the performance of action subsequent to the arising of knowledge. Since it is accepted that through knowledge there is both the destruction of past and future actions and their non-clinging, the aforementioned defect does not apply.

By means of knowledge (*jñāna*), there occurs the destruction of all previously accumulated sinful actions that have not yet begun to bear fruit (*aprārabdha*), as well as the destruction of those meritorious actions among one's merits that are likewise uncommenced, non-intentional, and non-desired; however, since other merits and sins remain, and because of the Smṛti rule "that which has not been experienced [must be exhausted]," the contradiction with that [rule] is resolved by taking that [Smṛti] to refer to those [remaining] objects. Furthermore, this is consistent with the statement that previously acquired merit serves as a support for the arising of knowledge, and that liberation occurs at the very moment following the birth of knowledge.

Likewise, since there is no contradiction with the method of praise (stutinaya)—given that one accepts that subsequent sin does not result in impurity or similar states due to its non-adherence (*aśleṣa*), and that merit not performed out of desire serves as a cause for the excellence of bliss in liberation—and because it is possible to exhaust both commenced (*prārabdha*) merit and demerit, as well as uncommenced (*aprārabdha*) merit and demerit from previous or subsequent actions not performed out of desire through experience (*bhoga*), there is no sublation [of the doctrine]. Therefore, the destruction of karma through knowledge and so forth is indeed logical; thus, liberation through knowledge is perfectly tenable.

Thus, for one who harbors hatred as well, because of the fulfillment of that hatred, there is the destruction of all previously performed *aprārabdha* merit, the non-attachment (*aśleṣa*) of all subsequent merits, and the exhaustion through experience of *prārabdha* merits and sins; therefore, the statement regarding the attainment of darkness (*tamas*) by the hater is also logical. As for the result, it is clearly the corroboration of the aforementioned subject matter. || 8 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the second quarter.

Therefore, since the destruction of karma through knowledge and experience for the sake of the fruit of liberation—the state denoted by the word "That"—was explained in the previous chapter (*pāda*), whereas here the sequence of the body's dissolution, which is to be accomplished by the destruction of karma, is being stated, the immediate succession of this chapter (*pāda*) to the preceding one should be kept in mind.
**Oṃ. Speech [is merged] in the mind, because it is so seen and because of scripture. Oṃ.** (1)
