|| Oṃ, and for this very reason, all [the other qualities] follow; oṃ.

Oṃ. For the wise, the dissolution of the body is of two kinds: for the gods, it is absorption (*laya*) into those superior to themselves; for others, it is by means of the upward departure through the *brahmanāḍī*. Among these, because the gods possess the highest qualification, their dissolution of the body is first described by the seven preceding sections (*adhikaraṇas*), beginning with the sūtra "Non-distinction [is attained], because of the scriptural statement" (*avibhāgo vacanāt*). In that regard, there arises the inquiry: regarding the absorption of the mind into the deity Vāc for the sake of liberation characterized by attaining the Lord, is this impossible to determine, or is it possible to determine?

Therefore, for that purpose, it must be determined whether the superiority of *manas* over *vāk* can or cannot be established. To that end, there is a mixed statement: "Speech is the prior form, mind is the subsequent form," and "Mind is the prior form, speech is the subsequent form. Since these two statements regarding speech and mind—by describing them as being born of one another—reveal their equal primacy, [the question arises: how can the superiority of *manas* be determined? [The answer is: because in the context of the Sūtra, "But the sequence is the reverse from this, and so it is logical" (*viparyayeṇa tu kramo'ta upapadyate ca*), dissolution must be stated as occurring into one's own immediate superior deity; therefore, the dissolution of speech is into mind.

"It is impossible to determine" [is the objection]. But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since it is established by the perception of all that speech is subject to the mind—as stated in the passage, "First one forms a volition with the mind, and then one speaks with speech"—the activity of speech [is preceded by the mind].

Furthermore, because the mind is characterized by its being preceded by the activity of the *manas* and is endowed with logical reasoning, it is possible to determine that the mind is superior; thus, the dissolution of the goddess of speech (*Vāgdevī*) into the god of the mind (*Manodeva*) certainly occurs. Nor is there any contradiction with the "mixed" statement (*vyāmiśrokti*), for that *Saṃhitā* is concerned with the dispute between Māṇḍūkya and his eldest son regarding whether the preceding or succeeding phonemes are the presiding deities and their respective status as subordinate or primary qualities. This is clearly explained in the *Aitareya Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the result, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is an objection based on the statement that because there is no liberation for the goddess of speech (*vāgdevī*), there is no fixed rule for all [deities]. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this is resolved. Here, the goddesses of speech are Vāruṇī and Sauparṇī; the gods of mind are to be known as Śeṣa and Suparṇa. By this, the dissolution of all deities into their respective superior deities is established through the force of such scriptural texts as, "All deities dissolve into Agni, and Agni into Indra," since there is no sublation thereof by statements such as those concerning mutual intermingling.

In this commentary, regarding the sentence expressing doubt as to whether [the mind] dissolves in the mind or not, one should consider the author’s intention to be either that there is no final determination, or that the ellipsis is "then it certainly does dissolve," and that in neither case is it possible [to conclude otherwise], which constitutes the commencement of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, one should not entertain the suspicion that this is inconsistent with the *pūrvapakṣa*. || 1 ||
Oṃ. That mind and vital breath [arise] from the subsequent [section]. Oṃ. 2.

In these three sections, the sequence for meditation should be understood according to the scriptural order beginning with "Speech merges into the mind" and so forth. Here, the question arises whether the deity of the mind originates from the deity of breath or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the deity of breath—is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the cause of activity everywhere for the four-faced Brahmā and others, so too the mind (*manas*)—the deity of the mind—is established as the cause of activity everywhere for Śeṣa and others. Since they are equal in being the impellers (*ceṣṭaka*), and since the deity of the mind possesses no less power than the deity of the vital breath, the deity of the mind does not dissolve into the vital breath. Consequently, there is no liberation (*mokṣa*). This is because, according to the direction stated in the passage beginning with "by the reverse order" (*viparyayeṇa*), that which is of lesser power must dissolve into that which is of greater power.

Nor can it be suspected that the mind dissolves there because it is born from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since the Lord's origination is stated in the sūtra: "And because of its being heard before that" (*tatprākśruteśca*). As for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*):

By the statement, "Speech merges into the mind," and because of the hearing of the merging—denoted by the word *sampatti*—of the deity Mind into the deity Breath in the passage, "The mind [merges] into breath," the deity Mind also merges into the deity Breath (the four-faced Brahmā) through the medium of Speech, on the strength of other scriptural texts. This is because the Aitareya Śruti, in passages such as "When the mind departs," etc., records that while there is an absence of the falling down and rising up of the body upon the departure and entry of the deity Mind from the body of Brahmā, there is the presence of these effects upon the departure and entry of the deity Breath; thus, [it follows] even from the deity Mind...

Because there is no equality in being an object of desire (*ceṣṭyatva*) due to the understanding of the superiority of the vital deity (*prāṇadeva*), and because [the soul's] origination from the Blessed Lord is possible through the medium of the vital deity according to the logic of the "ether" (*viyatpadīyanyāya*), and because the mind is born from the vital breath according to the scripture, "From the wind indeed Rudra arises," the mind also attains liberation. The result, however, is as before. || 2 ||
Oṃ. He is the presiding overseer, because of [scriptural passages] such as "approaching Him" (tad-upagama). Oṃ. 3.

Here, the connection [of the topic] is established either by the order of the Śruti texts or by the implication of the results of the two preceding methods. Here, the inquiry is whether Viriñca, who is designated by the term *prāṇa*, merges into Hari for the sake of liberation in the form of attaining the Blessed Lord, or whether he does not merge. For that purpose, the consideration is whether there is or is not a certainty regarding his subordination to the Lord (Īśa). For that purpose, the consideration is whether the abundance of scriptural texts concerning the independence of *prāṇa*, as well as his greatness consisting in being the eater while himself not being eaten, are without scope (*niravakāśa*) or have scope (*sāvakāśa*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows:

Because of the abundance of scriptural passages—such as "The vital breath (prāṇa) does not depend on anything," "In which all this is woven together," "All this that is established in the third heaven is under the control of the vital breath," and "By Vāyu, O Gautama, as by a thread"—which demonstrate that the vital breath is not dependent on anything else, its subordination to the Lord (Īśa) is certain; therefore, there is no dissolution of Viriñca (Brahmā) therein.

Nor should it be suspected that the Śrutis have scope [to refer to Viṣṇu] by means of the principle stated as: "The state of having no other Lord in Prāṇa is the exclusion of any Lord other than Him," and thus being intent on excluding any Lord other than Viṣṇu. For it is impossible to assume another interpretation for the Śrutis—which possess strength derived from their multiplicity—on account of a weak statement such as "having no other" (*ananya*). Furthermore, this is because the phrase "not being dissolved" (*ananya-māna*) declares the absence of dissolution for Prāṇa. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: there indeed exists the dissolution of Viriñca, who is denoted by the word "Prāṇa," into Hari.

Regarding the lack of independence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), although there is an abundance of scriptural texts concerning its dependence on the Lord, there exist many other scriptural passages such as "The vital breath [is merged] in the highest deity," "The vital breath goes to the Supreme," and "The vital breath breathes after the Supreme. Nor can it be determined that its dependence on the Lord is equal [to that of other things].

The scriptural texts concerning independence—such as "All go unto Prāṇa," "The gods breathe after Prāṇa," and "The state of having no other lord [means] the exclusion of any other lord besides Prāṇa"—are possessed of scope because they aim at [Prāṇa's] being the sustainer of all beings like Rudra and others, and at the exclusion of any other lord besides the Blessed Lord. This is because the quality of not being consumed is established by the fact that [Prāṇa] is not consumed by anyone other than Īśvara.

Regarding the scriptural statement, "The vital breath [merges] into heat," the mention of the dissolution of the vital breath into heat—that is, into the Śrī-tattva—is intended merely to indicate its attainment of that state, according to the Smṛti which states, "The dissolution of the vital breath into heat is merely a path"; it does not mean actual dissolution therein. It should be understood that because Viriñca alone is fit for direct dissolution into the Supreme Self, the vital breath's dissolution occurs there [in him], just as it does in the Supreme Self.

In the sūtra, "But like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them," although it was stated that the vital breath (prāṇa) is under the control of the Lord (Īśvara), here there is a suspicion of a distinction due to the abundance of scriptural texts [stating its] independence; thus, this is not a mere repetition of what has already been said. As for the result: in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), since there would be no liberation (mokṣa) for Viriñca in the absence of dissolution, and consequently no liberation for all those who have attained knowledge who enter into him, the two previously mentioned methods of reasoning would be subverted. Thus, by means of the objection stated as "no fixed rule" (aniyama), the established conclusion (siddhānta) provides the resolution thereof. || 3 ||
Oṃ, because that [Brahman] exists within all beings; Oṃ. 5.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised here by way of the objection stated previously. In the Śruti passage beginning with "Speech [merges] into the mind," there is an inquiry as to whether the gods—other than those specifically mentioned—dissolve into a single elemental principle (*bhūta*) for the sake of liberation consisting of attaining the Lord, or rather into other elemental principles as well. For that purpose, the question is whether the Śruti statement, "All the gods dissolve into fire," serves to determine the meaning of what was perceived [in the previous text], or not.

Regarding that matter, there is the following doubt: Is there no evidence for the dissolution of the elements into one another, and is the previously stated principle inconclusive? Or is there evidence, and is the previously stated principle decisive? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Based on the Vedic scripture stating, "All the gods are in Agni," all the gods dissolve only into the god Agni; furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for their dissolving elsewhere. Moreover, regarding the previously stated principle—that "whatever is the specific rule for something, it dissolves into that"—this principle is inconclusive because there are many such rules. Therefore, the previously stated view that dissolution occurs according to each thing's own specific rule is untenable. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

By the scriptural passage cited in the Commentary, "The gods dissolve into the elements," it is understood that within all five elemental categories, the presiding deities dissolve into their respective controllers. Even though there are many such controllers, a definitive conclusion can be reached according to the direction of other scriptural passages, such as: "All the gods dissolve into Agni; Agni into Indra; Indra into Umā; Umā into Rudra. Therefore, the previously stated reasoning is not lacking in its power to provide a definitive conclusion. The result, however, is the resolution of the objections raised previously. || 4 ||
Oṃ, for [the Lord] does not manifest [himself] in one [place], Oṃ. 5.

Here too, the connection [of the topic] arises from raising a doubt by way of an objection to what was previously stated. The doubt is as follows: do the deities mentioned in the preceding context dissolve into fire alone—which is a characteristic of liberation consisting in the attainment of the Lord—or do they dissolve into all five elements? Is the previously cited scripture stating, "the deities dissolve into the elements," one that has scope (sāvakāśā) or one that lacks scope (niravakāśā)? To determine this, it must be considered whether the scriptural statement, "all the deities [dissolve] into fire," is untenable otherwise (and thus lacks scope), or whether it does have scope.

To that end, since there is no specific evidence for the phrase "in all five" [of the elements], and because it is impossible for the Vedic scripture stating "in fire" to have any other meaning, and because there is no basis for postulating any alternative interpretation, the previously stated claim—that "the dissolution of all the gods occurs in fire alone"—is untenable. This is because the scripture using the plural form "in the elements" (*bhūteṣu*) is otherwise without scope; for even if the gods dissolve into fire, fire dissolves into its own progenitor, air, and air dissolves into its own progenitor, ether. Thus, by intending a dissolution through this successive lineage, the plural scriptural statement can be given scope, making the claim of dissolution in fire alone inconsistent.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Based on the two specific authorities mentioned in the Commentary—namely, "the *Ṛbhus* dissolve into the earth" and "the *Ṛbhus* [are] in the earth"—it is heard that the dissolution of the gods beginning with the *Ṛbhus* occurs individually within all five elements. Consequently, the scriptural statement "all the gods [dissolve] in Agni," along with the scriptural passage "the fires [dissolve] in Agni, Indra in Vāyu," and so forth, has a limited scope (*sāvakāśatva*) as it refers to the dissolution of those sons of Agni who are generally inferior and do not enter into other elements. Therefore, the dissolution of the gods occurs within the elements, according to the scripture stating "in the elements."

Since it is impossible for [the text] to imply a primary sense consisting of the intention of dissolution through a traditional succession, and because the aforementioned scripture states that [the gods] have "no other resort," it is logical that the dissolution of the gods occurs within all five elements as previously mentioned, and likewise within all five [categories] previously mentioned. The result is evident. || 5 ||
Oṃ. And [the soul] departs with the *samanā* [vital energy], because it begins its journey toward rebirth; and [it attains] immortality without having burned away [its karma]. Oṃ. 6.

|| Oṃ: And because of the merging into that [Brahman], and because of the designation of transmigratory existence, Oṃ. || Oṃ: And it is subtle, because it is perceived through that [scriptural authority] as being of such a nature, Oṃ. || Oṃ: Not by destruction, therefore, Oṃ. || Oṃ: And because this very [subtlety] is logical, there is warmth, Oṃ. || Oṃ: If it be argued "because of a prohibition," we say no, because [the prohibition refers to the soul] other than the embodied one, Oṃ. || Oṃ: For it is touched [as an object of perception] by some, Oṃ. || Oṃ: And it is also recorded in Smṛti, Oṃ. ||

The connection [of this section] is one of exception (*apavāda*), because a doubt arises here based on the previously stated principle of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and the specific scriptural statement regarding its dependence [on Brahman]. The inquiry is whether the conscious primordial nature (*cit-prakṛti*)—which is the subject under discussion either by virtue of being present in the mind as superior to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or by virtue of the sequence in the scripture—is merged into the Lord or not. For that purpose, the question is whether both the previously stated reasoning and the specific scriptural statement, "Light [merges] into the Supreme," are without scope (*niravakāśa*), or whether they have scope (*sāvakāśa*).

For that purpose, it was stated [in the previous section] whether the non-transmigratory nature of *prakṛti* mentioned in the passage "from desire" (*kāmāt*) is untenable or tenable. For that purpose, one must consider whether its state of liberation is adventitious or inherent. If it were inherent, would it result in her being equal to the Lord in all respects, or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: By the reasoning of subordination to the Lord and by the two scriptural texts beginning with "Fire" (*tejaḥ*), she too indeed merges into Hari; otherwise, the merging of speech and the other organs into the mind and so forth, as stated in those two [texts], would not occur either.

Nor can it be argued that there is an absence of dissolution because He is not subject to *saṃsāra*, for that very [state of being non-transmigratory] is untenable. Nor is it appropriate to say that [dissolution is absent] because He is liberated, since liberation is adventitious. If it were inherent, it would follow that the Lord is identical to all things; and if He were eternally free from *saṃsāra*, it would follow that He is equal to others in terms of other qualities as well. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "There are indeed two ways of not undertaking the path of transmigration: primordial nature (prakṛti) and the Supreme (parama)," since it is taught through the reasoning of the Supreme Person's omnipresence and eternity that there is never an absence of saṃsāra [for Him], and that His eternal liberation is caused by that very nature, liberation is innate because it is not something to be accomplished through means such as the worship of the Lord. Furthermore, since the Goddess—who possesses such liberation—cannot undergo dissolution in the form of casting off the body as Hari does, primordial nature does not dissolve [into her].

The intended inference—that [the mind] dissolves into Hari, its own superior, because it is dependent upon Him, just like speech and the other organs—is undermined by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). The scriptural statement, "It becomes fire" (*tejaḥ*), is likewise [subject to this condition].

This [liberation] is established as having the sense of extreme proximity (*atisāmīpya*), according to the scriptural statement: "The dissolution of Lakṣmī is proclaimed to be extreme proximity to Hari. Furthermore, the possibility of all beings attaining equality with the Lord of Prakṛti is refuted by the three sūtras—"*tadapīteḥ*," "*sūkṣmam*," and "*asyaiva ca*"—which provide the grounds for [the distinction between] being liberated and not liberated, subtlety and non-subtlety, the superiority and inferiority of the magnitude of qualities such as knowledge and bliss, and the possession or non-possession of heat.

Furthermore, as for the objection that if there were no equality in all respects, there would likewise be no equality even in terms of eternal liberation and so forth—as in the case of Brahmā and others—this is refuted in the sūtra "Not by the destruction [of qualities]" (*nopamardena*). This is because that sūtra states that the scriptural evidence establishes only a certain degree of equality, such as the pervasion of space and time, precisely through the non-destruction of the Lord’s specific attributes. Thus, the prohibition of equality regarding Hari in the Śruti text "This Supreme One is indeed unequal" (*asamo vā eṣa paraḥ*) pertains to the individual soul (*jīva*), according to the direction indicated in the three subsequent sūtras beginning with "Because of the prohibition" (*pratiṣedhāt*).

Regarding the result, however: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the Goddess is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) and because her merging into the Blessed Lord exists, there is an objection against [her] being the limit of the authority of those qualified [for knowledge], as stated in the scriptural authority cited under the Sūtra "Because of the mention of this much" (*iyad-āmananāt*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that objection is resolved. || 6 ||
Oṃ, those [elements] are beyond; for thus he has said, Oṃ. 7.

The connection with the preceding section arises from the doubt: since it was stated previously that "having dissolved into the Supreme, he indeed attains immortality" (*vilīnaḥ parame hyamṛtatvameti*), let immortality belong to the *prāṇa* mentioned in the phrase "he [dissolves] in the Overseer" (*so'dhyakṣe*), but not to the gods mentioned in the phrase "the gods dissolve into the elements" (*bhūteṣu devā vilīyante*). To resolve this, the inquiry is whether the gods mentioned in "the gods dissolve into the elements" dissolve into the Blessed Lord or not. For that purpose, the question is: are these [gods] reflections of the four-faced Brahmā (Caturmukha) denoted by the term *prāṇa*, or are they also reflections of the Blessed Lord?

For a reflection, which consists of similarity while being dependent upon that [original], indeed dissolves into its own controller, the archetype (*bimba*). Since the statement, "The life-breath (*prāṇa*) is the reflection of Hari; the other parts (*kalā*) are [reflections] of the life-breath in succession," establishes that the life-breath alone is the reflection of the Lord, it follows that liberation—which is entry into Him—belongs to that one [life-breath] alone and not to other knowers. Thus, the claim that liberation is unrestricted for all is incorrect. In response to this objection: although the deities are reflections of the life-breath in succession, because "all the gods, having entered the life-breath, [merge] into the God... [the text continues].

Because liberation consists in entering the Supreme Self through the gateway of the vital breath (prāṇa), as established by the Śruti text, "The liberated ones go to the supreme dissolution"; because when Viriñca—who is a reflection of the Blessed Lord—enters the Lord, his entry into the Supreme Self is unavoidable; and because, according to the direction of the Sūtra, "And [the soul] is merely a reflection," all souls in general are reflections of that aforementioned nature, it is logical that there exists liberation in the form of entry therein; thus, what was stated regarding the lack of restriction is correct. The result, however, is evident. || 7 ||
|| Oṃ, there is no division, because of the scriptural statement; oṃ. || 8 ||

The connection here is established by way of raising a doubt based on what was previously introduced. In the preceding section, it was stated that the gods possess liberation; the inquiry now is whether they are independent in liberation or dependent upon the Lord. To this end, the question is raised as to whether, if they were dependent on another, there would follow the consequence of experiencing the sufferings of saṃsāra and so forth, as well as the consequence of lacking the qualities of "truthful will" and the rest mentioned in the Śruti, or whether this is not the case.

If liberated souls were dependent on another, there would follow the consequence of suffering from saṃsāra and the like; furthermore, qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), as declared by the Śruti in passages such as, "These gods, having entered this Self, are true and possess true desires," would be impossible. Thus, since it has been previously stated that liberated souls are not dependent on another, the notion of their being reflections under the control of the Lord—characterized by dependence on Him—is untenable. To this, [the reply is: By the Śruti and Smṛti texts, "By my will, my desire comes" and "The liberated possess true desires," the possession of true desires and other qualities mentioned in the Śruti follows precisely from being in accordance with the will of the Lord.

Since there is no possibility of suffering and the like occurring [for the liberated], and since suffering and so forth are caused by the failure to obtain what one desires, and because those liberated ones who desire according to the will of the Lord lack the failure to obtain their desires, it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the possessors of knowledge remain dependent on the Lord even in liberation; thus, what was stated previously is justified. || 8 ||

Oṃ. Then [the soul] reaches the flame that issues from the door [of the heart], which is illuminated by that [flame]; by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), and by the application of recollection of the path that remains to be traversed, it is assisted by the one dwelling in the heart through the hundred-and-first artery. Oṃ. 9.

Oṃ, [the soul] follows the rays; Oṃ. Oṃ, if it is argued that [it does not go] at night, we say no, because of the connection; Oṃ. Oṃ, because it exists as long as the body, [the scripture] shows this; Oṃ. Oṃ, and therefore also during the southern course of the sun; Oṃ.

In the preceding section, liberation through the dissolution of the bodies of the gods into their respective superiors was described by seven principles for the qualified aspirant (*adhikārī*) according to the highest order, along with its exceptions. Here, however, it is stated that for human beings, liberation in the form of attaining the Blessed Lord occurs through the process of upward departure (*utkramaṇa*). Thus, the connection between this [section] and the previous one should be understood. Here, the inquiry concerns whether the departure from the body of the knowers (*jñānin*) is exactly like the death of the ignorant, or whether, by the power of knowledge, it is distinct from that.

For that purpose, one must consider whether knowledge is incapable of producing the state of being distinct from death, or indeed capable of it. For that purpose, one must consider whether the remainder of *prārabdha* karma acts as an obstacle to the power of knowledge, or not. For that purpose, one must consider whether knowledge is capable of yielding its fruit from its own arising, or only upon the exhaustion of karma. For that purpose, one must consider whether there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if it were capable of yielding its fruit from its own arising, or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
if knowledge is capable of yielding its fruit—consisting of the state of being distinct from the death of the ignorant—from the very moment of its own arising...

Since it would follow that the death of a knower (*jña*) lacks the distinction from the death of an ignorant person (*ajña*) unless it is admitted that [knowledge] is capable of yielding its fruit only upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma—and not while it still exists—the statement "as long as the body" (*ādeham*) implies that knowledge, its power being obstructed by *prārabdha* existing until the fall of the body, does not produce a distinction between the death of a knower and the death of an ignorant person. Nor is it reasonable to claim that *prārabdha* ceases at the time of death, for the death of a knower, like the death of an ignorant person, is likewise dependent upon *prārabdha*.

As for the statement, “Knowledge yields its fruit upon its own arising,” this must be understood as referring to another type of fruit. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: This would indeed be the case if we were to admit that the death of a knower (*jñānin*) produces a distinction by means of knowledge alone; then there would certainly be the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). But it is not so; rather, [the cause] is accompanied by the recollection of the path existing from one's own heart up to the attainment of the Lord, and is accompanied by the grace of the Lord residing in the heart, who is pleased by that wisdom (*vidyā*).

Likewise, that destruction occurs only at the conclusion of the karma and not otherwise; thus, there is no over-extension [of the argument]. Therefore, knowledge conjoined with both of these [factors] certainly brings about the distinction between the death of the ignorant and the death of the knower. Consequently, it should be understood that the efficacy of knowledge as described in the *Jñānapāda* is indeed logical. This is the result to be meditated upon.

The manner of this distinction should be understood according to the direction stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya and other texts, beginning with the phrase "the door revealed by that" (tat-prakāśita-dvāra): the departure of the knower occurs through the *brahmanāḍī*, whose opening is illuminated by the light of the Lord residing in the heart, and which is pervaded internally by the rays of the sun that persist as long as the body exists; such is not the case for the ignorant person. Although the general fact that the knower undergoes departure (*utkramaṇa*) is established here, it is appropriate to consider the specific point of whether this departure is distinct from that of an ignorant person who has died, or not.

Nevertheless, just as in the section on the ether (*viyat-pāda*), the dissolution (*laya*) is taken for granted by the very mention of birth, so that one considers whether it occurs in the order of creation or its reverse; here too, since the dissolution of the bodies of the gods is stated through their mutual entry, the departure (*utkramaṇa*) of others from their bodies is already established. Therefore, there is no fault in taking this as a settled fact and proceeding with this specific consideration. || 9 ||
Oṃ. These two [rites] are prescribed for the Smārta yogins; they are based on the Smṛti. Oṃ. 10.

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised by what preceded. In the preceding [section], there was an inquiry as to whether both the knowledge of the path (*vidyā-gati*) and the recollection [of that path], which were presented as being subsidiary to the primary [subject], are necessary for the journey or not. To that end, the Smṛti passage beginning with "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight" (*agnir jyotir ahaḥ śuklaḥ*), when assisted by its conformity with common worldly usage, is intended to show that the journey is dependent upon time and death.

The *smṛti* passage "whomsoever" (*yaṃ yaṃ vāpi*) and the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*) must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with common worldly usage; or else, the *smṛti* passage beginning with "Agni" is intended to show dependence on knowledge and the like, while the statement "whomsoever" is to be interpreted differently. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the Smṛti passages, "Fire, light, day, and the bright fortnight" and "Smoke, night," it is understood that the two paths—attaining Brahman and attaining the moon—are respectively dependent on the times of day and night. Furthermore, since in the world one is seen to obtain a result even without recollecting the result beforehand, the Smṛti regarding the path is not intended for the purpose of reaching the path; rather, it is simply the recollection of the time, such as day and so forth, that is required. And knowledge [of the path] is not required. However, the recollection of the time, such as day and so forth, is indeed necessary.

Nor should it be argued that, since the Smṛti passage "Whatever [being] he remembers" (*BhG* 8.6) states that only the object of remembrance is what is attained, this would contradict the scriptural statement "The teacher will tell you the way" (*BhG* 4.34)—which speaks of the attainment of the goal as a form of knowledge—were that the case. For at the moment of leaving the body, remembrance occurs with difficulty; therefore, the word "remembering" (*smaran*) must be interpreted as signifying mere knowledge, in the sense of "knowing through scripture and so forth" prior [to death].

By this, the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) is also refuted, since the teaching of that [path] is logically consistent with the purpose of knowledge; otherwise, it would contradict common worldly experience. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because of the qualifiers "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*) in the first *smṛti* and "yogi" in the *smṛti* concerning smoke, one understands from those two that [the attainment] is accomplished by means consisting of both knowledge and action; thus, there is no perception of its being dependent on time or death. Therefore, [factors] such as spiritual knowledge (*vidyā*) are certainly required. Otherwise, the specific qualifiers in those two *smṛtis* would result in meaninglessness.

Since day and so forth are deities by virtue of the principle of presiding deities (*abhimāninī-devatā*) and lack the nature of time, there is no impossibility of remembering [the Lord] at the moment of renunciation, as stated in the *Smṛti*: "Whatever [being] one may [be intent upon]... For great souls, because they always maintain the perception that the body is to be abandoned, there is an absence of suffering at that time; and for even common people, since suffering exists only in time, there is likewise an absence of suffering at that specific moment. Nor is there the fault of not conforming to worldly practice, for just as in the world one observes the persistence of actions such as plowing until the attainment of the fruit, here too we accept the persistence of the action in the form of remembrance.

In the world, action takes the form of plowing and so forth; here, however, it is mental—this is merely a distinction of sub-category. One should not, on that account alone, suspect that [the scripture] does not follow that [general rule], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). By this, it is also shown that the observation of the inferential mark (*liṅgadarśana*) is not to be interpreted otherwise. As for the fruit of knowledge, it consists in the refutation of the objection regarding its being the cause of the fourfold liberation (*mokṣa*). 10.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the third quarter.

In the preceding section, it was stated that for those who have departed through the *brahmanāḍī*, there is a recollection of the path (*gati-smaraṇa*) at the time of attaining Brahman as taught within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*). It should be understood that this present section follows the previous one because it describes that very path and its goal. Nor should it be feared that the division of the chapters would be compromised by the mention of both the path and the goal; for although the path and its final destination constitute a single entity insofar as the entire route is considered a "path," the text speaks of the "goal" here with the intention of distinguishing the final destination from the preceding portions of the path. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ arciṣādinā tat-prathiteḥ Oṃ* (1). The path begins with light (*arciḥ*), because that is how it is well-known [in scripture]. 1.1.1.

In the preceding section, it was stated that the remembrance of the path (*gati*) is necessary; the present inquiry is whether that path begins first with the light (*arcis*) or with both [the light and the wind]. To determine this, one must consider whether the two scriptural passages are without scope (*niravakāśa*) or possess scope (*sāvakāśa*). For that purpose, one must consider whether the priority of both is consistent with the path or inconsistent. Finally, for that purpose, one must consider whether that path is of two forms or of a single form, and whether—given the contradiction regarding the priority of both as implied by the distinction between different types of qualified aspirants—the passages are without scope or possess scope.

Regarding the two scriptural passages, "They enter into the rays" and "He reaches the wind," it might be concluded that the path beginning with both light (*arcis*) and wind (*vāyu*) is the primary route. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: according to the *Smṛti*—"Two paths alone are well-known for the wise: the one beginning with light and the other beginning with smoke for those who perform ritual acts"—there is in fact only one path.

And that [path] consists precisely of the *arciḥ* (flame) and so forth, and not of the *vāyu* (wind) and so forth; this is established by the expression "well-known" (*prasiddha*) through the word "famous. Because the Śruti text, "They [go] to the *arciḥ*" (*te 'rciṣam*), is more authoritative, and in accordance with it, there is only one path to Brahman whose first deity is named *arciḥ*, not many. As for the Śruti text, "He goes to the wind" (*sa vāyum gacchati*), it is explained as being consistent with the more authoritative Śruti by signifying arrival immediately after the *arciḥ*. [This has been explained] to the student in the *Ṭīkā*.

However, as for the fruit: although the two paths are established according to the distinction between qualified aspirants, because one has not determined "I am qualified for this [path]," there arises the impossibility of recollecting the way [to liberation] and its resolution. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The soul's departure] is due to wind and a specific sound, not due to poison; Oṃ. 2.

In the preceding section, the determination of the deities and others to be reached first on the path to Brahman was made. Here, the determination of the deity to be reached second is undertaken; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*). Alternatively, the connection arises from a doubt based on a perceived discrepancy with what preceded. The inquiry is as follows: on the previously mentioned path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), are both the deity Vāyu and the deity Day (*ahaḥ*) to be reached second, or is it the deity Vāyu alone?

For that purpose, it must be considered whether the two scriptural passages—"He [reaches] Vāyu" and "From the light [he reaches] the day"—establish that both [Vāyu and the day] are to be reached as the second stage, or not. For that purpose, one must further consider whether there are two paths or only one. As for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):

In the previous case, although it was understood that light (*arcis*) alone is the first [stage] due to the specific statement that there are only two paths, here, because there is no specific statement regarding air (*vāyu*) being the second stage to be reached, both light and air are the second stages to be reached by different paths. Since there is no contradiction in both being the second stages to be reached—given the authority of both scriptural passages, namely "from light to day" and "he reaches air"—both day and air are the second stages to be reached by the force of these two scriptures. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

Regarding the statement, "He goes to Vāyu," although the general expression might lead one to abandon the primacy of Vāyu—which has already been established—due to its contradiction with the well-known teaching that "only two paths are proclaimed," nevertheless, because the status of being the second destination is established by logic, and because of the specific scriptural text, "Having departed from here, he reaches the second path, Vāyu," it follows that Vāyu alone is the second destination, and the day (Ahar) is what is reached immediately after that.

The claim that both [results] are attainable through both paths is refuted precisely because it contradicts the well-known principle stated in the words "only two [results for each]. As for the result, however, it is as before. || 2 ||
Oṃ, Varuṇa is superior to Taṭit because of their relationship; Oṃ. 3.

"They reach the flame; from the flame, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months, to the year," and so forth. Regarding the path to the attainment of Brahman described in such passages of the *Chāndogya Śruti*, the first and second stages to be reached have been determined where there was dispute. As for the other stages up to the year, since there is no dispute regarding their sequential attainment, they require no further determination.

The inquiry is whether, after a year, both Taḍit and Varuṇa are reached by different paths to go to the world of Prajāpati, or whether they are reached by a single path, having first reached the world of Taḍit. To that end, the question is whether the two scriptural passages—"from the year to the world of Varuṇa" and "from the year to Taḍit"—establish the attainment of both, or not. Is there any evidence for the latter view (that they do not), or is there?

In the previous [section], although it was determined that Vāyu is the second destination by means of the specific statement "Vāyu," here such a proof is absent. Therefore, because both scriptural passages are authoritative, it is logical that both are destinations, depending on the distinction of paths governed by the difference in the qualifications of the seekers. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that both worlds are reached immediately after the world of the wind. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:

Because the specific scriptural statement, “From lightning he goes to Varuṇa, for by lightning the world of Varuṇa is reached,” declares with logical justification that the world of Varuṇa is attained immediately after lightning; and because it is logical that this does not contradict the well-known unity of the path to Brahman mentioned in the passage, “There are two paths... only these two,” which speaks of a single path; and because there is a contradiction in two [stations] being reached simultaneously on one and the same path; therefore, it is necessary that the two scriptural passages intend to convey that the two [stations] are reached as causes of attainment through a sequence of priority and posteriority. First...

Having reached the world of lightning, one subsequently reaches the world of Varuṇa; however, the result [of this] follows from the determination of the path, because otherwise the recollection of that [path] would be impossible, and for the sake of its successful accomplishment. || 3 ||
|| Oṃ, [the soul] is of a transportable nature, because of its characteristic marks; oṃ. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ. Because that [cognition] is established through the mutual delusion of both [parties], oṃ. ||

In the preceding section, the sequence between lightning and Varuṇa—two distinct entities occurring in separate sentences—was discussed; here, however, the sequence between two meanings of the single word "Vāyu"—namely, the *ātivāhika* (conductor) and the primary wind—is stated. Thus is the connection. Regarding the second path, there arises the inquiry whether the "Vāyu" mentioned in the scriptural text, "He goes to Vāyu," refers to the *ātivāhika* or to the primary wind. For that purpose, it must be considered whether, if he were the *ātivāhika*, the primary wind would be reached or not.

For that purpose, there arises a doubt as to whether the word "Vāyu" mentioned in the scripture—"The lightning indeed is the dyu; having reached its lord, Vāyu, one goes to Brahman by means of him alone"—refers to the primary Vāyu or to the *ativāhika* (conductor) Vāyu; and thus, through this doubt, there is a determination regarding the previous [doubt] as well, namely, the determination that it refers to the primary [Vāyu].

Although in the previous case the sequence was determined by the force of reasoned statements stating that "the lightning goes to Varuṇa," here there is no such determination because of doubt as to whether the former is the conductor (*ātivāhika*) and the latter is the primary (*mukhya*), or whether the former is the primary and the latter is the conductor; furthermore, since there is no evidence indicating that the former is the conductor, and because it is stated that Soma, Agni, Indra, and Dhruva are also reached sequentially on the path, the specific order of gradation is not intended here, making it possible for even the primary deity to be reached second.

Furthermore, because it is the primary meaning, the term "wind" (*vāyu*) in the second [stage] refers specifically to the primary wind and not to the *ativāhika* (conveying) wind; for if that were the case, it would follow that the primary wind could not be reached. Thus, there is a connection [to the previous discussion] due to the doubt arising from the disparity with what preceded. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: Since a determination is possible that the *ativāhika* comes first and the primary wind is last—based on the two marks of being previously reached and being the one who causes the falling of the speech denoted by the word "lightning" (*vidyut*)—the primary wind is indeed the final one.

Since even the primary meaning [the physical body] can be abandoned—given the inferential mark of being reached first and the scriptural statement cited in the Commentary, "But having departed from his own body" (CU 8.6.5)—it must be the *ātivāhika* body that is reached first. As for the result [of this discussion]: it is the refutation of the claim that the excellence of the presiding deity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) mentioned in the sūtra "Because of the teaching of this much" (BS 4.2.12) is inappropriate, along with its resolution. || 4 ||
|| Oṃ, then that [state] arises from the lightning-like [consciousness]; Oṃ. || 5 ||

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised by the discrepancy with what preceded. Following the primary air on the path to the attainment of the Brahman under discussion, there is an inquiry as to whether or not there is something to be attained prior to Brahman. To that end, the question is whether or not there is any obstacle to accepting an object of attainment in the interval between the primary air and Brahman.

In the previous case, although the final wind cannot be the *ativāhika* (conductor) because it is contradicted by its status as the Lord of the Day (*divaspati*), here there is no such contradiction in accepting some entity to be reached within the primary Brahman; furthermore, this is supported by the inference: "The primary wind possesses an interval other than itself that is distinct from Brahman, because it is an object of qualification, just like the earlier qualified souls. Nor should one raise the objection that the aforementioned superiority of the qualified soul mentioned in the Sūtra *iyadāmananāt* (B.S. 4.2.18) serves as a counter-argument, for that [objection] is itself refuted by the inference.

Regarding the passage, "Soma, Vaiśvānara, Indra, and Dhruva," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since the commentary on the preceding section cites a Smṛti text stating that Dhruva is inferior to Indra and is reached immediately after Indra, there is no sequence of attainment that conforms to the sequence of excellence; therefore, even after Vāyu, there may be someone else who is to be attained. In response to this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated.

Even if the superiority of the qualified person (*adhikārī*) does not contradict the acceptance of an intermediate goal to be reached, the fact that Vāyu is heard in scripture and tradition to be the one who leads to Brahman—as in the passages, "That person is Mānava," "He leads these to Brahman," and "Vāyu alone, having become lightning, shall lead [them] to Brahman, and no other"—contradicts the postulation of any other intermediate goal. Therefore, Vāyu alone is the final goal to be reached; for if anything else were the final goal, it would follow that it itself must be the one leading to Brahman, as is observed in the case of a king and others.
But as for the fruit, it is the application of preeminence to the wind and the meditative absorption (samādhi) upon that. || 5 ||
|| Oṃ. Bādari [holds that the soul] has a body [in the intermediate state], because the movement [described in scripture] is thus possible. Oṃ. || 6 ||

Oṃ. At the end of the task, [the soul departs] together with its presiding deity, because of the statement regarding that which is higher than this; Oṃ. And because of Smṛti; Oṃ. Jaimini [holds it goes to] the higher [Brahman], because that is the primary sense; Oṃ. And because of scriptural vision; Oṃ. Nor is there an intention to reach the effected [Brahman]; Oṃ. Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols, because of the fault in both cases and because of the nature of their resolve; Oṃ. And scripture shows a distinction; Oṃ.

The connection with the preceding section is established either by the description of the final attainment on the path to the realization of Brahman, or by the definition of the term "Brahman" occurring in the previously cited scripture: "He leads them to Brahman. Here, the inquiry is whether the "Brahman" heard in that scripture refers to the four-faced Brahmā alone, or to Brahman (the Absolute) alone, or to both. To determine this, one must consider whether the arguments for and against each individual position can be reconciled, or whether they cannot.

Likewise, regarding the position that both [attainments] occur, since it is impossible for both to be attained simultaneously, the question arises whether there is any authority for a sequential order or not. As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): this Brahman mentioned in the Śruti is none other than the four-faced one (Brahmā). For the Śruti says, "If he here indeed perceives the Supreme, he attains, he attains Brahmā, the four-faced one," and: "When the dissolution has arrived, all those [attendants], together with Brahmā..."

By the Smṛti passage, "At the end of the other [Brahmā], those whose self is the Supreme enter the supreme state," and by the reasoning that—despite the statement, "Nevertheless, bondage to Prakṛti is severed along with Brahmā," etc.—bondage continues until the liberation of Caturmukha (the four-faced Brahmā), and since it is heard that only Caturmukha exists prior to that [liberation] and it is logical that he alone is attained because he has been directly realized through means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, there arises a subverting factor (bādhaka) consisting in the understanding that the attainment is indeed of Caturmukha; thus, even the primary meaning, namely the Supreme Brahman, must be abandoned.

This is because it is logical to understand the term *viriñca* as not having its primary sense [of the four-faced Brahmā]. Nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, namely, "The knower of Brahman reaches the Supreme.

For that general statement is rendered consistent by being understood as having a secondary meaning—namely, proximity—since the previously cited specific scriptures and other evidence establish that after attaining the four-faced Brahmā, one reaches the Supreme Brahman with him shortly thereafter at the time of dissolution. As for the passage "He [leads them] to Brahman," the referent of the word *brahman* is indeed the Supreme Brahman, since the word *brahman* has its primary sense in that context.

The second [position] is that because [Brahman] has already been made directly perceived by the very means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, and because the Four-faced One (Brahmā) lacks the desire "May I attain the Four-faced One" since he has already attained realization through the means of hearing and so forth; furthermore, it is because the position of accepting both [simultaneous and sequential attainment] is untenable due to the impossibility of reconciling the aforementioned reasons, and because the position of sequential attainment is untenable for lack of authoritative evidence (*māna*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the four-faced one (*caturmukha*) alone is indeed the Supreme Brahman; for, since there is no specific reason [to restrict it] to each respective meaning through the exclusion of others, the stated reasons only establish the grasping of those respective meanings. Thus, both are intended here in the scriptural passage concerning attainment (*prāpti-śruti*) as being the referents of the word "Brahman."

As for the objection raised regarding the inclusion of the four-faced Brahmā—that it consists in the absence of the intention to reach [the goal]—and the objection raised regarding the inclusion of the Supreme Brahman in the sūtra "on account of the possibility of going" (Gatyu-papatteh)—namely, that bondage would be continuous—of these, the former is not a valid objection because, since those who take hold of symbols (pratīka) do not admit of reaching the Supreme, they lack such an intention.

The second [verse], "Those who do not rely on symbols (apratīka-āśrayāḥ) indeed go to the Supreme alone," is established both by the force of scriptural authority and by the acceptance that those who have reached the Supreme Brahman while still situated in the state of non-liberation attain it. Furthermore, for those who have attained the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and rely on symbols, there certainly exists the realization of the effected (kārya) Brahman through the path of practice and so forth; thus, even for them, this does not constitute a contradiction. Since the reasons stated for the two positions can be reconciled by accepting that they serve both purposes according to the distinction between the respective qualified aspirants, the two views can be harmonized.

For it is said: "Those who indeed have no reliance on the body go to the Supreme alone; by perceiving Brahman even in one's own body, one goes to the same world as Brahman. Thus, their attainment occurs through the sequence of fitness, both previously and at the time of dissolution. As for the fruit, however, it results from the determination or non-determination of the path to be traversed, and from the recollection of that path and its meditative absorption (samādhi). 6.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fourth quarter.

Having explained the threefold [liberation] among the fourfold fruits beginning with the destruction of karma, enjoyment, which is now reached in its proper turn, is discussed: "Oṃ, having attained [the state], he does not depart [from it], because of the word 'own' (svena). Oṃ. 1.

In the sūtra "But Jaimini [says] otherwise," the inquiry concerns whether the liberated soul under discussion—characterized by the attainment of Brahman—enjoys worldly pleasures after transcending Brahman, or without transcending it. To that end, the question is whether the scriptural passage, "Having crossed this bridge, he who was blind becomes sighted," intends a transcendence or a non-transcendence. Specifically, does it provide a basis for the sense of non-transcendence, or not? The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is as follows:

Since there is no grounds for interpreting the Śruti passage, "This is the bridge," as having any other meaning, the term *setu* (bridge) refers to Brahman; thus, by the statement that one attains liberation—which is the manifestation of one's true nature—immediately after crossing beyond (transcending) Brahman, it is understood that even one who has reached Brahman is not yet liberated. Since it is only the liberated one who experiences enjoyment, [the text means] that having transcended Brahman and being liberated, he enjoys worldly pleasures. However, this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Since the scripture, "Having attained the supreme light," describes liberation as the manifestation of one's own true nature for one who has indeed reached Brahman, and because the meaning of that same scripture—"having crossed this terrible, inauspicious river, having reached this bridge"—must be understood as "having crossed other [rivers] in order to go to this bridge" in accordance with the explicit Vedic text, and furthermore because of the scripture, "Having fully attained the Self, by means of this Self he experiences all desires according to his wish," the knower, having reached Brahman, does not depart from it.
"He enjoys enjoyments" (bhogān bhuṅkte). But as for the fruit, it is the refutation of the objection regarding Brahman being the final goal. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The soul] is released, because of the promise. Oṃ. 2.

The connection [of this section] is established by raising a doubt based on what was previously introduced. Regarding the remainder of the scriptural passage cited in the preceding Sūtra—namely, "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form" and "He moves about there"—there arises the inquiry: does the word "he" (*sa*) refer to one who is not yet liberated (*amukta*), or to one who is liberated (*mukta*)? To determine that, one must consider whether the pronoun "he" refers back to the immediately preceding subject or to the subject under discussion (*prākaraṇika*). To further determine that, one must consider whether, if it referred to the immediately preceding subject, the possession of actions described by "he moves about" and so forth would constitute a contradiction, or not.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: In the previous [sūtra], it was intended that the statement "he moves about there" serves as a proof for the experience of one who is already liberated, having attained the supreme light and manifested his true nature, without overstepping the Lord's sovereignty. Therefore, the citation of the word "by himself" (*svena*) from the śruti in the present sūtra is incorrect. This is because in the preceding passage containing the word "by himself," the manifestation of the true nature is stated for the meditator on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*); whereas in the passage "he moves about there," the one who is the cause of this world is specifically the non-liberated meditator on the *dahara-vidyā*.

For possession of activity is not possible for one who is liberated and has accomplished all that was to be done. However, for one who is not yet liberated—though such enjoyment is otherwise impossible—such enjoyment is possible once he has attained Brahman. Nor should it be suspected that this contradicts the second [sūtra], "Because of the teaching of movement" (*vihāropadeśāt*), where it is stated that since there is mention of movement in the form "he wanders about there," the agency of the liberated one must be merely imaginary; for that [point] too is implied here. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

In the Śruti cited in the Bhāṣya—"Day after day they enter this"—it is stated that for those who have attained Brahman while still in a state of sleep, there is an absence of divine enjoyment because they are not yet liberated; whereas for one who is liberated, such enjoyment is mentioned precisely because of their attainment of That. Since the possession of action (kriyāvattva), meaning the possession of volition (kṛtimattva), is established even in the case of the liberated, there is no obstacle to the word "sa" (he) referring back to what was previously mentioned. Thus, the referent of the pronoun "sa" is indeed the liberated soul. The purpose [of this discussion] is the resolution of the objection regarding the experience of enjoyment by the liberated. || 2 ||
|| Oṃ, [it is] the Self, because of the context. Oṃ. || 3 ||

In the preceding section, the meaning of the word *tat* (that) found in the remainder of the scriptural passage was explained by the phrase "by its own [light]". Here, the connection is that the meaning of the word *jyotis* (light) occurring in the preceding sentence is now being stated. The inquiry is whether the meaning of the word *jyotis* mentioned as "the highest light" (*paraṃjyotiḥ*) is the sun or Brahman. For that purpose, one must consider whether the designation (*samākhyā*)—namely, "he has reached the sun, which is light"—is more authoritative than the context (*prakaraṇa*), or whether the context is more authoritative. For that purpose again, one must determine whether the designation is without scope (*niravakāśa*) or with scope (*sāvakāśa*).

The word *jyotis* (light), while used for the sun—as in "We have gone to the sun, the light" (*sūryam aganma jyotiḥ*)—is also used for the Lord according to the aforementioned principle, as in "The light with four feet" (*jyotiś caraṇaḥ*). Nevertheless, because the name "He has merged into the splendor of the sun" (*sa tejasi sūrye saṃpannaḥ*) establishes a single referent, it follows that here *jyotis* refers only to the sun and not to Viṣṇu; for even if the context were Vaiṣṇava, a reference to another could occur incidentally, and the unambiguous name (*samākhyā*) would override it. This being the prima facie view, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The established conclusion follows: It is indeed Viṣṇu, because the context is Vaiṣṇava, and because the name [of the chapter] is applied to the whole section. Furthermore, the word *jyotis* is primarily used for Viṣṇu in the passage "The light which shines beyond this world" (*jyotiḥ śrīmad dṛśyatām etasmāt parataḥ*), and there is no contradiction with the name, since the name applies to the entire section. Moreover, the name is not without scope, as it can be explained by the fact that the merging into the sun occurs through the grace of Viṣṇu. Therefore, the word *jyotis* here denotes Viṣṇu alone. Thus it is concluded.

"Because the passage beginning with 'That Self which is free from evil' introduces Brahman through both Vedic texts and characteristics unique to Brahman; because this sentence is situated within a context concerning Brahman due to its mention of 'the highest light'; because the context is stronger than the name (*samākhyā*); and because that name is accommodated by having as its purport the liberation from commenced karma and the attainment of the inner sun on the path to the realization of Brahman; and because the term 'highest light' [denotes Brahman] according to the Smṛti: 'The highest light is the Supreme Brahman'."

Furthermore, because it is used in its primary sense for the Supreme Self alone, Brahman itself is the meaning of the term "supreme light. This is the resolution of the objection raised against the previously stated point that the fruit for the liberated one is enjoyment in the very vicinity of Brahman. || 3 ||
Oṃ. Because it is perceived as non-different [from Brahman], Oṃ. 4.

Thus, it being established that one who is liberated by the three means attains Brahman and enjoys enjoyments (*bhoga*), there arises a connection through the specific inquiry as to what the nature of that enjoyment is. Among those liberated ones who possess *sāyujya* (union), the inquiry is whether their enjoyment consists of that which has not been enjoyed by the Lord, or rather that which remains after having been enjoyed by the Lord. For that purpose, [the question is]: if there is a connection with the remnants of what was enjoyed, is the state of liberation diminished as the supreme goal of man, or not? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Because liberation is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and because that which has not been enjoyed by the Lord is easily available even though it is [inherently] to be enjoyed, one enjoys only those things already enjoyed by the Lord. Furthermore, if there were a rule that one must enjoy only what remains after being enjoyed by the Lord, then for some who have developed a desire for enjoyment, the absence of enjoyment would follow, resulting in the loss of liberation as a human goal; this is because the Lord, being eternally full of bliss, may at times not enjoy anything at all. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The rest of the passage continues with the formal argument.]

Although liberation is the supreme human goal and the enjoyments not yet experienced by the Lord are easily attainable, since the scripture states, "Those very [enjoyments] which I hear," indicating that the Lord is the enjoyer of the enjoyments being experienced, it must be accepted that the liberated souls are indeed enjoyers of the objects of enjoyment being enjoyed by the Lord. Nor should it be feared that, because the scripture "those very [enjoyments]" implies they are enjoyers of all things enjoyed by the Lord, they would thereby attain equality with the Lord.

The general Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating "to those very ones" is restricted by the specific Smṛti text: "Liberated souls, having attained the supreme Viṣṇu. Nor should it be suspected that liberation is not the supreme human goal on the grounds that, according to the aforementioned reasoning, there might occasionally be an absence of enjoyment; for in the Śruti text, "He is full bliss, full enjoyer, full doer," although full bliss is mentioned, the mention of "full enjoyment" precludes the possibility of an absence of enjoyment therein. The result [of this discussion] is the implication of Hari’s status as the enjoyer of all, as stated in the passage beginning with "the Eater" (*attā*), and its subsequent resolution.
|| Oṃ. Jaimini [maintains that the Self is] Brahman, on account of the introductory passages and so forth. Oṃ. || 5 ||

"Oṃ, [the soul is] by means of pure consciousness alone, because it has that as its essence; thus says Auḍulomi. Oṃ, even so, because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence [of the soul], there is no contradiction; thus says Bādarāyaṇa."

The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt raised by the preceding discussion: Is it not logical that enjoyment (*bhoga*) belongs to the liberated (*mukta*), or is it logical? For that purpose, one must consider whether they possess a body as the cause of enjoyment, or do not; and likewise, even in the absence of a material body (*bhautika-deha*), whether they are joined with another kind of body or not. In the previous section, it was stated that the enjoyment of the liberated—whether as non-excess over Brahman or as the enjoyment of what has been enjoyed by the Lord—is not logical, because, having reached the further shore of *saṃsāra*, they lack a body that serves as the cause of enjoyment.

If that [body] were to exist, it would contradict the state of liberation (*muktatva*). Furthermore, experience through a body such as that of Brahmā is not tenable, because even when such bodies exist at the beginning of a cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), there is an absence of experience. This being the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Even in the absence of all material bodies such as those of Brahmā and others, based on the Śruti and Smṛti cited in the Commentary—namely, "He indeed is this one established in Brahman" and "He takes [it] by the hand of Hari"—it is understood that for one who has entered the Supreme Self, experience occurs just like that of an embodied being, by means of that very [divine] body.
Furthermore, from the Smṛti statement, "I go by the two feet of Viṣṇu," it is understood that one performs actions such as going by means of the very limbs of Viṣṇu.

By the power of recollecting [past lives], by the reasoning that liberation involves the acquisition of that [divine] body, or by means of a Brahman-body—as supported by such Śruti as, "He, being liberated from this mortal state, becomes pure consciousness (cinmātra)," and such Smṛti as, "Having abandoned the mortal body"—the liberated one, through limbs consisting of the very essence of consciousness (svarūpabhūtacinmātra) favored by the Lord, experiences enjoyments and performs actions. As for the result, however, it consists in the refutation of the objection regarding liberation being the ultimate human goal (puruṣārtha). || 5 ||
|| Oṃ, and because it is seen from scripture that [the creation] occurs through mere volition, oṃ. || 6 ||

In the preceding section, it was stated that there is no dependence on extraordinary (alaukika) instruments; here, however, the connection is that it is now stated that there is no dependence even on worldly (laukika) means. The inquiry is whether the enjoyment of the liberated one mentioned in the context is accomplished by means of specific instruments achieved through particular methods, or whether it is accomplished by mere volition (saṃkalpa) alone. To that end, the inquiry is whether the reasoning regarding the Lord’s abiding in His own abode, when supported by conformity with the ways of the world, establishes that [enjoyment] is achievable through instruments, or not.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: "The one who has attained liberation while remaining in a world (*bhagavad-oka-stha*) possesses enjoyment (*bhoga*), because he is accomplished by means of various instruments that are themselves to be accomplished by various means; for, since he remains in a world, his enjoyment is like the enjoyment of those dwelling in worlds such as the earth. This is established through reasoning—namely, the observation in the world that enjoyment is accomplished by means of various instruments which are themselves to be accomplished by various means—and in accordance with worldly experience, the enjoyment of the liberated one must also be of that same nature. In response to this, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated:

"According to the Śruti text, 'If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will (saṃkalpa) the fathers arise for him,' the enjoyment of the liberated one is accomplished by will alone, not by means of specific instruments to be acquired through various methods. The previously mentioned argument, being sublated by the Śruti, is not a valid proof. As for the contradiction with worldly experience, it is actually an advantage in the case of the faultless abode of the Lord. The [objection regarding] the result is that liberation would lose its status as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) by falling into the same conditions as transmigratory existence; this is the objection, and the following is its resolution. **Oṃ. For this very reason, He has no other lord. Oṃ.** (Sūtra 7)

Here, the internal connection (*antarasaṅgati*) arises from the extension (*atideśa*) of the previously stated reason. The inquiry is whether the liberated soul under discussion is restricted to a lord other than those already established, or whether it is restricted to one of those already established. To that end, the question is whether the state of being restricted to a subordinate (*svāvara*)—even if not required for liberation—still applies to the liberated soul or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Just as in the world a person entering a king’s palace is necessarily subject to subordinates such as gatekeepers even if he does not require them, so too the liberated soul, because it has entered the house of another (the Lord), must be subject to subordinates; otherwise, it would contradict worldly experience. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: [The liberated soul is not subject to subordinates. This is because the previously mentioned reason is extended here. Furthermore, the soul is self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotis*), and since its nature is to be free from all dependence, it cannot be subject to anything else. Moreover, the Lord is the master of all masters, and there is no other master beyond Him. Therefore, the liberated soul is not restricted to any subordinate. Finally, the soul's true nature is freedom from all bonds, and this is not contradicted by worldly analogies. Thus, the liberated soul is not subject to the subordinates of others.

In the world, because the quality of having true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatva*) is absent, even though there might be the possibility of attaining what is not desired while remaining restricted to one's own lower state, for the liberated soul, precisely because of the possession of true resolve, it is not logical that there be the attainment of what is undesired; thus, the liberated souls remain restricted to their respective established levels. For the liberated, restriction to a lower state is not desired. Accordingly, the Smṛti says: "The supreme lordship belongs to them," and so forth. As for the result, however, it consists in the presence or absence of attributes common to the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). || 7 ||
Oṃ. Bādari says it is non-existence, for thus [the scripture] declares; Oṃ. (8)

Oṃ. Jaimini [holds that the meditation] has existence as its object, because it is manifold and free from conceptual construction. Oṃ. Bādarāyaṇa [holds that it is] of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice; therefore. Oṃ. In the absence of a body, it is possible as in the case of the twilight [meditation]. Oṃ. When there is a body, it is like the waking state. Oṃ. The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp, for so the scripture shows. Oṃ. It refers to either deep sleep or union [with Brahman], for this is clearly stated. Oṃ.

The connection [of this section] arises because a doubt is raised here by way of implying that enjoyment depends solely on mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), as was stated in the previous section (*saṃkalpādeva*). Since the phrase "in this very case" (*atraiva*) functions as an extension of the previously mentioned reason, it is incidental and does not constitute an interruption. Thus, the inquiry is whether the enjoyment of the liberated (*mukta*), which is the subject under discussion, is possible or not. For that purpose, the question is whether enjoyment can be established in the presence or absence of a body, and likewise, whether the presence or absence of a body for the liberated is untenable due to contradiction or tenable.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: If liberated souls possess a body, the experience of freedom from suffering is untenable due to the consequence of experiencing pain and so forth. Conversely, if they lack a body, experience is impossible. Nor can it be argued that experience is possible through a "brahmic body" (*brāhmadeha*), as suggested in the passage beginning with "by the brahmic [body]," because while such a body may exist for those who have attained *sāyujya* (union), it does not exist for others. Furthermore, experience cannot be established on the basis of a "conscious body" (*ciccharīra*), since even though it exists during states such as deep sleep, it is not observed to serve as the locus of experience.

Therefore, because enjoyment is difficult to establish whether through the existence or non-existence of a body, enjoyment is not tenable; moreover, both the positions of bodily existence and non-existence are untenable due to contradiction. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that enjoyment is indeed possible for the liberated (*muktas*). This is because enjoyment can be easily established under either of the two positions. In the case of an external body, although it is insentient (*jaḍa*), it consists of the nature of light (*tejas*) composed of pure *sattva*; thus, since it does not produce suffering and the like, the mere experience of pleasure therein is logically consistent.

Just as a lamp consumes only its oil and the like, but not the blackness inherent within it, so it is here; for the Śruti declares, "For then he has crossed beyond all sorrows. Even in the view that there is no physical body [in liberation], just as there is experience during one's own natural state (svapna) despite the absence of identification with an external body, so too in liberation, although there is no external body, experience is possible through the *ciñccharīra* (the body of consciousness), since the absence of identification is common to both cases. In deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is no experience because the mind has ceased its activity; and regarding the view that a body exists [in liberation], there is the statement: "It is either thought or non-thought."

This is because it is established by scripture in the passage: "He indeed becomes bodiless then. Furthermore, just as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is either an *ahīna* or a *sattra* depending on the sacrificer’s wish—being performed by one or many agents—there is no contradiction in liberated beings assuming or not assuming external bodies of light-form according to their own will; thus [the position] is logical. Accordingly, the Smṛti states: "Or, having voluntarily assumed certain bodies of light-form, they enjoy [pleasures] as if in the waking state, and at some point there is abandonment. As for the result: since there is an absence of experience of suffering, there is the objection that liberation lacks the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and this is its resolution. || 9 ||
Oṃ. [The Buddha is] exempt from activity toward the world. Oṃ. 9.

Oṃ. [The soul is not the object of meditation] because of the context and because it is not proximate; Oṃ. If it is argued that this is so because of the direct instruction, we say no, because of the mention of one who resides in the circle of authority; Oṃ. And it exists within the transformation, for thus the scripture shows. Oṃ.

Thus, the connection [of this section] is as follows: since it has been established that liberated souls possess enjoyment by way of refuting the argument for its impossibility, the present discussion concerns the limits thereof. The inquiry is whether liberated souls engage in the activities of the world or not. For that purpose, one must determine whether the word "all" (*sarva*) in the scriptural passage, "Having obtained all desires," functions in an unrestricted sense or in a restricted sense. For that purpose, one must determine whether there exists any text restricting that [meaning], and for that purpose, whether the phrase "all the gods" refers to those within the domain of Viriñca (Brahmā).
