The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Since the scriptural statement "to all gods" refers exclusively to the individual soul (*jīva*), and since the statement "all desires" occurs within a context concerning the individual soul—such as "having departed upwards after the dissolution of the body"—it must be understood that liberated souls indeed perform activities such as the creation of the world. This is because one may either postulate such power for the souls, or, even in the absence of such power, assume the capacity for universal sovereignty based on their possession of true desires; thus, there is no reason to restrict the scope of these scriptural passages. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: The liberated souls do not create the world or perform other such activities. Why? Because of the scriptural declaration: "He [the Self] does not eat food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.26). Furthermore, the scripture declares that the liberated soul possesses the same nature as the Lord: "He becomes like unto Him" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). Moreover, the scripture teaches that the liberated soul is dependent upon the Lord: "Having attained the Lord, he attains immortality" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Therefore, the liberated soul is subject to the will of the Supreme Lord. Consequently, the liberated soul cannot independently engage in the creation of the world or similar activities. Thus, the prima facie argument is refuted. Furthermore, the scripture states: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9). This indicates that the liberated soul attains a state of identity with Brahman. Since the Supreme Lord is eternally free from desire and agency, the liberated soul, having attained His nature, likewise becomes devoid of desire and agency. Therefore, the liberated soul does not create the world. This is the final position. Thus, it is established that the liberated soul does not perform the work of creating the world. This is the definitive conclusion. *Note: The term "sarvaiśvaryasambhavena" has been translated as "assuming the capacity for universal sovereignty," reflecting the argument that the soul's true desires might grant it sovereign power over all things.*

Because the passage beginning with "Māhācamasya" and ending with the Śruti statement "all [powers] belong to him" refers specifically to Viriñca (Brahmā), it does not apply to all liberated souls; consequently, there is no assumption of capacity for the creation and so forth of the world among individual souls, as they lack such power in that regard. Furthermore, the quality of having "true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) is consistent with the Smṛti: "Upon attaining their own superior bliss, the liberated have no desire even for activities such as creation and the like," which establishes that they possess no desires other than those concerning creation and so forth.

"Except for the activity of governing the world, he enjoys other desires; thus he is liberated. Here, it should be understood that while the liberated Viriñca possesses the activity of governing all liberated beings, the other gods possess the activity of governing only those liberated beings who are inferior to themselves. As for the fruit [of this discussion], it lies in the refutation and resolution of the objection raised against the definition-sūtra. || 9 ||
Oṃ. Thus he states their establishment: "And [the existence of] perception and inference is shown in this way. Oṃ. 10.
Oṃ. And because there is a scriptural indication of equality regarding mere enjoyment, Oṃ.

In the preceding section, the extent of the enjoyment of objects denoted by the word "kāma" was stated; here, however, the extent of the bliss of one's own nature—which is manifested by those objects—is stated in its natural state. This is the connection. The inquiry is whether the liberated soul possesses an increase or decrease of bliss, or whether it remains as it is. For that purpose, the question is whether practices such as meditation upon those [objects] become causes for increase and so forth, or not. The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:

In passages such as, “He sits singing this *sāman*,” since the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) is heard of even for the liberated (*mukta*), and because that [practice] would otherwise be purposeless—which implies it must necessarily have a fruit—and because the liberated possess the power of sovereignty consisting in self-mastery (*vaśitva*), whereby all desired specific enjoyments exist, it follows that their bliss increases when that [meditation] is present and decreases when it ceases. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: the bliss of the liberated remains in one and the same state alone.

Having stated the absence of growth and so forth in the scripture cited in the Commentary as "This is He," the statement regarding meditation, "Beholding the Self indeed," also serves to negate growth and diminution—denoted by the terms *āpatti* (attainment) and *vipatti* (loss)—because the absence of growth and so forth is established both by the direct perception of the great ones that the liberated one possesses no growth and so on, and by the inference that he lacks growth and so forth due to being devoid of any cause.

Furthermore, because worship is itself the fruit—since the *Smṛti* states, "And here, the worship of Hari is always of the nature of bliss"—it cannot be a means to any other fruit. Even when all desired enjoyments are obtained through mastery (*vaśitva*), there is an absence of desire for what is unattainable, and for what is attainable, it has already been attained; thus, even regarding specific enjoyments, there is cessation from them. Therefore, that specific enjoyment does not serve as a cause for the increase or decrease of happiness. Consequently, "the state of being free from increase and decrease would be the general rule for the liberated."

"An occasional particularity is not at all denied for them"—according to this direction, [the state of liberation] is established as being the cause of the variety of essential bliss. As for the result, however, it consists in the refutation of the objection that liberation would not be the goal of man because it would incur the same characteristics as saṃsāra. || 10 ||
Oṃ. There is no returning, on account of the scriptural statement; there is no returning, on account of the scriptural statement. Oṃ. 11.

In the previous [section], it was stated that there is no increase or decrease for one who has attained liberation; here, however, it is said that there is no end to the experience thereof—this is the connection. Is the liberated one [described] as...?

The inquiry concerns whether or not there is a return characterized by the attainment of birth, death, and so forth. To that end, it is considered whether the liberated soul’s dwelling throughout all time is an obstacle to such a return. For that purpose, it is further considered whether there is an end to all time or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Just as for one situated in heaven and other such realms, there is a return even for the liberated soul. This is because, even if the liberated soul dwells throughout all time, it is possible that all time might at some point come to an end.

Nor is it impossible for [the cycle] to reach completion because time is infinite; for in the *Mahābhārata*, regarding the battle, it is said: "The fourteenth, the fifteenth, and formerly even the sixteenth—this new-moon day, however, I do not recognize as being the thirteenth," which shows that the occurrence of a fifteenth day on a thirteenth day was considered impossible. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Since the completion of even the entirety of time is precluded by its being infinite, there is no return for the liberated one—even upon the recurrence of the dissolution of the *manvantara* and so forth—because he has attained that state. This is because of the Śruti: "And he does not return" (*na ca punarāvartate*). Furthermore, since the Śruti states, "He attains all desires," and because non-return is itself desired through the attainment of all desires mentioned in the scripture, there is no return; thus, the liberated ones are indeed those who experience eternal, sorrowless bliss. As for the result [of liberation], it consists in the resolution of the objection regarding liberation as the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 11 ||
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is filled with auspicious qualities, who is far removed from all defects, the lord of Śrī’s life-breath, and the bestower of the desired objects of his devotees.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyamuktāvalī*, composed by the ascetic Rāghavendra, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Sudhīndra Guru.
